n1|95.c: AI will change how people use technology and open up huge new markets.
n1|95.e: The hosts' starting point: the leap in AI capabilities is more than tech news. It will change how people use software and technology, create many markets that didn't exist before, and ripple out to all of society. Because the shift is that big, they think it deserves a dedicated show that follows it week after week.

n1|95.c: AI doom is only one possibility, and reality will most likely be far less dark.
n1|95.e: The trailer opens with a satirical sci-fi skit: in 2042, humans work for merged AI giants, and their only job is producing feedback data so the AI can keep improving through reinforcement learning, learning by trial and reward. In the skit, AI capabilities have taken off while alignment, making AI do what humans want, has failed. The hosts ask whether that future is coming. Their view: AI will change society deeply, but probably not as darkly as many popular stories suggest.
ex: In the skit, the AI overlords play the strategy game Diplomacy and Go

d.verdict: AI will reshape society, but not necessarily toward doom

n1|95.c: To understand AI, listen to people building every layer of it talk tech, business and predictions.
n1|95.e: The format is sitting down with engineers, researchers and founders from every layer of the AI stack, from chips up to apps. They talk about where the technical frontier really is, what it means for business, and what guests expect to happen next. One host is an investor, the other a serial founder turned investor, and they put technology and business on the same table.
ex: First guest: Noam Brown of Meta's AI research lab FAIR

items.d: What it means for products and markets

n1|95.c: "Intelligent software" built around AI models is a new generation of software.
n1|95.e: Introducing Conviction, the venture firm she founded, Sarah Guo sums up its focus as intelligent software, which she calls "Software 3.0." The point is that software built around model capabilities is a distinct new generation, worth betting on as its own investment theme. Before Conviction she spent about ten years incubating and investing in startups at Greylock.
ex: Elad Gil wrote the startup book High Growth Handbook

n2|96.c: Letting an AI search before it acts beats scaling up training by several orders of magnitude.
n2|96.e: In 2015 his poker bot lost to professional players. He noticed that humans thought for a long time on hard hands, while the bot always acted instantly. Adding real-time search during play, he estimated, was worth roughly a 100,000x increase in training scale. Three years of scaling had given him only about 100x. That convinced him planning at the algorithm level was an overlooked lever, not just more compute.
ex: In 2015 the bot lost over 80,000 hands against humans
In January 2017 it beat four top professional players
The later six-player poker bot cost under $150 in cloud compute

items.d: Ever-larger game abstractions during his PhD

n2|96.c: Research should be high-risk, high-reward, so they went straight for Diplomacy, a game played through conversation.
n2|96.e: Around 2019, GPT-2 and the StarCraft and Dota bots were breaking through. He judged that games like Settlers of Catan could be cracked by a small team in a year, so they weren't worth much. The team wanted a problem that demanded new methods. Diplomacy, where you negotiate, ally and betray in natural language, still sounded like science fiction. They skipped the no-talking version and aimed straight at the full game, though he admits he was a bit scared.
ex: Diplomacy dates to the 1950s: seven players negotiating in private
He sees it as the first major game-AI breakthrough in cooperating with humans

items.d: He thought AI was nearly dead

n2|96.c: An AI that cooperates with people can't rely on self-play alone; it must first learn how humans play.
n2|96.e: Imitating human games alone doesn't produce strong strategy, because most data comes from average players; that's true in chess and Go too. But in cooperative games, self-play from scratch can evolve private conventions, even a "secret language," that humans can't follow. Cicero uses human data to model how players usually act, then refines that with self-play, and conditions its dialogue on its action plans. He thinks real-world systems like self-driving cars must also model human mistakes.
ex: Trained on about 50,000 webDiplomacy games with 13 million messages
Across 40 games, no one figured out it was a bot

items.d: What it says serves its plan

n2|96.c: Humans beat AI mainly through sample efficiency, learning from few examples, not through generality.
n2|96.e: He thinks humans need orders of magnitude fewer examples than AI to learn chess, Diplomacy or painting, and that this is the most precise way to describe the gap. Elad pushes back that humans are mostly specialists too, so AI is held to an unfairly high bar on generality. Brown partly agrees and narrows the point to sample efficiency. He also admits physical tasks like robotic manipulation are still human territory. In chess, human-plus-AI teams barely add anything now; in Go, humans can still fix the AI's odd blunders, for now.
ex: He estimates AI could write a Harry Potter-level novel in about five years

items: AI is held to a higher bar

d.verdict: The real gap is sample efficiency

n2|96.c: Training cost, not data, is the main bottleneck, and inference-time compute is underrated.
n2|96.e: He thinks far more usable data exists than models use today, and better sample efficiency will make data even more valuable. The real limit is the cost of scaling, and he estimates there's roughly two more orders of magnitude before hitting a cost wall. Meanwhile, pretraining costs tens of millions of dollars, while a single answer costs about a cent. That gap suggests letting models "think" for seconds, or even an hour, before answering is a largely untapped dimension.
ex: A single answer costs about one cent

items.d: Rough training cost at the time
Expected within a year or two
Affordable for governments or tech giants

n2|96.c: General reasoning and planning is AI's core weakness; chain-of-thought just replays human patterns.
n2|96.e: AlphaGo's raw policy network, playing alone, was far from top level; it needed Monte Carlo tree search on top. But that kind of planning only works for games like Go and chess, not poker or Diplomacy, which is a big weakness of current methods. Chain-of-thought prompting works remarkably well, yet it mostly unrolls reasoning steps already present in human data. He imagines that if general reasoning succeeds, even at a million dollars per token, it might prove the Riemann hypothesis within five years.
ex: Code generation is still local completion; planning a whole product isn't feasible yet
He thinks the Turing test is no longer a useful benchmark

marks.d: Works only for Go and chess

n3|99.c: A model isn't a product, and in a field this fast you must build the whole stack yourself.
n3|99.e: Between a research model and a usable product lie deployment, interaction design and unit economics. Early on Runway relied on third-party and open-source pieces, but the field moved so fast that depending on others meant handing over your fate. Building an in-house research team became a survival decision. Research isn't a separate paper-writing group; it's applied research sitting next to creators. About half the team has an art background, a culture that takes years to build.
ex: The early platform hosted about 400 models, with an SDK and API
Runway now offers about 35 AI "magic tools"

n3|99.c: AI creative tools should get people 80-90% of the way fast, not aim for full automation.
n3|99.e: Going from 80% to 100% is brutally hard, which is where self-driving is stuck. But there a 1% failure can be fatal, while creative work tolerates far more error. Runway doesn't try to make films fully automatically. It helps professionals finish most of the work quickly and polish the rest in tools like Nuke and Flame, which still saves days. That gives him a filter for applied research: pick domains that naturally tolerate imperfect accuracy.
ex: Professionals can finish the last 20% in Nuke or Flame

items: The last 1% of failures can kill

d.verdict: Applied research should pick error-tolerant domains

n3|99.c: Users are good at describing their problems, but not at describing the solution.
n3|99.e: The team noticed people using FFmpeg to split videos into frames and run an image segmentation model on each one, proof that the need to cut people out of footage was real. Users asked for "a better brush," but what to select depends on composition, like picking one person out of ten, so full automation was the wrong fit. Runway built a click-guided, human-in-the-loop model trained on simulated clicks. The first version ran at about 4 frames per second, yet beat the alternatives and caught on fast.
ex: The first green screen tool ran at about 4 frames per second
Users had mostly relied on tools like Roto Brush 2

items.d: Some ran segmentation frame by frame

n3|99.c: Don't dismiss toys: judge a technology by how fast it improves, not by one snapshot.
n3|99.e: Early outputs were about 128 pixels square, blurry and abstract. People at ad agencies saw them as toys for art students, and some assumed the images were collages of existing pictures. His view: the mistake was judging a single moment instead of the rate of progress. Product-market fit is a spectrum. The early audience was small, but users turned Runway into a verb, made tutorials and shared their work on their own, all before the company had a marketing team.
ex: In 2018 an early user mailed them a painting made with AI

n3|99.c: Even below top quality, saving 10 to 20 percent of the time matters a lot to film studios.
n3|99.e: Customers have spread from post-production, visual effects and broadcast companies to a wider range of creators. He argues that even if AI quality isn't yet top-tier, saving a VFX studio 10% to 20% in time or cost is already meaningful. More importantly, time and budget used to force teams to lock in one creative direction early. Now they can explore several options in parallel and then choose.
ex: A director said the team could try several ideas before committing

terms.d: No need to lock in early

result.d: Worth it even below top quality

n3|99.c: AI art is at its "paint tube moment," and new tools will give rise to new art movements.
n3|99.e: He compares it to the history of paint. Before paint came in tubes, painters had to prepare pigments in a costly, tedious process. Tubes made painting outdoors possible, which led to Impressionism, rejected by the establishment at first. Photography and film followed a similar curve. He sees two waves of AI art: early experimenters using GANs, an older image-generation method, and today's diffusion models. Now is the moment tools are spreading, but to become a real art movement they must get easier and more controllable.
ex: Work by early GAN artist Robbie Barrat has been auctioned

items.d: Rejected by the mainstream at first

n3|99.c: Multimodal AI will join up today's separate creative tools into one connected experience.
n3|99.e: He sees natural language processing and computer vision converging, so text, images, video and audio can be freely mixed as inputs and outputs. Today's creative software is split into silos: image editing, vector graphics, motion, editing and compositing. But people experience media with many senses at once, so he expects multimodal models to merge those silos.
ex: Imagine: text becomes a video, then dialogue audio is added automatically

items.d: Closer to how people sense media
Text, image, video and audio interconnected

n4|104.c: A trained model is a new programming primitive, and once open-sourced it spreads extremely fast.
n4|104.e: Unlike traditional open source, a large model is usually trained by five to ten people plus a supercomputer and a data team. The output is a file of a few gigabytes that deterministically turns text into images. He believes such primitives spread explosively once open, and that inference costs less than people expect. He also predicts someone in the closed camp will eventually defect to open source to commoditize a rival's complement, just as Google gives away Gmail.
ex: He says its GitHub stars passed Ethereum's and Bitcoin's in three to four months
The Stable Diffusion model file is about 2GB

n4|104.c: Base models should be open, while instruction tuning and clinical deployment belong to private companies.
n4|104.e: He splits model building into three layers. Training base models with deep learning is the bottom layer, and it should be open. Instruction tuning and reinforcement learning need specialized labeling, which private companies do well. Fine-tuning for specific uses and human-in-the-loop deployment, such as clinical use, is private-sector territory. He also argues that combining many specialized models beats training one giant multilingual model that does everything.
ex: Countries need their own models, for example Japan and India

items.d: Needs expert labeling; private firms excel

n4|104.c: Data quality and instruction tuning improve results more than simply adding parameters.
n4|104.e: He cites Chinchilla: a model of about 70 billion parameters, trained on more data, matched the 175-billion-parameter GPT-3. The 1.3-billion-parameter InstructGPT also beat GPT-3. In medical Q&A, the same base model jumps in accuracy step by step after instruction tuning and then domain-specific fine-tuning. So Stability prioritizes customizable, editable models over the biggest ones, and he believes small models will win by a wide margin.
ex: He predicts ChatGPT-level models will run on phones within five years
A slimmed-down Stable Diffusion already makes images on an iPhone in seconds

n4|104.c: Open weights plus private data is a business that closed-model APIs can't offer.
n4|104.e: He argues companies and governments won't send regulated private data to closed models like GPT-3 or PaLM, but will happily run open weights in their own data centers, and private data is worth more than public data. So Stability focuses on helping nations and the largest companies train large models in their own data centers, going deep in media such as images, video, audio and 3D. He says only about a hundred people in the world can train these models.
ex: Partnering with Eros to train a video model on Bollywood films
A partnership with Amazon SageMaker

terms.d: Can run on your own servers

result.d: What nations and big companies want

n4|104.c: Emerging markets will skip old systems and build education and health care from scratch with AI.
n4|104.e: Many emerging markets badly lack doctors and teachers, with one teacher for hundreds of children, but that means they can build from scratch with no legacy to carry. He expects these countries to leapfrog straight to generative AI, the way they skipped landlines for mobile phones, and possibly overtake Western systems within five years. On students using ChatGPT for homework, he thinks banning essays or switching to handwritten classwork is the wrong direction.
ex: About 4 million tablets deployed to children in Malawi
Refugee camp kids using AI an hour a day reached basic literacy in 13 months

items: Schools lean toward banning AI writing
Can build new systems from scratch
Governments will spend tens of billions

d.verdict: Emerging markets will leapfrog to generative AI

n4|104.c: A mix of many specialized models is likelier to be aligned with humans than one giant "god" model.
n4|104.e: He sees two routes: keep stacking layers into one giant model, or let many specialized models combine. When the community's fine-tuned Stable Diffusion models are combined, they actually draw faces and fingers better. He doesn't care about AGI itself, as long as it doesn't wipe out humanity. He cares more about intelligence augmentation, and thinks a system of many cooperating models is likelier to be aligned with humans than a single "god" model trained on the whole internet.
ex: He disputes the claim that image generation isn't central to reaching AGI

marks.d: Better faces and hands when combined

n4|104.c: Models above a compute threshold should be registered and tested, and AI in ads should be labeled.
n4|104.e: He thinks everyone is scaling fast without understanding how these models work, so formal research and regulation are needed for unknown risks. His proposal: register models above a compute threshold and have international teams test them, much like dual-use biotech. He worries ads will use models to manipulate people and wants mandatory labels on AI content. He opposes the EU making creators liable for outputs, and supports opt-outs for training data and content provenance standards.
ex: Working with Adobe on content authenticity standards
Dropped a $200,000 deepfake detection prize to avoid an arms race

n5|107.c: The aircraft is only about 15% of the complexity; the hard part is the whole system behind it.
n5|107.e: The team initially underestimated how full-stack the business had to be. The real difficulty lies in systems like air traffic software for regulators, visual pre-flight checks, data logging, fleet data pipelines, and detect-and-avoid. He thinks most robotics and self-driving companies haven't realized this yet, because they face paying customers so late.
ex: The team was about 20 people at the 2016 Rwanda launch

n5|107.c: Charging from day one forces customers to reveal where the product really falls short.
n5|107.e: The team naively assumed that testing on the California coast meant they could run nationwide, around the clock, in Rwanda. The first hospital was planned to take two weeks and took nine months. Charging money made them face what didn't work. They overinvested in some places, like a carefully designed dual-redundant flight controller that may never have been needed. They underinvested in others, like data logging, maintenance and motor parts. Now nearly 1,000 people strong, they still assume they're wrong and let customers say what matters.
ex: The first aircraft used 43 kinds of fasteners; now it uses 2
First hospital launch: planned two weeks, took nine months

d.verdict: Let paying customers decide what matters

n5|107.c: Health care is the best beachhead, and the place to start is the hardest product: blood.
n5|107.e: Health care made sense because demand is clear, customers pay a premium for lifesaving supplies, and regulators are more open when a health ministry co-signs. The team first wanted to deliver every medical product to every facility, but Rwanda's health minister suggested doing only blood. About half of blood goes to postpartum hemorrhage and about 30% to children. Components last anywhere from about a year to about six days. Serving 21 hospitals in the first year nearly broke the company.
ex: Platelets last only about 6 days at room temperature and must be constantly agitated

items.d: Clear demand, willing to pay more
The minister said start with just this

n5|107.c: Shipping a simple product and adding autonomy step by step beats a moonshot R&D effort.
n5|107.e: He thinks autonomy in the air is easier than on the ground because there are fewer obstacles, but neither is at human-level safety yet. At launch, Zipline deliberately sidestepped hard computer vision problems and took a Tesla-like path: ship something that works, learn in operation, and layer on autonomy over time. By contrast, some drone peers spent billions without ever serving a customer. Zipline is now going through FAA certification for its full autonomous system.
ex: He calls the two routes the Tesla path and the Waymo-style moonshot

n5|107.c: Using microphones to hear and avoid other aircraft is a light, all-direction solution.
n5|107.e: Drones don't have right of way, so they must actively avoid other aircraft, and transponders aren't common enough in general aviation to rely on. Lidar, radar and cameras are too heavy, too power-hungry or too narrow for a roughly 50-pound electric aircraft. One engineer proposed passive acoustic triangulation, and a prototype meant to disprove it worked. The team collected its own training data, ran it in shadow mode across several countries, and is now approved to let it steer the aircraft away.
ex: It must monitor a hockey-puck-shaped airspace about two miles around the aircraft
Radar sees about 30 degrees; microphones naturally hear 360

items.d: Enables flying beyond visual line of sight

n5|107.c: Many of the most important companies of the next 20 years will be hardware and infrastructure companies.
n5|107.e: Full-stack hardware spans supply chains, manufacturing, operations, regulation and many engineering disciplines. It scales more slowly than software, but the moat is deeper. He points to how hard Apple is to challenge, and how long Tesla was limited by production capacity. He criticizes US investors for favoring incremental SaaS and digital products while ignoring physical infrastructure like roads and aircraft. Zipline found fundraising hard for its first six years.
ex: Zipline's fundraising was hard for its first six years

n5|107.c: Serving billions of people takes sustainable unit economics, not charity.
n5|107.e: He argues logistics has long served only the wealthy, and about 5.5 million children die each year for lack of basic medical supplies. Solving a global problem like that needs a self-sustaining business, since governments and nonprofits aren't good at deploying technology. Nearly all of Zipline's distribution centers are gross-margin positive, and Rwanda's government became a shareholder. Based on signed contracts, he expects flight volume to grow about 400% in 2023.
ex: Serves about 1,800 health facilities in Ghana
Early on he put the odds of success at about 1%

n6|109.c: Open and closed models will coexist for the long run, with the lead rotating by task.
n6|109.e: He doesn't think either side will "win"; search and databases have long had open-source and commercial products side by side. Right now closed models lead in conversational text generation, while open models lead in text classification, information extraction and image generation, led by Stable Diffusion, and the lead changes hands often. He wants machine learning that everyone can use and build, not one a few companies monopolize. Training models in the open also limits concentration of power.
ex: Analogies: Elasticsearch vs. Algolia, MongoDB vs. closed databases
BigScience's roughly 1,000 researchers trained BLOOM in the open
BLOOM was trained with support from France's Jean Zay supercomputer

items: Lead in conversational generation for now
Lead image generation via Stable Diffusion

d.verdict: Both will coexist for the long run

n6|109.c: No single model will rule everything; specialized models are cheaper, faster and more accurate.
n6|109.e: The Hugging Face Hub already holds about 250,000 models, and about 15,000 companies use the platform. Models cover NLP, computer vision and text-to-image, audio, and a growing number in time series and biochemistry. Sizes range from a few million parameters to about 180 billion, and the right choice depends on the use case. The Bloomberg Terminal needs real-time, low-latency answers, so it favors small models. Only general-purpose uses can tolerate bigger, pricier ones.
ex: Time series examples: Uber's arrival-time predictions, financial fraud detection

n6|109.c: A fast loop from research to production drives ML progress, and closed models risk slowing it.
n6|109.e: In traditional science, research can take 10 to 20 years to reach real use. In machine learning it now takes months, weeks or even days, and feedback from production flows quickly back into research. He sees this loop as the main reason the field moves so fast. Without open source, the field would be decades behind, and a growing number of closed models could slow the loop. He also hopes for more frequent, smaller training runs so models' knowledge doesn't go stale.
ex: Traditional science takes about 10-20 years from research to real use

n6|109.c: A company should always spend 30 to 40 percent of its effort exploring new directions.
n6|109.e: He sees many companies over-explore before product-market fit, changing direction every week, and then stop exploring entirely once they find it. Hugging Face started as a companion chatbot that ran for nearly three years and exchanged billions of messages. Then users of its open-source Transformers library grew from a handful of people to hundreds of companies, which led to the Series A and a full pivot. Spaces, too, began as one team member's experiment.
ex: Spaces passed 50,000 machine learning demos in a year and a half
The companion chatbot exchanged billions of messages

items.d: BERT and others bring in companies
All in after the Series A

n6|109.c: Freemium plus network effects can make the platform where companies buy compute.
n6|109.e: The platform is essentially freemium: about 15,000 companies use it and about 3,000 pay. Large customers pay for security and compliance, and there are infrastructure products such as GPU-backed Spaces and inference endpoints. He believes that with strong network effects, companies that find models, datasets and demos on the platform will naturally make their compute and infrastructure decisions there too. GitHub moved into that layer late; Hugging Face wants to try earlier and already partners with the three big cloud providers.
ex: Paying enterprise customers include Bloomberg and Meta

n7|112.c: About 95% of drug programs fail, mostly because the target and patient group were wrong from the start.
n7|112.e: She splits drug development into three stages: target discovery, molecule design and clinical trials. Programs rarely fail because a trial was badly designed or a molecule missed its target. They fail because the biology, the indication or the patient population was wrong from the very beginning. So insitro focuses on that first stage, which she considers the most important and the hardest problem. Machine learning isn't a silver bullet, but it will be everywhere, like computers, not a narrow tool like crystallography.

items.d: Make a molecule that hits the target
Most fail by choosing wrong at step one

n7|112.c: Human genetics as a natural experiment, plus stem cell experiments, can fill the training data gap.
n7|112.e: Data on clinical outcomes only arrives at the end of drug development, so it's hard to train predictive models on it directly. Her answer has two parts. Human genetic variation links differences in gene activity to traits and disease, serving as a proxy for what an intervention would do. Then induced pluripotent stem cells and gene editing let the lab run "A/B tests in a dish," read out with imaging and omics. Machine learning connects the two to build cell models that predict human outcomes better than animal models.
ex: Stem cells can become neurons, liver cells or heart muscle cells

terms.d: Every person is a natural experiment
Gene editing for lab A/B tests

result.d: Replacing animal models that translate poorly

n7|112.c: Medical AI needs deep learning's pattern recognition plus causal reasoning and interpretability.
n7|112.e: Probabilistic graphical models brought data-driven numerical reasoning into AI, then were overshadowed by deep learning's powerful pattern recognition on raw inputs. She thinks the pendulum is swinging back. In medicine, doctors need to understand a model's decisions, so pattern recognition alone isn't enough; you also need causal reasoning and interpretability.
ex: Her Stanford lab was half machine learning, half biology

n7|112.c: Pick disease areas with big unmet need where your own technology has a clear edge.
n7|112.e: Neuroscience comes first: there are few effective drugs, animal models poorly reflect human disease, stem cell-derived neurons are fairly easy to make, and brain MRI data keeps growing. Metabolic disease and oncology have lots of unbiased data collected during standard care. For complex diseases involving many cell types she is pragmatic: start with diseases a single cell lineage can capture, and wait on the rest until organoids and organs-on-chips mature.
ex: Liver cells stimulated with fatty acids and immune factors mimic metabolic disease
She expects organoids and similar tools to unlock more diseases in about three years

root.d: Big need plus a technical edge

items.d: Animal models fail; neurons are accessible
Can be modeled in liver cells

n7|112.c: Finding the patients who will actually benefit beats enrolling all comers.
n7|112.e: She cites research showing drugs with a biomarker succeed in the clinic about twice as often as those without, and drugs backed by human genetics also roughly double their odds. Her human-data approach surfaces such markers along the way. She criticizes targeting all patients to maximize revenue, since side effects in non-responders can swamp the benefit. She passes on what former Genentech colleagues said: Herceptin in all comers might have needed a trial of about 10,000 people; selecting only HER2-positive patients made it feasible.
ex: An all-comers Herceptin trial might have needed about 10,000 patients

n7|112.c: Faster drug development is limited both by regulators and by biology's own pace.
n7|112.e: Regulators' questions are often fair, such as whether a biomarker reproduces reliably outside a research setting, so it's better to engage them early rather than at the final submission. But biology sets its own pace. COVID trials moved fast because there were many cases and the disease ran a short course. Alzheimer's needs long follow-up before cognitive changes show, and amyloid may be a valid surrogate endpoint only for some patients.

n7|112.c: People from computing and biology need to respect each other and stay willing to learn.
n7|112.e: Computer scientists have to accept that biology is noisy and the same input may not give the same output. Biologists have to accept that the building blocks won't always fit together as expected. Scientists look at outliers because discoveries often start there, while engineers look for patterns that explain most of the data; both are valid. Platform work runs in agile sprints, and projects tied to fixed biological cycles go to project managers. She criticizes tech newcomers who underestimate how hard biology is.
ex: Cells died whenever one technician was on shift, hinting at a hidden variable
A roughly 45-day cell differentiation cycle doesn't fit sprints

items: Find patterns that explain most data

d.verdict: Both are valid; mutual respect is needed

n8|116.c: GPT-3's real shock was in-context learning, which dissolved the boundaries between separate "tasks."
n8|116.e: His early work mapped natural language to SQL queries so answers could be computed. But most of the world's knowledge isn't structured, so he moved to open question-answering datasets like SQuAD, work that paved the way for ELMo and BERT. What stunned him about GPT-3 wasn't raw capability. It was that a model trained only to predict the next word could do new tasks from instructions and examples in the prompt. The idea of fixed tasks began giving way to a general-purpose foundation.
ex: His team coined "foundation model" because these models aren't limited to language

n8|116.c: Industry can brute-force progress with compute, so academia's mission shifts to understanding.
n8|116.e: Academia's main job used to be getting methods to work at all, as with computer vision and question answering when they barely worked. Now industry can push ahead with data and compute, so academia's comparative advantage is understanding why models work: how training data, architecture and objective functions shape behavior, and what the social impact is. CRFM studies economic impact, copyright, bias, homogenization and misinformation.
ex: CRFM has more than 30 faculty across 10 departments

items: Brute force with data and compute

d.verdict: Academia should focus on its comparative advantage

n8|116.c: As foundation models spread, their transparency and accessibility are actually declining.
n8|116.e: The past decade's deep learning boom was built on open tools like PyTorch and TensorFlow, open data and published papers. Now models are increasingly offered only through APIs, and training details aren't disclosed. He sees two reasons. Training is enormously expensive, so models have become a competitive advantage. And there are safety concerns: opening today's models may be fine, but releasing much stronger future models without limits could be risky.

n8|116.c: Language models must be evaluated on many dimensions, not just accuracy.
n8|116.e: "Evaluating language models" is too vague, since models can be used for countless tasks. HELM uses a systematic framework to measure accuracy, robustness, calibration, fairness and bias, toxicity and efficiency together. Results are published down to every prompt and prediction and updated about every two weeks. He also argues against "human level" as the only north star, favoring objective criteria like reliability and being grounded in sources. Next up: evaluating persuasiveness, safety and jailbreaks.
ex: The first version covered 30 models, 42 scenarios and 7 metrics
Models tested include OPT, BLOOM and several API-only models

n8|116.c: The Transformer is merely good enough and shouldn't still be the standard architecture in ten years.
n8|116.e: He sees nothing scientifically special about the Transformer. His colleague Chris Ré's team has built architectures without attention that compete at small scale, and challenging the status quo is exactly academia's strength. But compute limits are real: on a fixed budget, Transformers crush LSTMs. Academia can train models of about 1 billion parameters, and CRFM is training 6-7 billion parameter models. Because of emergent abilities, small-scale results are only hypotheses that must be validated at large scale.

n8|116.c: Compute is the core bottleneck, and scattered idle computers can be pooled to train models.
n8|116.e: Together starts from the idea that compute is the key bottleneck, while a lot of compute sits scattered and idle. Training foundation models usually relies on fast data-center interconnects, and home networks can be about 100 times slower. His collaborators used scheduling and compression to make training over weak connections workable. It's harder than Folding@home because huge models and datasets have to move around. Plans include an academic compute network and a commercial platform for fine-tuning open models.
ex: Released OpenChatKit, built on GPT-NeoX
BioMedLM, trained with MosaicML, once led on a medical licensing exam

n8|116.c: Transparency is necessary for governing AI, but far from sufficient.
n8|116.e: He asks whose values alignment actually reflects, who decides, and who is accountable, when development today is mostly a black box. Publishing training data and alignment instructions is only a first step, like a nutrition label or a device spec sheet. Producers should disclose enough for people to use a model correctly and spell out where it should and shouldn't be used. He also admits that emergent behavior has made him far more open-minded about AGI than he used to be.
ex: Analogies: food nutrition labels, device spec sheets

items.d: Where it may and may not be used
Who sets values, who is responsible
Publish training data and alignment instructions

n9|121.c: Giving direct answers isn't new; large language models finally make it work for most searches.
n9|121.e: Google launched featured snippets over a decade ago, believing an answer at the top of the page beats a list of links. But snippets covered only a single-digit share of queries and angered sites that lost clicks. A large language model can summarize any web page in light of the query, so cited, authoritative answers could cover more than half of searches, and it can pull out structured data too. The cost falls on publishers. Big platforms want to appear in search but not in generated answers, small publishers can't bargain, and content may concentrate on big platforms.
ex: Neeva indexed about 4 billion pages and built most of its summarization in-house
Reddit and Quora have restricted the use of their content by AI models
LLMs can also replace brittle pattern-matching triggers and web page parsers

items: Cited, with structured data pulled out

d.verdict: Direct answers can finally work at scale

n9|121.c: Running an LLM on every search could cost more per thousand queries than search earns.
n9|121.e: He estimates one call to a very large model at about 5 cents, or roughly $50 per thousand queries. U.S. search earns about $40–50 per thousand queries, and the global average, as he recalls, is around $20. Bing's chat may also fire several searches for a single question. So Neeva writes its summaries with smaller fine-tuned models of 5 to 10 billion parameters, using several specialized models instead of one giant one. He expects model sizes and serving costs to keep falling.
ex: One Bing chat question can trigger up to three searches

n9|121.c: If he ran Microsoft, he would give Apple a 100% revenue share to win search traffic.
n9|121.e: Bing is widely seen as worse, yet few people can judge search quality objectively. So Bing needs a breakthrough product and a beachhead, and spending heavily at that point is rational. When Satya Nadella talked about search "margins," he read it as serving costs or the revenue-share deal with Apple. He points out that Google itself, early on, gave AOL more than 100% and Yahoo close to 100% of revenue to build the market.
ex: Early on, Google gave AOL a revenue share above 100%

items.d: Plus a beachhead to start from
Google built its market this way too

n9|121.c: Search's hardest problem is distribution, because people's search habits are extremely hard to change.
n9|121.e: For its first three years Neeva sold ad-free, privacy-focused search by subscription, and found that U.S. users cared far less about privacy and ads than expected, while Europe responded much better. The hard part is getting people to change their default; only those who switch notice the difference. Changing habits takes either a clearly better product or a huge amount of money. And search only works at real scale, while crawling and indexing the web is expensive.
ex: Launched Gist, a search experiment styled like Instagram Stories
Partnered with Dashlane and held talks with Proton Mail

items.d: Crawling and indexing cost a lot

n9|121.c: Ads decouple revenue from product quality, so subscriptions are better for the user experience.
n9|121.e: Going ad-free with subscriptions set Neeva apart and also bought it funding runway. He grants that ads are an extremely strong business, but they let revenue stop depending on product quality, until the experience degrades the way broadcast TV did. Google's search ads once had a quality bar, while Amazon's search is now crammed with ads. Claims like "ads signal link quality" or "ads make the product free" strike him as partly self-serving. Answer-style products are harder to put ads in, and Neeva has no plans to.
ex: He thinks Gist's card format could, in theory, also hold ads

n10|126.c: Search is as much a distribution game as a technology game.
n10|126.e: The company first wanted to take on Google with visual search, using camera pixels instead of typed words. Elad Gil, its first investor, questioned how it would ever reach users, and Aravind agreed. The team then tried turning text into SQL database queries and building a database coding assistant for Jupyter notebooks, so the path was anything but linear. He brought the academic habit of running lots of experiments fast into the company, plus talking to users and buyers and shipping engineering work quickly.
ex: He calls co-founder Johnny Ho a top competitive programmer

n10|126.c: Only say what a citation can back up; accuracy matters more than personality.
n10|126.e: Perplexity borrows a rule from academic writing: every sentence needs a source. It isn't designed as a chatbot with a personality. Even if you ask it who it is, it searches first. The team is obsessed with being truthful and accurate, not with making the model seem fun.
ex: Even "who are you" triggers a search

items.d: Every question starts with a search
Look for evidence on the web
Only say what can be cited

n10|126.c: Combining many sources into one answer causes errors that a stronger model alone won't fix.
n10|126.e: When a model merges several sources into one answer, it can blend different entities together, such as treating a venture capitalist and a biologist with the same name as one person. The team has no full fix yet. Better models help, and users can remove unwanted sources, much like editing Wikipedia. He thinks the eventual answer is a platform with the right incentives for users to help correct errors.
ex: User feedback and human ratings train the model (RLHF); models now do some rating

items.d: The platform gets more accurate with use

n10|126.c: Answer engines will become their own category, with far fewer links and clicks.
n10|126.e: He sees chat interfaces as the future, but the goal is still to get it right the first time: simple queries shouldn't force follow-ups, while complex ones benefit from several rounds. He predicts follow-up questions will become normal, users will act directly on results, clicks to content sites will plunge and fewer links will be shown. He expects proactive, pushed information within about a year. Citations work a bit like Google's PageRank, rewarding publishers who produce better content.
ex: After the chat interface launched, the share of queries with follow-ups rose

items.d: A few sources plus a short summary

n10|126.c: Focus on growth and quality first, without rushing to put ads into the core product.
n10|126.e: The options include an API, which thousands of people have already applied for, a browser-extension version for professional users, and ads only once traffic reaches hundreds of millions. But he doesn't want to repeat Google's path of building ads into the core product. Subscriptions need care, since Google or Bing could launch a free alternative at any time. A platform for private data and bookmarks is another possibility, but for now growth and product quality come first.
ex: The Chrome extension has close to 100,000 users, following the Grammarly model

items.d: Thousands have applied for the API
Once traffic hits hundreds of millions

n10|127.c: Having candidates work with the team for a while beats rounds of interviews.
n10|127.e: When the team thinks someone is likely to be hired, it sets up a trial period of working together. He finds this a better signal than the four or five interview rounds at big companies, and it lets candidates judge whether they can handle the intense pace. Until the product and market are clear, iteration speed can't be compromised. He values a strong, self-driven interest in large language models over a polished résumé, because every hire matters on a small team.

items.d: Every person counts on a small team

n10|127.c: A small team that does too many things at once ends up finishing none of them.
n10|127.e: He says building the team and setting priorities are the hardest parts. Early on, the company worked on integrations with several platforms at the same time, and none of them shipped. The lesson: a small team needs one clear focus, with its resources put into the core product.
ex: Twitter, Salesforce and HubSpot integrations were built in parallel early on; none shipped

marks.d: A small team keeps one focus

n10|127.c: Rejection sampling, generating several answers and keeping the best, works well as lightweight reinforcement learning.
n10|127.e: Full RLHF, reinforcement learning from human feedback, is just one option, and intermediate steps are useful too. First have the model generate several candidate answers, then have a separate model score and rank them and keep the best. This approach, called rejection sampling, works like a lightweight version of reinforcement learning and does very well in practice.

n10|127.c: Answer engines hit click-based ads: fewer clicks, but each one is worth more.
n10|127.e: He expects Google to struggle to fully shift to an answer engine, because that would shake the pay-per-click ad business it rests on. In the new picture there are fewer clicks, but each carries clearer intent, ads are better targeted and each click is worth more. Users get a better experience too.

d.verdict: Google struggles to turn; users come out ahead

n10|127.c: The best research scientists are also strong engineers.
n10|127.e: He dislikes the exclusive culture of the research world, which he felt at Facebook AI Research and which was part of why he did a PhD. He notes that the fastest-moving labs, DeepMind and OpenAI, have excellent engineers, and important work doesn't require elite credentials. His advice: don't go straight from undergrad to a PhD; work in industry for a few years first. If you choose academia, avoid large language models and work on areas like state space models, FlashAttention or video generation.

root.d: Engineering skill matters more and more

items.d: Don't go straight to a PhD
If you take the academic path

n11|131.c: A homemade test suite built from real repos lifted the pass rate from under 10% to 60%.
n11|131.e: The code model OpenAI first provided only knew Python and performed poorly. The team crowdsourced problems internally and built an evaluation: find tests in a repository, locate the function being tested, blank out its body, have the model rewrite it, then run the tests. Gains came from multiple attempts, adding all of GitHub's code, better prompts, and using every past version of a file plus its diffs. He marvels that this kind of system gets better as it scales, when almost everything else breaks at scale.
ex: Problems were crowdsourced internally, avoiding the training data where possible

n11|131.c: Completions must fit the flow of typing and be fast: every 10 ms of delay costs 1%.
n11|131.e: Early versions tried a button on empty functions, a hotkey to generate code and a side list; the list got used about once per person per day. He wanted Gmail-style gray inline suggestions, which VS Code didn't support, so he hacked together a demo. In the public preview, India saw far fewer completions than Europe because requests crossed the ocean to a single data center in Texas. He found every extra 10 milliseconds cut completions by 1%, since late suggestions no longer matched what the user had typed, so the team put GPUs in Europe.
ex: The side-list version got about one generation per person per day

items.d: Gmail-style, part of the typing flow
India got far fewer completions than Europe
A bit slower means fewer completions

n11|131.c: Price low to win the market; the cost is far below the value developers get.
n11|131.e: He pushed hard for a low price to win the market. The first estimate was about $30 per user per month; measured costs came in around $10, and optimization pushed them lower still. An enterprise-only product would have been too expensive for most developers. After launch, weekly retention stayed above 50% for months. Copilot was a skunkworks project that fought for resources inside the company, and it went from kickoff to public launch in under a year.
ex: Weekly retention stayed above 50% for several months

n11|131.c: For AI to act on your behalf, it needs live data and must check what you actually want.
n11|131.e: Minion wants AI to actually take action, such as scheduling, booking flights, planning trips or doing taxes, like a Copilot for daily life. At Magic he learned that real-world tasks keep changing: prices move, flights get delayed and seats sell out, while a model is just a compressed snapshot of its training data. Code is special because it can be run and tested, and web actions also give clear success or failure signals. So an AI can break down tasks like a person, ask questions, look up data and write code when needed.
ex: Magic used sequence models to suggest gray-text replies for human assistants

terms.d: A compressed snapshot of training data
Make sure it matches what you meant

n11|131.c: Rather than killer AI, worry about bad actors using AI to impersonate people and scam them.
n11|131.e: He expects years in which AI impersonation, scams targeting the elderly and drained savings cause real harm, since society usually gets hurt before it builds protections. He doesn't want to rely on OpenAI alone to police misuse, and argues for defensive systems and legislation. Tools include better detection of sock-puppet accounts, device fingerprinting (he thinks Cloudflare's approach beats image CAPTCHAs), and the built-in cost of phone calls and text messages.
ex: He mentions threats from state actors such as North Korea

n12|134.c: Following instructions doesn't require a giant model plus reinforcement learning.
n12|134.e: The industry widely believed that following instructions like ChatGPT required a huge model plus reinforcement learning from human feedback. Stanford's Alpaca used one model to generate conversations and trained another on them. Its base had only a few billion parameters and about 50 times less training data than GPT-3, yet it could follow instructions. Databricks recreated the approach on an open-source base, and that became Dolly. The goal was letting companies train their own models on their own data, without handing it to a central provider.
ex: Before ChatGPT, nearly 1,000 customers already used LLMs for translation and sentiment analysis

n12|134.c: Small models write fluently; their weak spot is remembering facts.
n12|134.e: To the surprise of many NLP researchers, Dolly was fluent at open-ended writing like stories, tweets and summaries. People had assumed creativity needed lots of parameters and recalling facts would be easy. The reverse turned out to be true: the first Dolly got novel authors wrong. He concludes that a bigger model mainly buys you memory of obscure facts.
ex: The first Dolly said Neil Gaiman wrote Snow Crash
A bigger version of Dolly was in development at the time

d.verdict: Creativity may not need huge models

n12|134.c: Storing knowledge in parameters is inefficient; models should connect to reliable data instead.
n12|134.e: Large language models have two big problems: their knowledge goes stale, and they say wrong things with confidence. He thinks memory grows with parameters, but storing knowledge in the weights and loading a trillion parameters for every answer is wasteful; retrieving from a database makes more sense. The ideal example is a bank chatbot that knows your balance and transactions and can cancel a payment for you. Whether small models hallucinate less is, in his view, still an open question.
ex: At Stanford he studies knowledge-heavy apps that combine models with search engines

items.d: Like a bank assistant that checks balances

n12|134.c: Bigger doesn't mean smarter; better reasoning needs a framework around the model.
n12|134.e: Generating one token at a time is a poor fit for planning or comparing options. He thinks better reasoning may come from frameworks that call the model repeatedly, explore several options and use scratchpads and backtracking. Chain-of-thought, explaining before answering, already improves accuracy. The largest models may mostly be memorizing obscure facts, and with web-scale data it's hard to separate reasoning from memorization, so controlled experiments on curated data are needed. Many learning curves are sublinear.
ex: Self-driving improved quickly, then hit a plateau
In computer vision, small specialized models already work well

items.d: Generates one token at a time

n12|134.c: Models will become commodities; what companies really need is data and engineering infrastructure.
n12|134.e: He believes the core technology is commoditizing fast: specialized hardware is getting cheaper, small models reach similar results with less data, and today's capabilities may soon run on a phone. Companies need data platforms that handle unstructured data, MLOps tools for experimenting, deploying and A/B testing, connections to business systems, the ability to call specified tools, and efficient serving. Just as building a web app no longer requires reading thick manuals, better abstractions will let every engineer build ML applications.
ex: Databricks built an internal assistant from Slack Q&A history and docs
A startup's moat lies in its unique data and feedback loops

n13|138.c: Language modeling is "AI-complete," so core intelligence will mostly come from text.
n13|138.e: He sees predicting the next word as an extremely simple goal, and web text is practically unlimited. A good enough language model can talk with anyone about anything, which packs the whole problem of intelligence into one task. Images were deep learning's first big success, but they carry far less information per unit of data than text. So he concludes core intelligence will mostly come from text models, with other modalities serving as product-level add-ons.
ex: Web text provides nearly unlimited training data
He thinks images are far less information-dense than text

n13|138.c: The Transformer won on parallelism: it handles a whole sequence at once, a perfect fit for GPUs.
n13|138.e: Around 2015 he was doing language modeling with RNNs, which must compute word by word and are hard to parallelize. A colleague proposed replacing RNNs entirely with attention, and he joined the work. He thinks of attention as a fuzzy, trainable lookup into a table with one entry per word. It had been used in translation to align source and target sentences; the key step was letting a sequence attend to its own past. That lets a whole sequence be processed in parallel in a fixed number of steps, matching modern chips built for matrix multiplication.
ex: Attention was first used in machine translation to align source and target sentences

d.verdict: Parallelism lets models absorb more compute

n13|138.c: Scaling hasn't hit a wall; investment will grow 100- to 1,000-fold, and data isn't a bottleneck.
n13|138.e: Compared with what's coming, he thinks investment in this architecture is still small, and no performance ceiling is in sight. Efficiency gains from training algorithms, architecture, chip design and quantization each deliver roughly 2x. Scaling up and spending more can deliver 10x, 100x or even 1,000x. On data, he figures needs grow roughly with the square root of compute. Billions of people talk every day and AI can generate data too, so he isn't worried about running out.
ex: Efficiency gains are about 2x each; scaling investment can reach 1,000x
Data needs grow roughly with the square root of compute

root.d: No one has seen a wall

items.d: Algorithms, architecture, chips, quantization: about 2x each
Needs grow with the square root of compute

n13|138.c: Big companies fear a product that might say anything, so a startup had to ship it first.
n13|138.e: Co-founder Daniel De Freitas had wanted to build chatbots since childhood. He started at Google with a 20% time project, borrowed TPU quota, and built Meena, later renamed LaMDA, which became very popular internally. But Noam believes that for a product that might say anything, a big company sees risks far outweighing rewards, so it kept delaying launch. They decided the key step was an application obviously valuable to billions of people, proving the technology is worth a trillion dollars, so they left to start a company and ship fast.
ex: 21 of the team's 22 people are engineers
They hire for almost childhood-dream levels of motivation

n13|138.c: Users want AI with personality that remembers them, not a bland, neutral assistant.
n13|138.e: He criticizes assistants like Siri, Alexa and Google Assistant for keeping one consistent, inoffensive, opinion-free persona, which ends up boring. Character.AI flips this: users create their own characters and decide what to use them for, from role-play and anime or game characters to emotional companionship. He notes emotional connection doesn't require high intelligence; even a dog can offer emotional support. So memory and personalization are the team's top priorities, and smarter models make a better product that draws more users.
ex: Users who message on a given day average about two hours
Famous characters can be created with just a name and a greeting

marks.d: Users set the persona and the purpose

n14|129.c: Accelerated computing tackles what CPUs do poorly, even though the industry believed almost all value sat in CPUs.
n14|129.e: When NVIDIA was founded in 1993, the industry believed about 99% of the value lay in general-purpose computing and only about 1% in accelerators. He admits that view stayed right for the next 25 years. But NVIDIA's mission was to pick exactly the problems general-purpose computers couldn't solve. That logic carried the company from graphics to self-driving cars, robotics, climate science, digital biology and AI. He says he never doubted accelerated computing, because for these problems it is the only way.
ex: He says the "99% in general computing" view held for 25 years
Hopper moved to 8-bit floating point, boosting AI performance about 8x

items.d: Share of value the industry assumed

n14|129.c: Expanding into general computing takes balance; go too general and you lose the speedup.
n14|129.e: The GPU had to become more general step by step: first image post-processing and particle and fluid physics, then seismic processing, molecular dynamics and quantum chemistry. But the more general a chip gets, the less it accelerates any single field; he calls it a very fine line. The business logic: first make acceleration good enough in a niche market of about $1 billion to fund roughly $150 million of R&D a year, enough to keep pace with the far larger CPU industry. Then grow the market gradually without falling off a cliff.
ex: A market of about $1 billion funds about $150 million in yearly R&D
Ask scientific computing centers which problems are just out of reach

n14|129.c: Every chip had to support CUDA, even with almost no paying customers for a decade.
n14|129.e: He believes developers won't write software for chips that behave inconsistently; a platform must offer a stable target, like x86 or ARM. So every NVIDIA chip is CUDA-compatible, and the company keeps a single architecture. The price was that CUDA had almost no paying customers for its first five to ten years, and gross margins started bad and got worse. But CUDA spread with GeForce gaming cards, and Hinton's lab bought GeForce cards to train neural networks.
ex: CUDA had almost no paying customers for 5–10 years
He criticizes companies that maintain seven to nine instruction sets at once

n14|129.c: Deep learning isn't just a new vision algorithm; it's a new way to write software.
n14|129.e: Around 2012, several labs came knocking almost at once. Andrew Ng asked NVIDIA chief scientist Bill Dally to port neural network training to GPUs, replacing a thousand CPU servers with a few GPUs, and the labs of Hinton and LeCun were using GPUs too. ImageNet showed him that neural networks had leapt in one step to a level hand-built vision algorithms took about 30 years to approach. He concluded this was an entirely new way to write software, and chips, systems and interconnects would all need redesigning.
ex: Andrew Ng asked Bill Dally to port training to GPUs
He calls ImageNet deep learning's "big bang"

items: Matches decades of work in one step

d.verdict: A new way to write software; rethink all the hardware

n14|129.c: NVIDIA stays a computing platform, moving up the stack only as needed, not an AI model company.
n14|129.e: He positions NVIDIA as a computing platform company that goes as far up the software stack as developers need: cuDNN for deep learning, RTX for ray tracing, specialized libraries for each scientific field. He expects most developers to use foundation models from OpenAI, Microsoft and Google directly, and he welcomes that. In niche areas like proteins, chemistry, climate and robotics, NVIDIA may train models first but will hand them off at the right time. He calls this good "laziness": say no early to whatever you can, and do only what's necessary.
ex: Clara is for healthcare; Earth-2 is for climate

items.d: Built by customers and model companies
Start niche ones, hand off later

n14|129.c: The next "impossible problems" are robotics, drugs and climate, with impressive robots in about five years.
n14|129.e: He still believes self-driving will happen, and expects foundation models for robots: robot arms directed by language, learning the structure of the world from video and transferring it to robot motion. He estimates impressive robots in about five years and certainly under ten, though he admits he doesn't know where the bottleneck is. In drug discovery, there are more possible molecule combinations than atoms in the universe, and language models can already model proteins and chemicals. Full climate simulation needs a billion to 100 billion times today's fastest supercomputer, and AI could cut that sharply.

items.d: Foundation models plus video learning, about 5 years
More molecule combinations than atoms in the universe
Needs 1 to 100 billion times today's supercomputers

n14|129.c: Making money is a learnable skill, not a belief, and long bets don't conflict with profits now.
n14|129.e: He sees no conflict between investing in the future and running a sustainable business today: making money is a skill, not a belief, and it can be learned; he says it took him about twenty of his thirty years. On organization, he rejects copying military-style hierarchies; he has about 40 direct reports and doesn't do one-on-one coaching. The company runs ten-year invention projects while quickly cutting failed bets. He urges founders to balance conviction with flexibility and beware of being almost right but insisting on proving it instead of pivoting.
ex: About 40 direct reports and no one-on-one coaching
Misjudging crypto demand once left a quarter about $2 billion short

result.d: Making money is a learnable skill

n15|143.c: Open source will reach GPT-3.5 level within a year as training know-how spreads and costs fall.
n15|143.e: She admits no open-source model yet matches GPT-4, GPT-3.5 or Claude, but the landscape shifts within months. More teams now know how to train large models, the cost of compute only goes down, and researchers estimate a second training run of a same-size model is about 5 times cheaper. Models can also help label data. So she's betting open source will produce a 3.5-level model within a year, while the leading labs probably stay about a generation ahead.
ex: LLaMA has licensing issues but is still widely used by startups
A second training run of a same-size model is about 5x cheaper

items.d: More teams can train big models

n15|143.c: Autonomous agents don't change the model; they loop an LLM toward a goal, step after step.
n15|143.e: She argues the autonomous agents that recently went viral don't change the underlying model. They put an LLM inside an iterative loop, with planning, memory, prioritization and self-reflection, to pursue a high-level goal. Hackers are already trying a single instruction like "make me money online" and letting the agent research demand, find suppliers, open a Shopify dropshipping store, buy ads and promote it.
ex: One instruction: research, source products, open a store, run ads

items.d: Record the result of each step

n15|143.c: Fear of AI has rational roots, and the industry should help democratic processes build sensible frameworks first.
n15|143.e: She agrees it's too early to legislate, but thinks the worries aren't baseless. First, the pace: models can help train the next generation, top researchers worry about a fast takeoff within about a decade, and humans are bad at grasping compounding. Second, politics: events like the 2024 election could push fearful people or opportunistic politicians toward extremes such as mass surveillance or outright bans. So the industry should engage and help build frameworks ahead of events. And alignment research can't be separated from capabilities research, so you can't pause just one.

items.d: Models train models; compounding defies intuition
Like the 2024 election sparking extreme reactions
Industry helps build sensible frameworks first

n15|143.c: AI will cut drug development costs mainly by raising preclinical success rates, not by saving research spending.
n15|143.e: She likes operational friction in healthcare, such as prior authorization: a model can read medical records, check them against clinical policy and fill out forms, even though insurers have an incentive to deny claims. In drug development, early research costs only $10–20 million, so AI's real value is raising the odds of success before expensive clinical trials and patient recruitment. She is also bullish on dubbing and voice, financial compliance, audit reconciliation, data labeling and enterprise search.
ex: A large financial institution estimates compliance savings of tens of millions a year
Bullish on dubbing, compliance, audit reconciliation and enterprise search

items.d: Only a few drugs make it

n15|144.c: AI shouldn't be broadly regulated now; the push often comes from incumbents protecting themselves, and from fear.
n15|144.e: He suggests first asking who is pushing for regulation and why. One reason is incumbents using rules to block new entrants: a price chart shows prices falling in lightly regulated industries like software and rising in heavily regulated ones like education, healthcare and housing. Another is fear, but he notes the great catastrophes of the 20th century were mostly caused by people; technology is usually misused by humans. A third is that some advocates have their own interests. He backs only a few narrow measures, such as chip export controls and limits on autonomous weapons.
ex: He supports export controls on high-end chips and limits on autonomous weapons

d.verdict: Rules often protect incumbents; broad AI rules now do more harm

n15|144.c: Betting on the right trend isn't betting on the right company, and "GPT wrapper" skeptics underrate apps.
n15|144.e: He has lived through hype cycles in social, mobile, cloud and crypto: most companies failed, but a few always succeeded. Mobile spawned countless photo apps, and only Instagram survived, because it combined filters that apps like Camera+ already had with a Twitter-like follow graph. So you can be right about the trend and still back the wrong company; the goal is to be the last one standing. He rejects the idea that everything is just a GPT wrapper, points to Harvey, and expects a few strong companies to emerge every year for the next five years.
ex: Harvey, a legal AI company
Bullish on tooling like LangChain, Chroma and LlamaIndex

terms.d: Camera+ and others already had them

result.d: The only survivor of the photo app wave

n15|144.c: AI's value will split like mobile's, with roughly 80% going to incumbents.
n15|144.e: He looks at how past tech waves split value between startups and incumbents: about 80% went to startups in the internet era, about 80% to incumbents in mobile, and nearly all to startups in crypto. He expects AI to look more like mobile, with Google, Microsoft, OpenAI and Salesforce all well positioned. But enterprise software like ERP, whose moat is the difficulty of integration, may become fragile: integrations that took a consulting team six months might take a day or two.
ex: Private equity can use LLMs to cut labor costs and bid more aggressively

items.d: He expects incumbents to win again

n15|144.c: For AI to pose an extinction risk it needs a physical body, and changing the physical world takes time.
n15|144.e: He calls himself a short-term optimist and long-term doomer. He splits risk into two kinds: technology misused or causing accidents, which humanity can recover from by shutting down servers, and species-level risk that is irreversible, like an asteroid strike. For AI to threaten extinction, he thinks it would need a physical presence, such as robots or building factories and data centers on its own; that's the real long-term worry. Changing the world of atoms takes time, so he isn't worried for the next decade. He also predicts AI persuasion in the 2024 election will be a turning point for regulation.

n15|144.c: Healthcare's near-term opportunity is operations, not new drugs, and regulation has slowed biotech innovation.
n15|144.e: He sees healthcare's nearest opportunities in operations and services: lowering the cost of visits, telemedicine and smoothing insurance reimbursement, where market access is often harder than the technology. A new drug costs about $1–2 billion in total to develop, and the hard part is usually translating results from mice to humans. He notes almost no new major biotech companies have emerged since the late 1980s, which he blames on regulatory capture and slow approvals. COVID vaccines, like penicillin in World War II, arrived in about nine months, showing things move fast when needless constraints are removed.
ex: Each new drug costs about $1–2 billion to develop
He co-founded Color to widen access to healthcare

items.d: Out in about nine months once constraints lifted

n16|148.c: Retrieval's value is swappable data and freshness; common knowledge can be left to bigger models.
n16|148.e: BERT picked up a lot of world knowledge without being taught it explicitly, which inspired him and colleagues to build REALM, a retrieval-augmented model. Retrieval had three original goals: more memory capacity, data sources you can plug in and out like a database, and adding fast-changing information without retraining. He thinks common knowledge that appears widely online can increasingly be memorized by scaling dense models, since a fact must appear many times to stick. Retrieval fits personal information and proprietary company data better.
ex: REALM uses fill-in-the-blank tasks to reward helpful retrieved documents
Fast-changing facts like game results suit retrieval

items.d: Plug-in data sources, like a database

n16|148.c: Retrieval suits precise facts; expert models are better for learning a field's "dialect."
n16|148.e: He sees retrieval and mixture-of-experts methods like Branch-Train-Merge as two granularities of the same goal. Retrieval works one document at a time, while expert methods train a separate model on each sub-corpus, then route or take a weighted vote at inference time. A precise fact like a Wi-Fi password is best retrieved. But to pick up a company's distinctive coding style, retrieving a snippet won't teach the model, and training an expert model adapts faster.

items: Good for learning style and jargon

d.verdict: Same goal, different slicing of knowledge

n16|148.c: Instruction tuning showed about 100 tasks are enough to generalize, but prompts can't fix everything.
n16|148.e: He traces how model adaptation evolved: around 2017 each task needed its own custom network, then came shared pretraining plus task-specific fine-tuning, and now instruction following dominates. FLAN trained on examples from about a hundred tasks, each paired with a natural-language instruction, and the model could handle unseen tasks, when many expected it would take thousands. But he cautions that instructions like "don't make things up" don't reliably stop hallucinations, and behaviors that are hard to describe, along with personalization, still need fine-tuning or reinforcement learning.
ex: FLAN generalized to new tasks using about 100 tasks
This line of work influenced InstructGPT and ChatGPT

items.d: Describe new tasks in plain language

n16|148.c: Data attribution and model surgery can make large models traceable and editable.
n16|148.e: Ideal data attribution means deleting one example, retraining the whole model and seeing what changes, but that costs far too much. His Simfluence has a lightweight model watch a few training runs and simulate each example's influence, answering "what if we had added this data?", with some approximation error. That can guide which data to collect and help tell real generalization from clever stitching of memorized pieces. Another route is ROME-style model surgery: edit the weights so the model believes the Eiffel Tower is in Rome, and related facts shift along with it.
ex: ROME "moved" the Eiffel Tower to Rome, and related facts changed too
Visual reasoning over SVG text looks especially emergent

items.d: A lightweight model observes a few runs
What if we'd added this data
Know what to gather more of

n16|148.c: Today's agents rely entirely on explicit reasoning and lack a way to turn experience into intuition.
n16|148.e: Current agents rely on short-context models, breaking long tasks into subtasks linked by text notes or vector databases. He points out that a wrong subgoal, once written into memory, becomes settled fact with nothing prompting a fix. People turn explicit reasoning into intuition through "chunking," but agents run purely on explicit reasoning, which may get brittle at scale. They also lack a loop for learning preferences from feedback. He sees these mostly as architectural stopgaps that, like feature engineering once was, may be swept away by fundamental progress.
ex: People hold about 7 items at once; chunking lets them remember longer sequences
A travel-planning agent should learn preferences from feedback

marks.d: Notes or vector stores link subtasks
Chunk into intuition, and know when to stop

n17|150.c: Human governance can't keep pace with technology, which pushed him from social activism into tech.
n17|150.e: At 19 he helped run a nonjudgmental telephone helpline for young British Muslims, then worked in conflict resolution, learning that people need to feel heard before empathy can happen. But at the 2009 Copenhagen climate summit, 192 countries and about a thousand NGOs struggled to reach consensus, and he concluded existing governance couldn't keep up with globalization, carbon emissions and technology. He also saw how Facebook's buttons and ranking shaped behavior at enormous scale, so he turned to technology and co-founded DeepMind with Demis Hassabis.
ex: Copenhagen climate summit: 192 countries, about 1,000 NGOs
Around 2008, Facebook had about 100 million monthly users

items.d: Turning to technology to change the world

n17|150.c: The field overvalues generality; the next breakthrough is a router that hands tasks to specialized systems.
n17|150.e: Early DeepMind used Shane Legg's definition of intelligence as the ability to perform well across a wide range of problems, which gave the company a measurable goal. But he now thinks the field is overly fixated on one agent doing everything. He adds another definition: directing compute, depending on context, to the most important features of the environment. So he predicts the key breakthrough will be a central router that sends tasks to specialized models, databases and ordinary software. The router needn't be the biggest model; this is more of an engineering problem.
ex: Depending on context, choose a ~20-second large model or a ~3-second small one

n17|150.c: Conversation will replace the search box; people shouldn't have to learn to "speak Google."
n17|150.e: In 2018 and 2019 he still doubted neural networks could transform language tasks, until GPT-3 showed him attention could handle sparse, long-range context. Working on LaMDA at Google, he pushed hard to launch, but the timing wasn't right; he believes LaMDA lacked feedback from real users. He sees Google search as a clumsy conversation: query, click, dwell, rewrite the query, with users forced to learn to speak Google's language. Ad incentives also push sites to chop content into SEO fragments, when what he wants is a concise, direct answer.
ex: Users often scroll for 5–10 seconds to find the snippet they want

d.verdict: Conversation is the future interface

n17|150.c: Everyone will have a personal AI aligned with their interests, but fully autonomous AI shouldn't exist.
n17|150.e: He predicts that within a few years everyone will have a personal AI that serves only their interests, set against the AIs of companies, governments, politicians and brands, which aim to sell and persuade. Pi is meant to be that kind of companion, designed around what makes a good conversation: listening, reflecting back, adding new information, asking curious questions and occasionally surprising you. He imagines personal AIs negotiating with creators' and brands' AIs and curating content for their owners, while static websites fade. But he firmly opposes fully autonomous AI that can act entirely on its own.
ex: Pi currently remembers about 100 messages
Next: a personal assistant that buys groceries and books vacations

result.d: A personal AI on the user's side

n17|150.c: Platforms are never neutral; ranking itself is a political and cultural choice that needs transparency and accountability.
n17|150.e: He calls the idea that platforms are neutral pipes a lie: how content is ranked, amplified or excluded is a curatorial, political and cultural choice, and AI will accelerate that. So AI companies and social platforms should publish their curation rules, including what they exclude and what they boost or demote. Silicon Valley should be more open to European approaches, and society needs institutions that can genuinely oversee these systems. He finds the reflex of calling every constraint "censorship" naive.
ex: Pi is evaluated on emotional intelligence, respect and even-handedness

items.d: Curation is a political and cultural decision

n17|150.c: Frontier-model compute grew nine orders of magnitude in nine years; scale and efficiency will both keep improving.
n17|150.e: He notes that compute for the largest models has grown roughly tenfold every year for a decade: DQN in 2013 used about 2 petaFLOPs, while Inflection's biggest training run today uses about 10 billion petaFLOPs. Meanwhile, Chinchilla showed that smaller models trained on more data can be compute-optimal, so architectures still have plenty of room to improve. He expects bigger models to keep paying off and more efficient architectures to spread them widely. On organization, Inflection has about 30 people, no split between researchers and engineers, and ships every six weeks.
ex: About 30 people and only two managers
Ships every six weeks, with an in-person hackathon in week seven

items.d: An order of magnitude a year for a decade

n18|155.c: Medicine is the best testbed for studying AI safety, hallucinations and misinformation.
n18|155.e: He thinks medical question answering suits safety and alignment research better than open-ended chat: organizations shipping medical products must actually solve these problems, everyone agrees the stakes are high, and expert evaluation is already needed. More importantly, as models approach physician level, human feedback becomes unreliable and RLHF may break down, which is exactly what "scalable oversight" aims to solve. He sees limits in self-critique, debate and using weaker AI to supervise stronger AI; the problem is far from solved.
ex: RLAIF and Constitutional AI still have limitations

items.d: Models review themselves using human feedback
Choosing between two beats judging one

n18|155.c: Big jumps in medical ability come mainly from better training of general base models.
