n18|155.e: He attributes much of the progress of PaLM, Med-PaLM and even GPT-4 on medical benchmarks to improvements in base model training. Minerva's sudden jump on science benchmarks from near-random to usable prompted them to test medical ability with multiple-choice questions. Flan-PaLM became the first model to pass the MedQA threshold, but its long answers fell clearly short of physicians', so they used instruction prompt tuning to align it to the domain. Med-PaLM 2's gains came from mixed training objectives, compute-optimal data mixtures and better data.
ex: PaLM is a 540-billion-parameter dense model
Flan-PaLM was the first to pass MedQA

n18|155.c: Which method you use to adapt a model depends on how much data you have.
n18|155.e: He offers a framework organized by data volume. With lots of relevant domain data, you can pretrain from scratch; if web pretraining transfers well to the target domain, such as medical reasoning, build on an existing model. With only three to five examples, use prompting. With ten to fifty, prompt tuning and fine-tuning perform similarly, and prompt tuning is cheaper when costs are tight. With more than a hundred examples and a goal of the best results, do full fine-tuning. Physician labels are expensive, so they favor data-efficient methods.

n18|155.c: Declining to answer is also a decision, and big companies are too conservative about health information.
n18|155.e: He notes that about one in ten internet searches is health-related, and even doctors search, so refusing to answer is a choice too. He thinks big companies and health information providers are too risk-averse, weighing risks but not benefits. What's really missing are evaluations that prove safety and patient benefit within specific workflows. On deployment, clinical documentation tools are already appearing. Higher-stakes "physician assistants" need specialized models, such as helping radiologists read scans using medical records and prior images, which he thinks is feasible in the short to medium term.
ex: About 10% of internet searches are health-related
A radiology assistant reads scans alongside records and prior images

d.verdict: Prove safety and benefit in real workflows

n18|155.c: Strong results are possible without patient data; privacy tech and closed-loop data come next.
n18|155.e: He notes the Med-PaLM models used no patient health data at all and performed well just by aligning PaLM, as GPT-4 did too. People are already pasting de-identified, or even identifiable, medical records into GPT-4, which he calls an ongoing experiment; automatic de-identification models are low-hanging fruit. Federated learning fits healthcare well, but the biggest near-term gains will more likely come from the largest models, with trusted execution environments as a compromise. Longer term, deployed physician assistants can generate outcome data, closing the loop.
ex: Trusted execution environments keep employees from accessing data directly

items.d: Aligned general models already do well
Outcome data feeds back into medicine

n19|159.c: Reusable pretrained models turned AI into a platform, so Microsoft pooled its compute and went all in.
n19|159.e: He credits transfer learning, meaning models like ELMo, BERT, RoBERTa and Microsoft's own Turing that are trained once and reused for many tasks, with turning AI from isolated systems into a platform. That was the catalyst for Microsoft's bet. When he arrived, AI spending was scattered, so he pooled the GPU budget and aimed it at work that improves with more compute. In Satya Nadella's framing it was a no-regret bet: at worst, Microsoft would learn to run huge training facilities. Analysis showing frontier training compute growing about 10x a year firmed up his view, despite heavy internal disagreement.
ex: Compute used to train frontier models grows about 10x a year
Microsoft began building an AI supercomputer in 2019, and GPT-3 was trained on it

items.d: Bet where more compute pays off

n19|159.c: Open and closed models aren't rivals: good products mix several, picked for cost and quality.
n19|159.e: He rejects framing the industry as open source versus closed. Microsoft's Bing Chat, Microsoft 365 Copilot and GitHub Copilot all combine several models, chosen for cost, performance and quality. He sees no reason to stop building bigger models, yet he's excited by open-source work like Databricks' Dolly 2.0, which has 12 billion parameters and runs well on a single machine. His main worry about public models is whether they get used safely and responsibly. He also expects projects like RedPajama to produce stronger open models.
ex: Databricks' Dolly 2.0 has 12 billion parameters and runs on one machine

marks.d: Mix models by cost and quality

n19|159.c: Most AI value comes from copilots that help people work, and partners will build most of the apps.
n19|159.e: He thinks most of the value comes from AI helping people do their work while humans review the results, with GitHub Copilot as the first example. The Copilot stack he describes has an interaction layer, a plugin ecosystem, orchestration software like LangChain and Microsoft's open-source Semantic Kernel, meta-prompts, retrieval-augmented generation (looking things up before answering), and safety filters on both inputs and outputs. Businesses also need data privacy, clear visibility into where their data goes, and plugin switches they control. No company in history has built every useful thing on a platform by itself.

n19|159.c: Models aren't products, and the best openings are tasks that just went from impossible to merely hard.
n19|159.e: He says many people mistake models and infrastructure for the product, when you still have to work out what a great product on top looks like. The most interesting openings are tasks that used to be impossible and are now hard. Things that suddenly became easy tend to be trivial. He compares it to smartphones: early iPhone apps were mostly novelty toys, while lasting businesses like TikTok, Instagram, WhatsApp and DoorDash solved problems that weren't obvious. Sprinkling a bit of LLM magic on existing products only brings small, incremental gains.
ex: Lasting businesses: TikTok, Instagram, WhatsApp, DoorDash

d.verdict: Look for hard problems that just became possible

n19|159.c: AI's barriers to entry have collapsed, which could make one-on-one tutoring available to everyone.
n19|159.e: He wrote Reprogramming the American Dream for non-technical readers like the people of his rural Virginia hometown, hoping they won't fear AI and that its gains get shared more fairly. In 2003-04, a machine learning project took him piles of papers and six months of coding. Today a high schooler could do it in four hours over a weekend, and the cost of running models keeps falling. He thinks the media fixates on regulation and says too little about beneficial uses. Bloom's research shows one-on-one tutoring works remarkably well, and AI could make it widespread and cheap.
ex: Bloom's two-sigma finding: one-on-one tutoring has a dramatic effect
He cites Sal Khan's talk on AI tutoring

terms.d: Six months of work becomes four hours

n19|159.c: AI is a cognitive revolution, so demand for hands-on work like nursing and skilled trades will grow.
n19|159.e: He sees this wave as a leap in cognitive ability, while robotics hasn't caught up. So demand for surgeons, nurses, physical therapists, elder-care workers, electricians, mechanics and solar installers will keep growing, pushed higher by an aging population and grid upgrades. People still want humans at the center of the story: a forklift lifts more than any person, yet nobody watches forklift weightlifting. He admits there will be disruption, but people value doing things, and the predicted four-hour workweek never arrived. In his view, optimism and taking safety seriously can go together.
ex: Forklifts out-lift people, yet nobody watches forklift weightlifting
He thinks the US should respect skilled trades the way Germany does

root.d: A cognitive revolution; robots haven't caught up

items.d: Grid upgrades need electricians and installers

n20|163.c: Future defense depends on huge numbers of cheap systems, not a few expensive, exquisite platforms.
n20|163.e: He grants that the big defense contractors are good at building expensive high-end platforms, but he thinks the future belongs to large numbers of low-cost systems. The US relies on costly crewed systems like aircraft carriers, fighter jets and bombers, yet faces pilot shortages and recruiting shortfalls. The industrial base for nuclear submarines is shrinking and its workers are aging. On that model, the US can't outproduce China. Cheap systems only work with smart software, and Silicon Valley's best software talent has long avoided defense.
ex: Pilot shortages and recruiting shortfalls
The nuclear submarine industrial base is shrinking, and its skilled craft workers are aging

d.verdict: Numbers plus software win; exquisite platforms alone can't keep up

n20|163.c: You have to own both hardware and software, because governments buy complete capabilities, not parts.
n20|163.e: He argues a company must control both hardware and software to move the technology forward, because governments buy a complete capability that solves a problem: support, training, logistics, manufacturing, integration and security. Delivering that takes Anduril about 50 different skill sets. From day one the company built Lattice, software that tracks and makes sense of huge streams of sensor data, identifying tanks, ships, aircraft and people. Products started with base protection and border security, then grew into small autonomous drones, school-bus-sized unmanned submarines and counter-drone systems.
ex: The unmanned submarine is about the size of a school bus and runs for weeks
Delivering one capability takes about 50 different skill sets

terms.d: Fuses sensor data to identify targets

n20|163.c: Anduril targets urgent problems nobody is solving well, so work like counter-drone moves in months.
n20|163.e: He says Anduril picks problems that nobody is getting right and that are urgent. Cheap drones cost on the order of $100,000, far less than cruise missiles at over $1 million, and they've become a widespread threat. A counter-drone program can move in months instead of the decade a traditional program takes. Technically, there are only about five kinds of sensing, and the processing methods are highly general. The company doesn't do basic AI research. It applies state-of-the-art techniques and uses the fact that defense problems can be analyzed and simulated to predict results.
ex: Cheap drones cost around $100,000, while cruise missiles cost over $1 million
There are only about five kinds of sensing

n20|163.c: A person must answer for every lethal decision, so autonomy has to be predictable and expanded gradually.
n20|163.e: He says the US won't adopt systems that make lethal decisions on their own, and responsibility always rests with the person using the weapon. Operators must trust a system and know what it will do once switched on, so autonomy advances in a crawl, walk, run sequence. Reinforcement learning (training by trial and reward) and large language models are inherently unpredictable, so their behavior must be bounded and quantified. Autonomy should extend human agency with the right synthesized information. For long missions like a submarine's, the hard part is turning human intent into machine behavior that copes with surprises, with extremely high reliability.

n20|163.c: LLMs are useful for synthesizing intelligence and drafting plans, but defense can't tolerate hallucinations.
n20|163.e: He sees two main uses for large language models in defense. One is synthesizing huge volumes of text-based intelligence. The other is generative work, such as hooking into various APIs to draft mission plans, giving operators a draft that's about 95% usable for a human to revise, so a human stays in the loop. But intelligence can't contain hallucinations, because made-up intel is dangerous. The Defense Department cares intensely about operations and predictability, so generative creativity has limited value there. Cyber offense and defense is another possible use, and he expects a big wave of new applications within 18 to 24 months.
ex: Draft mission plans come out about 95% usable
He expects a wave of new applications within 18 to 24 months

items.d: A human stays in the loop

n20|163.c: Ukraine shows massed forces are easy to spot, and dispersed autonomous systems favor defending Taiwan.
n20|163.e: He notes that Russia never ran a traditional air campaign because the air-defense risk was too high. With commercial satellite imagery everywhere, massed troops have nowhere to hide, which pushes militaries toward small, dispersed, autonomous units. He thinks these lessons favor the defender and would make invading Taiwan very hard. Satellite constellations made possible by cheap launch, cheaper hypersonic missiles and drones could spare the US from putting carrier groups at risk. He estimates the change driven by cheap launch is only about 5% of the way along.
ex: The shift driven by cheap launch is only about 5% done

items.d: No need to risk carrier groups

n20|163.c: Silicon Valley hurts itself by shunning Washington, and defense startups must understand government from day one.
n20|163.e: He points out that HP, Cisco, Microsoft and Amazon all once worked closely with defense, and the internet itself grew out of DARPA funding. Anduril had a lobbying team from day one and hired former government staff to help it understand budgets drawn up years in advance, far slower than Silicon Valley moves. He thinks the Valley hurts itself by avoiding Washington while getting beaten up on encryption, AI and social media regulation. The war in Ukraine and China's military modernization have shifted the mood. Anduril says openly that it builds weapons and believes they can be developed ethically.
ex: About 1,600 employees, headquartered in Orange County, California
Orders can jump from 10 units a year to 5,000

n21|95.c: Generative AI is a new technical leap, not a continuation of old machine learning, and it's very early.
n21|95.e: They think many people treat generative AI as a continuation of a decade of convolutional and recurrent networks, and overstate the idea that whoever has the most data wins. In fact it's a jump to diffusion models and large language models that can chain reasoning, take actions and synthesize information. Few products have truly worked at scale yet. ChatGPT has been in public view for about six months and GPT-4 for about three, roughly one planning cycle at a big company. So the investor who met a hundred companies and concluded AI doesn't work for enterprises is calling it too early.
ex: ChatGPT is about six months old, GPT-4 about three
A growth-stage investor turned bearish after meeting about 100 companies

d.verdict: Too early to draw conclusions

n21|95.c: The industry is naive to rush toward regulation, and nuclear power's decades-long approval freeze shows why.
n21|95.e: They think tech leaders calling for regulation don't understand how it works. Expecting a panel of industry experts to write the rules is unrealistic. The more likely result is a new agency. Nuclear power is the cautionary tale: under the US approval process, almost no new reactor designs were approved for about 50 years, which blocked safer designs. Meanwhile France gets about 70% of its electricity from nuclear with few incidents. They also worry that issues like bias get bundled with existential risk, and that overregulation would undercut AI's potential to make healthcare and education fairer.
ex: Nuclear's share of power: about 20% in the US, 30% in Japan, 70% in France

items.d: Few new nuclear designs in about 50 years

n21|95.c: Context windows will keep growing, but using all that context efficiently is still hard.
n21|95.e: Context windows, the amount of text a model can take in at once, are growing fast, but they think headlines about two million tokens are overblown. Context always gets filled, and the cost of attention grows with the square of the length. At a developer hackathon Conviction ran, the Kubernetes documentation alone filled the window. The two disagree here. One thinks windows will be big enough within two years and is willing to bet on it. The other thinks efficiency is the key, and that ordering information, memory and data structures will still decide results.
ex: The Kubernetes docs alone can fill the window

items.d: Attention cost grows with length squared

n21|95.c: Big companies adding AI is expected, and how fast they ship is the real test of management.
n21|95.e: It's no surprise that Microsoft, Google and others are adding AI to their products. Building on someone else's platform has always been risky, as with Facebook games, G Suite and the Shopify ecosystem, yet Klaviyo still built a business worth hundreds of millions of dollars on Shopify. Founders should ask what happens when the incumbent adds this feature, and whether that takes one year or three. Incumbents vary widely. Salesforce often announces things that don't get widely adopted, Teams won through distribution, and Adobe shipped AI products surprisingly fast. Adoption speed is a good proxy for management quality.
ex: Klaviyo built a business worth hundreds of millions on Shopify
Incumbents may need 12 to 24 months to ship solid AI features

n21|95.c: AI could erode the integration advantage of ERP giants and open the door to fat startups.
n21|95.e: The edge held by Salesforce and ERP vendors, the makers of enterprise resource planning software like SAP, comes from dense integrations and product breadth. Deploying SAP often takes six months, much of it spent on consultants writing integrations. They think AI can generate connectors automatically, handle data transformations and even extract custom configurations for migration, sharply cutting implementation costs. That opens the door to "fat startups" like Rippling, Ashby and HubSpot that build broad suites from the start. Other ideas they like: triaging security alerts, root-cause analysis and postmortems for operations, and automatically recording economic events like payments in CRM and ERP systems.
ex: Deploying SAP takes about six months
Reference points: Rippling, Ashby, HubSpot

root.d: Decisions on top of company data

items.d: AI cuts integration costs to take on ERP

n22|171.c: AI makes writing code easy, so value shifts to understanding, running and fixing that code.
n22|171.e: He's bullish on the demand generative AI will create. More people will write more software and engineers will be more productive, so value moves from writing code to understanding, securing, running and fixing it, which is exactly what Datadog sells. AI training and inference workloads will also drive infrastructure usage and bring a whole set of new components. Because AI needs data that's digitized and in the cloud, it will speed up cloud migration. He isn't sure what the killer app is, and doubts chatbots are the long-term interface: starting your car shouldn't mean playing twenty questions.
ex: Starting your car shouldn't require a game of twenty questions

items.d: Writing code is no longer the bottleneck
Harder to understand, secure and fix

n22|171.c: LLMs turned nearly every developer into a model user, which is giving rise to LLMOps.
n22|171.e: He says Datadog used to watch MLOps from a distance, because its users were a small group of data scientists building their own tools. LLMs have made nearly every developer a user, and those developers care about using models reliably, not building them. Each new component, from API models to vector databases to self-hosted models on GPUs, needs monitoring of inputs and outputs, whether answers are right, and how components interact. Metrics, traces and logs still apply. Customers often prototype with a top API model, then keep open-source models around and route requests by cost.
ex: On narrow tasks, open-source models already match or beat closed ones

items: Relies on APIs and open models

d.verdict: A bigger user base sets off a surge in monitoring needs

n22|171.c: Statistical methods still beat LLMs at anomaly detection, while LLMs shine at combining information.
n22|171.e: He says Datadog deliberately avoids overhyping AI, worried that inflated expectations will disappoint customers. He doesn't think older methods will disappear. For spotting anomalies in metrics, statistical methods are still more accurate, and customers can't tolerate frequent false alarms. What LLMs open up is unstructured data that used to be out of reach, like knowledge bases, emails and wikis. They can also work like a calculator for language, combining results from several numerical models and metadata. Paste a stack trace into ChatGPT and the answer is often wrong. Add the runtime variables and it gets far more precise.
ex: A stack trace alone often gets wrong answers, but runtime variables make them precise

terms.d: A language calculator that combines info

n22|171.c: Automating production operations is still far off, because most companies look like old Rome, not highways.
n22|171.e: He expects more and more automation, but the industry isn't there yet. Even Google, with its huge scale and uniform environment, isn't highly automated. He uses a self-driving analogy: Google's systems are like a highway, while most companies look like the dense streets of downtown Rome. Troubleshooting production issues is hard and takes experts who often disagree. Generating images and text is easy because a person can spot mistakes at a glance. Debugging systems is much harder. He expects production use to start in about a year, with a clearer picture in a few years.

marks.d: Uniform, yet still not highly automated
Messy and varied, harder to automate

n22|171.c: A strong platform plus disciplined acquisitions took Datadog from one product to many.
n22|171.e: For six or seven years Datadog did only infrastructure monitoring, then expanded by following customers. When customers built their own application performance monitoring (APM) on Datadog, it built a real APM product. About half the engineers work on the core platform, half on products. Acquisitions buy a two-to-three-year head start. Datadog picks founders who want to keep building, asks for a joint launch within three months to build trust, then spends about a year moving onto the shared platform. In security, crowded with tools that work poorly, he wants to win through ubiquitous deployment and usage-based adoption, not top-down sales to security chiefs.
ex: About half the engineers work on the core platform
Joint launch within three months of a deal, full migration in about a year

items.d: One product for six or seven years

n23|174.c: Generative AI should let software answer the way people think, and even the search box is fair game.
n23|174.e: Instacart has used AI from the start and is essentially a search engine handling about a billion searches a quarter. To her, what generative AI changes is that users can ask questions in plain language. When people shop for groceries they think about budgets, dietary needs and menus, not keywords, and software should answer the way they think. She tells teams to start by asking which old problems can now be solved far better, not to build an AI roadmap for its own sake. Just as Facebook's mobile ads succeeded by riding the new News Feed format, Ask Instacart should let the search box take questions.
ex: About 1 billion searches a quarter
About 1 billion product replacements suggested so far

items: Users break down their own needs
Software answers the way people think

d.verdict: Start from old problems, not AI for AI's sake

n23|174.c: Instacart wants to be the layer linking bits and atoms, turning early intent into delivered groceries.
n23|174.e: ChatGPT plugins showed her that users arrive with intent that goes far beyond buying groceries, such as planning a birthday party. Instacart currently sits at the bottom of the funnel, and generative AI can help it capture intent much earlier. She's doing similar work with Bing and Bard, and plans to open the platform so apps such as nutrition apps can send food-related intent to Instacart. She believes the real advantage is LLMs combined with proprietary data, including the product catalog and billions of purchase data points.
ex: About 80,000 stores and more than 1,000 retailers
Delivery in about two hours

n23|174.c: Automated warehouses sit too far from customers to beat existing stores plus delivery on cost.
n23|174.e: She grants that if you rebuilt grocery from scratch, it might be fewer, highly automated dark stores that only serve delivery. But nobody is starting from scratch. Retailers have already paid the fixed costs of their stores, which sit close to customers, so Instacart orders are incremental demand on top and very efficient. Automated warehouses have to be built farther from customers, turning same-day delivery into next-day. That neither cuts costs nor improves the experience. Her rule: technology that improves neither cost nor experience won't spread widely anytime soon.

n23|174.c: Digital experiences inside physical stores will define the grocery industry over the next five years.
n23|174.e: She thinks grocery is going digital not just online but inside stores too. Caper, the smart cart Instacart acquired, uses computer vision to recognize items so shoppers can check out right in the cart. Its screen can also suggest items that go together, point to where things are, and show deals and budgets. Her data shows omnichannel customers, who shop both online and in store, are worth more than single-channel ones. Ads will get more personalized, with generative AI producing many creative variations. Conversational interfaces reveal clearer intent, which makes them a natural home for sponsored results.
ex: Deployed at Kroger, Sobeys and Wakefern
Omnichannel customers are worth more than single-channel ones

n23|174.c: AI in healthcare is stuck on clinical adoption, and AI-discovered drugs still have to prove they work better.
n23|174.e: About three years ago she was diagnosed with a chronic illness and learned that new research takes about 14 years to change clinical practice. So she co-founded Metrodora with a doctor and a scientist, combining clinical care with research. She's excited about AI finding patterns people can't see in clinical genomics, pathology and immune analysis. But doctors don't have time to read new literature, so AI has to be built into clinical workflows and verify its sources. She also wants evidence that AI-discovered drugs succeed more often in trials, and she opposes halting AI over speculative risks.
ex: New research takes about 14 years to reach clinical practice

n24|176.c: Organizations naturally slacken, so leaders must raise the pace and the bar in every interaction.
n24|176.e: He believes people naturally slow down when nobody is pushing, so leaders have to raise the pace, urgency, intensity and standards in every meeting, every message and every interaction. Many CEOs hire good people and wait for results. He argues for confronting conflict head-on, even though it goes against most people's instincts. One founder he mentions had the CFO carry out layoffs and stayed home that day. High standards push out people who don't fit, which strengthens the culture. There's no universally good culture. Culture should serve the company's specific mission.
ex: One employee quit after two weeks because the pace was too fast
He eliminated customer success departments at the companies he ran

n24|176.c: Snowflake is a database rewritten for the cloud, not an old engine moved onto it.
n24|176.e: He says Snowflake's two French founders were Oracle architects who never set out to build a traditional data warehouse, and the system handled semi-structured data from day one. They rewrote database management for cloud computing instead of porting an existing engine. Storage and compute are separate and scale independently. Clusters are stateless, so many jobs run at once without queuing. Billing went from per node and per hour down to per second. He rejects the data warehouse label, which he sees as just one kind of workload.
ex: Workloads are moving over from Teradata, Hadoop and Oracle

d.verdict: Architecture sets flexibility and cost

n24|176.c: Compute should go to the data, instead of copying data out to every application.
n24|176.e: He thinks handing data out to every application creates silos, and silos lock up the data's value. He warns bank CEOs not to rebuild silos in the cloud, or their data science teams will suffer. Data management also has to reach beyond the company: a hedge fund may take in hundreds of outside data feeds, so a data cloud can't live on just one public cloud. Applications should run inside the platform's governance boundary rather than pulling data out, which is what Snowpark and the native app framework are for. Software vendors shouldn't keep building their own data containers.
ex: A hedge fund takes in hundreds of data feeds
Blue Yonder moved its supply chain system onto Snowflake

items.d: Data shared across clouds and companies

n24|176.c: Natural language is the last mile of using data, but business questions still need business-specific models.
n24|176.e: He sees large language models as fundamentally about language. Natural-language queries continue SQL's original promise of letting non-experts benefit from data. But generated content is good for planning a trip, while companies need answers grounded in their own structured data. An insurer wants to know why personal injury claims in Florida spiked, whether it will happen again and how to adjust pricing. A language model alone can't answer that. It takes models built for the business, such as car insurers using telematics data to set prices, which both cut rates and raised profits.
ex: Why did personal injury claims in Florida spike?
Geico and Progressive price policies using telematics data

result.d: Like why claims spiked and what to do

n24|176.c: Search and chat will merge, and governed, trustworthy data is a precondition for enterprise AI.
n24|176.e: He says traditional search matches keywords without context, so it can't tell Snowflake the company from a snowflake in the weather. Adding context and enrichment turns ordinary data into data with predictive value. Snowflake bought Neeva for search, and he expects search and chat to merge into one conversation. It bought Streamlit so business users can work with Python models interactively, and spent about two years making its Python environment leak-proof. An ungoverned data lake is a landfill, and chief data officers should be responsible for publishing trusted data products.
ex: About two years to make the Python environment leak-proof
BI dashboards will remain, while Q&A suits ad hoc questions

items.d: Published by the chief data officer

n24|176.c: Usage-based pricing is fairer than subscriptions, even though growth looks worse right away in a downturn.
n24|176.e: He dislikes contracts that lock customers in, seeing it as unfair to make them pay for idle seats and wait for renewal. With usage-based pricing, customers pay only for what they use and can cut spending in real time by adjusting compute, how often jobs run and how long data is kept. The cost is that growth takes an immediate hit: investors love the model in good times and hate it in bad ones. He avoids mass layoffs in favor of constant pruning. He treats downturns as normal, says to lean into them, and advises startups to run toward their fundraising milestones.
ex: A bank CIO said the bank grew 3% while Snowflake grew 22%

cells.d: Customers cut spending in real time

n25|186.c: Video generation can be learned in parts: appearance from image-text data, motion from unlabeled video.
n25|186.e: Paired image-text data already teaches a model what things look like and how people describe them, so video only needs to add how things move. That means less to learn. The rich range of subjects in image datasets, like dragons and unicorns, carries over for free. And there's no need for scarce paired video-text data. In practice, the team started from a pretrained image model and trained it to keep frames consistent over time.
ex: A flying corgi combines the motion of flight with a corgi's look
She stresses big models are hard to interpret, so this is intuition, not proof

n25|186.c: Video won't simply follow the progress curve of images and text, and current methods may be missing something.
n25|186.e: Nearly a year after Make-A-Video came out, the field has improved resolution and quality but hasn't seen the kind of leap images did. Today's results are essentially moving pictures: a few seconds long, with the same objects throughout and no scene transitions. Telling complex stories needs longer videos, consistency across shots and some kind of memory. So she suspects video is harder than people assume when they extrapolate from images.
ex: Make-A-Video produces clips of about four seconds
Nine months to a year after release, still no major leap

items.d: Objects enter and exit, transitions, memory

n25|186.c: Video is stuck on four things: infrastructure, representation, model architecture and the data recipe.
n25|186.e: Video files are big, so storing, processing and generating them is expensive, which slows iteration. Neighboring frames are highly redundant, yet models mostly treat them as separate images, so an efficient representation is missing. Long videos and scene transitions are extremely high-dimensional and may need hierarchical structures and memory. The community also knows far less about cleaning video data than text or images. Clips that are too short or static teach no motion, and ones too long or complex can't be learned. She leans toward curriculum training, from easy to hard, but the recipe isn't settled.
ex: Video understanding has long lagged image understanding in computer vision too

items.d: Costly storage and processing slow iteration

n25|186.c: To become creative tools, generative models must go beyond text prompts to multimodal inputs and targeted edits.
n25|186.e: Text prompts are a step up from random sampling, but users can still only accept a result or regenerate, rewriting prompts again and again. She wants to set the composition with a sketch, use reference images, audio or short clips as inputs, and tell the model to change just one spot, all through an intuitive interface. She expects quality to mature before control does. And richer combinations of inputs can actually open up unexpected creative space.
ex: Runway and others already offer video stylization edits
Text-to-audio can only produce a few seconds to tens of seconds

items: Hard to say exactly what you want
Sketches, reference images, audio as input
Point to the part to change

d.verdict: More control opens more creative room

n25|186.c: AI-generated content will flood social networks, and its social impact is underestimated.
n25|186.e: She says she isn't a product person, but expects personalized GIFs, short animations and marketing material to come first, along with uses nobody expects. Just as Instagram and TikTok lowered the bar so ordinary people could create, generative models will let millions of non-professionals express themselves. Some artists already treat AI as a medium or collaborator. AI agents might even become part of the social graph.
ex: Lensa drew tens of millions of users sharing AI avatars
Sofia Crespo and Scott Eaton use AI as their artistic medium

marks.d: Realize the exact image in mind

n26|189.c: Work backward from the customer's problem and make forward deployed engineers own real outcomes.
n26|189.e: As Palantir's 13th employee, he led the creation of the forward deployed engineer (FDE), a role that blends product, customer success and engineering. The idea came from an analogy by Alex Karp, Palantir's CEO: a great restaurant's waiters understand the kitchen. The measure isn't whether the software meets spec, but whether the customer is actually better off today. Back then cloud infrastructure was immature, so the company had to own most of the tech stack itself to guarantee results.
ex: Palantir's 13th employee and its first business hire
Apollo delivers about 550 microservices autonomously on air-gapped networks

items.d: Start from needs in the field
Build it when the cloud falls short

n26|189.c: What LLMs lack is an ontology, and packing a company's meaning into context makes them reliable.
n26|189.e: Foundry manages data like code and feeds it into an ontology: a semantic layer that captures both the nouns and the verbs of a business and can write back to transactional systems like SAP. He thinks LLMs are good at non-algorithmic reasoning but bad at things like orbital simulation or inventory forecasting, so they need tools. The ontology supplies those tools and packs the company's context into the model's window, grounding the model without changing it.
ex: Customers launched inventory allocation and claims adjudication copilots within weeks
Palantir decided to bet heavily on AIP last Q4

items.d: Business nouns and verbs, with write-back

n26|189.c: LLMs are statistics, not calculus, so you tame them with evals, telemetry and ensembles of models.
n26|189.e: Engineers used to traditional code often assume LLMs are deterministic, so they get dazzled at first and then hit sudden failures. He argues for replacing unit tests with evals over many runs, and using telemetry and traces as health checks in production. Pick use cases where being right pays off a lot and being wrong does no harm. Treat the model as a slightly mad genius, and run several models to compare where they agree and disagree.
ex: An internal tool routes tasks to several models and compares outputs and latency
Classified networks can't use GPT-4, only open-source models

d.verdict: Treat LLMs as statistics, not calculus

n26|189.c: Chat is a limited interface, so models should return structured output that directly updates application state.
n26|189.e: He thinks prompts are ultimately for developers and shouldn't leak into the user experience. The ideal pattern is current state plus user intent equals new state: the model returns a DSL or JSON, the system uses it to update the map, the resource table or another view, and the user approves with one click. Replacing parts of the interface with language makes development much faster and lets users handle last-mile customization.
ex: An evacuation plan generated automatically from a war-planning document
A feature scoped at two people for two months took one engineer a few hours

result.d: Structured output, approved in one click

n26|189.c: Companies run on state machines, so skip autonomous agents and start human-AI teaming with one state transition.
n26|189.e: He mostly avoids the word agent because it implies autonomous planning, while companies actually run on explicit or implicit state machines, where work moves from one defined step to the next. The safer path is to give AI the context, permissions and guardrails for one piece of the state machine, start with a single transition, assign a human owner to each step, and build trust through logs. In hospital operations, that means moving from pushing alerts to pushing proposed plans for approval, with clinical decisions staying with doctors.
ex: Healthcare is about a third of Palantir's business
He compares it to Tesla's step-by-step path to self-driving

n27|193.c: Data matters more than models, so ML practitioners should own data collection themselves.
n27|193.e: In grad school, his papers often improved accuracy by just two points, not far above the baseline of always guessing the most common answer, and he doubted the results were reliable. Later, working on multilingual search ranking at Yahoo, he saw the same model perform very differently across countries, depending on how carefully the training data had been collected. That convinced him it doesn't work to write requirements in long documents nobody reads and hand them to a labeling team.
ex: Accuracy rose from 68% to 70%, against a baseline of about 64%
Yahoo's ranking moved from hand-tuned weights to machine learning

items.d: Always guess the most common answer

n27|193.c: Machine learning adoption comes in jumps driven by new technology and new markets, not smooth growth.
n27|193.e: His first company, Figure Eight, did data labeling. Early on it had only a few big customers and couldn't find a second market, so it stalled for years. Expansions the board pushed, aimed at crossing the chasm into the mainstream market, all failed. Only when self-driving cars created huge labeling demand did revenue take off again, and then Scale AI won that market. He sold the company and later somewhat regretted not holding on longer.
ex: Early customers included eBay, Google and Bloomberg
Competitors went under one after another, yet the market stayed small

n27|193.c: Researchers aren't software engineers, so simplicity matters more than power in ML tools.
n27|193.e: He compares bad tools to painting with a lousy brush. For researchers, Docker and Git are too complex, and versioning data in Git is even more painful. Many early MLOps companies were rebranded DevOps teams who thought Kubernetes was easy and didn't understand ordinary developers. They often sold big deals to executives and got stuck in a model that couldn't grow through self-serve adoption. W&B stayed developer-first, and its founders are themselves the target users.
ex: The core product is experiment tracking, extended to data versioning and a model registry
Being closed source lets them see click data to cut features and set defaults

n27|193.c: LLMs let prompts replace training, the first real existential threat to W&B's core business.
n27|193.e: Tasks like sentiment analysis and entity extraction used to require training a model. Now you can just ask an LLM. He thinks customers are rational, and most have switched to GPT, yet at first the board couldn't see the danger in the metrics. So the company made LLM tooling its top priority. He also notes that few companies have LLMs in production. Big enterprises plan on roughly six-month cycles, so wide deployment is still a year or two away.
ex: He estimates about 95% of people use GPT for these tasks
Early adopters are tech-savvy companies like Notion and Zapier

n27|193.c: Founders should care more about user needs than they think, and less about outside metrics like ARR.
n27|193.e: For his second company, he first picked a type of customer he genuinely liked, which kept the team focused. He's competitive and loves numbers, but found that chasing ARR and user growth hurt the product and long-term growth. He's skeptical when people claim to do lots of customer interviews, since even booking three calls a week is hard. So every call needs sharp questions that force customers to say whether the product really works for them.
ex: He thinks booking three customer calls a week is already hard

root.d: More confident than the first time

items.d: High ARR doesn't mean a good product

n28|95.c: The GPU shortage comes from concentrated supply and manufacturing bottlenecks, and demand will keep rising.
n28|95.e: Nvidia dominates high-end chips for training and inference, and it depends on a handful of foundries like TSMC. A new fab costs billions of dollars, yields depend on a huge number of variables such as temperature, pressure and chemical concentrations, and packaging equipment is another bottleneck. Meanwhile, many companies decided they needed AI compute at the same moment, and inference demand will keep growing.
ex: Big cloud providers' GPUs are reportedly sold out until next April
Microsoft is buying from other providers to cover short-term demand

n28|95.c: Compute scarcity creates new businesses and makes overlooked efficiency research valuable again.
n28|95.e: The shortage sets off a chain reaction. GPU clouds and aggregators like CoreWeave are springing up, renting crypto-mining GPUs to AI companies pays better when crypto prices are low, and AI chip startups are winning orders. The industry had been racing down the Chinchilla-style scaling path, growing models and data together, and efficiency research was undervalued. When compute is constrained, methods like routing queries between models, distillation into smaller models and selecting training data matter more.
ex: Cerebras signed with the UAE's G42 to build nine supercomputers
FrugalGPT-style routing sends each query to a cheaper model

items.d: Pays off when crypto is down

n28|95.c: Big companies' AI products will take one to two years to launch at scale, and revenue ramps then.
n28|95.e: Transformers bring entirely new capabilities, not an extension of older architectures. Right now the users are mainly AI-native companies, a few early adopters and the first wave of startups. Big enterprises plan on six-to-nine-month cycles, then spend about a year on prototypes before launch, so scaled deployment is one to two years out. ChatGPT was just the starting gun, and most activity so far is still demos.
ex: Early adopters: Notion, Zapier
First-wave startups: Perplexity, Harvey, Character

n28|95.c: Agents should first delight a few people on a narrow task, then expand into general platforms.
n28|95.e: Agents are systems where a model plans and calls tools to finish tasks on its own, and both general and specialized ones will exist. But historically, winners mostly started with one or two things done extremely well. Facebook began with just a few colleges. Many founders pitch agents that will make you happy, which is hard to deliver. Narrow tasks like fixing bugs across a whole codebase, paired with test-time search that can be checked by running the code, are easier to crack.
ex: Agent examples include Inflection, MultiOn and Harvey
One host: happiness is never writing boilerplate code again

items: Vague goals, like making you happy
One or two things done extremely well

d.verdict: Start narrow, then grow into a platform

n28|95.c: About a third of 2021's non-AI unicorns will fail, and the real problem is their cash burn.
n28|95.e: The hosts split 2021's late-stage non-AI companies into thirds: about a third will fail or sell cheaply, a third will stall at their peak valuation and a third will surpass it. As cash runs out, 2024 and 2025 will be bumpy, with knock-on effects on hiring, commercial real estate and venture fundraising. One host advises founders to let go of their old valuations. The other worries more about models that spend over $100 million to generate a few million in revenue.
ex: Public tech stocks fell 30% to 90% over the past 18 months
Burning $50-100 million to reach only $5-10 million in revenue

items.d: Another third stall at the peak

n29|200.c: Moving classes forward by age piles up knowledge gaps, and mastery learning is how you fill them.
n29|200.e: Tutoring his cousins, he found students usually got stuck not because the current material was hard, but because of gaps in earlier skills like decimals or exponents. Traditional schools group kids by age and push them forward whether or not they've mastered the material, so gaps pile up layer by layer and eventually turn into tracking. He borrows Bloom's idea of mastery learning: learn it before moving on, with instant feedback and hints.
ex: Bloom found one-on-one tutoring improves results by about two standard deviations
A seventh grader understood exponents but needed a calculator for 3×7

n29|200.c: Personalized practice plus human interaction can move students ahead 1.5 to 2 grade levels a year.
n29|200.e: Khan Lab School started on the ground floor of the office and now covers kindergarten through 12th grade. He also co-founded an online school with Arizona State University built around daily Socratic seminars, discussions where teachers guide students through questions. He says lab school students consistently advance at least 1.5 to 2 grade levels a year, versus about 0.7 at traditional schools. A school district in Newark adopted Khan Academy at scale even before generative AI arrived.
ex: Steve Levitt's analysis: students learn 3 to 4 times faster
About 6,000 students in Newark's North Ward, roughly 70% using it effectively

n29|200.c: Khanmigo is meant to be a Socratic tutor, with guardrails so AI guides thinking instead of doing the work.
n29|200.e: OpenAI approached him in late summer 2022. He saw GPT-4 explain AP Biology questions and write new ones, but also make math errors and hallucinate. In the product, the system prompt tells the AI not to give answers, only to ask guiding questions. Parents and teachers can see minors' conversations. Another AI monitors chats and alerts an adult if a student seems to be in trouble. An integration with Canvas also records the writing process, answering worries about cheating.
ex: Bill Gates used the AP Biology exam as a test challenge
Students can talk with fictional or historical figures like Don Quixote

n29|200.c: AI will help teachers first, and within three to five years every student will have an AI tutor.
n29|200.e: He expects AI to be a substantial supplement for the next year or two, with teachers benefiting first. Lesson plans, rubrics, grading and feedback take about half their time. Within five years nearly every teacher will use AI, possibly by the end of next year. The cheating crisis will force schools to find solutions. Within three to five years, AI tutors with memory that can talk by voice or even video will become mainstream.
ex: Inspired by the Young Lady's Illustrated Primer in The Diamond Age
He imagines an AI tutor someday writing a student's college recommendation

n29|200.c: Pricey middle-tier colleges with weak returns are most at risk, and schools should share responsibility for student debt.
n29|200.e: He doesn't think generative AI has fundamentally changed trends already under way in higher education. Elite universities essentially sell status and networks. Community colleges are cheap and flexible, good for stacking credentials. The riskiest are middle-tier schools that charge a lot but deliver mediocre returns. If colleges had to carry part of their students' loans, their career services and choice of majors would change right away. He also supports skills credentials that employers recognize.
ex: Middle-tier colleges cost about $60,000 a year with room and board
A pilot with Howard University lets high schoolers earn credit through mastery

n29|200.c: The AI era demands stronger basics in reading, writing, math and coding, as people become architects and editors.
n29|200.e: He compares it to the camera: photography didn't kill painting, it freed painters. Once everyone has an AI assistant, work will look more like being an architect, editor or manager, which takes deeper skills, not shallower ones. Basics like knowing multiplication tables and historical dates are what let people use AI well, and he rejects the idea that you can just look things up. He also values human connection and started a separate free platform for live tutoring by volunteers.
ex: About 10,000 people a month join tutoring on Schoolhouse.world

n30|206.c: Transformers won because they ran well on the chips of the day, not because of theory.
n30|206.e: His starting point is that language has structure. You don't have to read strictly left to right; you can process pieces in parallel and combine them. Attention compares every pair of words, which costs more as text gets longer, but that kind of math happened to suit the parallel accelerators of the time. The real difference from earlier, similar methods was not the idea but an implementation that fit the hardware. So he sees efficiency and engineering as the core. He adds that researchers staying optimistic through years of failure, and the field's energy compounding once something works, mattered just as much.
ex: Earlier "decomposable attention" had a similar idea but lost on implementation

items.d: No need to read in order

n30|206.c: GPUs weren't built for Transformers, so hardware and model design should be explored together.
n30|206.e: His reasoning is simple: GPUs were not designed with Transformers in mind, so there is no reason to think they strike the best balance of memory bandwidth, parallelism, and latency for them. Hardware and architecture evolve together like chicken and egg. New accelerators are already bending to fit Transformers. He expects that trying several hardware-and-model combinations would find better options fairly quickly, and that architectures might even get simpler as a result.
ex: Mixer, a vision model built only from simple layers, matches vision Transformers

n30|206.c: Models should spend compute based on how hard a problem is, not how long the text is.
n30|206.e: He points out that today's models spend compute in proportion to the length of the input and output, with no regard for how hard the problem is. A hard problem with a short answer, like factoring a large number into primes, gets very little compute. Meanwhile, a long-winded question about simple addition burns a lot of it for nothing. He wants models to decide for themselves how much effort to spend at inference time. Attempts like adaptive depth have not caught on yet, which he attributes to results not being good enough rather than the direction being wrong.
ex: Asking GPT-4 "what is 2+2" in a long-winded way wastes compute
Searching over answers like a compiler checking code works, but is a "patch"

n30|206.c: Biology doesn't need the mechanism first; deep learning can treat the cell as a black box.
n30|206.e: He argues that biology has neither a complete list of mechanisms nor many theories that predict anything, and full understanding is not coming soon. But given enough observed inputs and outcomes, deep learning can learn the pattern without the mechanism, and AlphaFold 2 has already shown this works. Aspirin and metformin were used for years before anyone understood how they worked. So he thinks regulators who demand a proven mechanism first may be wasting time and money. The real test should be whether a treatment works and how its benefits weigh against its harms.
ex: AlphaFold 2 proved the black-box approach works
Aspirin and metformin were used long before their mechanisms were understood

n30|206.c: mRNA is biology's bytecode: today it can only "print" one protein, but it could run programs.
n30|206.e: He compares today's mRNA vaccines to a program with a single line: print this protein. But RNA can do more. Riboswitches change shape in response to nearby molecules, which works like an if-then condition, and self-amplifying RNA copies itself, which works like a loop. The number of possible variants of a single antigen is far too large to screen one by one, so the only option is to generate designs with a model. Inceptive's lab can synthesize almost any RNA to produce training data, and the model and wet-lab experiments feed back into each other in tight loops.
ex: A single antigen has roughly 10 to the 60th power possible variants
He says RNA production could reach 6 to 8 billion doses within two years

n31|209.c: Foundation models are "cloud 2.0," and the value comes from redesigning products around AI, not bolting on features.
n31|209.e: He sees foundation models as a new layer of cloud. Just as SaaS companies were built on AWS and Snowflake, AI-native companies will be built on top of models. He's against sprinkling in bits of AI just to check a box. Instead, teams should treat AI as a design input and rethink the problem from scratch. You don't need to train or fine-tune a model to build a great product. Vercel's AI SDK lets developers plug into multiple model providers without changing their backend.
ex: Jenny.ai grew annual recurring revenue from $1 million to $1.5 million in two months
The RoomGPT template uses image generation to redesign rooms

items.d: Designed around AI from the start
One interface to many model providers

n31|209.c: AI apps are slow and expensive, so they need new infrastructure for streaming, abuse prevention and caching.
n31|209.e: Traditional backends aim to respond within 100 milliseconds, but an AI model can take ten-plus seconds to finish "thinking." That calls for long-running streaming from edge functions, servers that sit close to users. Many apps leave their AI keys exposed on the public internet, and scrapers and bots grab the "free intelligence." He says every customer running AI at scale has hit this. Vercel offers rate limiting, bot detection and response caching, and he expects the AI-versus-AI arms race to escalate.
ex: OpenAI is the most common backend among Vercel customers, per anonymized telemetry

n31|209.c: Google is no longer the only front door, and answer engines will reshape SEO, crawling and content licensing.
n31|209.e: With real-time answer engines like Perplexity on the rise, customers started asking him whether Google is still king and whether the old SEO rules still apply. Google doesn't open its index and Bing is expensive, so more companies build their own crawlers. They rely on pre-training for breadth, then layer fresh vertical indexes on top. Traffic is highly concentrated, so crawling the top sites covers most usage. He predicts APIs will become a two-way stream of content plus citations.
ex: The top 1,000 websites account for roughly half of all page views
Phind (developer search) and Casetext (legal) build vertical indexes

n31|209.c: AI-generated interfaces will replace the blank canvas, and taste becomes the frontend engineer's core skill.
n31|209.e: He calls "a new frontend framework every week" a myth. The data shows React, Svelte and Vue are all stable, and big companies mostly use React. Where AI really lands is generating code and UI. Like Midjourney, it can offer a good-looking starting point while avoiding the sameness that templates create. Product engineers will shift toward exercising taste and iterating on prompts, and they'll do it inside the tools they already use.
ex: Templates produced look-alike websites full of purple gradients
GitHub Copilot won by fitting into developers' existing editors

n31|209.c: AI makes copy-paste easy, so code may swing back from third-party packages to code you own.
n31|209.e: Dependencies bring supply-chain risk and surprises, while AI makes copying and pasting code painless. The UI world already works this way. He agrees that copy-paste beats a bad abstraction and thinks over-abstracted codebases are the worst. Code you own is easier to audit, and AI security assistants can flag memory bugs in real time. He also notes GPT-4 is strongest in JavaScript and Python, which have lots of training data, while HTML's redundant closing tags waste tokens.
ex: shadcn/ui has you copy code instead of installing a dependency
Vercel built Turborepo to support monorepos

n32|212.c: They bet AI workloads would choke on memory bandwidth and work-splitting, so they built wafer-scale chips.
n32|212.e: In late 2015, a group of former colleagues concluded that AI workloads would become enormous, and the hard parts would be memory bandwidth and splitting work across many small machines. Rather than make incremental improvements, they bet on a technology that had never worked before: turning an entire silicon wafer into one chip the size of a dinner plate. He says it's his fifth startup and the first time he underestimated the market. The architecture was locked in before the Transformer appeared.
ex: Their 2015 pitch deck already named slow training as the top problem
Eight pitches produced eight term sheets

n32|212.c: A dataflow design puts memory next to compute and parameters off-chip, so simple data parallelism scales linearly.
n32|212.e: The chip is made of many identical units, each with its own processor and memory just one clock cycle away, and a unit computes only when data arrives. Lots of on-chip SRAM removes the bandwidth bottleneck and lets the chip exploit sparsity, skipping work on zeros. Parameters live off-chip and stream in, so memory and compute can be sized as needed. The system uses only data parallelism, which avoids the months of model-parallel engineering that GPUs require.
ex: About 850,000 identical compute units
He says a 64-node cluster scales linearly

n32|212.c: Benchmarks can be gamed; the real metric is how long a customer takes to go from model to trained.
n32|212.e: He doesn't trust standard benchmarks. At AMD he had about 30 people tuning for them, and his CTO's team at Sun had 70. What matters is how long it takes customers to train their own model, including the hyperparameter sweeps. Training open-source models is another kind of demo: when others released one model, Cerebras released seven at once, because distributing work on its system is simple.
ex: One customer trained on GPUs for 60 days without converging, then converged after switching
Open-sourced the 3B-parameter BTLM and helped build an open Arabic model

n32|212.c: A chip company is about 75% software, and hardware mistakes are costly, so don't build circuits for one model.
n32|212.e: A first chip takes two to three years and $50–60 million, and customer feedback arrives late. One hardware bug can cost $20–30 million to re-spin the chip, so each designer needs several verification engineers. Cerebras's compiler stack lets PyTorch users work with it the way they would with GPUs. The company skips Transformer-specific circuits, which would sit idle on other models, and focuses instead on the sparse linear algebra underneath every model.
ex: A first chip takes 2–3 years and $50–60 million
One hardware bug can cost $20–30 million

d.verdict: The chip is the muscle, software is the brain

n32|212.c: GPU shortages stem from rigid foundry supply, and companies with unique data will train their own smaller models.
n32|212.e: He blames the shortage on TSMC's inflexible supply chain. Fabs cost a fortune and take six to eight months to adjust capacity, so even Nvidia forecast wrong. He thinks demand will be many times larger in two or three years. Running big models is expensive, so many companies will stop at 3B to 13B parameters. He disagrees that training will concentrate in a few labs. Any company with unique data will get in, because data is the new gold.
ex: Running a 175B model costs about 17.5 times as much as a 10B model
Fabs need 6–8 months to adjust capacity

result.d: Training isn't just for big labs

n33|216.c: Once an AI has an on-chain account it becomes an economic actor, and AIs could someday run organizations.
n33|216.e: NEAR started out trying to teach machines to code and moved to blockchain only to pay students in countries with poor access to banking. He sees language models as the first machines that can talk directly with people, and with an account they can pay humans or other AIs. He imagines an AI "CEO" pushing a mission in the direction a community sets, cutting out layers of middle management. DAOs, organizations run by on-chain rules and votes, would come first because their coordination work is already repetitive.
ex: An AI could coordinate cancer research, picking labs and allocating funds
He has heard people accept feedback more readily from an AI

items.d: AI can pay and get paid

n33|216.c: The real alignment problem is people, and AI amplifies a misinformation problem society never solved.
n33|216.e: He thinks the harm comes from the people using the tools, so what's needed is human alignment. Seen through Byzantine fault tolerance, the study of systems that keep working when some participants lie, society has never systematically defended against large-scale misinformation, and AI amplifies it sharply. He expects 2024 to bring a flood of fake or per-visitor tailored political content. Law enforcement will struggle to tell real audio and video from fake, and voice-cloning scams will become a major consumer fraud problem.
ex: About 30 seconds of audio is enough to clone a voice for scam calls
Expect web pages that tailor a candidate's message to each visitor

n33|216.c: Cryptographic signatures, device security chips and trust networks can give content a "green lock" of authenticity.
n33|216.e: Web3 already offers ready-made building blocks. A phone's secure chip can sign a photo the moment it's taken, recording time, place and edit history. Tie that signature to a real identity and reputation, and content can show something like the browser's SSL green lock, telling you it came from someone you trust. Phones already have face ID and secure chips, so what's missing is the product layer. A NEAR account can hold multiple keys with different permissions, which can be delegated to an agent and later revoked.
ex: He finds using Social Security numbers as secret IDs absurd
Like SSL, it needs critical mass before it becomes the default

items.d: Shows when it's from your trust circle
Signature tied to a real person
Time, place and edit history attached
Signs at the moment of capture

n33|216.c: Decentralized training isn't realistic yet, but inference and data labeling suit decentralized marketplaces.
n33|216.e: Training clusters need extremely fast links between GPUs, far beyond ordinary internet connections, and old crypto-mining cards are bad at the math AI needs. Inference is different: demand is huge, the same model can run anywhere, and techniques like multi-party computation and zero-knowledge proofs can protect privacy. A labeling marketplace spares workers worldwide the hassle of setting up companies and payroll. Escrow guarantees payment by the rules, while honeypot questions, staking and cross-checking keep quality up.
ex: Training needs about 800 Gbps links; 100 Mbps won't work
Sweatcoin, with about 120 million installs, is moving to NEAR

d.verdict: Web3 is good at creating marketplaces

n33|216.c: Most SaaS is a database with a custom UI; users will own the data and UIs will be generated.
n33|216.e: CRM, recruiting, marketing and project management tools share much the same underlying data model, yet connecting them is expensive and brittle. He imagines users owning their data, with interfaces generated from shared components or natural-language descriptions, and different dashboards for different roles. On models, he thinks the Transformer will be hard to dislodge. Progress will come from letting models "think" before they answer and learn to correct themselves.
ex: Same workflow: marketing watches conversion, someone else watches retention
Transformers and GPUs are locked together, much like Wintel once was

terms.d: Built from components or plain language

n34|220.c: AI coding is in its demo era; the opportunity is around the model: context, tools and agents.
n34|220.e: He sees today's AI coding tools as primitive, with the models' potential far from tapped. The gaps are around the model: better context, and the ability to read files, install dependencies, run code, browse the web and even write whole features. He also suggests training models on execution results and runtime behavior so they learn semantics, not just syntax. Even if model capability stayed flat, basic agent experiences are about a year away.
ex: A 2012 paper, "On the Naturalness of Software," showed code can be modeled like language
He estimates a "build me a login page" agent is 6–18 months away

items.d: Debugging, deploying, turning requirements into code

n34|220.c: AI helps beginners first, but eventually programmers will review AI-written code like engineering managers.
n34|220.e: Replit's internal research shows AI raises productivity 30–50% in the coding step itself, and beginners benefit most today. Once AI covers the whole chain, from debugging and deploying to meetings and turning requirements into code, professional programmers will see gains of several times. He expects that within three to five years, software development will mostly mean reviewing and directing code that AI writes.
ex: A founder with no coding background built a product earning about $250,000 a year within months

n34|220.c: Replit's edge isn't the size of its user data but the full loop from first line to deployment.
n34|220.e: People often stress the value of data from Replit's 20-million-plus users, but he thinks that's easy to overrate. The real advantage is an end-to-end platform: writing the first line of code, running, deploying, then production crashes and fixes all happen in one place. Usually those steps are scattered across several tools. The loop yields execution feedback plus something the industry lacks: data pairing a complete requirement with the code that fulfills it.
ex: The usual workflow is spread across GitHub, VS Code and AWS

n34|220.c: Train your own model only if the product needs it; 3B parameters is the sweet spot for code completion.
n34|220.e: Commercial APIs were expensive, slow and shifting toward chat-only interfaces, which made code completion hard, so Replit trained its own model. The team found 1B parameters too weak and anything larger too costly and slow, with about 3B just right. Following Chinchilla and LLaMA, they trained a small model for longer and added their own data, which improved results markedly. They open-sourced the base model to give back. He opposes training models for benchmarks and says to start from the use case.
ex: Adding Replit's own data beat the open-source version by about 50%

marks.d: Sweet spot for quality and cost

n34|220.c: Open-source AI is short on talent, not money, and needs new corporate backers if Meta steps back.
n34|220.e: In early 2022 he worried that only big companies could build products on commercial APIs, and he urged Zuckerberg to open-source a large model. He thinks money isn't scarce. What's scarce is talent and the nerve to release, since safety worries keep many companies away from open models. Linux, too, had IBM behind it. He also calls GitHub stars a fake currency and wants bounties and a native currency to make open source sustainable, even letting AIs take paid jobs.
ex: A prototype or MVP on Replit can cost as little as $50–100
The bounty market lets developers in places like India and Serbia earn money

n35|224.c: DNA is like code, but cells aren't chips; bioengineering means reverse-engineering a system nobody designed.
n35|224.e: DNA is like bits on a tape, but it's a physical polymer. Proteins behave like nanomachines bumping into each other at random, and a cell isn't a human-made, clocked system you can isolate. People from computing who try lab work often find the same protocol gives different results, with "bugs" coming from processes nobody understands. It's worth it because biology can copy and assemble itself. He also thinks analyzing neural networks will look more and more like systems biology.
ex: MIT computer architect Tom Knight switched to programming DNA in the 1990s

d.verdict: Worth it: biology self-replicates and self-assembles

n35|224.c: Automating lab work into a "foundry" lets Ginkgo test designs at scale and build the data AI needs.
n35|224.e: Ginkgo borrows the division of labor from electronics and computing. On one side is a lab foundry that copies the semiconductor playbook, automating and scaling experiments. On the other are DNA programmers who send it orders. Scientists were reluctant at first to let someone else run their experiments. Scale produces large amounts of tested design data, which is fuel for training AI. Commercially it works like software outsourcing: agree on specs with pharma and ag companies, deliver strains, and earn milestone payments and royalties.
ex: A roughly 300,000-square-foot robotic lab, built over nearly a decade
A cold-water laundry enzyme project tested about 1,000 designs in the lab

items.d: Thousands of designs tested in batches

n35|224.c: DNA was never a language for human brains, so AI will beat experts faster in biology than in English.
n35|224.e: Fields like law rest on language that evolved alongside the human brain, so AI there mostly replaces junior staff. DNA was never meant for humans to understand, so AI will outdo experts faster here, a change he likens to splitting the atom. Ginkgo plans to train a foundation model that "speaks protein," then fine-tune it on its own enzyme data. There's still no AI-discovered drug, and the bottleneck is that everyone uses the same public data.
ex: In English, AI replaces the intern, not the law firm partner
Partnering with Google to train a protein foundation model

n35|224.c: Society is still badly exposed to pandemics and needs a biosurveillance network that works like antivirus software.
n35|224.e: COVID showed that even rich countries' health systems can't stop a pandemic. He wants two things: fast vaccine platforms and a "bio radar" like hurricane tracking. Hurricanes get early warnings, yet COVID was only spotted once it reached New York. He thinks the near-term risk of a lone actor using AI to build a bioweapon is low, because data such as lethality is missing. Still, defense should work like antivirus software, with automatic detection and global alerts.
ex: Working with the CDC to sequence wastewater from arriving flights
Doha's airport and Ukraine run similar monitoring programs

n35|224.c: Employees who bear the consequences, not capital, should govern powerful platforms, so all staff get super-voting shares.
n35|224.e: He thinks tech treated social networks as "just bits" and underestimated the consequences. Drugs go into human bodies, and AI is forcing tech to face similar risks. Control of a platform usually sits with founders or big asset managers. Ginkgo chose a third way: employees hold Class B shares with extra votes that lapse when they leave. Votes build up with tenure and can back hard decisions, and he admits it's an experiment.
ex: Class B shares carry 10 votes each, Class A shares one
Early on, DARPA and other government grants kept it going for five years

n36|95.c: Without waiting for bigger models, today's models can get 10 to 100 times better along several fronts.
n36|95.e: Elad lists five or six directions: multimodal input and output, context windows long enough to hold an entire codebase, customization through fine-tuning and RAG, memory, recursive calls on a model's own output, and a router that dispatches work to many small expert models. Many in the industry believe all of these will arrive and noticeably improve results. The only question is timing.
ex: Magic uses long context to work across an entire codebase

items.d: A whole codebase in the window

n36|95.c: Fine-tuning is really about injecting lots of feedback, while RAG gives a trusted, citable, controllable source.
n36|95.e: ChatGPT is GPT-3.5 after RLHF, reinforcement learning from human rankings of its answers. The base model barely changed, yet usability leapt. Companies can fine-tune on medical data or internal HR Q&A. RAG retrieves from a chosen set of documents and then lets the model reason over them. Its core value is trust and citation. It also avoids retraining, keeps information fresh and sharply cuts hallucinations such as made-up legal cases.
ex: Google research found AI feedback can rival human feedback in some settings
Med-PaLM 2, trained on medical data, beats doctors on some tasks

d.verdict: They complement each other; pick by task

n36|95.c: Meta open-sourcing models is like MySQL and Linux: sharing the cost of non-core infrastructure with an ecosystem.
n36|95.e: One explanation borrows from MySQL. The open-source database gave big companies an alternative to commercial software, and internet companies like Facebook helped harden it and gave back to the community. For Meta, models are infrastructure for data center efficiency, ads and consumer products, not something it sells to enterprises. Open-sourcing spreads the cost and grows an ecosystem. The counterpoint: IBM funded Linux as a check on Microsoft, and sustaining an open-source ecosystem can be expensive.
ex: In some years IBM spent about $1 billion a year funding Linux
Llama 2 is seen as the leading open-source model

n36|95.c: Generative AI may be the first new opening in consumer social since TikTok.
n36|95.e: TikTok, the last big social network, launched seven years ago. Users' time is locked up by the giants, and startups mostly copy Twitter and Facebook. ByteDance solved the cold-start problem for users with its recommendation algorithm. Generative AI could do for content what Instagram filters did, solving content cold start by making creation easier. The open question is whether creation tools grow into standalone social products or stay tools.
ex: Midjourney, Pika and Character grow through creation
Can of Soup, a new YC company, is worth watching

items.d: Tool or standalone network, still open

n36|95.c: Early in a tech shift, go after easy, high-value problems, and buy no GPUs before product-market fit.
n36|95.e: The hosts advise picking easy, valuable markets while a technology is young and saving the hard problems for five years later, when the tech has matured. The exception is a technical breakthrough that unlocks a major use case. If you've slogged for a long time without customer pull, your time is better spent elsewhere. They mention founders with strong research backgrounds aiming at extremely hard code-generation problems, while shorter, achievable wins let a team take more shots and lower risk.

n37|232.c: Buyers had already tuned out interruptions, so marketing had to shift from push to being found.
n37|232.e: The Boston startups he saw were all copying the outbound playbook: buy lists, cold-call, blast emails, exhibit at trade shows. But buyers had caller ID, ad blockers and DVRs, and that playbook had stopped working. Co-founder Dharmesh's blog, written in business school, drew more traffic than well-funded companies, which showed buyers were doing their own research on Google and blogs. So HubSpot bet on inbound marketing and deliberately framed the market as inbound versus outbound, giving the idea an enemy so it would spread.
ex: Dharmesh's personal blog outdrew venture-backed companies
The first Inbound drew about 400 people; now about 12,000 attend in person
"Inbound sales" never caught on, so HubSpot supported outbound too

items: Blocked by caller ID and ad blockers

d.verdict: Marketing should attract, not interrupt

n37|232.c: Go against the grain: bet on the small businesses everyone dismissed and skip building a third enterprise suite.
n37|232.e: Early on, VCs widely saw selling to small businesses as a bad business and asked who had ever succeeded. His math: inbound lowers customer acquisition cost, steady upselling raises customer lifetime value, and net revenue retention above 100% lets the model scale. He also judged the market didn't need a third big enterprise marketing suite, so he didn't chase enterprise giants. In hindsight he was right, though the founders were diluted more than they expected.
ex: Sequoia invested early, and buying Performable filled in the middle of the funnel

n37|232.c: Going from one product to a suite means giving the new business its own team and a fresh start.
n37|232.e: After Salesforce bought several marketing companies, HubSpot went from partner to rival, so it did the counterintuitive thing and launched a simpler, cheaper freemium CRM. Changing the product form and the go-to-market at once was risky.
