His answer, modeled on Apple's Mac team, was to put the sales product in a separate building with its own tech stack and sales team, led by him and Christopher O'Donnell. The sales product grew faster with better margins, and the freemium playbook was then applied back to marketing. He calls it his best chapter at HubSpot.
ex: The sales team had its own building and its own tech stack
At IPO the sales business was still small, but confidence inside was high

items.d: Adds free CRM and sales tools

n37|232.c: Culture is how a company scales, and it should be iterated for employees like a product.
n37|232.e: HubSpot avoided talking about culture early on. In a CEO peer group, people like iRobot's Colin Angle changed his mind: culture is how employees decide when leaders aren't in the room. The company measured employee satisfaction with an NPS-style survey, then wrote a culture code modeled on Netflix's, updated every six months, with quarterly survey answers posted on the internal wiki. He admits his limits too. He resisted when the board urged him to hire a COO, and at about $2 billion in revenue he decided going to $20 billion wasn't his strength, so he handed over and became chairman.
ex: The culture code, modeled on Netflix's, is updated every six months
The first HR head came from marketing
He handed the CEO role to Yamini Rangan

items.d: Culture code updated twice a year
People know what to do without leaders present

n37|232.c: AI is a rare win for incumbents this time: years of data are an edge startups can't easily match.
n37|232.e: The usual disruption story has upstarts beating incumbents, but he thinks this time incumbents like HubSpot and Salesforce have an unfair advantage: years of massive customer data that startups can't easily get. More than two years before ChatGPT, Sam Altman told him not to rush into hiring lots of PhDs, because AI would improve slowly and steadily, then suddenly jump. So HubSpot stayed prepared. He also predicts AI assistants will answer questions about brands directly, search traffic to websites will fall, and brands will need higher-quality content.
ex: There are roughly a thousand CRM companies, and few move fast
He tried to co-invest in OpenAI but couldn't
HubSpot has shipped a content assistant, ChatSpot and more

root.d: Upstarts don't automatically win this time

n38|236.c: The hard part for enterprises isn't calling an API but deployment, monitoring and governance.
n38|236.e: He sees much of the enterprise excitement coming from quickly building prototypes on APIs, and he calls it genuine engineering enthusiasm, not hype. The real difficulty starts after deployment: monitoring for model drift, chaining multiple models together, and keeping answers reliable and on topic. Scaling also means logging who accessed what and when, enforcing permissions, and keeping each customer's data, models and weights inside its own tenant. Rollbacks are costly, so set checkpoints and don't rush.
ex: Model Garden offers Google's own, third-party and open-source models
Med-PaLM 2 can verify and organize clinical notes

n38|236.c: Enterprises adopt AI in steps: efficiency first, then productivity, then creativity.
n38|236.e: He sees customers usually start by using AI to make existing processes more efficient, measured with clear metrics like customer service CSAT. The capacity freed up by efficiency then turns into productivity gains. As trust in the model's predictability builds step by step, people can shift their energy to creative work. That's why models must behave as expected, without going off topic or making things up.
ex: Customer service measures results with CSAT scores

n38|236.c: Sales and marketing adopt first, and engineering teams have embraced AI faster than expected.
n38|236.e: Producing and distributing content is the bottleneck for sales and marketing, so AI's efficiency gains show up fastest there and those teams adopt first. Customer service follows, including vendor support in B2B. Internal employee Q&A, such as HR questions, is also growing. What surprised him is how fast engineering teams took to it, since coding models ease staff shortages. Multimodal AI is still early. Gaming is a fast-growing use, but deepfakes and storage and retrieval costs will come with it.
ex: Google piloted it internally in Workspace, then launched Duet AI
Gmail helps him translate emails for his Hindi-speaking mother

n38|236.c: Success depends more on choosing to be a first mover or fast follower than on technology choices.
n38|236.e: He thinks whether a company positions itself as an industry first mover or a fast follower depends on its investment, conviction and ambition, and that matters more than which technology it uses. The strategy and culture changes involved belong in board-level discussions. Whether to train your own model or use a domain model depends on guardrails, use cases, cost and whether the organization knows how to build and tune models. Model access and platform costs are falling fast, which will drive wider adoption.
ex: More than 10,000 people have earned Google Cloud generative AI certifications

n38|236.c: TPUs and GPUs are largely interchangeable; what's truly scarce is people who can optimize for TPUs.
n38|236.e: He considers the two fairly interchangeable, and the goal is to abstract away the infrastructure so developers can focus on their projects. The real difference is talent: few people know how to optimize for TPUs, and most of them were trained at Google, which wants to spread that know-how. Google is investing heavily in inference to cut costs and help customers scale. When GPU shortages come up, he says conversations with customers quickly turn to security, access control and data residency.
ex: Customers like Character AI rely on scaling up inference

items: Can be abstracted by the platform

d.verdict: The bottleneck is talent and operations, not chips

n39|238.c: Assume the attacker is already in, and hide the sensitive data in the mailbox first.
n39|238.e: Material grew out of the string of email breaches during the 2016 US election. His approach is defense in depth: assume the bad guys are already inside, find the sensitive content in mailboxes and archives, redact it and leave clean copies. An attacker who downloads the whole mailbox gets nothing useful, while legitimate users can still retrieve the originals after stronger authentication. Business email is nearly a Google–Microsoft duopoly, so their vulnerabilities affect the whole system, which he sees as fragile.
ex: The first prototype protected ordinary mailboxes through the Gmail API
Later expanded into anti-phishing and account takeover protection

n39|238.c: Off-the-shelf models already understand security; fine-tuning for a "moat" is mostly a story.
n39|238.e: He thinks models trained on huge amounts of internet text have already absorbed a lot of security knowledge. Material's first production use was having a model filter and triage raw security signals like email headers before a human reviews them, and the model is very good at cutting noise. Tasks that were extremely hard for computers 18 months ago are now easy for off-the-shelf models. So he doubts heavy fine-tuning is needed and suspects many startups just need to pretend they have a moat.
ex: Socket uses models to analyze NPM dependencies
Detecting leaked secrets in codebases
Summarizing logs and alerts, possibly making some old tools obsolete

d.verdict: Off-the-shelf models handle most security tasks

n39|238.c: AI lets one attacker do the work of a roomful, and security is always cleaning up after innovation.
n39|238.e: Voice cloning and texts impersonating banks or CEOs are already happening, and they work because people trust whatever looks human. Phishing emails with bad grammar still succeed at scale, and off-the-shelf open-source models will noticeably raise attack quality. Automation lets a single attacker cycle through thousands of targets. He compares cybersecurity to the "waste heat" of all computing innovation: society adopts technology because it's useful, and side effects and security get patched afterward.
ex: Texting new employees while posing as the CEO

n39|238.c: Intelligence is now an arms race, so regulation should watch for capability jumps, not data centers.
n39|238.e: He sees intelligence as a commodity nations can race over, a "Red Queen" situation where everyone has to keep running just to stay in place. Open Western societies adopt technology fast and are widely exposed, while authoritarian states can seal off their information environments. He gave people at the White House an analogy: if your neighbor goes from bronze to iron, you're in trouble. Capability gaps come in steps, so simply restricting data centers misses the point. He also thinks policymakers know models through ChatGPT headlines and underestimate their real abilities.
ex: He thinks DARPA runs plenty of interesting projects, and deterrence often works

n39|238.c: Security buyers can't verify what works, so winners are often distribution giants, not innovators.
n39|238.e: He makes Ian Grigg's "The Market for Silver Bullets" required reading at the company: buyers can't confirm whether a security product works, so vendors with distribution and bundling power win. Cisco, Palo Alto Networks, Google and Microsoft rarely create new categories and mostly buy startups, which he calls the "cybersecurity industrial complex." Still, technology shifts open windows, so startups keep a chance, and a common good outcome is acquisition. His advice to founders is to pick big markets, since startup difficulty is roughly inversely proportional to market size.
ex: Cisco acquiring Splunk
He once advised passing on Snowflake's Series B, one of his biggest mistakes

n40|243.c: OpenAI's goal has always been AGI; only the structure changed, from nonprofit to capped-profit.
n40|243.e: The goal has always been autonomous systems that can do most economically valuable work, built to benefit all of humanity. The original plan was a nonprofit plus open source, but real progress turned out to need enormous compute, and a nonprofit couldn't raise enough to build big clusters. So it became a capped-profit company, where investor returns are limited to a multiple of what they put in. The reasoning: if AGI can automate most work, its builders shouldn't have an unlimited profit motive. He admits competition among several companies complicates that logic.
ex: He says that, as far as he knows, it's the world's only capped-profit company

d.verdict: The structure serves the AGI mission

n40|243.c: Reaching AGI takes big engineering: making Transformers bigger and bigger.
n40|243.e: Most of OpenAI's early, conventional academic research is now forgotten, and he drew a lesson from that: AGI requires large engineering projects with lots of compute. Dota 2 was the first big bet, but the domain was too narrow and the network too small. Predicting the next word is linked to compression, and that idea led to large Transformers. GPT-1 showed early signs, and the jump from GPT-2 to GPT-3 woke everyone up. The nearest bottleneck now is data, which he thinks research can overcome. Cost slows things down, while investment and talent speed them up.
ex: A Dota 2 neural network reached top human level
GPT-2 to GPT-3 was the "great awakening" moment

n40|243.c: Reliability is the biggest bottleneck: after 20 right answers, you still can't trust the 21st.
n40|243.e: He thinks models are becoming more reliable, but reliability is what still stands between them and real usefulness. Even after 20 correct answers in a row, you worry the 21st will be badly wrong, so important decisions need human checks. It's like self-driving, where "mostly works" is nowhere near enough. Reliability improves with model scale and task-specific fine-tuning. Small models can serve many niche applications, but high-value uses like trustworthy legal advice need bigger ones, so the future is an ecosystem of many sizes.
ex: Research at 7B, 13B and 34B scale isn't wasted

n40|243.c: Neural networks are small brains, and Transformers are enough to get to AGI.
n40|243.e: Before AlexNet, neural networks were shunned because you couldn't prove theorems about them. He believed artificial and biological neurons aren't fundamentally different, so a big enough network can replicate what the brain does. The real question is computational efficiency, not whether Transformers can reach AGI. Other architectures might just be more efficient. His evidence is that the cortex is fairly uniform: children who have half their brain removed grow up largely normal, and when a ferret's optic nerve is rewired to the auditory cortex, the neurons there come to resemble visual neurons.
ex: AlexNet relied on a big network, two GPUs and training tricks
Children with half their brain removed grow up largely normal
Experiments rewiring a ferret's optic nerve to its auditory cortex

root.d: Artificial neurons aren't fundamentally different from biological ones

items.d: A big enough network can see

n40|243.c: Reliable, autonomous AI is close to digital life, so it must be made to care about humans.
n40|243.e: He thinks AI that is reliable enough and highly autonomous comes close to digital life, though today's systems can't yet do your homework or taxes on their own. If progress continues, data centers far smarter than people within five to ten years isn't out of the question. So the goal of superalignment is for superintelligence to feel warmly and positively toward humanity. Open source is similar: the benefits win out today, but once models can do science and run companies on their own, that's no longer obvious. Now is the time to study alignment, he says, because it's under-studied and today's AI is strong enough to study.
ex: He expects open-source models to catch up with closed ones in about two years

items.d: Close to a non-human life form

n41|248.c: Chinchilla's correction didn't go far enough; models can get smaller and cheaper to run.
n41|248.e: He says a poorly executed 2020 scaling-law paper led the field to train models on too few tokens. Chinchilla showed that for a fixed compute budget, training tokens should grow in step with model size, which makes a model trained with the same compute about four times cheaper to serve. He thinks that road is far from finished, and Mistral 7B, which runs on a laptop and is still useful, is the proof. Inference costs, just like training costs, decide whether the business works.
ex: He worked on RETRO, sparse mixture-of-experts and Chinchilla
Mistral 7B runs on a laptop

items.d: Compressed further, runs on a laptop

n41|248.c: AI is still immature and closed research holds science back, so the field should return to openness.
n41|248.e: He says machine learning has always advanced through open publication at conferences, with labs building on each other's work. Around 2020 it turned opaque, and expensive large-scale experiments were duplicated in secret. Yet today's models reason poorly, have a shallow grasp of memory and causality, are hard to steer and carry biases, and a technology this new needs open, shared experimentation. Mistral has enough money for compute and wants to push the whole field back toward openness. He welcomes Meta's moves on open source too.
ex: Welcomes Meta pushing open source

d.verdict: It's too early to work behind closed doors

n41|248.c: Open-sourcing today's models is a manageable risk: moderation is solvable, and bio and existential risks lack evidence.
n41|248.e: He sees no evidence that large models help bad actors more than search engines do, and knowledge may not be the bottleneck for doing harm anyway. That should be reassessed once models get stronger. The bioweapons worry traces back to one observation in the GPT-4 system card, after which policy papers cited each other without scientific grounding, and COVID trauma amplified the story. Existential risk is more of a philosophical question. He trusts only visible evidence and thinks complexity is more likely to cause paralysis than loss of control. Climate change is more pressing.
ex: The bioweapons narrative stems from one observation in the GPT-4 system card

n41|248.c: Regulate capabilities, not compute thresholds, and handle safety with composable guardrails.
n41|248.e: The proposed 10^26 FLOPs threshold is arbitrary. He estimates it's roughly $300 million of compute, and no one has shown dangerous capabilities emerge at that scale. Datasets matter more than raw compute, so regulation should target capabilities directly. Banning open source would entrench the giants and hurt small players, which amounts to regulatory capture. He argues a base model should "know everything," which also makes it useful for moderation. Modular filters can be stacked on inputs and outputs, with application builders responsible for compliance and guardrail startups competing to supply them.
ex: The 10^26 FLOPs threshold is about $300 million, by his estimate

n41|248.c: Inference must be cheap: small models make agents affordable, and one GPU can serve hundreds of customers.
n41|248.e: He sees cheap, fast inference as the precondition for models being everywhere and for agents to be affordable. Running agents on GPT-4 burns through money fast. Today's agents repeat themselves and get stuck in loops, a kind of "mode collapse," so research is needed on reasoning and on allocating compute by task difficulty. Big models still matter: reasoning needs scale, and large models can be distilled or used to generate synthetic data to train stronger small ones. Commercially, the API time-shares one GPU across hundreds of customers, and enterprises that need full control can deploy models themselves.
ex: Mistral 7B uses sparse attention to cut memory use
Mistral is training larger models

n42|253.c: Agents should act for people, not leave people to check a chatbot's output.
n42|253.e: She thinks chatbots leave both the doing and the checking to the user, and today's computers do nothing unless someone is sitting in front of them. The vision for agents is a computer that understands natural-language instructions and accomplishes goals for you. She sorts technologies into three kinds: never going to work, achievable now with engineering, and inevitable but still a ways off. Agents mostly fall in the middle. They're evolving along two axes: from specialized to general, and from copilot to autonomous.
ex: Her earlier AI recruiting company was an early autonomous system
Customer service bots that hand off to humans are already deployed

cells.d: Human in the loop, takes new tasks
Like support bots with human handoff

n42|253.c: Reliability is the core bottleneck for agents, and reasoning is essentially a set of error-correction techniques.
n42|253.e: Compared with lossy Ethernet or analog computers, today's models are very unreliable, and it's the problem founders raise most. She defines reasoning as everything needed to finish a task: knowing when to go back to the user, recognizing uncertainty, comparing possible actions and deciding which path to try first. Chain-of-thought and tree-of-thought are error-correction methods, and Imbue has other techniques in-house. Treating agents as a reliability problem lets progress accumulate step by step.
ex: Chain-of-thought and tree-of-thought are both error-correction techniques

items.d: Ask the user or switch paths

n42|253.c: Prototype with the strongest model, ship with the "minimum viable model," and small models will dominate.
n42|253.e: She sees teams usually prototype with the strongest model, then switch to a cheaper or fine-tuned open-source model to save money. A general agent can also specialize the workflows it runs again and again: if it's going to make ten thousand similar calls, it might as well write a piece of Python instead. She leans toward giving each capability a smaller, narrower minimum viable model, just as the personal computer market ended up far bigger than the supercomputer market.
ex: The PC market is far bigger than the supercomputer market

n42|253.c: Agents the team truly uses every day push the research forward, ratcheting reliability up step by step.
n42|253.e: Imbue's method is serious use: building coding agents the team itself uses every day, plus operations agents for tasks like recruiting outreach. Going from 60% to 70% to 80% reliability, the pressure at each step forces new techniques. Training one giant model and waiting for a miracle doesn't work. Tasks are chosen for being useful, frequent, feasible and general, for pushing the technology, and for extending to harder versions. A large share of the $200 million Series B goes to compute rather than headcount, and she hopes a small, tight team can punch above its weight.
ex: A large share of the $200 million Series B goes to compute
Example: auto-running a linter and fixing type errors on every PR

items.d: Like auto-fixing type errors in PRs

n42|254.c: Language models can't learn general algorithms, so reasoning needs an outer control loop.
n42|254.e: Language models are good at predicting the next word and classifying, but they have hard limits. A model can learn modular addition almost perfectly yet fail to learn the general addition algorithm, and general multiplication is beyond the context window entirely. Running general algorithms takes an outer control loop that decides what to do next, when to gather more information and whether the model is confident. The idea of putting everything into the language model doesn't work, and that outer loop is the truly interesting open problem.
ex: Modular addition can be learned; general multiplication can't

items.d: Decides next steps and when to verify

n42|254.c: Evaluation is key: break "is it good?" down until every sub-question has an objective answer.
n42|254.e: To define what a good coding agent looks like, you have to break down what users actually want: speed, how much changed, whether there are bugs, whether there are tests, style, variable naming, whether the change is minimal. Keep going until every sub-question can be answered objectively. Code comes first because it's easier to judge whether tests pass or a function is correct, and the approach then extends to qualitative tasks. The same method works for recruiting. Looking only at whether the final answer is right throws away a lot of information.
ex: The same breakdown approach is used for recruiting tasks

n42|254.c: Everyone will become a programmer, and agents are tools for programming in natural language.
n42|254.e: He cites his co-founder: Imbue is essentially a software developer tools company. The reasoning is that in the future everyone will work like a software engineer, so everyone will need developer tools. "Agent" is just a technical term. In practice it works like a natural-language programming layer. Computers keep getting more intuitive, and future computers will let more people direct them to do what they want, like customizing a research workflow.
ex: In five years, individuals could customize their own agents in natural language

n42|254.c: Once compute produces code, even small companies can write more and better software.
n42|254.e: Software is badly undersupplied because writing code is so hard, and the bottleneck now is finding good engineers. If compute can produce good code, small companies can write far more code than big ones. Agents won't just write more. They can add tests, fix old tests, find security holes and simplify code. Software can also be personalized, with interfaces cached and reused. Imbue uses coding agents to build its coding agents, and progress comes not from sudden leaps but from small daily improvements that compound.
ex: Built a custom prompting interface for Midjourney in one weekend
About 13 or 14 people training frontier-scale models

result.d: With tests, security and custom interfaces

n43|95.c: The OpenAI saga showed that governance, capital and employees' interests all matter a great deal.
n43|95.e: They see the outcome as broadly good for OpenAI: the company stabilized, still has the leading model in GPT-4, and the board was reshuffled. Lesson one is that governance matters. Nonprofit performance is hard to measure, so decisions drift toward politics and status. Lesson two is that money matters, and the compute Microsoft controls is itself a form of capital. The board also underestimated how strongly employees backed Sam Altman and Greg Brockman, and part of their anger was about the value of a promised tender offer for their shares. Board members' outside incentives deserve scrutiny too.
ex: The employee tender offer valued OpenAI at about $86 billion
Shopify came up as an example of a board focused on performance

root.d: People with real stakes hold the power

items.d: Nonprofit performance is hard to measure
Their tender offer payout was at risk

n43|95.c: Companies will move from betting on one model to using several: prototype first, then cut costs.
n43|95.e: The saga made companies realize they shouldn't depend on a single model vendor. Tools like Braintrust's AI proxy already let code written for OpenAI's SDK call other providers' models. The typical path is to prototype on GPT-4, then switch to GPT-3.5 or a fine-tuned Llama or Mistral for cost, throughput or latency. Few teams fine-tune unless they run at large scale or have proprietary data. Big enterprises have always wanted a second supplier to strengthen their hand in negotiations.
ex: Juniper to Cisco and AMD to Intel: classic second suppliers
GPT-4 still leads in code generation and in GPT-4V

items.d: First prove it can be done

n43|95.c: Diffusion models are cheap to train, so small teams can reach the frontier, and video is taking off.
n43|95.e: After ChatGPT launched, many founders switched to large language models, but work on diffusion models, the kind that generate images and video, never stopped. That is why video and digital-avatar products are now popping up. Diffusion models cost far less to train than frontier LLMs, in the millions of dollars for modern ones, and the data is easier to handle, so startups can train their own. Video is still early: it needs lots of data, is hard to caption, is expensive to generate, and keeping frames consistent over time is hard. Small teams can reach the frontier and approaches vary widely, which favors startups.
ex: Pika was founded by two Stanford PhDs
Stable Diffusion took about 600,000 GPU hours to train
Midjourney has kept a very small team for a long time

items: Small teams can reach the frontier

d.verdict: Diffusion is friendlier to startups

n43|95.c: AI will turn labor-heavy, low-margin services revenue into high-margin software revenue.
n43|95.e: Companies spend about $500 billion a year on software but roughly $3–5 trillion on services. AI can turn low-margin, people-heavy services revenue into high-margin software revenue. The total may be smaller, but it is more profitable. They use an Anduril-style example: a $1 million drone sold at a 5% cost-plus markup earns the same profit as a $100,000 product with a 50% gross margin. Technology often grows the market while pushing unit prices down. Video production has gone from hundreds or thousands of dollars per hour to single digits per minute, and the audience has grown with it.
ex: $1 million at 5% earns the same profit as $100,000 at 50%

n43|95.c: AI today is like the early internet: few real use cases yet, but value is hard to predict.
n43|95.e: There's a joke that only a few AI businesses are really working: foundation models, Midjourney, Copilot and inference platforms that run models for others. They think it has some truth to it but isn't that funny. The early internet also had a handful of real use cases plus many experiments that looked silly at first. Some investors once doubted Midjourney could get big, and it proved there is huge demand for creative tools. Adobe's size shows the creative market is large too. The traction these products already have is a positive sign.
ex: Adobe is worth roughly $280–300 billion

marks.d: Once doubted it could get big
Shows how big creative tools can get

n44|262.c: Salesforce picks the model per task: big firms bring their own, smaller ones let the platform choose.
n44|262.e: Salesforce's customers vary enormously. Large enterprises want to bring or fine-tune their own models, while small businesses want Salesforce to choose for them. So the platform picks the best model for each task based on cost, performance and latency. Options include models from its own research team and industry-tuned versions, models customers fine-tune on their own data in Data Cloud, and third-party models from Anthropic, Cohere, OpenAI and Google Vertex. She also pushed for shared services so each product line doesn't build its own.
ex: Customers can buy through Salesforce or bring their own API keys
Some in-house models are open-sourced on Hugging Face

items.d: Plain language across Salesforce clouds and Slack

n44|262.c: Enterprise AI is only in the second or third inning, and most companies' data is still scattered.
n44|262.e: She puts enterprise adoption early, around the second or third inning. Enough companies have proven the value, but most are still experimenting and cleaning up their data. Customer service can start before the data is fully sorted. Connectors, vector search and embeddings can unify knowledge articles scattered across systems. That enables retrieval-augmented generation, where the AI looks things up before answering, for both self-service bots and human agents. The demand for data has made Data Cloud the fastest organically growing product in Salesforce history.
ex: Zero-ETL integration with BigQuery, Databricks and Snowflake

items.d: A few service centers are there

n44|262.c: Retrieval-augmented AI helps brand-new advisors tell the brand story and handle tough cases.
n44|262.e: During the pandemic Gucci had high staff turnover and hired many new client advisors. Retrieval-augmented generation gave them brand stories and expert-level troubleshooting knowledge, with suggested replies grounded in knowledge articles and similar past cases. Average handle time went down, and advisors could have deeper conversations with clients. With a 360-degree view of each customer, advisors could also see related items in the cart and ongoing marketing and sales conversations, breaking down the walls between departments.
ex: The most popular feature was suggested replies for agents

n44|262.c: AI is becoming the new enterprise interface, but processes that must be exact should stay hard-coded.
n44|262.e: She thinks agents, AI that can take actions on its own, will change how software is built, replacing hard-coded branches and screen-by-screen design with dynamic execution. Chat interfaces like Slack are becoming AI's new UI, and "generative canvas" prototypes let charts and records appear in the conversation on demand. But as with the move to the cloud, workflows that must run exactly the same way every time, such as authentication, financial transactions and medical processes, should stay deterministic. Engineers and product managers will shift from specifying "how" to describing "why" and "what."
ex: The Slack, Tableau and MuleSoft acquisitions happen to fit AI well

d.verdict: Migrate case by case, like the cloud

n44|262.c: AI pricing should be simple and tied to ROI, not make customers estimate token usage.
n44|262.e: She admits pricing is hard: it has to cover costs and still be easy to understand, and customers shouldn't need a complex calculator to forecast their token usage. The real test is visible ROI, such as shorter handle times or higher sales conversion. When the gains are clear, customers will pay. Model costs keep falling while the value may rise by orders of magnitude, so she is optimistic. For founders, she likes vertical models, the tooling layer and rebuilt applications, and advises building close to the data layer.
ex: She says generative AI surprises her every week

n45|265.c: Small merchants know they should market but lack time and money. AI can unlock that latent demand.
n45|265.e: Most small business owners are craftspeople, not MBAs. They know they should do marketing but lack the time, skills and budget, and consultants are too expensive. Easier, cheaper tools can open up demand that was never served, which she calls white space. Generating product photos or short videos is mostly work nobody did before, not a replacement for existing jobs. AI can help with almost every part of running a business. Quantitative tasks like finance still suffer from hallucinations, but that will improve quickly.
ex: Square once used GPT-2 to power a messaging assistant for sellers
Like word processors and card acceptance, it lowers the barrier

n45|265.c: Physical retail lags far behind e-commerce in going digital, and generative AI is lowering the barriers.
n45|265.e: E-commerce photos, descriptions and inventory are digital by nature, while physical and local businesses lag far behind. Square's Photo Studio began as a physical studio in Brooklyn where sellers mailed in products for 360-degree photos. It then became an iPhone app that removes backgrounds with AI, so nothing had to be shipped. New tools keep lowering the barrier. Her summary: generative AI can make things ten times faster and ten times cheaper.
ex: Photo Studio went from a Brooklyn studio to an iPhone app

n45|265.c: Today's tools are fragmented, and the next phase will be bundling and consolidation.
n45|265.e: Business owners juggle a pile of browser tabs and move data between tools by hand. Integration is poor, and offline workflows are worse. She expects today's unbundled phase, where each product tries to be best in class, to give way to a bundling phase where categories merge and boundaries blur. Technology itself cycles between scaling up and scaling out, and chiplets and advanced packaging let systems swap parts like microservices. After each burst of innovation, most experiments drift back to the main path.
ex: Blockchain saw a flood of Layer 1s, then a shift to Layer 2s

n45|265.c: Every cloud provider is betting on several models, so one model dominating the world is unlikely.
n45|265.e: AI brings new, GPU-heavy training demand on top of existing CPU workloads rather than replacing them, so this is a land grab with many players. Amazon invested in Anthropic, Google invested in Anthropic while building Gemini, and Microsoft partners with OpenAI while building its own models. Everyone is hedging. Enterprises want multiple models too, so a single dominant model is unlikely. From her S3 experience, she believes simple APIs become the foundation. Enterprises like open source, but it is hard to monetize, and Confluent is one of the few successes.
ex: Amazon Bedrock brings many companies' models together
Confluent, the company behind Kafka, made open source pay

items.d: Partners with OpenAI, builds its own

n45|265.c: Every computing wave has a clear number one and number two, so Nvidia won't hold a monopoly.
n45|265.e: She has noticed that each computing wave produces a clear first and second place, like Intel and AMD or ARM and Qualcomm, and being third is very hard. Nvidia sells the most GPUs today, but she doesn't expect a monopoly. A clear number two will emerge, and the toolchain moving up the stack opens room for it. She is less confident than before that the Transformer architecture will stay dominant. Looking ahead, infrastructure is settling into a few players, and the biggest opportunity is in applications, where large parts of the service economy get turned into code.
ex: She still sits on the boards of Intel and Confluent

items.d: Each new wave draws a rush

n46|270.c: AI is a "steam engine of the mind," and human-AI amplification matters more than pure automation.
n46|270.e: He thinks AI may be the biggest technological shift of his lifetime, perhaps in human history: the steam engine gave people physical power, and AI gives them mental power. A loop where humans and AI amplify each other matters more than pure automation. Self-driving cars are the exception, since they can run on their own and the goal is to cut traffic deaths. People always overestimate what changes in a year and underestimate what changes in ten or twenty. The printing press and electricity drew doomsday talk too.
ex: About 40,000 people die in US traffic accidents each year

items: People boost their minds with AI

d.verdict: Humans working with AI is the main story

n46|270.c: A doctor and a tutor in every phone is the biggest access opportunity he's seen in twenty years.
n46|270.e: About 5 billion people have smartphones, yet far fewer than 1 billion can see a doctor. He thinks a medical assistant in every phone is a realistic near-term goal, and AI tutors for every subject and age are achievable too. He cites a 15-year-old who used GPT-4 to understand a dense organic chemistry paper. He calls this the biggest global health and equity opportunity he has seen in about twenty years in the industry, and says government policy should focus on making these tools widely available.
ex: About 5 billion smartphones, but far fewer than 1 billion people can see a doctor
A 15-year-old used GPT-4 to understand an organic chemistry paper

n46|270.c: Doomers extrapolate wrongly: exponential growth in compute doesn't mean "IQ" soars along with it.
n46|270.e: Doomers see compute growing exponentially and assume "IQ" will rise in step until superintelligence arrives. He thinks that extrapolation is unfounded. If progress looks more like narrow, savant-like abilities, the outcome is completely different. GPT-4 already beats humans in some narrow areas, yet it isn't scary, and mostly it amplifies its users. He questions the open letter calling for a six-month pause, saying its authors wrongly assumed the whole world would stop together. Sci-fi movies always pit humans against evil machines, and he wants the stories to include good machines too.
ex: The open letter calling for a six-month pause

marks.d: Superhuman in narrow areas, not scary

n46|270.c: On net AI lowers humanity's existential risk, and talking only about danger may do more harm than good.
n46|270.e: He didn't sign the 22-word extinction-risk statement because, unlike climate change or pandemics, AI also has a positive column: it could help humanity handle pandemics and climate. He grants that AI adds some existential risk, but its net effect on the overall risk portfolio is positive. He respects signers like Sam Altman and Mustafa Suleyman and simply disagrees on this point. Critics who stress only the dangers paint no future worth heading toward, which may do more harm than good. He also rejects the idea that technology is all good and safety can be ignored, especially with biological risks.
ex: The 22-word statement on AI extinction risk
Biological risks like viruses and gene manipulation need extra care

items.d: Helps fight pandemics and climate change
So he didn't sign the statement

n46|270.c: White-collar workers should learn AI now, the way they learned Excel. Resisting the shift won't work.
n46|270.e: He advises white-collar workers to start using AI as an amplifier right away, the way people learned Excel, without waiting for it to be perfect. The history of coachmen and Luddite weavers shows resistance goes nowhere. AI that replaces jobs can also help people move on, for example helping customer service reps find, learn and succeed at new jobs. Transitions take time, but smartphone-scale distribution may make this one faster. Middle and some senior white-collar roles will change first and most sharply. Try AI on things that really matter to you, not on writing sonnets.
ex: Even if every truck factory went autonomous, they'd need about 10 years to be the majority
Asking GPT-4 how to make money investing in AI gets useless answers

items.d: Try it on what matters to you
AI helps people learn new skills

n46|270.c: Pi is a personal AI companion with its own views, designed to steer people back to real relationships.
n46|270.e: He co-founded Inflection with Mustafa Suleyman and Karén Simonyan on the premise that everyone will one day have a personal intelligence. Pi is designed as a knowledgeable, empathetic everyday companion you can ask about anything from fixing a flat tire to parenting. It is not a therapist. Unlike the movie Her, it encourages users to return to real human relationships. It also has its own point of view and won't go along with harmful talk like racism.
ex: A Greylock colleague, a new parent, used it for parenting advice
A user asked it how to fix a flat tire

items.d: Steers people back to real relationships

n46|270.c: Technology is never value-neutral, and regulating before innovating means clinging to the past.
n46|270.e: He rejects Silicon Valley's claim that technology is value-neutral and wants developers to state their values openly, as The Economist does. Big platforms shape how many people think and carry social responsibilities, such as refusing to help terrorists or promote genocide. Some bias is unavoidable and gets fixed by deploying, learning and iterating, and critics should offer concrete benchmarks. You can't know how to regulate a technology before you see it. He criticizes the UK AI Safety Summit's regulate-first stance and thinks the EU AI Act trades the future for the past.
ex: AI can't be built by a "UN committee"
He thinks AI safety and tools for white-collar transitions are underrated

n48|287.c: Developers spend most of their time understanding old code, and that toil kills their flow.
n48|287.e: While he and co-founder Quinn were embedded at big banks and Fortune 500 companies for Palantir, they saw that these customers' legacy code and context problems were far worse than their own. Developers spend much of their time reading and understanding existing code instead of building features. That toil breaks the flow state that draws people to programming in the first place. Sourcegraph's core is fast code search plus navigation over a graph of references, so you can jump to definitions and find references without setting up a build environment.
ex: Working on-site for Palantir exposed him to big-company legacy code

n48|287.c: Context is the key: retrieval makes models more accurate and less prone to hallucinate.
n48|287.e: What sets Cody apart is that it uses Sourcegraph's code search and code graph to feed context to the LLM, much as Bing Chat and Perplexity ground answers in web search. Retrieval has two layers. First, several retrievers, including keyword, regex, vector nearest-neighbor and filename matching, aim for near-total recall. Then a slower but more precise reranker pushes the most relevant results to the top. He says keyword search alone gets you surprisingly far. Indexing by function and class works far better than indexing whole files or naive chunking.
ex: Cody works in VS Code and JetBrains
He says many people doing RAG quietly find keyword search is enough

n48|287.c: Retrieval for models differs from retrieval for people: more forgiving, and data quality sets the ceiling.
n48|287.e: When people search, the right result has to be in the top few. Models have much larger context windows, so there is more room for error. Embedding models and chunking strategies depend heavily on the domain, and domain-tuned embeddings have lots of room to improve. He mentions working with Voyage on this. Data quality is decisive, and no model architecture can make up for bad data, so selecting high-quality code and structuring it well matters most. He expects search-like pipelines to be attached to LLMs in every field.
ex: Working with Voyage on domain-specific embeddings

items: The right answer must be in the top few

d.verdict: Retrieval pipelines will show up in every field

n48|287.c: Near term, remove toil from the inner loop. Long term, an AI engineer that turns issues into PRs.
n48|287.e: In the near term, the focus is the inner loop each developer runs all day: removing toil like writing unit tests, writing docstrings and explaining code, because it breaks flow. The long-term goal is an "AI engineer" that turns an issue or bug report directly into a PR without supervision. The path starts with boring, low-risk tasks like dependency upgrades and moves gradually toward high-risk work. He ranks tasks on a two-by-two of how tedious and how risky they are. He admits that day is still some way off.
ex: Inline completion, codebase Q&A, generating unit tests and docs

n48|287.c: Chaining many steps compounds errors, so better context is the main lever for reliability.
n48|287.e: Breaking a feature into subtasks and chaining them works in principle, but errors compound. Even at 90% success per step, a long chain falls apart quickly, and today's per-step success rates are far below 90%. Sampling heavily and then verifying, as AlphaCode does, is too expensive for building features in a large codebase. When the context engine works, generation quality is night and day: the model reuses existing APIs, patterns and test frameworks. He is optimistic that the AI engineer will arrive sooner than many expect.
ex: AlphaCode-style mass sampling suits programming contest problems

items.d: Errors add up step by step

n48|287.c: Start with the simplest baseline: RAG before fine-tuning, and small models with good context are strong enough.
n48|287.e: Machine learning research taught him to do the simplest thing first and set a baseline, since fancy methods are often matched by simple ones. A Nature paper that used a large neural network for climate prediction was later matched by a model with a single neuron. So Sourcegraph did RAG first rather than fine-tuning, and even alongside fine-tuned models, RAG is the last mile. He is very bullish on small models but still uses large models for chat, because they are better at using retrieved context.
ex: Inline completion uses StarCoder 7B
Cody chat recently added Mixtral

n48|287.c: Software's core problems are coordination and visibility, and CS fundamentals will matter more.
n48|287.e: The argument of The Mythical Man-Month still holds: software is hard-to-measure knowledge work, and counting lines of code or commits like a factory is wrong. The core problems are coordination and visibility. AI can raise individual output from the bottom up and help leaders summarize what changed in a codebase from the top down. One person may do what a team once did, but demand for software is nowhere near saturated, so large teams will remain. AI will compress the middle layers of abstraction and glue code, making product goals at the top and data structures and algorithms at the bottom more important.
ex: He disagrees that people no longer need to learn to code

n49|290.c: Robots will follow the foundation-model path. The bottleneck is data, which only a deployed fleet can collect.
n49|290.e: He expects robotics to repeat the path of language models: train multi-task models on huge amounts of data, which generalize and transfer better and even do single tasks better. The hard part is that the physical world has no ready-made datasets, and lab collection can't scale. The only scalable way is to deploy robots in production, doing real work for customers while sending data back, much as Tesla trains self-driving on fleet data. The roadmap should also go product by product, with every milestone generating revenue and data.
ex: About 200 people, with customers roughly split between Europe and North America
Robots in 10+ countries on three continents share one foundation model

n49|290.c: Over 99% of robots are "dumb," and AI should open up new tasks that need adaptability.
n49|290.e: Nearly all robots in use today repeat one preprogrammed motion and can't adapt. Covariant isn't trying to replace those hand-programmable jobs. It targets new use cases that need adaptability and are orders of magnitude more numerous. Picking, packing and shipping in warehouses means handling hundreds of thousands of products with very high reliability, which traditional robots can't do. Meanwhile e-commerce has made logistics more complex, and late-night shifts at warehouses far from cities are getting harder to staff.
ex: Customer warehouses average over 100% annual staff turnover
He likens a put wall to a "physical router" for goods

items: Like moving car bodies in auto plants
Handle hundreds of thousands of products

d.verdict: Growth is in tasks that need adaptability

n49|290.c: Robots need precision and action-outcome data that the internet can't provide.
n49|290.e: Multimodal models like GPT-4V have learned some ability to map concepts onto the physical world from image-text pairs, but that is far from what robots need. First, precision: online descriptions are coarse, and when grasping, being two centimeters off at an object's edge is already too coarse. Second, there is no record of what was done and what happened, such as how much force will crush a tomato. Human videos on YouTube don't show force or precision, and learning from video is still a research problem.
ex: Whether moving too fast damages an item is also missing data

root.d: Not covered by internet images and text

items.d: Two centimeters off is too coarse
How much force crushes a tomato

n49|290.c: The future of robotics belongs to whoever has the most data. Simulation can only supplement it.
n49|290.e: Model architectures have changed about five times in recent years, so Covariant doesn't tie itself to one. Its only bet is robot data. He doesn't buy simulation alone: self-driving simulation is mostly about not touching things, while manipulation requires contact, and contact physics is especially hard for soft objects. A warehouse may hold about 100,000 kinds of items, and modeling each one is harder than learning from real data. He thinks scaling laws hold for robots, but a domain model only needs to cover its target tasks and doesn't depend on emergence.
ex: Model architectures have changed about five times recently
A customer warehouse may stock about 100,000 different items

marks.d: Learn from real data, explore what-ifs
Mostly real data, simulation as a supplement

n49|290.c: Robotics' ChatGPT moment has a higher bar and will come first in industrial settings.
n49|290.e: That moment needs generality, meaning robots quickly learn new settings, plus high reliability: no one accepts a robot that succeeds 70% of the time and fails catastrophically 30% of the time. It also needs high-quality data covering the target skills and cost-effective hardware. Factory robots run around the clock, which spreads out hardware costs, while a home robot might be used two hours a week. He doesn't expect fully unmanned factories soon. One person may supervise 10 to 30 robots as their "physical copilot."
ex: The first consumer robot may resemble Amazon Astro, mostly navigating and talking
Industrial sites already have safety cages and certified controllers

items.d: Runs all day, spreads hardware cost
Safety and alignment get much harder

n50|294.c: Big problems are often org problems: merge business units and let former founders make the calls.
n50|294.e: In 2020 checkout broke in several places, and the company declared a "code red" that pulled in 200 to 300 people at its peak. The postmortem traced the root cause to structure: 12 to 15 fragmented business units were merged into three or four larger ones that matched the product better. Many Shopify leaders are former founders who hold clear views, push through hard things and say uncomfortable truths, which avoids design by committee and speeds things up. CEO Tobi Lütke is also increasingly willing to set direction directly.
ex: The 2020 checkout code red mobilized about 200–300 people at its peak
Most of his nine or ten direct reports are former founders

n50|294.c: Never run two systems for the same layer of the stack, and merge duplicates as early as possible.
n50|294.e: Duplicate systems often grow by accident. A small feature for editing discounts on a placed order can slowly turn into a second, checkout-like negotiation engine. After that, changing shipping, adding items or international pricing all have to be built twice. The cost keeps landing on internal teams and on merchants, who run into inconsistent behavior. So teams need an instinct for avoiding duplication and should merge quickly when it appears. Wait too long and it's like rebuilding a house's foundation while living in it.
ex: Google faced a similar problem consolidating its identity layer

n50|294.c: AI may propose but never submit, and acceptance rates decide when to allow automation.
n50|294.e: Shopify positions Sidekick and Shopify Magic as partners, not replacements: AI can propose changes, but nothing takes effect until the merchant reviews it and clicks save. Feedback falls into three buckets, accepted as is, accepted after edits, or rejected, and feeds continuous iteration. He admits LLMs reach 75% quality fast, but the climb to 95% is slow and takes curated datasets, user feedback and evals, with each new foundation model lifting the whole curve. They will take risks with Shopify itself, but not with merchants' businesses.
ex: Three feedback buckets: accepted as is, accepted with edits, rejected
Full automation might come only near a 99% acceptance rate

n50|294.c: Structured product data plus semantic search translates directly into visibility and sales.
n50|294.e: Shopify's product data model barely changed in over a decade, yet it supports about 10% of US e-commerce. It handles products with many colors and sizes poorly, so Shopify is expanding variants and moving to paginated APIs. It is also launching a standard product taxonomy, using AI to detect categories and attributes from images and descriptions. Even at 90% accuracy, that saves a lot of work for merchants with thousands of SKUs. Structured data improves on-store search and helps rankings on Google, Facebook and Amazon.
ex: A store search for "sweater" found nothing because the product said "sweatshirt"
Semantic search understands queries like LBD or "Christmas-themed shoes"
AI image editing can swap product photo backgrounds

n50|294.c: Search should route queries by intent. LLMs don't need to handle every query.
n50|294.e: He sees a three-way contest: ChatGPT is great at LLM interaction but weak at search, Google is great at search but hasn't nailed the LLM experience, and Perplexity sits in between with LLM-native search. Users want answers, not a search process, and some LLMs get slower and full of disclaimers once they go online. Queries fall into navigational, factual, opinion and shopping types, and a router should send each to the right system. Shopping itself varies a lot. Google's distribution is hard to shake, but user expectations are shifting, which gives new players an opening.
ex: For classic books for a six-year-old girl, ChatGPT beat Google Shopping and Amazon
ChatGPT struggles with whether a New York store has sneakers in a given size

items.d: Specific items and stock, still hard

n51|298.c: Even non-AI companies should let employees adopt AI bottom-up. Internal use spreads on its own.
n51|298.e: Three engineers built an internal chat tool, LLM Explorer, in three weeks, with safeguards like stripping and re-inserting personal information from day one. Within days about a third of employees were using it. Today it has about 3,000 weekly active users, close to half the company, across engineering, sales and marketing. Leadership deliberately encouraged bottom-up experimentation with a Slack channel and hackathons, but it barely needed a push. Saveable, shareable prompt "presets" reached about 300 within a single day.
ex: Supports multiple models, starting with GPT-3.5 and GPT-4
A "style guide" preset that rewrites text in Stripe's voice still has thousands of users

n51|298.c: Applied AI runs on time-boxed "accelerator" teams plus a centralized LLM platform.
n51|298.e: An accelerator is an independent group the size of one or two pizza teams, funded by the CTO's office for about six months with a loose charter and milestones. Members are mostly long-tenured employees, so it doubles as talent rotation. The foundation is centralized: a shared LLM API already powers more than 60 applications, with a default model per use case that teams can override for cost or latency. The most expensive apps' costs are charged back to the teams using them. Stripe builds when needs are unusual, like a highly reliable experimentation platform, and buys when good tools exist.
ex: LLM Explorer came out of an accelerator
Buy Weights & Biases, build the experimentation platform

terms.d: About six months from the CTO's office

result.d: The right size is still unclear, she admits

n51|298.c: In payments products, LLMs help most by letting non-technical users write rules and query data in plain language.
n51|298.e: She sees LLMs doing two main things in customer-facing products: writing code automatically and speeding up information retrieval. Radar Assistant turns plain language into custom fraud rules, so fraud teams don't have to wait on developers, which matters because speed is critical against fraud. It also helps small businesses with no engineers. Sigma Assistant turns business questions into SQL, so users can query their own Stripe data directly. This pattern of writing policy in natural language could extend to other decision engines, such as underwriting.
ex: Sigma examples: December revenue, and which customers often pay late

items.d: Describe it, get a fraud rule

n51|298.c: Payments data points toward a financial foundation model and an "economic operating system."
n51|298.e: Stripe has long used traditional ML: optimizing authorization retries, smart dunning for failed payments, and scoring about a thousand transaction features in under 100 milliseconds. She estimates a foundation model trained on financial data could improve payment optimization by another 100 to 200 basis points. Further out, Stripe could become its users' "economic operating system," offering customer-level predictions and automating pricing, discounting and international expansion decisions. Real-time payments data could also give macro signals months ahead of lagging indicators like CPI.
ex: Optimized retries recover about 10% of false declines
Smart dunning cuts recurring payment failures by about 30%

n51|298.c: AI startups carry compute costs from day one, so they must monetize like real businesses much earlier.
n51|298.e: Unlike past software startups, AI companies face meaningful compute costs the day they open, so the pressure to make money comes sooner. Many products face global demand at launch, and consumer products are mostly subscriptions. So even tiny teams have to get revenue and finance operations running early, which pushes them to adopt Stripe's revenue and finance automation tools. The number of generative AI companies on Stripe surged in the past year, from two-person teams to scaled companies like Midjourney.
ex: More than half of last year's Forbes AI 50 used Stripe
OpenAI, Mistral and Runway are among its users

items.d: Small teams run like big companies

n52|301.c: Software should be composable blocks, but most people just want the job done, so ship templates.
n52|301.e: Notion doesn't hard-code every use case into the product. It builds basic blocks like text editing, relational databases, permissions and comments, and lets users assemble their own workflows. This comes from his college ideal of malleable software, inspired by Engelbart and Smalltalk. He thinks SaaS fragmentation has trapped users in separate apps for about twenty years. But the practical lesson is that most people don't want to build software. They want to get their work done, so the blocks have to be packaged into ready-to-use templates.
ex: Uses range from weddings and trip planning to company docs, tasks and wikis

items.d: Ready to use out of the box

n52|301.c: AI's most underrated opportunity is retrieval: people will no longer need to organize their information.
n52|301.e: He thinks agents and automation get more attention, but the sleeping opportunity is retrieval: models can understand content, so users no longer depend on keywords or careful organization. Notion Q&A lets people ask questions in plain language about everything they have saved, giving individuals and teams near-perfect memory, and someday it could push information to the people who need it. Snap a photo of a whiteboard, dump it into a note, and let the system organize it. Even Notion's signature left-hand sidebar tree may become unnecessary.
ex: He estimates a routine Slack question takes 10 minutes to write and 20 to answer
Such as how big the new office should be, without asking three people

items: Dump it in, the system organizes

d.verdict: Retrieval is perfect memory, and next it acts for you

n52|301.c: GPT-4 made him bet the company: knowledge work is mostly routing information between people.
n52|301.e: Early GPT-3 output was unreliable, and for a while he thought it was only good for marketing copy. Seeing a GPT-4 preview made him realize its potential for reasoning and workflows. His logic: most knowledge work is passing information between people, and language models are getting better at doing exactly that. Five-plus years of building blocks let Notion quickly add AI writing, AI in databases and Q&A. He believes change has to be gradual, and RAG is easy to accept precisely because it keeps familiar habits.
ex: High-end OpenAI and Anthropic models for reasoning, cheaper and faster ones for summaries

items.d: Saw potential for reasoning and workflows

n52|301.c: Software history cycles between bundling and unbundling, and this LLM round bundles around data.
n52|301.e: He reads the software industry through "history doesn't repeat, but it rhymes" and the Romance of the Three Kingdoms idea that what is long divided must unite. The 1980s were fragmented, the 1990s bundled around Microsoft's operating system, the mid-2000s brought SaaS unbundling, and the last decade-plus of cheap money fragmented things again. Now cost pressure and AI's need for centralized data are driving a rebundling. He disagrees with the YC-style view that distribution is the main wedge: Microsoft's bundle ran on distribution, while the LLM-era bundle runs on synergy from shared data.
ex: HubSpot and Rippling: each product 80% as good, but sold as a bundle
Oracle also succeeded by buying number-two products and bundling them

items.d: Cost savings plus AI's need for central data

n52|301.c: Design is how the whole system fits together, so it must be decided centrally, like an operating system.
n52|301.e: To him, design isn't surface appearance but how the whole system fits together. So Notion's design decisions are highly centralized, more like Apple than Amazon, much like designing a programming language or an operating system. The team is relatively small, and about 80% of designers can code, so they can make cross-disciplinary tradeoffs themselves. The office's classic furniture, lighting and jazz echo the product's aesthetic. He positions Notion as the front office of daily work and leaves vertical back-office systems to specialized software.
ex: The first three offices were shoes-off with heated floors
Companies use it to replace separate project and ticketing tools, and CFOs like that

marks.d: Centralized, like designing an operating system

n53|304.c: RAG is really semantic search. It cuts hallucinations a lot and narrows the gap between models.
n53|304.e: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) looks up relevant documents when a question comes in and hands them to the model along with the question, so the answer is more accurate. It works for public data and for a company's private data the model has never seen. His team ran experiments on Common Crawl, a public snapshot of the web: adding retrieval to several models cut hallucinations by up to about half in some cases, and models that had started out far apart in accuracy ended up close together. Text is the main data type, and legal documents, medical records, internal wikis, and sales calls are typical uses.
ex: They tested GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama, Mixtral, and Anthropic's models
Notion Q&A and the sales-analytics company Gong both run on Pinecone

result.d: Hallucinations down by up to half

n53|304.c: Neither keyword search nor a vector plug-in on an old database is the right answer.
n53|304.e: He thinks bolting a vector index onto a traditional database like Postgres (pgvector, for example) works at small scale but breaks down on performance and cost in production. Keyword search in the style of Elastic or Algolia points the wrong way entirely, because meaning lives in high-dimensional embeddings (long lists of numbers that capture what a passage means), not in the literal words. Everyone has failed to find an email by keyword. Pinecone supports both sparse vectors (close to keyword matching) and dense ones, so users can weight them, but his research shows that well-tuned embeddings rarely need keywords, and he expects the hybrid approach to fade.
ex: RAG needs hundreds of millions to tens of billions of vectors; early recommendation systems were far smaller

d.verdict: Search by meaning, not keywords

n53|304.c: A complex managed system doesn't need to be open source; reliability and service earn trust.
n53|304.e: Open source usually serves three purposes: building trust, attracting contributors, and reaching users. He argues trust can be earned through stability and service quality instead. As for contributions, more than ninety percent of the code at open-source companies comes from their own staff, so the community adds little. And Pinecone is a complex multi-tenant managed system (many customers share one infrastructure), which would be hard for anyone else to run even with the code. RAG also needs huge numbers of vectors, controlled cost, and easy operations, unlike earlier recommendation and anomaly-detection uses, which is why they rewrote the system almost from scratch a fourth time as serverless.
ex: Over ninety percent of code at open-source companies comes from their own employees
Serverless has been tested on live traffic with tens of billions of vectors

items.d: Hundreds of millions to billions of vectors

n53|304.c: Infinite context isn't the way forward; reasoning and knowledge should be kept separate.
n53|304.e: He is skeptical of very long context windows (how much text a model can take in at once). Providers charge per token, so selling bigger windows is good business, but the evidence shows that dumping in everything without care does not improve results. It just costs more. Stuffing all your documents into every query is like attaching the whole internet to every Google search. He would rather see foundation models broken into components. Today's models cram enormous amounts of knowledge into GPU memory, which he calls a blunt instrument. Separate reasoning from knowledge, and the same task gets much cheaper.
ex: Some users pair a model with a few billion parameters with huge vector data and get better results

n53|304.c: Don't fine-tune on private data; retrieve at query time, keep nothing, and compliance gets simpler.
n53|304.e: He sees two leak risks. One is the model provider keeping your data or training on it. The other is fine-tuning on private data (continuing to train the model on your own documents), after which that content can surface in someone else's answers. His advice is not to fine-tune on proprietary data at all. Retrieve the relevant records at query time, discard them afterward, and nothing ends up inside the model. That also makes GDPR, the EU privacy law, easier to satisfy: delete a document from the vector database and the model can never see it again, with no complicated "unlearning" needed. He admits fine-tuning works when done well, but without experts it is easy to break a model.

items.d: Never ends up in the model

n54|308.c: AMD rebuilt its CPUs before turning to AI, and its edge is having both CPUs and GPUs.
n54|308.e: AMD started out as the second-source supplier for components and x86 processors. When Lisa Su took over, the first job was to become competitive again, starting with CPUs. From 2012 to 2017 revenue came mostly from PCs and gaming, so those building blocks had to be strong before the company could pivot to AI. The Zen architecture in 2017 drove big growth in Ryzen and EPYC processors. He believes the industry needs heterogeneous computing: CPUs for step-by-step work, GPUs for massively parallel work. AMD has both, and since 2011 has shipped APUs that combine a CPU and GPU on one chip.
ex: Products span supercomputers, cloud servers, Xbox and PlayStation, and embedded devices
Acquired Xilinx and Pensando to add embedded and networking chips

items.d: APUs combining CPU and GPU launch

n54|308.c: He opposes closed software stacks: open ecosystems give customers choice, and competition forces better products.
n54|308.e: He admits GPU software took longer to mature than CPU software. AMD chose to go fully open: its compiler is built on LLVM and its ROCm software stack is open source, which was key to winning supercomputer contracts. It supports PyTorch, ONNX, and TensorFlow, and models from Hugging Face are tested on Instinct chips with nightly regression runs. He rejects locking customers into a proprietary walled garden and wants to win on the best solution. The CPU market before AMD's revival, he says, showed that without competition the whole industry stalls, which is bad for everyone.
ex: AMD is a founding member of the PyTorch Foundation
He says MI300 is competitive in training, leads in inference, and beat 2x in FP16 tests

n54|308.c: As Moore's Law slows, speed comes from mixed engines, chiplets, packaging, and hardware-software co-design.
n54|308.e: His view is that each new manufacturing node costs more and saves less power, so gains have to come from holistic design. That means matching each kind of workload to the right compute engine, splitting a big chip into chiplets so each function uses the most suitable process, connecting them with advanced packaging, and designing the hardware together with the software. MI300 is the example: CPU and GPU chiplets, memory controllers, and high-bandwidth memory are packaged together both side by side and stacked. He stresses that AMD relies on deep partnerships rather than trying to own the whole stack itself.
ex: MI300's pitch is more compute from less power and less rack space

n54|308.c: AI is spreading from training clusters to devices, and cloud and device should split work by latency.
n54|308.e: He sees demand shifting from giant training runs toward many smaller, fine-tuned models built for specific jobs, with inference moving into factories, embedded devices, and personal computers. AMD began adding AI inference acceleration to PC chips in 2023 and showed the next generation at CES 2024. Applications should put heavy work in the cloud and latency-sensitive work on the device: a self-driving car cannot depend on a network connection, and lag in VR makes people sick. From his time at Apple he learned that new hardware succeeds only when it meets a real need and creates a new category.
ex: An AI PC can do real-time translation with almost no delay
Generative AI mostly runs on GPUs, but much general inference still runs on CPUs

n54|308.c: Packaging and electricity are AI's bottlenecks, and chip capacity must be spread across regions.
n54|308.e: He sees semiconductors as a matter of national security now, so continuity of supply matters. Advanced packaging, the process of tightly assembling multiple chiplets, is one of AI's main bottlenecks, and electricity may become the tightest constraint on data centers, which makes energy efficiency the top design priority. AMD has worked with TSMC for decades and can usually anticipate shortages; during the pandemic it locked in substrate capacity (the board a chip sits on) ahead of time. He supports building fabs in several regions and spreading packaging capacity too, but warns that unlike software, hardware takes years to scale up.
ex: He backs TSMC in Arizona, Samsung in Texas, and new fabs in Europe and Asia

items.d: Capacity locked in during the pandemic

n55|95.c: Google is a sleeping giant that just woke up; all it lacked was the will to focus on AI.
n55|95.e: They see Gemini 1.5 as a strong release, especially its context window of about one million tokens, which matters for very long sequences like proteins. Google has top research talent, compute, data from the web, YouTube, and Gmail, distribution to billions of users, and years of experience running ad auctions. The only question was whether it could focus on AI among all its other missions. Elad, who used to work at Google, says this makes him more bullish: competition has reawakened the company's will to execute, and its release pace has clearly picked up in recent months.
ex: Gemini 1.5 has a context window of about one million tokens
Mistral reached roughly GPT-4 level in about nine months

n55|95.c: Long context won't replace retrieval; inference-time compute and domain models are the next step.
n55|95.e: They argue that longer context widens the trade-off space between retrieval, reasoning, and fine-tuning rather than making retrieval disappear, so the two will coexist. Game-playing AIs like poker bots do much of their thinking at inference time, and agent systems will lean on inference-time compute too. Training will also shift, from spending about $100 million on a single run that is used for a year toward continuous training on live feedback. They expect a wave of specialized models for chemistry, materials, biology, and robotics in 2024 and 2025.
ex: LLMs still can't reliably design a DNA sequence that expresses CRISPR-Cas9

root.d: Where new model capability comes from

items.d: Borrowed from poker and Go AIs

n55|95.c: AI returns are starting to show, and the services spend AI can replace dwarfs the software market.
n55|95.e: They note that the big AI money comes from large tech companies and cloud build-outs, not venture capital. About 5 percentage points of Microsoft Azure's growth came from AI, which they roughly estimate at $5 to 6 billion in new annual revenue, and Meta plans $30 to 37 billion in capital spending for 2024. On the return side, Klarna's AI customer service handled about 2.3 million conversations in four weeks, roughly two thirds of all inquiries, doing the work of about 700 full-time agents. Their back-of-envelope math: the US spends about $500 billion a year on software, while services wages AI could address total $3.5 to 5 trillion. Converting just a tenth of that equals the entire software market.
ex: Klarna's average resolution time fell from 11 minutes to 2
Adoption tends to start slow then accelerate: one leader forces rivals to follow

n55|95.c: 2024 is the year of applications: narrow agents work first, and app builders have just arrived.
n55|95.e: They think general-purpose agents accumulate errors across multi-step tasks, but agents already work in narrow domains with a feedback loop, such as coding, constrained web environments, and customer support. Paid human feedback makes the cost of polishing one task predictable. They describe three waves of talent: researchers founded the model companies and early applications first, infrastructure engineers came next, and application builders only started showing up about 15 months after ChatGPT launched. Many categories still have no one working on them. Technically strong big companies will build their own, while small and mid-sized businesses are more likely to buy.
ex: Meta, Shopify, and Klarna can build their own customer-service AI
Several medical-records apps are growing well

n55|95.c: Nvidia's edge is the whole system, and chip markets usually settle into one leader plus a strong second source.
n55|95.e: They see Nvidia's advantage as the combination of chip performance, its CUDA software that developers rely on, and the networking that links chips together; the 2019 purchase of Israel's Mellanox filled in the networking piece. Challengers include AMD and Intel, startups like Groq and Cerebras, and in-house chips like Google's TPU and AWS Trainium, which only need to run their owners' own workloads well. Chips built specifically for Transformers are a bet that the architecture stays put, and state-space models could open a new window. Historically, they note, chip markets tend to end up with one leader and one strong second supplier.
ex: Slow environmental reviews delay US fabs; Japan may become a second production base
TSMC's capacity, yields, and talent are hard to replicate

items.d: The whole system, not just transistors

n56|314.c: The collapsed Adobe deal brought clarity, and the team kept building through the long review.
n56|314.e: He saw selling to Adobe as a "one-way door," a decision you can't undo, and chose it hoping to speed up Figma's vision and learn from Adobe's team. Regulators objected, the review dragged on for about 16 months, and the deal ended at year's end. He told the team on the first day of the holidays, feeling that the clarity was valuable for starting the new year. The review was draining, but the team kept working. It finished a lot of foundational platform work, including Dev Mode, which hadn't been announced when the deal was signed.

items.d: Hoping to speed up the vision
Team told on the first holiday day

n56|314.c: Play isn't a gimmick: a playful mood makes people feel safe to speak up, which improves decisions.
n56|314.e: FigJam, Figma's online whiteboard, grew out of existing behavior: people already whiteboarded and drew diagrams, and usage surged when teams went remote during the pandemic. The team built a beta in about six to eight months. What sets it apart is fun: stickers, emoji reactions, cursor chat. He believes play creates psychological safety, so more people speak up and outcomes improve. At first, leadership doubted enterprises would buy it. Meetings in FigJam often turn into structured, visual decision documents, and AI can help teams set up that structure faster.

n56|314.c: Design is art that solves problems, so AI for design needs both diffusion models and LLMs.
n56|314.e: He maps diffusion models, the AI behind image generation, to art, and large language models to problem-solving. Design can be defined as art used to solve problems, so it may need a blend of the two. Figma deliberately slows its AI launches so features are at least useful and ideally great. A prompt can't hold culture, emotion, user context and product needs, so AI works best as a first-draft collaborator, refined through back-and-forth between people and the model. It lowers the bar for non-designers and takes repetitive work off professional designers' plates.
ex: Image generation that updates live as you type
Sliders that control a parametric 3D model

n56|314.c: AI won't kill the interface. New media add to old ones, so we'll get more software and UI.
n56|314.e: He disagrees that AI will make UI vanish into chat or invisible agents, AI that acts on your behalf. New media don't wipe out old ones: TikTok didn't kill YouTube. He doubts voice will become the main way people take in information all day, and he isn't sold on Minority Report-style gesture controls, though he still supports exploring new modes.
