He is especially bullish on smart cameras, because people struggle to describe a scene in words but almost everyone can take a photo. Nor does he think designers will be replaced. AI will mostly augment them and expand the field.
ex: Engineers will spend more time designing, and programming will move to higher abstractions

items: New media layer on old ones

d.verdict: New interaction modes add; they don't replace

n56|314.c: Figma wants to be more than a design tool, covering everything from idea to launch.
n56|314.e: Figma has three parts today: FigJam for brainstorming, Figma Design for design, and Dev Mode for turning designs into code. Developers are very active but not very satisfied. They often build the wrong thing, struggle to find their way around Figma, and want better links to design systems and plugins. So Dev Mode added annotations, properties, change tracking, and plugins such as Jira. Next, Figma wants to use AI to connect ideas, design and code, simplify the product so more people can take part, and eventually extend into launching, measuring and experimenting.
ex: Developers make up about a third of Figma's users
The company value in focus now is "Run with it": see a chance, take it

items.d: Shipping and experiments, the future direction

n57|319.c: Engineers want code, not no-code: easy abstractions that still let them tune the internals.
n57|319.e: Baseten is about four and a half years old, and its early product leaned no-code. Over the past three or four years, the team learned that engineers want to write code and need access to the internals. No-code doesn't always remove the knobs, but it makes them hard to turn. So Baseten's pitch is selling efficient code: intuitive abstractions that make common tasks simple, with room for deep tuning, supporting customers from launch to large scale. It also doesn't offer bare GPUs, and he thinks adding another abstraction layer for AMD chips would be too complex and slow the company down.
ex: Customers range from weekend projects to AI-native and established firms like Descript and Patreon

n57|319.c: Inference and training are different businesses, and inference cares most about latency, workflows and reliability.
n57|319.e: Inference, running a trained model to answer user requests, needs to sit close to users and respond fast, while training cares more about networking between GPUs inside one cluster. Inference has lots of workflow that repeats across customers: versioning, CI/CD, cold starts and deployment. Training teams often just want raw compute. When inference goes down, end users feel it immediately, so the reliability bar is much higher. Customers usually start on shared endpoints, move to dedicated compute, and large enterprises eventually deploy into their own AWS or GCP accounts.
ex: Picnic Health extracts information from medical records using its own data

d.verdict: Inference is an ongoing, productizable business

n57|319.c: Speed is the top advantage, so buy infrastructure and spend your energy on models and data.
n57|319.e: He believes speed trumps everything in this market, and companies that don't compete on speed will fall behind, so enterprises would rather buy than build. A customer's truly proprietary assets are its models, data and workflows. Infrastructure is the part everyone duplicates. Many companies say at first they'll build it themselves, then change their minds a few months later because they underestimated the complexity and scale involved. His example: a company with a two-year-old AI infrastructure team moved onto Baseten in 36 hours, freeing four engineers to work on what sets it apart.
ex: A six-person chatbot company processes about a billion tokens a day
An outage during a launch wrecks the user experience

n57|319.c: Inference speed improves through three stacked levers: better hardware, software optimization and smaller models.
n57|319.e: He says language model output speeds have climbed from about 90 tokens per second to 100, then 200, and some now reach three or four hundred. On the software side, the gains come from continuous or dynamic batching, speculative decoding and handing some steps to smaller models. Baseten also worked with Nvidia to improve TensorRT-LLM. On hardware, the move is from H100 to H200 chips. Models will shrink and specialize through distillation, and more inference will run locally. Performance will eventually become a commodity, so you have to stay at the cutting edge or risk not surviving.
ex: Sourcegraph runs Cody on-premises for many customers
Gamma wants image generation faster than today's four to five seconds

items.d: He says three or four hundred

n57|319.c: Enterprise AI adoption is overhyped in the short run and underestimated over three to five years.
n57|319.e: Most enterprises are still planning, mostly using Copilot-style tools and just starting to plug into OpenAI or Anthropic. Pfizer reportedly set aside tens of millions of dollars from the top down, and he worries this echoes the CIO-driven buying of 2018–2020, disconnected from user value. Long term, though, 10x growth is possible: one customer with under a thousand users spends hundreds of thousands a year on a single use case and is already cash-flow positive. Inference may become one of the biggest costs on the P&L, so the roughly 80% gross margins of traditional SaaS are no longer a given.
ex: One customer refused to prepay a year of compute: it's their second-biggest expense
Medical note apps built on Whisper are growing fast

items.d: Most still at the Copilot stage
Under 1,000 users, six figures a year

n58|321.c: The low-level abstractions stay fairly stable; what changes fastest is how the pieces get combined.
n58|321.e: LangChain began as a side project in late 2022, and ChatGPT's launch a month later made it take off. The integrations and core abstractions have stayed fairly stable, and the team only had to add new abstractions when model APIs moved to a chat format. They also built a low-level runtime focused on streaming and structured output, plus LangGraph, which supports loops, because an agent is basically an LLM running in a loop. The biggest change is in how components fit together at the top layer: the field is moving from free-running agents toward controlled state machines.
ex: About 700 integrations today
The first version drew on Nat Friedman's NatBot web agent

n58|321.c: Planning is agents' biggest weakness, and UX and testing practices are far from mature.
n58|321.e: He sees LLM planning as the biggest gap. For now, developers have to break tasks into small pieces and encode domain knowledge into the flow of information. Research on explicit up-front planning and "reflection" checks is moving forward but still falls short. UX isn't settled either: apps need to explain what an agent is and isn't good at, and let users see and correct intermediate steps. Testing also lacks a mature process. The agents actually in production cluster in customer support, coding and recommendation-style chat, all of which have clear feedback loops.
ex: In customer support he likes Sierra, and Klarna's launch is a good example
Cognition's coding agent demo impressed him

items.d: Biggest weakness; humans break down tasks
Show intermediate steps and allow corrections

n58|321.c: AI memory comes in two kinds, system-level and personal, and the whole field is very early.
n58|321.e: System-level memory means knowing how to use tools and finish tasks no matter who the user is. It mostly comes from few-shot examples, sometimes fine-tuning. Personal memory means remembering facts like a user's interests. He sees ChatGPT's memory as the model actively calling functions to save and fetch facts, and he also likes passively distilling conversations in the background. Each approach has tradeoffs. He isn't very satisfied with progress here, and says that if he were starting a company today, he would build an app that makes full use of long-term memory.

items: Model calls functions to save it
Or distills it in the background

d.verdict: Both early; long-term memory apps are the opportunity

n58|321.c: Long context won't kill RAG, and needle-in-a-haystack tests are too narrow.
n58|321.e: Long context windows make single tasks simpler, like pulling information from a long PDF or doing RAG (retrieve documents, then answer) over a few long documents. But some data still won't fit in any window, and iterative tasks that interact with an environment and get feedback still need chains and agents. Real RAG often means combining several facts and reasoning over them. His colleague Lance Martin's tests show performance drops as you add more needles, and drops further when reasoning is required. Retrieval itself is becoming multi-step: analyze the query, then pick a retriever, extract keywords and add filters.
ex: Text chunking is where he's least sure; a parent document retriever is one approach

n58|321.c: A few-shot data flywheel beats fine-tuning in practice and points the way to continual learning.
n58|321.e: People talk about fine-tuning a lot, but few actually do it, and mostly only at large scale. Datasets are hard to collect, results are hard to evaluate, and each iteration is far slower than tweaking prompts and examples. He finds few-shot examples faster and cheaper, and easier than programmatic prompt optimization. Continual learning can work like this: the app makes a mistake, the user corrects it, and that correction goes back in as a new example, so the app learns from both successes and failures. He sees this as close to Stanford's DSPy, except done online and driven by user feedback.
ex: Switching models is hard because prompts are tailored to each model
He thinks open-source models still trail GPT-4 and Claude 3 at reasoning

n59|327.c: If humanoid robots work, they'll be the biggest business in the world.
n59|327.e: His starting point is that human labor is about half of GDP, an order of magnitude bigger than the entire transportation market. Robots doing real work every day could bring goods and services into an "age of abundance." The world is designed around the human body, so a humanoid is like a computer's keyboard and mouse: a general-purpose interface to the physical world. One hardware platform can be spread across millions of tasks, while building a thousand specialized robots would need a company, a team and capital for each one.
ex: He says it could be an order of magnitude bigger than other businesses
He admits many roboticists think two legs are unstable

items: Each needs a company, team, capital
Fits a world built for humans

d.verdict: The question isn't the form, but whether it can be built

n59|327.c: Batteries, motors, walking and AI have matured at once, making humanoid robots feasible.
n59|327.e: He thinks that ten years ago, neither battery life nor actuator strength was good enough. Battery energy density has improved only modestly, but motors have gained power and torque density. Bipedal walking has advanced hugely: at the DARPA Robotics Challenge about a decade ago, robots stumbled and fell, while Figure got its robot walking in under a year. AI compute and algorithms have also reached a usable level. He expects speech to be the default interface, with even out-of-box setup done by talking to the robot.
ex: Figure is about 21 months old
In the demo, a neural network outputs the motion directly

result.d: Any one alone wasn't enough before

n59|327.c: Industry before homes: factories let Figure ship sooner, gather data and scale up.
n59|327.e: Industrial settings let Figure ship faster, build a data engine and scale up manufacturing. Homes are unstructured, failures carry bigger safety risks, and consumers are more price-sensitive. The first public customer is BMW, at its Spartanburg plant. Figure has identified and ranked five use cases, and the first is moving toward reliable end-to-end operation. He rejects the idea that robots will always be expensive: design for manufacturing plus the experience curve will drive costs down, much like Ford's Model T.
ex: He says BMW's Spartanburg plant builds about 1,400 cars a day
Customers have already paid for robots delivered this year

items.d: Design for manufacturing plus experience curve

n59|327.c: OpenAI's models handle high-level reasoning, while Figure's handle low-level movement.
n59|327.e: OpenAI supplies top vision-language models and high-level language reasoning, and Figure builds the low-level neural networks that control the motors and hands. He compares it to a brain: a central model turns a request like "fold the laundry" into a task plan, and Figure's models carry it out physically. With more than 30 degrees of freedom, the robot has a huge space of possible movements, so behaviors must be learned rather than hand-coded. He also thinks large models are weak at physical reasoning and planning, and data from robots may be key to reaching AGI.
ex: A demo with voice conversation and memory came about 13 days after the deal was announced

items.d: Figure's neural nets drive the motors

n59|327.c: Hardware cycles run 10 to 100 times longer than software, so speed culture and fast prototyping matter.
n59|327.e: Speed is one of Figure's five values, alongside "aggressive optimism": when you hit an unknown problem, the answer is to work harder. He drew the org chart himself, made about 300 calls and emails over six months to recruit, and hired 30 to 50 people in the first year. There's a 9 a.m. daily standup, and people are expected in the office five to seven days a week. With no mature supply chain, Figure had to build most parts itself, including actuators. The process starts from customer needs, runs trade studies and several design reviews, and prototypes early to learn from failures.
ex: Most parts are built in-house, except battery cells, GPUs and CPUs
The focus for the next 12–24 months is reliability and speed

n60|95.c: Frontier-class models spread faster than expected, but the very top will stay a small club.
n60|95.e: A year ago, most people expected a monopoly or oligopoly. Now it looks like there may be several GPT-4-class models by year's end, including open-source ones. Mistral and Databricks' DBRX built strong models with compute in the tens of millions of dollars. Databricks claims the cost of the same capability falls about 4x a year, though the hosts doubt that rests on solid theory. Still, capital requirements will keep the frontier limited to a few players, and strong models can help label data and train the next generation.

marks.d: Several by year-end, open source included

n60|95.c: Model companies are funded mostly by cloud providers, and their compute spending flows back as cloud revenue.
n60|95.e: The hosts think foundation model funding comes mainly from cloud providers and big tech, Nvidia included. VCs supply only early rounds of tens to hundreds of millions of dollars, and in China big internet companies play the same role. Clouds pay up because model companies drive compute usage, and hosting all kinds of open and closed models on the cloud is itself profitable, a point people underrate. Microsoft hiring the Inflection team shows it doesn't want to rely on OpenAI as its only outside partner.
ex: About 5 points of Microsoft Azure's growth came from AI, roughly $1.5 billion a quarter
They expect fewer new LLM companies and more funding for video, biology and robotics

items.d: Training and inference run in the cloud

n60|95.c: The app layer is wide open, and AI video is a deep product problem, not just a modality.
n60|95.e: Gaps they list include reasoning over time-series data with common sense (anomaly detection, infrastructure monitoring, security, healthcare), robotics, which needs embodied control data, and finance, where few people understand both AI and accounting. Many teams chase the same idea, just as lots of photo apps came before Instagram, so success depends on the product. Demand for video generation is huge, but length, quality, controllability and interfaces all fall short. Adding some constraints to creation actually makes it easier for ordinary people to get started.
ex: HeyGen launched a feature that swaps the script but keeps the speaker's motion
Several companies may have strong voice models held back over deepfake concerns

n60|95.c: Agent interfaces are moving beyond the chat box, and using one feels like managing an eager intern.
n60|95.e: Cognition's Devin, an AI that writes code on its own, shows a useful interface: the plan, a terminal, the code being written, a browser and a chat channel side by side. Users can watch progress, change direction at any time, and supply login credentials when needed. The hosts compare these agents to eager junior interns who need guidance and regular check-ins. Human-in-the-loop interfaces are a transitional form: as agents and reasoning get stronger, many of these interfaces may eventually disappear.

items.d: Plan, terminal, browser side by side
Agents finish alone as reasoning improves

n60|95.c: Prosumers will embrace AI before enterprises, because a $10-a-month tool is an easy call.
n60|95.e: Enterprise sales mean security reviews, procurement and risk assessments, so they move slowly, while an individual can decide on a $10-a-month tool on the spot. Prosumer companies can later grow into professional-grade products. History follows this pattern: the internet in the '90s went consumer first and B2B later, the mobile era was led by consumer apps like Uber, Instacart and WhatsApp, and email took the same path. So they expect the first wave of AI adoption to be driven by prosumer apps.
ex: About $1 billion of Canva's roughly $1.7 billion ARR comes from prosumers

n61|333.c: He picked images because the bar was low, the output spreads itself, and rivals weren't focused.
n61|333.e: In 2022, DALL·E 2 and Stable Diffusion showed him image generation had matured early, yet people were still tinkering in Colab notebooks with no good product. He considered music but couldn't think of a useful product form. Language was crowded with well-funded companies. Images are both creative and practical, and people naturally share what they make. OpenAI's commitment to DALL·E was unclear, and Stability was spread too thin, which left room for a company focused on doing one thing well.
ex: In 2022 he got about two weeks of early access to SD 1.4
Language had 20-plus companies, several with over $1 billion raised

items.d: Creative and practical, built to be shared

n61|333.c: Training from scratch is far harder than expected, and the final fine-tune on curated data matters most.
n61|333.e: The team kept the SDXL architecture to see how far a research team could push the existing recipe. After switching to EDM's noise schedule, SDXL's washed-out gray look mostly disappeared and colors and contrast got richer, so much that he first thought the eval images had a bug. Tricks like power EMA, offset noise and DPO each added 10–20%. But the biggest impact came from a final supervised fine-tune on hand-picked data. That takes aesthetic judgment, and images depend on taste even more than language does.
ex: After switching to EDM, blacks got deeper and contrast stronger
A single trick adds about 10–20%, a few up to 2x

terms.d: EDM, power EMA, DPO and more

result.d: Testing the limits of the existing recipe

n61|333.c: Industry benchmarks mostly serve marketing and miss what users actually care about.
n61|333.e: He thinks many benchmarks are like having a language model do homework problems: the scores look good but don't mean the model is useful. Playground's model scored well overall, yet its photorealistic portraits went wrong, with faces that looked tired. Celebrities, paintings, 3D, illustration and logos all need coverage, so the team manually reviews thousands of images across checkpoints to pick a release. He admits their own evals still aren't strong enough. User votes can supply preference data, but they must be dead simple, because users come to make images, not to label them.
ex: High overall scores, but realistic faces looked tired
Thousands of images reviewed by hand before each release

d.verdict: Evals should track users, not leaderboards

n61|333.c: The next step is moving from loot-box generation to editing images users already have.
n61|333.e: He reckons Playground ranks about second in text-to-image and is catching up fast by training from scratch, but its long-term edge lies in editing. Generation today feels like pulling a slot machine: getting what you want takes a lot of effort. Meanwhile users have plenty of images they want to tweak: swapping a person, keeping a character consistent, adding their own logo, or restyling a real photo while matching the lighting. Models can do far more than turn a description into art, and limiting them to art caps their practical value.
ex: Consistent characters, logo placement, restyled photos

n61|333.c: Pixels carry more information than text, and vision will eventually merge with language in big models.
n61|333.e: The long-term goal is a large vision model that can generate, edit and understand images. Images come first because video is extremely expensive to train and run, and 3D struggles to earn creators money. He likes diffusion transformers such as DiT and MMDiT, but thinks training only on caption-image pairs isn't enough, since the model lacks the knowledge language models have. Language is compressed information, while images carry lighting, physics and spatial relationships. Visual data can be collected almost without limit, while internet text may run out sooner.
ex: Two people describing a shattered glass will write very different text
Video models are often pretrained on about a billion images first

items.d: Generate, edit and understand in one

n62|336.c: Generating realistic video requires understanding the world, so Sora is a path to world simulators.
n62|336.e: Take the snowy Tokyo street scene: the camera moves through crowds and market stalls. To generate that, the model has to learn how people, animals and objects move and interact. He thinks continuing to scale along this path will produce world simulators that people can interact with and even hand tasks to. That is where video generation connects to AGI.
ex: A winter street in Tokyo, with the camera weaving past crowds and stalls

n62|336.c: Sora is on the early GPT path, and new abilities will emerge as it scales.
n62|336.e: The team has always compared Sora to the GPT series. GPT-1 and GPT-2 had limited abilities, and impressive capabilities only appeared as they scaled up. He sees today's Sora as an early point on the scaling curve for vision, and expects the same pattern to repeat for video.

n62|336.c: Many safety measures carry over from DALL·E 3, but release must be gradual so society can adapt.
n62|336.e: Practices like blocking gory or violent content can be inherited directly from DALL·E 3, OpenAI's image model. The new problem video brings is mainly misinformation. How responsibility should be split among the model maker, the platforms where content is posted (for example, by labeling untrustworthy content) and users is still an open question. The team wants to give people creative freedom while opening up step by step, so society has time to adjust.

items.d: Content filters carried over from DALL·E 3
Gradual release so society can adapt

n62|337.c: There's no product timeline yet; artists and red teamers try it first to shape the direction.
n62|337.e: OpenAI wants outside input before deciding what the product looks like, so it has opened Sora only to a small group of artists and red teamers, people who probe for risks, looking at both usefulness and safety. The most common feedback is about control: text is the only input, which makes precise control hard, so the team is considering other input methods. For now the focus remains core research, not specific applications like digital avatars.
ex: Feedback centers on control: text is the only input

n62|337.c: Diffusion transformers improve steadily as compute and data grow.
n62|337.e: Sora starts from pure noise and removes it step by step until a video emerges, which is what diffusion means. The denoising network uses the same transformer architecture as GPT, so adding data and compute reliably improves results. In the technical report, the same prompt run at increasing compute levels gives clearly better quality each time, and the team expects that trend to continue.

n62|337.c: The biggest value is letting creative people without resources tell their stories.
n62|337.e: He is most excited for people with ideas but no budget or tools to make their work. The shorts artists made with Sora show that the value lies in a complete story, not a single stunning shot. In the next few years more films will be made with tools like this, but he is more excited about new content forms and ways of interacting that don't fit existing categories yet, and about educational videos tailored to each person.
ex: Shy Kids' short Airhead, whose hero has a balloon for a head

marks.d: More in the next few years

n62|338.c: Video holds physical knowledge that text lacks, and it's vital for robotics and embodied AI.
n62|338.e: How limbs move and how objects touch the ground are details you almost never find in language data, but they can be learned from raw video. He sees this knowledge as a necessary foundation for embodied intelligence and robotics, and an important reason to bet on video beyond language.

d.verdict: Vision is a necessary step toward embodied AI

n62|338.c: Cutting video into spacetime patches used as tokens unifies all kinds of visual data.
n62|338.e: A key to language models' success is that tokens put all kinds of text into one format. Earlier vision models trained only on short clips at a fixed small size, throwing away lots of usable data. Sora cuts compressed video into spacetime cubes, small patches of image across a slice of time, and treats them as tokens. That lets it handle different resolutions, durations and aspect ratios, and generate images too. It became the first visual generator to approach language models in breadth of data, at the cost of rebuilding much of the data infrastructure.
ex: The old way: fixed 256×256 clips of about 4 seconds
Handles aspect ratios from about 1:2 to 2:1

root.d: A unified unit for visual data

items.d: No more cropping to fixed sizes
An image is a one-frame video

n62|338.c: Video models have scaling laws too, and the goal is lower loss for the same compute.
n62|338.e: One benefit of using transformers is that they inherit the scaling behavior seen in language models. The team is systematically studying scaling laws for video, looking for ways to push loss lower for the same compute. He believes the most scalable methods all predict the data directly, as GPT predicts text and Sora predicts visual data, rather than optimizing complicated proxy objectives.

items.d: Lower loss for the same compute

n62|338.c: Sora understands 3D without being taught it, but complex object interactions still often fail.
n62|338.e: The team never explicitly fed the model 3D information, yet it learned three-dimensional structure from video. It can also keep track of state: a burger keeps its bite mark, and a watercolor brush leaves a trail. But fine-grained object interactions are still unreliable. A kicked ball might vanish or appear out of nowhere, while simple motions like walking are already stable. Reaching more people will take lower costs and faster generation, and first dealing with misinformation risks in settings like elections.
ex: A burger keeps its bite mark after being bitten
A kicked ball may vanish into thin air
Generating a long video takes several minutes

items: Keeps state like bites and brushstrokes

d.verdict: These should improve with scale

n63|343.c: Competitive programming and startups are alike: both mean questioning assumptions and reasoning from first principles.
n63|343.e: In informatics olympiads every problem is new. Classic algorithms like shortest paths and binary search trees are just the foundation, and what matters is applying them creatively. Progress comes from sustained effort and honesty about your own weaknesses. To him, a startup is the same: finding ideas the world doesn't believe yet and challenging premises nobody has tested. Cognition was founded around November 2023, and its founders all came from the competition world, where many people later started companies or went into AI.
ex: He knew Alexandr Wang back in high school
Almost everyone on the team has founded or seriously considered founding a company

n63|343.c: Devin is an AI engineer that makes its own decisions and completes tasks end to end.
n63|343.e: You describe what you want built, and Devin works like a human engineer: writing and editing code, using the command line and browser, reading docs, deploying, testing and debugging. Its panels for the plan, terminal, code and browser were designed by working backward from how the team itself would want to collaborate with an AI teammate. Early agents often ran heads-down for hours and came back with useless results. Checking in and course-correcting regularly, as you would with a junior engineer, produces much better work.

items.d: Like looking at a coworker's screen

n63|343.c: AI multiplies each engineer's output, so there will be more engineers, not fewer.
n63|343.e: He gives two reasons. First, demand is nearly unlimited: lots of convoluted Excel workarounds should really be code, and multiplying capacity will only unlock more demand. Second, Devin doesn't decide what to build, so people still define the problem and the solution. He estimates engineers spend about 20% of their time thinking through the core problem and 80% writing implementation code, and AI could let them do about 5x more. It's like when human computers, people who did calculations by hand, disappeared and moved on to more valuable work.
ex: About 30 million engineers worldwide, only 0.4% of the population

items.d: AI can take over much of it

n63|343.c: Agents excel at step-by-step, trial-and-error setup and analysis, but can't set direction themselves.
n63|343.e: Encyclopedic knowledge plus a loop of running commands, reading errors, checking ports and installing dependencies is exactly what agents are good at. The team once spent an hour stuck on a database and Kubernetes setup, and Devin got it working. It can also do data analysis end to end. But it needs people to give precise specs. When fixing a GitHub issue, the good approach is to reproduce it, add logging and look things up, rather than stare at the code and guess. Much of Cognition's work is teaching Devin to plan this way.
ex: Devin finished a database and K8s setup the team was stuck on for an hour
Find data, clean CSVs, analyze and chart, all in one go

n63|343.c: Future engineers will be more like architects plus product managers, but fundamentals still matter.
n63|343.e: He agrees English is becoming a programming language, but fundamentals like network protocols, logic gates, algorithms and logical reasoning won't go out of date. Within a year or two, engineers who use AI well will multiply their output. In five to ten years, engineers will mainly break business problems into concrete solutions and leave implementation to agents. People may someday find it strange that we learned obscure languages and read stack traces just to talk to computers. Foundation models are improving at reasoning, planning, tool use and speed, and he can't say which will improve fastest.

items.d: In 5–10 years, focused on defining solutions

n64|95.c: Small models will run on devices, and local AI assistants will be standard within a year or two.
n64|95.e: Apple releasing roughly 1-billion and 3-billion-parameter models on Hugging Face shows developers need models that run on edge devices. Local inference is fast and cheap, and it enables proactive experiences. The hosts expect Apple to wire local models into its ecosystem, and apps that index your files, build embeddings and let you chat on your desktop should become common within a year or two. They suggest splitting capabilities like reasoning, synthesis, multimodality and stored knowledge one by one, seeing which can run on-device now and which need the cloud, and tracking that line as hardware improves.
ex: Apple released 1B and 3B parameter models on Hugging Face

marks.d: Most uses still need the cloud

n64|95.c: Platforms tend to absorb the most valuable features built on them, so standalone apps should be careful.
n64|95.e: One view is that platforms pull the most valuable things into themselves, so building an app on someone else's platform is risky. The spreadsheet, presentation and word processing tools in Office all started as third-party products. A counterexample is Veeva, which began as a layer on top of Salesforce, grew into a roughly $40 billion vertical SaaS company for pharma, and later replaced its Salesforce foundation. The other view holds that the outcome depends on the product itself and whether it works across platforms.
ex: Veeva is worth about $40 billion, Salesforce about $266 billion

items: Office apps began as third-party tools

d.verdict: It depends on going cross-platform and standing alone

n64|95.c: AI compute spending is huge, but not unprecedented in the history of infrastructure.
n64|95.e: Investors often ask how much the world should spend on AI and whether it's rational. The hosts think "should" comes down to a few decision-makers willing to bet on exponential growth. The cloud giants will spend nearly $200 billion combined on AI compute this year, with Meta alone at an estimated $30–35 billion. Compared with roughly $80 billion a year for oil majors and about $100 billion for broadband buildout, that isn't outlandish. Meta found performance kept improving after training past the so-called optimal point, which favors the giants. Countries may also fund sovereign models for their own languages and cultures.

n64|95.c: Like bandwidth, context windows will keep getting longer for a long time.
n64|95.e: So-called infinite context is really about actively managing context. Magic launched a 5-million-token window (Sarah is an investor), Gemini 1.5 reached 1 million, and the hosts expect many providers to hit tens of millions within a year or two. At that point whole codebases, legal files and large batches of support tickets can go straight into the prompt. In biology models, longer context has already improved the accuracy of protein structure prediction. Just as internet access went from dial-up to broadband to fiber, longer will stay valuable for a long time.
ex: Gemini 1.5 handles about 1 million tokens, Magic 5 million

items.d: Expected to spread within a year or two

n64|95.c: The bottleneck is shifting from chips to data centers and energy, with nuclear power a key variable.
n64|95.e: The constraint has moved from chips to packaging and now to data centers and power. No one has built a 500-megawatt to 1-gigawatt data center yet, roughly the output of a nuclear plant, and training requires GPUs to sit in one place. Permitting slows construction, a physical-world problem. The US largely stopped building nuclear plants in the 1970s, and nuclear now supplies about 17–18% of its power, versus about 70% in France and 30% in Japan. Plentiful cheap power would change the economics of compute and reduce dependence on oil-producing countries.
ex: Nuclear share of power: US 17–18%, France about 70%, Japan about 30%
Microsoft invested $1.5 billion in Abu Dhabi's G42

items.d: GPUs must be in one place

n65|347.c: Audio lags far behind images and text, and music offers more creative room than speech.
n65|347.e: He has a physics PhD and later did machine learning at Kensho. After S&P acquired the company, the team's first audio project was automatically transcribing earnings calls. That got them hooked on audio AI, and showed them that audio was clearly behind images and text, with the gap still widening. After open-sourcing Bark, they chose music over speech: speech just has to be accurate, while music is about how people feel. He admits a B2B speech business would have been more straightforward.
ex: S&P Global acquired Kensho in 2018
The team open-sourced the audio model Bark

d.verdict: Choose music: harder, but more creative

n65|347.c: The model is a plain transformer; the real work is audio tokenization, with no music theory hard-coded.
n65|347.e: Suno openly uses transformers: they scale well, and the open-source text community has already paved the way. Its own research focuses on turning audio into tokens. Audio is a continuous signal sampled about 50,000 times per second, so it has to be compressed into manageable discrete units using heuristics or learned models. He deliberately avoids building music theory, scale systems or lists of instruments into the model, believing that would limit the output. Borrowing next-token prediction from text works surprisingly well.
ex: Audio has about 50,000 samples per second

n65|347.c: Music has no right answer, so quality can only be judged by ear and A/B tests.
n65|347.e: Technical metrics like stereo and bitrate are easy to measure. The hard part is emotional impact, which varies by culture, age and audience. A language model can be scored on the bar exam, but music has no objective standard, and whether a song takes off may depend on hard-to-pin-down factors like graininess or length. He warns that AI is prone to over-optimizing benchmarks and losses that have nothing to do with real value. Suno relies mainly on team listening sessions, internal reviews and A/B tests, and admits evaluation still has a long way to go.

marks.d: Affects hits but hard to explain

n65|347.c: Suno is for everyday people, and charging early reveals why users are willing to pay.
n65|347.e: The product isn't for hobbyists making music late into the night, or a plugin for professional audio software. It's for ordinary people like his mom. Because Suno is creating a new behavior, charging early is the best way to learn what people will pay for. He thinks generative AI companies mostly copy crude SaaS subscription pricing out of habit, since the same investors and founders keep doing it, and that it may not be the long-term answer. They haven't figured out the business model yet.

items.d: Learn what people will pay for

n65|347.c: The line between making and listening will blur, and people will spend far more time on music.
n65|347.e: Users enjoy the act of creating itself, like jamming with friends: writing lyrics together, taking turns on verses, passing songs back and forth, even putting their names in song titles to climb the trending chart. Writing a song for a few friends to capture a shared moment barely exists in music today. He expects lots of lean-in listening and lean-back creating. Just as DAWs, software for recording and producing music on a computer, let more people make music and sped up cultural change, time and money spent on music will grow sharply, without pulling people away from the artists they love.
ex: Users put their names in song titles to climb the trending chart
His recent favorite genre is sitar trap

n66|245.c: Of AI's three pillars, algorithms, compute and data, data was the one neglected first.
n66|245.e: At MIT in 2016, he realized neural networks are essentially products of their training data. Big labs were working on algorithms and Nvidia on compute, but no one was focused on data, so he dropped out and founded Scale. The company started with labeling for self-driving cars, fusing camera and lidar data, then moved into satellite imagery for government. Starting in the GPT-2 era, it worked with OpenAI on early RLHF, which led to InstructGPT. Today nearly every major large-model team is a customer.
ex: Self-driving customers included GM, Toyota and Stellantis
Supported the US Department of Defense's first AI program of record

n66|245.c: The easy data is used up, but the industry can choose data abundance over scarcity.
n66|245.e: Public internet data has largely been consumed. What's needed next is frontier data with stronger supervision: expert reasoning chains, many languages, multiple modalities, and traces of agents working through enterprise, consumer and coding tasks. One source is top experts such as mathematicians, doctors and lawyers. The other is the vast private data held by companies and governments. The best approach is hybrid human-AI synthetic data, where AI does the heavy lifting and experts check the work. Tens of billions spent on compute must be matched by equal investment in data.
ex: JPMorgan holds about 150 petabytes of private data
GPT-4 was trained on less than one petabyte

n66|245.c: The question isn't whether models beat humans, but whether humans plus models beat models alone.
n66|245.e: Models have many quirks unlike human intelligence, such as lopsided performance on rot13 versus rot8 ciphers, or the reversal curse, where learning "A is B" doesn't teach "B is A." What they're good at is a small cup of human intelligence, and they struggle to reason over long stretches or pursue goals persistently. Med-PaLM 2 beats general doctors on some questions, but cardiologists still do better. Experts can catch factual and reasoning errors and guide long chains of reasoning, so human-AI complementarity will last. Closing the gap on long-horizon ability will take data, not just architecture.
ex: Med-PaLM 2 beats general doctors but trails cardiologists

n66|245.c: Public benchmarks are widely contaminated, so trust requires private holdout sets and expert evaluation.
n66|245.e: AI runs on a loop of data, training and evaluation, and only reliable measurement lets governments, companies and labs adopt models with confidence. Many models overfit public benchmarks because the questions have leaked into training data. Scale's held-out math set, GSM1k, showed some models performing well below their self-reported scores. He argues for transparent leaderboards and expert evaluation, and Scale launched private evals that are rerun regularly, starting with math, coding, instruction following and adversarial robustness.
ex: GSM1k: some models scored well below their self-reported numbers

n66|245.c: Reaching AGI looks more like curing cancers one by one than developing a single vaccine.
n66|245.e: He doesn't buy the single-breakthrough story. Capabilities transfer only a little: training on one modality doesn't help much with others, so each capability area needs its own data flywheel, the way cancers have to be tackled one type at a time. That means progress will be steady and incremental, giving society time to adapt. He is also skeptical that models can learn a world model just by watching video, calling it a nice story with little evidence. Recent multimodal launches are horizontal expansion, and the industry needs smarter models more.

items: A data flywheel for each domain

d.verdict: AGI will arrive step by step

n67|350.c: "GPT wrapper" is a wrong-headed insult; AI is a technology that has to be put to work.
n67|350.e: About 70% of the current YC batch are AI companies, and about two-thirds of those build application software on top of frontier models. Calling them wrappers is like calling every SaaS company a MySQL wrapper. The turning point was GPT-4. Casetext's Jake Heller got early access, found it barely hallucinated anymore, and broke a lawyer's real work (reading a brief paragraph by paragraph, flagging key points, building a timeline) into prompts, workflows, tests and scoring. Many YC companies are doing this kind of detailed breakdown.
ex: Casetext broke legal work into prompts, tests and scoring

items.d: About 1/3, testing, prompt collaboration and more
A few, such as biology and robotics

n67|350.c: AI application startups are growing early revenue faster than anything YC has seen.
n67|350.e: He says the last batch went from about $6 million to more than $30 million in ARR in three months (he was a bit vague on whether that's average or combined), mostly from teams of two or three people who had just built their first demo. The reason is that they automate work people already do and find painful, often replacing offshore outsourcing, and software multiplies the payoff. He also cautions that today's models are like eager interns with an IQ of about 85, needing tight constraints and careful workflow breakdowns.
ex: He likens models to eager interns with an IQ around 85

n67|350.c: The bar hasn't changed: strong technical skills, clear communication and a narrow wedge into the market.
n67|350.e: YC still favors founders who are deeply technical and can explain themselves clearly. Weak applications build generic products, haven't talked to customers and lack a narrow wedge. He ranks founders by where their information comes from: talking to customers is firsthand, hearing it from other founders is secondhand, from investors thirdhand, and media and Twitter are even further removed. Good teams zero in on a niche like corporate litigators. He compares it to chess: the rules are easy to learn, and the hard part is being smart. Find smart people, and the community can teach them how to play.

n67|350.c: Incumbents' secure advantages make them sluggish, which gives startups a real chance to win.
n67|350.e: Startups are like mice running around an elephant, but he thinks today's elephant is a weak one: secure advantages leave incumbents without urgency. Google, and Amazon with Mechanical Turk, both had the resources for data labeling, yet Scale AI is the one that made it. Not everyone has to spend hundreds of millions training models either. Early on, Cruise used a retrofit kit costing about $10,000 to get an Audi driving on the highway, and that demo attracted talent and money. He also admits he used to underestimate the harm of raising too much: too much money can send a company off course.
ex: Cruise's 2013 highway demo cost about $10,000
After raising big, cutting 50–80% of staff is brutally hard

d.verdict: A weak elephant gives the mice a chance

n67|350.c: In the AI era, engineering skill is nearly enough, so founders keep getting younger.
n67|350.e: The vertical markets in vogue three to five years ago required deep industry experience, such as running a shipyard overseas, so YC founders skewed older and more international. Today's AI market is wide open, and solid software engineering is nearly enough. The summer batch's average age may be just 25 or 26, and many founders are dropping out to avoid missing the moment. Every time YC raised its investment amount, a wave of innovation followed. He believes going from zero to one means being around the smartest people, and right now they're clustered within five miles of each other in San Francisco.

n68|355.c: RAG is easy to build, but answer quality depends mostly on retrieving the right documents.
n68|355.e: RAG, or retrieval-augmented generation, first finds relevant material and then hands it to a large language model to write the answer. The retrieved text acts as an anchor that curbs hallucination and lets the model use a company's private knowledge. Text, code and other data are turned into vectors and stored in a vector database, then searched with the query's vector. He thinks wiring the pieces together is easy. The hard part is answer quality: once the model sees the relevant documents, even a model like Llama 70B writes good answers. Prompting matters less now, because models follow instructions well.
ex: Customers include a chemical company that uses RAG to search product and chemistry documents

n68|355.c: Context is short-term memory and RAG is long-term memory, and RAG will stay cheaper.
n68|355.e: The context window is what a model reads in one go. Stuffing a huge number of tokens into it costs orders of magnitude more. Caching the model's intermediate results, the KV cache, saves some but still can't match RAG. Better hardware and models help RAG just as much, so he expects it to stay cheaper. You don't need to carry a whole library in your head to answer one question, and like a computer's layered caches, two tiers of memory are more efficient. Chains of agents don't conflict with embeddings and reranking, he says, but using a giant model to manage knowledge is wasteful.
ex: For 100 million tokens of data and a 1-million-token window, costs differ about 100x

n68|355.c: Speed limits keep embedding models small, so specializing in one domain pays off noticeably.
n68|355.e: Retrieval usually has to finish in about a second, sometimes in 200 or even 50 milliseconds. That caps embedding models, which turn text into vectors, at roughly 10 billion parameters, so limited capacity is better spent on one domain. Voyage first trains a general embedding model from scratch, then keeps pre-training it on domain data, such as about 2 trillion tokens of code or 1 trillion tokens of legal text. Code gains more because there is lots of data and it requires understanding algorithms. Legal starts from a higher baseline, so gains are smaller. Fine-tuning on a customer's private data adds another chunk.
ex: Code retrieval improves 15–20%, legal 5–15%
Fine-tuning on customers' private data adds another 10–20%

n68|355.c: RAG systems will shrink down to a few powerful neural network components.
n68|355.e: There are two ways to improve retrieval: better networks, meaning embedding models and rerankers that re-sort search results, or more software around them, like chunking, multi-step retrieval and metadata. As the networks improve, the software layer shrinks. An embedding model that can take in a roughly 50-page PDF means you no longer cut documents into 512-token chunks. He expects systems to end up as an LLM, a vector database, an embedding model and maybe a reranker, while admitting this view may favor his own company's direction. He advises measuring retrieval quality and end-to-end quality separately from day one of a prototype.

n68|355.c: Academia shouldn't compete on scale. It should bet on breakthroughs three to five years out.
n68|355.e: Scaling takes huge amounts of capital that universities and nonprofits don't have. So instead of improving the next GPT, he says academics should ask what breakthroughs might arrive in three to five years. Optimizers, the methods that adjust a model's weights during training, are one example: his Sophia optimizer is about twice as efficient as the standard Adam in pre-training. If efficiency improved 5 to 10x within five years, a $100 million training run could cost $10 million. Reasoning is another: scaling laws and web-scraped data alone are unlikely to produce a mathematician who can crack the Riemann hypothesis.
ex: Sophia is about 2x as efficient as Adam; Meta measured about 1.6x at scale

d.verdict: Academia and industry should split the work, not race on scale

n69|357.c: The popular AGI definition measures economic value, not general intelligence.
n69|357.e: The popular definition calls AGI a system that can do most economically valuable work. He grants that this captures "useful AI" well, but says it really describes what human jobs are made of. He sides with François Chollet's definition: the ability to efficiently acquire new skills and solve open-ended problems. AI already beats humans at poker, Go, protein folding and driving, yet a system trained for one task can't learn another. People, by contrast, pick up a new car or a new game with very little data and energy.

d.verdict: Measuring the wrong thing overstates how close AGI is

n69|357.c: LLMs are vast memorization systems, and scaling them up alone won't reach AGI.
n69|357.e: Memorization is a kind of intelligence, he says, but not general intelligence: the patterns needed to discover new physics or new treatments aren't in the training data. Today's agents work because the reasoning chains they need already exist, in some abstract form, in the training data. As an empiricist he looks at results. ARC predates the current scaling wave, yet the best score has only climbed from about 20% to 34%. Ten times more parameters and data won't be enough. Transformers may serve as the perception piece, but something key is still missing.
ex: The GPT-4 and Gemini papers reveal almost no technical details

n69|357.c: Breakthroughs may come from outsiders, so the prize aims to steer smart people toward new ideas.
n69|357.e: The ARC Prize is a nonprofit public contest with over $1 million in prizes, and winning solutions must be open-sourced. A smaller 2023 contest drew about 300 teams, mostly one or two people from around the world, not from AI startups. He's betting the answer will come from people not locked into the "LLM plus scale" mindset. The puzzles are small, and a solution might take only 10,000 lines of code. Program synthesis, where a computer writes programs to solve tasks, has already scored just over 20%, and with cheaper compute, neural architecture search is worth revisiting too.
ex: About 300 teams entered the 2023 contest
Program synthesis approaches reached just over 20%

items.d: Offsets the pull of LLM startups

n69|357.c: Agents will spread in rings as reliability grows: individuals first, then teams, then enterprises.
n69|357.e: In summer 2022 he and Zapier's CTO stepped back from management and spent about six months building prototypes themselves. They found that models are frozen at training time and need tools, and with about 6,000 integrations Zapier became a launch partner for ChatGPT plugins. The platform has now run over 50 million AI tasks, mostly content generation, information extraction and summarization. He thinks agents will catch on first in low-risk personal and small-team uses. To reach further, products must let users limit what the bot is allowed to touch.
ex: The platform has run over 50 million AI tasks
About 6,000 integrations made Zapier a ChatGPT plugins launch partner

items.d: Need tighter limits and more reliability

n69|357.c: Regulate today's AI with existing laws, not with AGI legislation based on theory.
n69|357.e: Existing agencies already have the authority to handle most harms from today's narrow AI. Writing prescriptive AGI laws without evidence is dangerous, he says, and restricting research directions, such as allowing only LLM work, is short-sighted, since AI looked completely different five years ago. He wants to see what systems can actually do before deciding how to release and control them, and he won't trade away individual freedom to stop AGI. Openly shared papers and datasets are where new ideas come from, and frontier labs going closed is slowing progress.

items.d: See what systems can do first
AI looked totally different five years ago
New ideas come from open sharing

n70|363.c: AI can create content directly, so it will replace the camera as the tool for making video.
n70|363.e: He spent about six and a half years at Snapchat, first on ad recommendations, then on AI camera features. A 2018 filter was the first time he saw a computer generate something that doesn't exist in reality. Snap is a camera company, but AI can create content directly, so AI could become the new camera. Remove the barrier of filming, and visual storytelling opens up to everyone, a big step forward for all content creation.

n70|363.c: Filming, not editing, is the costly part of video, so HeyGen started with avatars.
n70|363.e: The team first wanted to automate the whole video pipeline: filming the on-camera A-roll, plus editing B-roll, voiceover, music and transitions. Customers said editing was cheap and standardized, while filming was expensive. For a CEO to record a message, they had to book a crew and studio two weeks ahead, then cut 20 minutes of footage down to a two-minute video. So HeyGen built on-camera avatars first, then used AI editing to assemble the final cut. Uses fall into three groups: creating with templates or a digital twin, translating into 175+ languages and dialects, and personalizing at scale.
ex: Videos can be translated into more than 175 languages and dialects

d.verdict: Replace the costliest step, filming, first

n70|363.c: Businesses need quality, control and consistency, so assembling components beats end-to-end generation.
n70|363.e: One approach, like OpenAI's Sora, generates a whole video end to end. The other breaks video into components such as the avatar, B-roll, voice and music, then orchestrates them. HeyGen chose the second. A company's logo and fonts must be exactly right and shouldn't be generated, and brand style has to be learned for each customer. He sees Sora as a generator that can plug into the pipeline, not a rival. Quality has a threshold of about 90 out of 100. Below it, customers can't use the output, and full-body avatars haven't crossed it yet.
ex: Video translation = lip sync + voice cloning + ChatGPT translation

items.d: OpenAI's text models as the brain
Logos and fonts used as-is, never generated

n70|363.c: Generated video is a new format that can be personalized for each viewer in real time.
n70|363.e: Video no longer has to be a fixed MP4 file. Ads can be generated to match the viewer, so someone who loves avocados sees a Coca-Cola ad featuring avocados. Personalized education used to be too expensive, and generated video could make it practical. One customer created more than 100,000 localized thank-you videos for employees worldwide, each with the person's name and details. Before, they could only send one generic executive video. Real-time avatars already work as virtual salespeople and support agents.
ex: One customer made over 100,000 personalized employee thank-you videos

items.d: A different video for every viewer

n70|363.c: Safety must be built into every step of creation, and only customers can judge quality.
n70|363.e: HeyGen bans political and election content and any unauthorized use of someone's likeness. It relies on identity verification, consent videos from the real person, dynamic passcodes and fast human review, so safety runs through every step instead of being patched on later. In research, lower loss doesn't mean better-looking video, and the last mile comes down to taste. Quality can't be turned into a formula the model trains on directly, so HeyGen runs in-product A/B tests and feeds the results back into training. At Snap he learned that objective metrics aren't enough: the phone with the highest resolution isn't always the most popular.
ex: A team of 40-plus people with over 40,000 paying customers

n71|366.c: SSMs keep updating a compressed state, so compute grows only linearly with sequence length.
n71|366.e: A state space model processes one input at a time and compresses the history into a state it keeps updating. That's a bit like how the brain encodes information, and it connects to dynamical systems, which he finds elegant and fundamental. Each new token costs roughly the same, so compute grows linearly with length. A Transformer looks back at the entire history at every step, so its cost grows with the square of the length. His S4 work with Karan showed what SSMs could do, and the later Mamba brought them into language modeling.

n71|366.c: The best models are hybrids: mostly SSM layers with a little attention mixed in.
n71|366.e: A Transformer's attention can look up every token it has seen, which suits exact recall, but it's slow. He argues for giving most of the work to the SSM as a fuzzy compressor, with attention filling in as a cache or retrieval mechanism. Hybrids beat any single architecture. By his account, at least five or so teams found independently that the best ratio is about ten SSM layers to one attention layer.

items.d: Like a cache, adds exact recall

n71|366.c: No architecture wins everywhere, so models must be designed together with data type and tokenization.
n71|366.e: Early SSMs were good at raw perceptual signals like audio and pixels but weaker on text. Transformers were the opposite, and only newer variants like Mamba caught up on text. Applying Transformers directly to raw pixels or audio samples doesn't work well without a lot of special engineering. He thinks today's architectures actually co-evolved with tokenization, the way text is split into tokens, and with data pipelines, and tokenization itself is counterintuitive and imperfect.

n71|366.c: AI's first wave proved scaling pays off. The second wave is about efficiency.
n71|366.e: He compares this moment to phones getting more powerful each year. The first wave proved that scaling up pays off. The second is about building the smartest models that are cheap enough to run over and over. Apple's roughly 3-billion-parameter on-device model has limited ability, while running a 7-billion-parameter model on a Mac slows it down and eats memory. The hard part is high capability in a small package. He values beauty when picking research problems and likes clean solutions, what Erdős called "proofs from the Book," even though machine learning is often messier.

items.d: Smart models cheap enough to run repeatedly

n71|367.c: Sonic is built for ultra-low-latency speech generation, aimed at games and voice agents.
n71|367.e: Sonic is a very fast text-to-speech engine for situations that need instant interaction. Game characters could respond in real time to millions of players, and voice agents are extremely sensitive to latency. He says Sonic already cuts about 150 milliseconds of latency compared with common alternatives, and the team plans to cut more. The company's approach is to first build general, efficient models and a training stack, then apply them to audio generation conditioned on text.
ex: Latency already cut by about 150 milliseconds

n71|367.c: Speech synthesis is far from solved. Would you talk to it for more than 30 seconds?
n71|367.e: His test is simple: would you keep talking to the system for more than 30 seconds? If not, the problem isn't solved, and most current systems fail. People engage with them far less than with a real person. Quality is hard to measure, and the key is control over emotion and tone. Speech should also fit a social role, since a nurse, a lawyer, a judge or a venture capitalist each sounds different, and today's models struggle with that.

n71|367.c: Efficient models can move intelligence out of the data center and onto every device.
n71|367.e: Audio is highly compressible and continuous, and it needs low-latency streaming, which makes it a natural fit for SSMs. Their efficiency can also move inference from the data center onto the device. His vision is that capability costing about $1 million in a data center today could one day run on ordinary hardware for about $10. People now accept that each model call is expensive. Once costs collapse, new products appear, like security cameras that keep only the footage that matters, or a personal musician built into a device.
ex: His vision: about $1 million of capability for about $10

n71|367.c: Chained speech pipelines are clunky and inefficient. The goal is one unified multimodal model.
n71|367.e: Converting speech to text, running it through an LLM, then turning it back into speech stacks up latency and orchestration overhead. He finds this heavy on engineering and inelegant. Near term, the plan is to improve Sonic's audio quality, language coverage and controllability, run it on devices (already demoed on a MacBook), add text reasoning, and then accept audio input natively. The long-term goal is a large multimodal model built on Cartesia's own technology that is cheap, runs on devices and prioritizes audio fidelity.

items.d: Sonic is only the output side

n73|95.c: The skeptical report misreads AI: abilities that come from scaling differ from old-style machine learning.
n73|95.e: One side of the report argues AI affects fewer than 5% of tasks and that trillion-dollar capital spending is wasted. The other says AI is expensive from the start and competition will wipe out any efficiency gains. The hosts think the first view treats Transformers like old-fashioned regression models and ignores the measurable gains from scaling data and compute. The second wrongly assumes gains get spread evenly, when the internet's rewards went to a few winners.
ex: The report's view: AI affects under 5% of tasks
Some healthcare AI startups hit $5–10 million in annualized revenue in year one
IBM's chief once called internet companies "fireflies before the storm"

d.verdict: It's early days, not a bubble

n73|95.c: General-purpose models, ready-to-use APIs and "we must do AI" mandates are opening new markets together.
n73|95.e: One large model can cover language, images, biology, robotics and more, replacing a pile of narrow models. Companies don't need their own MLOps, the infrastructure for running machine learning, because they can call a model through an API. Boards everywhere are demanding an AI plan, much like everyone wanted to become an e-company in the 1990s, so buyers will try products they wouldn't have considered. Enterprise adoption is still early, though. Most usage at scale today comes from consumer products like ChatGPT and Perplexity.
ex: Companies buy from AI vendors, rebuild internal tools, or build AI products for customers

items.d: Buyers willing to try new things

n73|95.c: The bigger market is roughly $5 trillion of service labor, not $500 billion of software spend.
n73|95.e: The U.S. spends about $500 billion a year on software, versus about $5 trillion on service labor in law, accounting, sales and similar work. Much white-collar work is moving information between spreadsheets, email and CRMs, and some of it can now be automated. Klarna used models plus custom workflows to replace about 700 customer service roles. It now offers support around the clock in about 20 languages, with higher satisfaction and faster responses.
ex: Klarna replaced about 700 customer service roles with AI
Support now covers about 20 languages, 24/7

items.d: About $500 billion a year in the U.S.

n73|95.c: AI-driven acquisitions can skip slow adoption, but the team must understand both finance and technology.
n73|95.e: Buying a services business outright and using AI to rebuild its cost structure skips change management and long sales cycles. In effect, you're buying customer relationships. Past "tech-enabled" roll-ups often just put a software veneer on a cash-flow business and raised money at tech valuations, and latecomers lost money. AI offers far more leverage than a veneer. Incubation has historically failed more often than not, and the winners usually go deep in one industry and have exclusive access to customers.
ex: Snowflake is one of the few successful incubations
The hosts have already backed one or two AI acquisition companies

result.d: Buy distribution, then rework the cost structure

n73|95.c: Big cost-structure changes await mature coding agents, so early-stage teams have nothing to cut yet.
n73|95.e: Today's coding assistants bring modest productivity gains, nowhere near 5x. Truly changing cost structures may take coding agents that can work at scale, perhaps two or three years out. Early teams have only a few engineers and designers, and the first ten hires won't be replaced soon. The first roles hit will be SDRs, the reps who find prospects, and customer support once a company reaches hundreds of people. The hosts also think speed matters more than seniority, and that an AI product's taste depends on the founder's choices about data and output style.
ex: Midjourney, Suno and Pika each reflect their founders' taste in style

n74|376.c: Airtable is really an app platform that uses the familiar spreadsheet to make getting started easy.
n74|376.e: After his previous company was acquired by Salesforce, he saw that Salesforce won CRM through a customizable platform design, and he wanted to hand that power to "citizen developers" who don't code. Traditional low-code platforms required real technical skill, while project management tools were too simple, and Airtable sat in between. Keeping the grid interface, keyboard shortcuts and direct pasting from Excel meant users didn't have to learn a new category of software. Templates later covered the long tail of use cases.
ex: Launched in 2015 after about two and a half years of polishing
He rejects the dogma of "build a killer app, not a platform"

n74|376.c: Going enterprise needs a low floor and a high ceiling, and pivoting too early can crush the product.
n74|376.e: The 2012 vision document already pointed to the enterprise, but the strategy was to make getting started easy and raise the ceiling step by step, rather than start out complex like SAP. The platform grew from thousands of rows to hundreds of thousands and added scripting and serverless extensions. Bottom-up usage revealed "hot spots," such as global content production at media companies, and Airtable built end-to-end solutions around them and sold to those use cases directly.
ex: Rows grew from thousands to hundreds of thousands, with millions planned
Now winning business from Salesforce Service and QuickBase

items.d: Fill in what the hot spot needs
Market and sell by use case

n74|376.c: Product managers wear three hats, market, execution and design, and the team must cover all three.
n74|376.e: He thinks people misread Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky's "getting rid of PMs" remark, which was really about separating product marketing from project management. He adds a third hat: hard design problems like information architecture and complex interactions, modeled on early Google PMs. One person needn't wear all three, but each needs an owner. Borrowing Jensen Huang's line about loving hard problems, he picks distinctive hard problems so Airtable doesn't become one more interchangeable vertical SaaS company.

n74|376.c: AI's value lies mostly in structured, repetitive workflows, not one-off chats.
n74|376.e: Chat and internal RAG assistants are useful but cover only a small slice of what's possible. The bigger value comes from embedding model calls in data, workflows and automations, such as drafting a PRD automatically for every new feature record. Point solutions each handle one corner. Covering a company's long tail takes either Palantir-style heavy services or a flexible platform, which he estimates maps to trillions of dollars of labor. The barrier today isn't features but customers' imagination and know-how.
ex: About 1,000 customers joined the AI beta
A top-five law firm automated parts of its contract process with it
Strong PRDs in a table serve as few-shot examples in prompts

d.verdict: The long tail of workflows is a trillion-dollar opportunity

n74|376.c: Code generation won't replace no-code, because non-developers need something they can edit directly.
n74|376.e: Generating small snippets of code is easy and very helpful to developers, who can check and fix it. But complex end-to-end business apps are hard to generate in one shot before AGI, because requirements need repeated clarification. Non-developers can't read code, so the output has to be visual: data structures, flowchart-style automations and interface layouts. Editing those directly is also more efficient than rewriting prompts again and again.
ex: A translation chain that drafts, self-critiques, then revises gives better quality

n75|378.c: Chat won't replace search: search adds citations to answers, and models summarize search results.
n75|378.e: He uses both and thinks each has its place. In chat products, search can add citations and reduce hallucination. In search products, large models can summarize and reason. He expects search to be greatly enhanced by large models, but which interface wins is for the product teams to decide based on what models can do. The research side stays open.
ex: Gemini came from merging the Brain and DeepMind LLM teams
California and London hand off, so training runs around the clock

n75|378.c: Very long context is more powerful than expected and will be standard within a year or two.
n75|378.e: Older RNNs and LSTMs could in theory remember forever, but in practice kept only a few hundred words. Today's million-token context windows let users upload an hour of video and ask anything about it. Retrieval often squeezes a whole book into a single vector, while long context can reason over every word, so he expects hybrid, layered memory systems. In the next year or two, commonly available context length could grow another tenfold or so.
ex: Project Astra keeps personal information in context, not in the weights
Point your phone at a screen and it helps debug code

items.d: Remembered only a few hundred words
Can take in an hour of video

n75|378.c: Models are inherently probabilistic and err at any scale, so they need more explicit reasoning.
n75|378.e: A model assigns a probability to every sequence, so wrong answers never have zero probability. Even 95% accuracy on hard problems still means many visible errors across a global user base. One path is to keep scaling models and algorithms to push error rates close to zero. The other is to make reasoning more explicit, for example by slowly running a small program with an LLM at its core, to push reliability toward 99.9%.
ex: It can do olympiad-level math yet slip up on simple puzzles

items.d: Slowly run a program around an LLM

n75|378.c: Compute will shift from pre-training to reinforcement learning, perhaps cutting pre-training to half.
n75|378.e: He broadly agrees with "the bitter lesson": what scales is learning and search. Scaling learning has been proven, but language lacks a clear win-or-lose reward like Go's. When the reward model is imperfect, reinforcement learning has to stop early, or the model learns to game it. Today over 90% of compute goes to pre-training. With good rewards, he imagines pre-training dropping to about half, with more going to reinforcement learning.
ex: AlphaGo spent most of its compute on self-play
Reward hacking: even outputting emojis could earn high scores

items.d: More of the rest goes to RL

n75|378.c: Checking is easier than generating, so models judging their own work can bootstrap reinforcement learning.
n75|378.e: Human labeling can scale, as ImageNet showed. But having models judge their own outputs may bootstrap better, because checking is often easier than generating. Generative reward models, which use a model to judge answers, are a promising direction. Once models can correct themselves, bootstrapping gets much easier, though this won't happen evenly across all domains.

n75|378.c: General models should rise across the board, but important hard problems still deserve specialized models.
n75|378.e: Today's general models are roughly "20% good at everything," and he wants that level to rise evenly rather than over-specialize. But for important problems like protein folding, fusion and weather, specialized models pay off faster. They're worth it even if retired later, and the results can flow back into general models. He doesn't see math and games as dead ends, because math has a formal signal of correctness.
ex: Climate modeling is hard: there's data from only one Earth
LLM research still has 5–10 years of open problems

marks.d: Results flow back to general models

n75|378.c: AGI won't arrive in a single moment but gradually, like a "cloud."
n75|378.e: DeepMind co-founder Shane Legg predicted in 2009 that AGI would arrive around 2028, and forecasts on sites like Metaculus are similar, perhaps closer to 2030. He thinks abilities will show up unevenly, so different people will feel "it's here" at different times, but basic, obvious mistakes must be fixed first. He cares less about a strict definition than about how useful AI is for science. He advises young people to follow their interests and learn to work with AI tools.

n76|382.c: An AI assistant should act like an executive assistant, handling employees' expense chores for them.
n76|382.e: His starting question: if employees suddenly had free time, what would the company have them do? In expense management, the answer is to let AI take over an executive assistant's work. He built a prototype over one weekend with Python and GPT-3.5. It inferred expense memos from the calendar, categorized spending and found receipts in email. It worked surprisingly well, and the team shipped it into the product within a week.
ex: About 30,000 customers use the Brex assistant
Over a third of expenses are completed automatically

n76|382.c: Show users how confident the AI is and build trust gradually, instead of giving one answer.
n76|382.e: High-confidence suggestions are executed directly, medium ones are offered as options, and low ones aren't shown at all. He criticizes chatbots for giving a single answer with no alternatives or context. Instead of full automation, the interface offers batch suggestions, such as "You've categorized this three times. Apply it to 15 similar transactions?" As users come to trust it, the confirmation step can be safely dropped.
ex: Accounting suggestions are accepted about 80% of the time
Like the early days, when people feared typing card numbers online

marks.d: Like applying a category in bulk

n76|382.c: AI-written emails are a commodity now. The real edge is your own customer data and signals.
n76|382.e: Custom marketing to large enterprises used to need a dedicated team, and generative AI has pushed the marginal cost of personalized outreach toward zero. But generic AI SDR tools are available to everyone. The hard part is managing the whole addressable market as a system: measuring the value each kind of customer gets from Brex, then using LLMs to parse unstructured signals like hiring and news. Tools like Salesforce can't handle those signals, so Brex built its own customer data platform, which he thinks most companies can't do.
ex: Multinationals save on foreign exchange fees, making them high-value customers

n76|382.c: Moving money is a lasting advantage, and AI will make traditional ERP systems unnecessary.
n76|382.e: He sees money movement as fundamental. Brex connects directly to card networks and local payment rails without middlemen, which lets it run a global card program that settles in local currencies. The strategy has three steps: corporate cards, all spending, then "continuous finance." Finance teams today resemble software teams 20 years ago, planning only once a year. Accounting is mostly cleaning data across systems. If AI can integrate it at near-human accuracy, the result is a real-time data layer you can query directly.
ex: 130 public companies use Brex
AI monitors negative news to meet compliance requirements

items.d: Non-card spend on the platform too

n76|382.c: Focus gives choices meaning, and Brex deliberately dropped about 20,000 small customers.
n76|382.e: Brex once served small businesses, the mid-market, large enterprises and startups. It was fine at each but world-class at none. The real bottleneck wasn't headcount but leadership attention. So the company chose startups and large enterprises, growing alongside customers like Scale AI. It was painful, but he sees it as the reason Brex is where it is today.
ex: Dropped about 20,000 customers
About a third of startups use Brex

n77|385.c: Credit cards profit from encouraging spending. Ramp does the opposite, helping companies spend less and save time.
n77|385.e: Its predecessor, Paribus, scanned users' email receipts and claimed refunds when prices dropped. That showed the founders that the credit card industry's incentives are misaligned with customers': rewards points encourage spending more.
