Bigger companies waste more, so they moved to business customers. And compared with status symbols like airport lounges, time is the truly scarce luxury. The end goal is "self-driving money," with bookkeeping, payments, approvals and receipt matching all automated.
ex: Paribus had about a million users and an acquisition offer from Capital One
Founded in March 2019, now serving about 25,000 businesses

d.verdict: Customers really want more money in the bank

n77|385.c: Give your best salesperson an "Iron Man suit" first, rather than building an AI rep from scratch.
n77|385.e: Ramp had one extremely productive sales rep, and engineers shadowed his daily workflow. They automated each manual step one by one: building lead lists, finding emails, writing copy and running A/B tests. He says Ramp's SDRs book several times as many meetings as the closest competitor's. The organizational design behind it: engineers own business outcomes and P&L, instead of sitting in a traditional IT cost center.
ex: Lead-list signals come from fundraising, personnel changes and similar events

n77|385.c: Ramp is a productivity company that sells back time, so it must win on results, not AI hype.
n77|385.e: Finance teams face overhead budgets that no longer grow, and Ramp offers leverage: doing more without adding people. He thinks the best near-term use of AI is raising output per hour, not just cutting costs. The product can be tried for free and points out savings directly, and provable results persuade more than an "AI" label. He also notes early data suggesting companies using Ramp go bankrupt less often.
ex: Early on, Ramp saved customers money by catching duplicate SaaS subscriptions

n77|385.c: Taste is marketing's scarce skill, so AI should clear out repetitive work and keep output flowing.
n77|385.e: He sees marketing as a system with bottlenecks and dependencies, and the answer is to redesign the bottlenecks rather than slow down. He compares it to Andy Warhol's studio: abstract away the complexity of production and focus on what actually moves people. A marketing lead at Stitch Fix gave stylists video tools instead of using agencies, with better results at almost no cost, if less polish. Ramp keeps its marketing team structure and uses more tools to maintain its cadence.
ex: Stitch Fix had stylists shoot their own videos instead of hiring agencies

items.d: Hand it to AI and tools

n77|385.c: Automation eliminates chores like chasing receipts, and finance staff will move to higher-value work.
n77|385.e: Reports say bookkeeper jobs are shrinking, but he points out that other finance and accounting roles are growing. Depending on how you count, only about 4–9% of finance jobs are strategic finance. The rest are mostly chores, and he thinks that mix should change. As companies grow, nobody wants to deliver bad news, so the team uses AI to condense huge volumes of customer calls into a few minutes of "podcast" so everyone hears the complaints directly.
ex: Strategic finance is about 4–9% of finance jobs, depending on the measure
Tens of thousands of hours of calls condensed into a 5-minute podcast

n77|386.c: AI's edge comes from context: structure card, email and ERP data first, then automate.
n77|386.e: Ramp holds card transactions, emailed receipts and ERP connections. Only after merging and structuring that data can it automate an entire workflow. Products are designed around the job to be done, such as the month-end close. A general model plus each customer's own constraints scales better than custom work for every client. Finance users care about speed, accuracy, visibility and control, not whether AI is involved.

n77|386.c: Constrain problems into verifiable decisions, and AI risk in finance becomes manageable.
n77|386.e: Some decisions have clear right answers, like paying on the last due date, or early when there's a discount, and those can be tested. Fraud checks can use three-way matching of purchase order, invoice and goods receipt, which AI does faster. Models are bad at arithmetic, so Ramp mainly uses them to translate accounting language. Pre-filled forms, pre-sorted lists and targeted questions based on the calendar are all ways to box in risk.
ex: Three-way match: purchase order, invoice, goods receipt
Models are weak at math, so they mainly translate accounting language

items.d: Right or wrong can be checked

n77|386.c: Pick vendors for how fast they improve, not today's features, and don't neglect buying decisions.
n77|386.e: Build decisions are easy to judge after the fact, but buying decisions rarely show up in performance reviews, and almost no one measures procurement skill. Ramp talks directly with vendors' engineering teams and weighs their speed of iteration over today's feature gaps. Choosing the "safe" incumbent can actually be risky. For "AI employees" that replace human roles, good evaluation frameworks don't exist yet.

n77|386.c: Rather than fine-tuning, build an evaluation system that lets you swap models quickly.
n77|386.e: Ramp tried fine-tuning and found the gains smaller than simply waiting for stronger new models. So it built its infrastructure to swap models quickly and evaluates each subtask separately. When GPT-4o mini came out, the team found it could handle about 90% of tasks and switched over within a day.
ex: GPT-4o mini handled about 90% of tasks and was swapped in within a day

n77|386.c: The AI stack still lacks agents that can operate apps and controls that go beyond prompts.
n77|386.e: Getting agents to browse websites and operate apps end to end is still hard, especially when products change fast and need guardrails. Interfaces need better controls than prompts, and he praises Claude's Artifacts for generating small apps you can edit. Brand review could work like CI/CD tests, automatically checking each new email against brand guidelines and for a clear call to action. Future teams will need people who can build tools with systems thinking.
ex: Claude Artifacts generates small apps you can edit

n78|389.c: Give more teams the compute leverage of frontier labs, and breakthroughs will come more often.
n78|389.e: AlphaFold 2 and ChatGPT look like small-team miracles, but they were backed by Google's infrastructure and OpenAI's enormous compute, so they weren't really underdog wins. Foundry wants to spread the compute leverage now concentrated in a few labs. His goal is to cut the cost of a major breakthrough from about $1 billion to $100 million, then to $10 million, so breakthroughs happen more often.
ex: He says OpenAI has about 400 people and about $13 billion in compute

items.d: A few labs hold the leverage

n78|389.c: GPU utilization is generally low, and system complexity makes failures in large clusters nearly inevitable.
n78|389.e: Even at top labs doing pre-training, utilization is often below 80% and sometimes under 50%. Teams typically hold back 10–20% of their GPUs as a buffer for failures, and there are gaps between jobs. He estimates market-wide H100 utilization at only 20–25% or lower. A single H100 system has more than 35,000 parts, and when thousands are networked together, failure odds compound, so the more advanced the system, the more likely it breaks.
ex: An H100 system weighs 70–80 pounds and has over 35,000 parts
Teams reserve 10–20% of GPUs as a failure buffer

n78|389.c: Today's AI clouds are just co-location, and without elasticity, "fast is free" breaks down.
n78|389.e: Cloud computing's original promise was "fast is free": a job that takes 10 machines 10 days can run on 10,000 machines in 15 minutes for the same cost. But AI compute usually requires three-year reservations, so customers must commit capital up front and carry the risk, with no hedging tools like futures or options. Along the path from on-premises to co-location, hosting, virtualization and serverless, AI hardware is stuck somewhere between co-location and hosting.
ex: Compute reservations often run three years
Public clouds hold only a tiny share of the world's GPU compute

n78|389.c: Like a shared parking space for GPUs: others use idle reserved capacity, and all three sides win.
n78|389.e: When the owner of reserved capacity isn't using it, on-demand users can temporarily take over, and automation moves workloads seamlessly. Depending on the share of capacity that's reserved, he estimates this can multiply effective capacity about tenfold. Another product, Mars, handles monitoring, alerts and fault tolerance, so a failed GPU can be swapped without users noticing. Partners can also rent out their own failure buffers through Foundry.
ex: Spot GPUs with high-speed interconnect are rare
Used mainly for training and batch inference

n78|389.c: Compound AI systems gain by sampling many answers and verifying them, reducing reliance on giant clusters.
n78|389.e: The field is shifting from training one giant model to compound systems that combine many model calls, synthetic data and filtering. The key principle is verifiability: when checking an answer is easier than generating it, sample many candidates and pick the best with unit tests, simulators or a model acting as judge. These workloads parallelize across many machines and don't need tightly networked mega-clusters, which helps ease bottlenecks in power, space and interconnect.
ex: His paper raised prime factorization accuracy from 3.7% to 36.6%
Small Llama 3 models were distilled using synthetic data from the 405B model

items.d: AlphaCode 2: about a million candidates per problem

n79|392.c: AWS won by offering familiar building blocks, not by forcing developers to work in a new way.
n79|392.e: Around 2003, Jeff Bezos pushed Amazon to move from one monolithic system to separate services, and AWS concluded that other companies would hit the same scaling problems. Unlike Google and Microsoft, which pushed new architectures, AWS offered familiar primitives: a virtual Linux server was just a Linux server, available in 30 seconds instead of after months of procurement. Only once developers were comfortable did AWS launch less familiar services like Lambda and Bedrock.
ex: He was AWS's first product manager and has been there about 18 years

n79|392.c: Win the hardest customers first, and other companies' objections stop holding up.
n79|392.e: Around 2008, Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan said their core workloads would never move to the cloud. AWS kept asking why and spent about a decade meeting compliance and audit requirements. AWS also won the U.S. intelligence community's classified cloud contract. IBM's protest sparked a public fight that ended with the agencies publicly declaring AWS's technology the best. He estimates about 85% of workloads are still on premises, so migration alone leaves roughly 10x room to grow.
ex: The intelligence cloud contract beat IBM, HP and Oracle
About 85% of workloads still run in on-premises data centers

n79|392.c: Generative AI will have many coexisting models, and companies will stand out on private data and security.
n79|392.e: After OpenAI's breakthrough, AWS didn't build consumer apps. It asked what building blocks every company would need, and it made three bets. Security remains customers' top concern. There will be many models of different sizes and uses, not one winner. And a company's edge comes from its proprietary data, which must not leak into models. So AWS offers Bedrock, its own chips and a catalog that includes open models, without locking customers in through proprietary licenses.
ex: He considers Claude one of the best models today
Llama 3.1 was on Bedrock on launch day
Aurora is fully Postgres-compatible, so customers can leave anytime

n79|392.c: Compute will stay scarce for now, and inference must outgrow training for investments to pay off.
n79|392.e: Fabs, memory and data centers all take years to build, while demand may grow faster than exponentially, so the industry will be capacity-constrained for a long time. AWS draws on more than a decade of experience allocating capital and securing power, and says it is the largest corporate buyer of renewable energy. Today training and inference are roughly 50/50, but for big model investments to pay off, inference has to dominate. AWS's own Trainium and Inferentia chips add supply beyond Nvidia.
ex: Nvidia's own training cluster runs on AWS
Some model companies talk about gigawatt-scale compute needs

items.d: Needed for investments to pay off

n79|392.c: Value will shift from Nvidia to applications that solve business problems, and inference will become a basic primitive.
n79|392.e: Right now most of the value goes to Nvidia, which is typical of an early market. It will shift to companies that actually solve business problems, and startups that help enterprises move from proof of concept to production will win. Most enterprises won't build their own models and shouldn't manage GPUs. Within three to five years, inference will be a building block like compute, storage, databases and networking. He also urges founders to plan for revenue early: his first startup raised $27 million and burned through it in about 18 months.
ex: Bedrock users just send and receive tokens and never touch GPUs

n80|393.c: An AI that builds its own successor must code and run experiments, so he starts with code.
n80|393.e: He works backward from AGI, meaning AI that can do most human work. A system that can build the next version of itself has to write code, come up with ideas and test them with experiments, which makes the goal more manageable. Focusing on code also avoids the endless use cases of a general product, so most things get simpler, though it needs just as much compute. He admits he overestimated how fast compute would get cheaper and underestimated how seriously rivals would take coding. He is catching up with a very large new computing cluster.

n80|393.c: Bring compute to the data: having the model read everything at once beats retrieving pieces.
n80|393.e: He wants models to learn from the long history of their own and their collaborators' actions, and to absorb lots of fast-changing data. Learning from whatever is in the context is exactly why Transformers are so powerful. Retrieval picks a subset of data each time, while his models use all the data all the time. By the "bitter lesson" (methods that learn from compute beat hand-built rules), if retrieval were truly best, the model would learn to do it itself. And in long-running use, fine-tuning the model on every new chunk of context would cost far too much.
ex: About a year ago, Magic announced models that read 5 million tokens at once

items: Picks a slice of data each time
Uses all the data all the time

d.verdict: Learned methods eventually beat hand-written rules

n80|393.c: Skills should be learned once in training, while users choose how much compute to buy per question.
n80|393.e: Performance depends on two kinds of compute: what you spend training the model and what you spend when it answers, and the budget should be split well between them. Having a model learn something like programming on the fly is wasteful, because that cost repeats on every query. Expensive skills should be trained in once. But what users will pay for a single query varies hugely, so letting them pick a compute tier only helps. The hardest problems take even top mathematicians a long time, so thinking time when answering still matters.

terms.d: Paid per query, by difficulty and user

result.d: Split the budget wisely between both

n80|393.c: Usage jumps only once engineers trust AI code enough to stop reviewing it.
n80|393.e: The goal is an assistant that feels like a colleague, not a tool. A half-good assistant just adds review work, which is worse than not shipping at all, so he'd rather delay the next product. Usage won't grow gradually. Once engineers can safely skip reviewing AI-written code, the share of tasks given to AI jumps from about 5% to about 90%. Until then it stays near zero. Existing systems will also be reshaped to suit AI, the way websites optimize for search engine crawlers.
ex: Code completion is live, but the next product's prototype isn't good enough yet

n80|393.c: Use AI to keep solving AI safety, while outcomes after AGI are heading toward two extremes.
n80|393.e: He compares the long-term risk to the way humans dominate other species. The most workable path, he thinks, is having AI systems help solve alignment (keeping AI's goals in line with ours) and safety, round after round: 100,000 great AI researchers beat 100 human ones. He believes competition with guardrails is humanity's best optimizer. After AGI, computer-based work gets automated and people won't need to work for income. But meaning becomes a big problem, and universal basic income won't fix it.
ex: His rough guess: 10%–20% feel deeply frustrated, about 70% don't care
Handmade goods may be prized more because a human made them

n81|397.c: Tesla is ahead of Waymo because its remaining problem is software, while Waymo's is hardware.
n81|397.e: About ten years ago he rode in a nearly perfect Waymo demo around the block, yet it took roughly another decade to become a paid service, mostly because of the technology. He thinks software problems are easier to solve than hardware cost and sensor complexity, and Tesla already has a huge fleet. Tesla plays a cost arbitrage: it trains with data-collection cars carrying expensive sensors, then distills that into production cars that use only cameras. Neural networks are also steadily "eating" the hand-written C++ rules.
ex: Sensors matter more at training time than on the road

d.verdict: Software problems are easier to solve

n81|397.c: Humanoids make sense: the world is built for humans, they're easy to teleoperate, and skills transfer.
n81|397.e: A car is already a robot, and Tesla's early Optimus ran the car's own networks. What was missing was mainly actuators and motion data. The humanoid form makes sense because the world is designed around the human body, people can easily teleoperate it to collect data, and each platform carries high fixed costs, so one general platform pays off. A single multi-task network can also transfer skills across tasks. He expects them first in Tesla's own factories moving things, then in warehouses and other businesses, and only last in homes.
ex: He bought a Unitree G1 humanoid himself
An ideal early task: quietly sweeping up leaves

n81|397.c: The Transformer is a trainable general-purpose computer, so the bottleneck is now data and objectives, not architecture.
n81|397.e: The Transformer combines residual connections, layer normalization and attention into a general computer that configures itself through backpropagation, and scaling laws are largely a property of it. Today, architectures like Llama's barely change. Progress comes mostly from data and training objectives. What he wants most is the "inner monologue" people have while solving problems. Synthetic data, generated by models, is essential, but outputs can quietly collapse into a few patterns, so diversity has to be injected on purpose.
ex: Recent architecture changes are mostly small tweaks like RoPE
About a billion synthetic personas are used to add diversity

items.d: For example, generate from different personas

n81|397.c: A model's thinking core could be tiny, maybe a billion parameters, with facts looked up by tools.
n81|397.e: Today's models waste much of their capacity memorizing trivia because the training data isn't curated. He roughly estimates that only about 0.001% of the internet is real cognition. Strip out the memory, keep only the reasoning, and let the model call tools to look things up, and even a billion parameters may be too many. Distillation, where big models teach small ones, works surprisingly well. He pictures the future like an organization: a capable "CEO model" hands tasks to cheap worker models, and hard problems get passed back up.
ex: About 0.001% of the internet is real cognition, he estimates
Distillation, with big models supervising small ones, works amazingly well

items.d: About a billion parameters or fewer

n81|397.c: AI should augment people, not replace them: own your external brain, and scale one-on-one tutoring.
n81|397.e: Phones and AI tools are already an external brain, sitting in the cloud on top of our neocortex. Like GPS, they let us outsource some thinking, and he's happy to spend the freed-up brainpower elsewhere. But renting that layer of cognition from a company is unsettling, so open-source models must keep improving. He is on "team human": at Eureka Labs, experts design the courses and AI acts as the tutor up front, aiming to bring the effect of one-on-one tutoring to everyone. Learning, he says, is like the gym: it takes effort.
ex: He cites the classic study showing one-on-one tutoring sharply boosts results
The first course targets technical learners at an undergraduate level

terms.d: Humans in charge behind the scenes
Many languages, tailored to each learner

n82|95.c: Foundation model rounds have outgrown what venture capital can fund, pulling the market toward big tech.
n82|95.e: Parts of Inflection, Character and Adept joined Microsoft, Google and Amazon through acqui-hires or partnerships. Each funding round for a foundation model now costs billions or even tens of billions of dollars, which only cloud giants and sovereign funds can afford, and cloud providers invest partly to drive usage of their clouds. On the other hand, benchmarks keep improving, prices keep falling and open-source players are real, so the market has actually grown more competitive over the past 18 months.
ex: Parts of Inflection, Character and Adept were absorbed by big tech companies

d.verdict: Consolidation and competition can happen at once

n82|95.c: Plunging API prices push model companies to specialize and find ways to lock customers in.
n82|95.e: Data compiled by the hosts' team shows API costs fell about 200x in 18 to 24 months, thanks to both distillation and new generations of GPUs. Selling raw API access is getting harder, which pushes companies toward specialized models, post-training and vertical applications. Labs are also building AWS-style lock-in with features like prompt caching, JSON output and fine-tuning. High-profile product hires are another way to build a moat.
ex: Product talent: Krieger joined Anthropic, and Weil joined OpenAI

n82|95.c: Claims that models are now interchangeable keep proving wrong, and different players will each win a slice.
n82|95.e: In the early days of social networks, everyone thought Friendster would win, and it was Facebook. Then Instagram, Twitter, Snapchat and TikTok rose even as people declared social dead. The LLM market could likewise split into segments owned by different companies. Images and video are heating up too: Midjourney was once seen as the default winner, then Ideogram showed very high fidelity, and small teams of about five people can build competitive video models.
ex: Runway, Pika and Luma's video generation is closing in on OpenAI's Sora

n82|95.c: Small models are catching up to big ones, and real-time multimodal experiences are months away.
n82|95.e: Through distillation and similar techniques, much smaller models now reach strong performance, something few expected a year or two ago. The human brain handles general cognition on about 20 to 30 watts, which shows how much room for efficiency remains. Smaller, faster models, such as Cartesia's new architecture, could make real-time image, video and audio experiences actually happen.
ex: The human brain runs general cognition on about 20–30 watts

n82|95.c: Data and content limits are a business risk: learn from Google and Uber, but separate the risk types.
n82|95.e: Early Google crawled the web and showed snippets, and after more than a decade of lawsuits things settled into robots.txt, fair use for snippets and content licensing. Airbnb and Uber also challenged regulators first and caught up on policy later. Napster, though, was sued into shutting down by the music industry. They split the risk into three kinds: litigation, regulation and reputation. In their view, generating content is closer to free speech, while distribution platforms should carry more responsibility for policing it.
ex: Google's path: robots.txt, fair-use rulings and licensing deals

items.d: Like Napster, sued out of existence
What the model is allowed to say

n83|404.c: There are three kinds of agents: personal ones are hardest, and company agents can be built today.
n83|404.e: "Agent" is so broad it's like a Rorschach test: everyone reads their own meaning into it. A personal agent handles your email and calendar, with almost no limit on what it must reason about or connect to, so it's the hardest and will likely be led by Apple, Google and OpenAI. Role-based agents are narrow but deep, like Harvey for law or coding agents, with benchmarks, compiler errors and integration tests as scaffolding. Company agents face customers, with well-defined processes and systems of record, and he thinks they can be built now.

marks.d: Almost unlimited scope to reason over

n83|404.c: Branded conversational agents will be a company's digital presence, the way websites were in 1995.
n83|404.e: In 1995, having a website was how a company existed online, and he believes branded conversational agents will play the same role. Within three or four years, a company's agent will cover almost everything a customer can do with it, like filing an insurance claim, comparing prices or adding a child to a policy. A phone support call costs about $13, and AI can bring that well under $1. Once conversations are cheap, support stops being a cost center to squeeze.
ex: Sonos: troubleshooting issues like a speaker's flashing orange light
SiriusXM's agent "Harmony" handles subscription changes

n83|404.c: Valuable support takes actions, not just answers, so software must move from rules to goals and guardrails.
n83|404.e: RAG, which looks things up before answering, is popular, but the valuable interactions are actions like upgrades, returns, exchanges and claims. These often span more than ten systems of record and carry business goals like retention, plus compliance rules. Traditional enterprise software is a rules engine. Future software must express goals and guardrails, and spell out where the AI may be creative. Too tight and it feels robotic. Too loose and you get hallucinations and violations. Programming non-deterministic, creative software is a new problem.

d.verdict: Balance robotic against out of control

n83|404.c: The AI market will rhyme with cloud computing, and most companies will buy solutions rather than build.
n83|404.e: Pretraining is enormously expensive, so only a few frontier labs will do it, allied with cloud providers. There will also be pick-and-shovel tool companies like Scale AI. Just as companies rarely build their own CRM or ERP software, most will buy solutions like Sierra or Harvey. If a single model release weakens your product, you're just a thin layer. Then again, Salesforce and Shopify were once dismissed as wrappers around a database.
ex: He doesn't think latency or security will force everything onto one platform

n83|404.c: Outcome-based pricing aligns vendors with customers, much like ads shifting to pay-per-click.
n83|404.e: Charging for work completed, rather than per token or per seat, could be a shift as big as subscriptions, he thinks. At Google he watched ads move from paying per impression to paying per click, and customers would pay more for results they could attribute directly. An agent's results can likewise be measured with metrics like cost per contact. Many CIOs are disappointed by the return on their software spending, and outcome-based pricing makes the vendor a real partner.
ex: Klarna: he recalls the work of about 700 support agents being automated

n83|404.c: Bad customer service comes from waiting, so instant gratification is AI's core value.
n83|404.e: Human agents aren't bad at service. They're dragged down by queues and waiting, a mismatch of scale. AI can resolve issues almost instantly, which is the main value in itself, and everything else is a bonus. An agent is also a brand ambassador. Its tone can be tuned with prompts, post-training and "supervisor models," with tighter controls in sensitive areas like medical or financial advice. It can also reply in the customer's own language and learn a new product in one click.
ex: A free-text box reveals long-tail needs the company never anticipated

items.d: Waiting is the main pain point

n83|404.c: Phones stay central, but interaction will shift to voice, and technology should fade into the background.
n83|404.e: Touchscreens carry most human-computer interaction, and smartphones have swallowed other consumer devices. He thinks conversational interfaces crossed the usability threshold around GPT-4, so interaction will move toward voice settings like earbuds and CarPlay. Early iPhone apps were flashlight-style gadgets. Only later came services like Uber and WhatsApp that combined location and connectivity, and conversation-first services will follow a similar path. He hopes AI can cut screen time and filter notifications for people.

n84|406.c: Companies want to consolidate onto a few software platforms, and the compound startup rides that wave.
n84|406.e: Rippling spans HR, IT and finance, with about 25 separately sold products built on one deep employee data model, its core asset. Customers want fewer vendors, both to save money and to stop juggling multiple sales teams. Mature SaaS growth increasingly comes from cross-selling to existing customers, so more products means more room to grow. The company has more than 150 former founders, and letting them keep acting like founders speeds up product work.
ex: About 3,500 employees and tens of thousands of customers
He reads buybacks and dividends as a sign of no good places to reinvest

items.d: Where mature SaaS growth comes from

n84|406.c: Performance reviews get skewed by managers' gut feel, so they should rest on the actual work produced.
n84|406.e: Managers rarely go back over six to twelve months of someone's work, and calibration meetings don't fix that. Talent Signal reads work output such as code, sales calls and support tickets, combines it with HR data like job level, and flags each person as high potential, typical or needing attention, with concrete work examples to coach from. Of the inputs they compared, work output correlated most strongly with promotion, performance-based exits and long-term stagnation.
ex: Work output was the input most correlated with promotions and departures

items.d: High potential, typical or needs attention

n84|406.c: It gives a single signal at day 90 of a new hire's tenure, building trust step by step.
n84|406.e: The first version looks only at a new hire's first 90 days of work and issues one signal per person, while existing employees are used only for backtesting. That builds trust gradually, lets real outcomes about a year later test its accuracy, and avoids pushing public acceptance too far too fast. The model gets no demographic data like race, age or location, and uses only job level to calibrate across companies. Managers decide whether employees can see their own signal.
ex: An engineer in India was flagged as high potential soon after joining

n84|406.c: AI signals are only a cheat sheet and can never decide promotions or firings on their own.
n84|406.e: Rippling's internal rule is that no promotion or hiring decision can rest on the model alone, and managers must form their own view first. Attribution can go wrong too: one CTO found that a "weak" engineer flagged as high potential owed the good code to the CTO's own hands-on pairing. Hallucinations, amplified bias and growing numb to the impact on individuals are real risks, so users must understand the stakes and check the context. He welcomes criticism and calls feedback a gift.
ex: The CTO case: the good code came from his own pair-programming coaching

d.verdict: The signal assists; people decide

n84|406.c: Scarce AI engineers should build products that sell subscriptions, not chatbots.
n84|406.e: Rippling didn't build a chatbot or copilot because those don't drive subscription sales, so its expensive, scarce AI engineers went to higher-value work. Its edge is data: GitHub and Salesforce don't know who got promoted or who was fired for performance, but Rippling does, and it can match an employee's identity across systems. The first customers are sales, sales engineering and support teams, who already review and coach regularly. He thinks AI in performance reviews is only 0.1% of the way there.
ex: GitHub code and Salesforce data are copied into a secure environment for analysis

n85|410.c: Antitrust shouldn't fixate on short-term prices, because market structure is itself a policy choice.
n85|410.e: As a business reporter, she watched airlines, publishing, chicken farming and aluminum consolidate under forty years of lax enforcement, hurting consumers, farmers and small businesses. She argues antitrust narrowed to short-term prices and output and missed a lot of harm. When she wrote her Amazon paper, sellers and investors felt the platform's structural dominance well before prices rose. She credits America's historic tilt toward competition for its economic growth and its many big companies.
ex: Airlines, book publishing, chicken and aluminum kept consolidating
In law school she wrote her Amazon paper from interviews with sellers

d.verdict: Policy shapes markets, so weigh long-term competition

n85|410.c: Merger review is a prediction: does this deal eliminate a future competitor?
n85|410.e: The law asks agencies to judge whether a deal "may" substantially lessen competition, so they must forecast whether firms compete on price, quality or innovation, and whether the deal removes a rival in a current or future market. Digital markets have network effects, data advantages and winner-take-all dynamics, so early leaders entrench and dominant firms can buy up threats while they're small. She cites the old Microsoft case over Netscape: that enforcement made room for the later rise of Google, Amazon and Facebook.
ex: The FTC sued over Meta buying a small VR fitness app
The Microsoft–Netscape case made room for later platforms

items.d: One fewer competitor in tomorrow's market
Network effects entrench the first mover

n85|410.c: Acquisitions aren't banned; deals get close scrutiny only when the buyer is already a monopolist.
n85|410.e: She stresses that there are thousands of mergers a year, and fewer than 3% of deals reported to the agency get investigated, with even fewer challenged. The real red flag is a buyer that already holds a monopoly in that market. Sanofi wanted to buy Maze, which was developing an oral alternative to Sanofi's Pompe disease drug, and the FTC worried it would slow the rival's launch. Maze instead partnered with a company without monopoly power, on good terms, and the drug may reach patients sooner. She concedes that fewer buyers means weaker bargaining power for founders.
ex: Fewer than 3% of reported deals get investigated
The FTC sued to block Sanofi's purchase of Maze

n85|410.c: Open-weight models lower barriers to entry, and the more complex the rules, the more they favor incumbents.
n85|410.e: She publicly supports open-weight models: they keep companies from being cut off from a key input and let people tinker and innovate cheaply, and openness has long been a major source of innovation. The FTC will watch for points in the AI stack where competitors could be squeezed, and it has heard writers, designers and journalists worry about their work being used for training without pay. She says her job is to enforce existing law, not design new regimes, and complex rules only suit big companies that can afford lawyers and lobbyists.
ex: Creators say their work was used for training without compensation

marks.d: Same rule for big and small

n85|410.c: Banning non-competes lets people and ideas move freely, as California shows.
n85|410.e: The FTC has finalized a rule banning non-compete clauses in the vast majority of employment contracts. She points to California, which has long refused to enforce non-competes, where research shows this boosted innovation: when people can move freely, ideas spread. Her yardstick for the FTC's success is whether it tackles the big problems within its mandate, such as hospital mergers and practices that drive up drug prices, and whether markets stay open to the next wave of founders.
ex: California has long declined to enforce non-competes
Challenging hospital mergers and practices that inflate drug prices

n86|413.c: Evals look like a simple for loop, yet doing them well sets how fast an AI product improves.
n86|413.e: At Impira he built eval and data-collection tools for traditional AI, then built nearly the same thing at Figma for LLM features, a sign the problem outlasts each technology generation. Prototypes work on a few examples and break at scale. Only systematic evals turn anxious guessing into measurable improvement. Reviewing results is especially hard, harder still with agents, and the faster you review, the faster you iterate. Early customers like Zapier and Notion had all built internal versions and learned how hard it is.
ex: He built nearly the same tool twice, at Impira and at Figma
More than half of evals are scored by an LLM

n86|413.c: Nearly every customer moved from fine-tuning to prompts with examples, since fine-tuning was a means, not the goal.
n86|413.e: What customers really want is their workload optimized automatically, and fine-tuning is just one hard path there. When GPT-4 was hard to get, fine-tuning GPT-3.5 was the main way to improve quality, and customers re-tested it every two or three months. Now almost all of them use instruction-tuned models with few-shot prompts, and it works well. Changing a prompt is like writing high-level code. Changing weights is slower, costlier and can hurt real-world performance if done badly. So the fine-tuning features Braintrust planned early on went unused.
ex: Customers re-ran evals on fine-tuning every two or three months
About 50% of production use cases use some form of RAG

d.verdict: Almost every customer now prompts with examples

n86|413.c: Early adopters are retreating from free-form agents to deterministic workflows with embedded LLM calls.
n86|413.e: Many early adopters bet heavily on free-form agents, then found them hard to control and error-prone, with mistakes compounding step by step. So they moved control flow back into code and embedded LLM calls throughout the product. He also sees a typical path: explore fine-tuning or open source, switch to GPT-4, build your own tooling, and finally realize the product itself matters most. Many say at first they don't need an eval tool, then come back about three months later.
ex: Many teams come back needing an eval tool about three months later

items.d: The model decides on its own
Code controls the flow, with embedded LLM calls

n86|413.c: Data warehouses are the wrong tool for AI, and embedding-based search will become central to querying data.
n86|413.e: Years of hoarded structured data are worth less than companies hoped: LLMs trained on internet text beat models trained only on company data at many tasks. Many customers' logs stored in Braintrust never reach a data warehouse, and they don't care. Warehouses were built for ad hoc SQL on structured data, while AI workloads are mostly text and semantic search. Leading companies already use embeddings to find underrepresented examples. He thinks the vector database fight matters little. Analytical systems are what really get disrupted.
ex: Using embeddings to pick rare support tickets for an eval set
A relational database plus an HNSW index is enough

root.d: Built for SQL on structured data

items.d: Embeddings become the way to query

n86|413.c: Hire strong product engineers first, and save ML rigor for after you find product-market fit.
n86|413.e: Many early LLM adopters had no traditional ML team and moved faster for it. Traditional ML people often resisted LLMs out of identity, even though GPT-3 already beat any model they had trained in-house. He advises starting with product engineers who can see which parts of a product AI will reshape, then adding evals, fine-tuning or cheaper open-source models after product-market fit. Product engineers drive the innovation, so most customers use TypeScript, whose type system also helps turn uncertain outputs into fixed structures.
ex: Vercel's v0 is a model of strong product engineering
Most customers build their AI features in TypeScript

n87|95.c: This wave of consumer AI is about information utility and content generation.
n87|95.e: Past consumer waves centered on e-commerce, search and social. This one centers on processing information and generating content. NotebookLM turns uploaded documents into a conversation between two AI hosts, and one host mostly uses it as a ready-made search interface for personal files. They think embedding AI in users' existing workflows and material solves the cold-start problem of not knowing what to use it for. ChatGPT, Perplexity and Midjourney all started from consumer or prosumer uses.
ex: NotebookLM turns documents into a two-host podcast
Midjourney gets used to illustrate fundraising decks

n87|95.c: AI will bring truly interactive NPCs and modding tools that let players extend game worlds.
n87|95.e: Since the GPT-3 era, people have imagined NPCs that talk like humans, and public demos can now teach, chat and trigger in-game actions within the latency games can tolerate. A Stanford student team uses generative methods to produce endless levels on fixed mechanics, much like the Angry Birds series keeps its gameplay and refreshes levels and art. Modding is already a big market, and if players get powerful AI tools to extend worlds, gameplay and visuals, the impact could be large.
ex: A student team generates endless levels on fixed mechanics
Angry Birds: same mechanics, ever-new levels

items.d: Trigger game moves with low latency

n87|95.c: Many people will date AI, and human conversation may become cheap as a result.
n87|95.e: An AI lab researcher thinks his son will likely have an AI partner someday, and both hosts expect AI romance to be common. One host admits that ten years ago they'd have backed artificial wombs, but now worries that mass use could deepen isolation. Unlike COVID lockdowns, AI companionship keeps socializing but cuts real human contact. When human-like conversation becomes cheap and abundant, people may stop valuing it, for example feeling less obliged to answer a real person's email.
ex: A researcher expects his son to have an AI partner
A host's view on artificial wombs flipped over ten years

n87|95.c: o1 opens test-time compute as a new scaling dimension, but it's still unreliable.
n87|95.e: OpenAI says o1 can spend more compute at inference time on long-horizon planning, which suits iterative reasoning like math, code and crosswords. But it doesn't beat GPT-4o everywhere, and early reactions were mixed. The hosts lean toward seeing it as a new scaling curve, like early GPT-2, that will improve fast with more compute and data. Still, one host tested it on a coin-flip puzzle from a colleague, and even with hints it couldn't answer reliably. On the Nobels, they call the chemistry prize for protein structure prediction a real breakthrough, while the physics prize looks more like borrowing physics ideas.
ex: A coin-flip puzzle took the host about 3.5 hours to solve
The Nobel Prize in Chemistry went to protein structure prediction

items: Base model isn't good enough yet

d.verdict: Bullish on test-time compute, but labs should improve steering

n87|95.c: AI's biggest opportunity is replacing labor rather than SaaS, and thin layers over data are most exposed.
n87|95.e: They see the bigger opportunity in augmenting or replacing human labor at scale, not just swapping out SaaS. Customer support, customer success and many email-heavy, text-processing jobs come first, and AI can work in many languages around the clock. Niche vertical software rolled up by acquirers, and website hosting, could be replaced by software users generate themselves. By contrast, regulated railroads and deeply bundled Rippling are more "AI-durable." Systems of record that are just a wrapper on data storage will erode, starting with smaller customers.
ex: Sierra and Decagon use AI for customer support
Constellation has bought up lots of niche vertical software

n88|421.c: Hardware matured over generations, and Waymo dropped driver assistance early to aim straight at full autonomy.
n88|421.e: When the Google project started in 2009, about a dozen people spent roughly 18 months completing ten 100-mile routes without a human takeover. The original idea was driver assistance, but once the core technology advanced, they pivoted to full autonomy around 2013. In 2015 the third-generation hardware made the first driverless trip in the custom Firefly. The fourth generation opened to the public in Chandler, and only the fifth-generation Jaguar I-PACE was seen as a platform that could scale. Going straight for full autonomy, he believes, kept them from stalling at driver-assist level.
ex: About 100,000 paid rides and over 1 million miles a week
Operating in Phoenix, San Francisco, Los Angeles and more

n88|421.c: Prototypes are easy; full autonomy is about the long tail and adding more nines of reliability.
n88|421.e: Today you can fine-tune a vision-language model and drive a few hundred impressive miles, but safely handling rare events over tens of millions of miles is a different level of difficulty. He doesn't think highways or trucks are easier. Routine conditions are more regular, but high speeds bring rare dangers like construction zones, debris and out-of-control vehicles. Some events happen roughly once per million miles, and nobody in the industry has large samples of them. There's no silver bullet: you don't get to skip the core complexity.
ex: A fine-tuned vision-language model can drive hundreds of miles
Some dangerous events occur about once per million miles

items.d: A fine-tuned model can do it

n88|421.c: Imitating human drivers alone plateaus too low, so full autonomy needs simulation and synthetic data.
n88|421.e: Pure end-to-end imitation learning plus a data flywheel keeps improving, but it plateaus at a level fine for driver assistance and not enough for full autonomy. Breaking through takes synthetic data, closed-loop simulation and even simulation in latent space, since full sensor-level simulation is too inefficient at scale. He stresses that model architecture is only one piece: the data engine, evaluation metrics and simulator around it matter just as much. Evaluation has to be built alongside the driving system, and it's as hard as building the "driver" itself.
ex: They track hundreds of metrics using both open- and closed-loop simulation

n88|421.c: Multiple sensors are an advantage; cameras alone can drive but can't clear the bar for driverless scale.
n88|421.e: Humans drive with two eyes, but a computer needs to see more to meet Waymo's safety standard, so it combines cameras, lidar and radar. They can now test experimentally what happens if a sensor is removed: cameras alone can drive, but they don't clear the bar for driverless service at scale. Driver assistance with a human backup can make different trade-offs. Each hardware generation adds capability while cutting cost and complexity, and safety data shows crash rates clearly below the human benchmark.
ex: About 22 million miles of data: roughly 6x fewer airbag-deployment crashes
A study with Swiss Re: about 4x fewer property damage claims

n88|421.c: Trust, not capital, limits expansion, and scaling is a dial you turn gradually, not a switch.
n88|421.e: Trust is hard to build and easy to lose, so Waymo stays transparent with regulators and communities and expands step by step as safety evidence accumulates, rather than flipping a switch. Experience changes minds: riders in cities where it operates often call it magic, while people who haven't ridden are more anxious. Choosing cities depends on market appeal, technical complexity and the regulatory climate. The business centers on ride-hailing. Waymo sees itself as a tech company building a general-purpose "driver," partnering with automakers and operators instead of building cars.
ex: The sixth-generation vehicle is designed for riders: flat floor, sliding doors
Riders are encouraged to connect to public transit hubs

n89|424.c: Financial markets only grow big once regulated, so Kalshi put compliance first.
n89|424.e: He thinks people naturally want to take positions on things they care about, like weather, climate or AI, so prediction markets could be the next big financial asset class. But historically, markets only grew large once the right regulation existed. So Kalshi, like Coinbase with crypto, put legal work, compliance and trust first: it spent nearly three years in CFTC review, and the team helped draft the rules for prediction markets. Money held in positions also earns about 4.1% interest, so it isn't just sitting idle.
ex: Nearly three years to get CFTC approval
Money in open positions earns about 4.1% interest

n89|424.c: Elections have real economic consequences, so trading on them is hedging, not gambling.
n89|424.e: Even after Kalshi got its license, the CFTC refused to let it list U.S. election contracts. Kalshi sued and eventually won, though its board first thought suing the government was a bad idea. To the charge that this is gambling, he answers that rolling dice has no economic meaning, while election outcomes affect the real economy, so people have legitimate reasons to hedge or forecast them. Futures began as a way for farmers to hedge price risk, and from Japan's Dojima rice market to U.S. grain futures, they too were once denounced as gambling.
ex: In 1905 the Supreme Court upheld grain futures
Japan's Dojima rice market: futures began as hedging

d.verdict: Election contracts are tools for hedging and forecasting

n89|424.c: Price is probability, and crowd judgment backed by real money beats polls.
n89|424.e: People who've done research are rewarded for bringing information into the market, and those who disagree can bet against a mispricing: wisdom of crowds plus skin in the game. Speculators are essential too, because they provide liquidity. He stresses that Kalshi is more accurate than alternatives, not always right. Its inflation forecasts beat Bloomberg and Economist surveys, and it has a good record on Fed decisions and the TikTok ban. Polls are biased samples, and media often misread a 55% chance as a 10-point lead, when it's closer to a slightly weighted coin.
ex: Trump's chance of winning was then about 55%
A TikTok ban taking effect by May was about 35%

result.d: Beats polls, but isn't always right

n89|424.c: Liquidity is an exchange's hardest problem, so start with retail and forecasting communities, then add institutions.
n89|424.e: An exchange has to match both sides, which makes it one of the hardest businesses to start, so Kalshi began with retail traders and forecasting communities. After the court win, sign-ups and volume soared day after day, and some institutions wanted to place $10 million to $20 million orders, making compliance onboarding the bottleneck. Launching a new market dropped from 18 months for the first one to about 24 hours, and about half of markets are proposed by users. Kalshi also bought a clearinghouse and plans margin, leverage and conditional markets within a year to eighteen months.
ex: Launching a new market: 18 months down to about 24 hours
About 50% of markets are proposed by users

items.d: Soaring daily after the court win
Orders in the tens of millions
Over the next year or so

n89|424.c: Humans are wired to take risks, and amateur stars on the leaderboard often beat professional firms.
n89|424.e: Evolution made people comfortable with risk, he thinks, and casinos and startups both draw people in by showcasing visible winners. Startups have more social value, but they come from the same appetite for risk. He partly agrees with Nassim Taleb that a grandmother's intuition beats a data scientist, but finds that too conservative. By his account, the best inflation forecaster of the past year or two is a self-taught person in Kansas who never traded professionally, and trading firms now recruit from the leaderboard. Personally, he thinks the market underprices the chance of Musk leaving Tesla.
ex: Some weather-market users make hundreds of thousands of dollars a month
Someone inferred jobs data from the Labor Department's lights at night

n90|129.c: Moore's law's two pillars have run out, so NVIDIA co-designs hardware and software for 2–3x gains a year.
n90|129.e: Dennard scaling and Carver Mead's VLSI scaling have both run out of steam, so a new way to scale is needed. His answer is co-design: fit algorithms to hardware and hardware to software, which only a company that controls both can do, such as cutting numerical precision down to FP8 and FP4. The network also has to become part of the computing fabric, which is why NVIDIA bought Mellanox and built out NVLink. The goal is two to three times more performance per year at the system level, with cost and energy falling too: a "hyper Moore's law" curve.
ex: Precision: FP64 to FP32 to BF16 to FP8 to FP4
Cost per million tokens for GPT-4-class models fell 240x in about 18 months

terms.d: Algorithms and hardware shaped for each other

result.d: Two to three times better per year, system-wide

n90|129.c: The new unit of computing is the whole data center, which NVIDIA builds itself, then sells in parts.
n90|129.e: You can't validate a system without running the full software and network stack, and peak numbers on a slide often differ greatly from real performance. So NVIDIA builds every configuration itself at scale, air and liquid cooling, x86 and Grace, Ethernet and InfiniBand, then sells the pieces, while CUDA lets customers build once and run on every major cloud. It already has five supercomputers in-house and plans about five more next year. The goal is to deliver a working data center about 30 days after a customer provides space, power and cooling.
ex: xAI's 100,000-GPU cluster was running within weeks
Goal: deliver a data center in about 30 days

items.d: Air or liquid cooling, x86 or Grace

n90|129.c: NVIDIA never abandons a software version, and compatibility keeps old clusters valuable for inference.
n90|129.e: Software is the most expensive investment: the hardware industry is about $1 trillion, while industries driven by software are worth about $100 trillion. Because CUDA's foundation is stable, the layers above can iterate fast, and Hopper's performance on Llama rose about 5x within a year. Training clusters can later be repurposed for inference, and most ChatGPT inference runs on systems like those used for training, so customers can keep investing with confidence. Inference will span every model size, with big models generating synthetic data that is distilled into small ones.
ex: The seven-year-old Shield TV box still gets updates
Hopper's Llama performance improved about 5x in a year

n90|129.c: Data centers are becoming AI factories that produce tokens, and generative AI is no passing fad.
n90|129.e: He sees computing being reinvented after about 60 years. The marginal cost of computing fell roughly a millionfold over the past decade, so computers can now write software themselves by brute-force search. Data centers become factories that produce tokens, a new commodity that may be worth trillions of dollars and that every company and country will need. NVIDIA's market value rose from about $500 billion to over $3 trillion in about 18 months, but he says the company itself hasn't changed that fast. No law of physics blocks scaling to hundreds of thousands or a million GPUs. The hard parts are capital, energy and supply.
ex: The marginal cost of computing fell roughly a millionfold in ten years

n90|129.c: Companies will mix human and AI employees, and SaaS platforms are sitting on gold mines, not facing disruption.
n90|129.e: He expects companies to have AI employees for marketing, design, supply chain and more, prompted to work the way human staff are directed. Chip design is the first field AI is transforming: Hopper couldn't have been built without AI designers, because human time is limited and people can't explore the whole design space. He imagines renting AI chip engineers from Synopsys and Cadence, and SaaS platforms growing specialized agents to work alongside people. In robotics, if actions can be tokenized, robots can be prompted like language models.
ex: Renting AI chip engineers from Synopsys and Cadence
NVIDIA will build its own OpenUSD agents

items.d: First to be transformed by AI
Platforms sit on a gold mine
A basis for breakthroughs within years

n91|433.c: Math has no opponent to self-play against, so the only way forward is to think longer.
n91|433.e: In board games you improve by playing a copy of yourself at your level, but math has no opponent and no physical experiments, so all you can do is think more. He has long focused on systems that solve harder problems with more compute, and math is one of the last grand-challenge domains. This year AlphaProof solved four of six IMO problems, reaching silver-medal level. But math's search space is enormous, and many proofs require inventing new constructions, not just picking from known techniques.
ex: Solved four of six IMO problems, silver-medal level
Strongest at algebra and number theory, weaker at combinatorics

d.verdict: Math only improves by thinking longer

n91|433.c: AlphaProof can't build theories yet, and cracking the Riemann hypothesis will need new mathematics.
n91|433.e: It can't invent new mathematical objects or frameworks, which harder problems often require. Combinatorics problems are hard to translate into Lean, a language that lets computers check proofs, partly because its library lacks definitions like "agent, environment, policy," so autoformalization would have to create them first. The Riemann hypothesis and the Millennium Prize problems probably need entirely new theory, and no one knows how far off that is, perhaps orders of magnitude. Hilbert's 23 problems show that good questions can set a field's agenda.
ex: Lean's library lacks definitions that combinatorics problems need

n91|433.c: On the hardest problem, Problem 6, it found a construction top mathematicians missed for hours.
n91|433.e: Problems 3 and 6 are usually the hardest, and only about 5 of roughly 500 contestants solved Problem 6. It asked for an upper bound on how many distinct values an expression can take for a certain class of functions. AlphaProof first proved the bound is at most 2, then built a special function with a zigzag term that hits exactly two values, settling the answer. The guest notes that Fields medalist Tim Gowers spent hours without finding this construction, but stresses this doesn't mean it's better at math than people overall.
ex: Only about 5 of roughly 500 contestants solved it
Fields medalist Tim Gowers spent hours without finding it

n91|434.c: When stuck, it generates variant problems to solve, doing reinforcement learning even at inference time.
n91|434.e: Facing a hard problem, the system generates many variants of it, solves those easier versions and learns from them, then works its way toward the original. In effect it keeps doing reinforcement learning at inference time. Some problems used up to three days of inference compute. This is the team's core interest: systems that solve harder problems by spending more compute.
ex: Some problems used about three days of inference compute

n91|434.c: A little expert data provides a starting point, then reinforcement learning surpasses humans in its own style.
n91|434.e: A small amount of expert data can take a model from almost nothing to a usable starting point. Reinforcement learning then builds on those priors and may surpass humans in a style of its own. AlphaProof's proofs look rather "alien." You could optimize for proofs that humans prefer and find readable, but that's a preference, not something capability requires. Human data's other value is saving years of exploration compute.
ex: AlphaProof's proofs have an "alien" style

items.d: No need to explore from zero

n91|434.c: Machine-verifiable domains can scale, and formal proofs can also be used to verify code.
n91|434.e: A math proof can be checked automatically, so training can scale up massively. Domains without a right answer, like humor, can only be rewarded by human judgment or real-world feedback, so scale is limited by how many people can give feedback. The same idea applies to code: formal proofs that software satisfies certain properties can reduce bugs and security holes. Today that work is done by hand, mostly in critical areas like avionics and cryptography.
ex: Formal verification is used today mainly in avionics and cryptography

marks.d: Needs human judges, hard to scale

n91|434.c: The better machines get at finding answers, the better humans must get at asking good questions.
n91|434.e: He considers himself a software engineer, and thinks taste matters more and more in every field AI assists, though it's much harder to teach than a concrete skill like Lean. Once machines are good at solving, people need to get better at choosing problems and breaking big ones into interesting smaller ones, and the same goes for software engineering. The team positions AlphaProof as a grad-student-like assistant that isn't good at posing problems, and hopes mathematicians will supply them.
ex: Mathematicians can't use AlphaProof yet

n91|435.c: A verifiable formal language lets AlphaZero-style reinforcement learning work for math.
n91|435.e: A former Go player, he worked on AlphaGo, AlphaZero and MuZero, as well as AlphaCode and AlphaTensor. AlphaProof keeps AlphaZero's three ingredients: a neural network, large-scale trial-and-error reinforcement learning, and search and planning. It just swaps board moves for a nearly infinite space of proof steps. Proofs are written in Lean, whose checker confirms whether each one is correct, and correct proofs become new training data, creating a self-improving loop.
ex: Writing proofs in Lean is like writing math as code

n91|435.c: Mathematicians should learn Lean early, because it tells you for certain you aren't fooling yourself.
n91|435.e: Lean is becoming an increasingly important collaboration tool, and it's good for teaching, since a proof can be expanded to any level of detail on demand. A formal language checks itself: you know exactly what remains to be proved and whether you've fooled yourself. Formal verification also makes large, distributed collaboration possible, because collaborators' work doesn't need to be checked one by one by hand, and AI can be one of the collaborators.

n92|439.c: Cohere isn't building a ChatGPT rival: the model is the foundation, but enterprises win on deployment.
n92|439.e: As a Google Brain intern he co-wrote the Transformer paper, the architecture behind today's models. Seeing GPT-2 convinced him that models trained on web-scale data would become useful, so he started Cohere. A weak foundation sinks a company, but enterprise success also depends on customer support, reliability and security. Finance and healthcare data often can't leave a private cloud, so Cohere deploys wherever the customer needs it. He says many 2023 proofs of concept failed because people treated the model like a human.
ex: Healthcare: a patient-history briefing generated in under a second
Even with no new models, working AI into the economy takes about five years

n92|439.c: Enterprises should customize cheap first: fine-tuning, then post-training, and continued pre-training only last.
n92|439.e: He tells customers to start with fine-tuning, then move to post-training such as SFT and RLHF, which teach the model from example answers and human ratings, and only then consider continued pre-training. Some needs truly require pre-training, like the Japanese model Cohere built with Fujitsu. A large company with hundreds of billions of tokens of its own data can continue pre-training for about $5 million rather than $50 million. For startups and small businesses it usually doesn't pay off. Some lab leaders say only AGI labs should pre-train. He thinks the evidence says otherwise.
ex: Building a Japanese-language model with Fujitsu

n92|439.c: Matching GPT-4 on business tasks costs just $10–20 million, so lagging a few months beats burning billions.
n92|439.e: He estimates that a model matching GPT-4 on enterprise-relevant tasks now costs about $10–20 million, if you accept being 6 to 12 months behind the frontier. So Cohere doesn't race for the frontier. It focuses on the capabilities customers rely on, does them well at lower cost, and avoids burning billions a year. Supercomputers still cost hundreds of millions a year, so this is a capital-intensive business, but it can be capital-efficient. He also argues that fine-tuning open models like Llama gives you fewer levers than owning your training data end to end.
ex: Supercomputers cost hundreds of millions of dollars a year

n92|439.c: Test-time compute is a new lever: pay for more thinking at answer time and get smarter answers.
n92|439.e: Early models had no inner monologue, so they couldn't catch and fix their own mistakes, and chain-of-thought prompting only imitated reasoning after the fact. He sees reasoning models as a genuinely new category. A more capable model used to mean waiting 6 to 12 months for new training. Now a customer can pay for more inference compute and get a better answer right away, and the model maker doesn't have to double its supercomputer. Inference doesn't need tightly interconnected supercomputers, so chip design and data center priorities may shift. He thinks the market hasn't priced this in.
ex: Training on reasoning traces from humans and synthetic data

d.verdict: Test-time compute is an underrated new lever

n92|439.c: Model progress is flattening, AGI is arriving gradually, and models are not becoming commodities.
n92|439.e: He compares it to painting: broad strokes are easy, details are hard. Code and math can be checked, so synthetic data keeps scaling them. Biology and chemistry are limited by scarce experts, and eventually models must run their own experiments, which is still far off. Casual vibe checks no longer reveal differences, so domain experts must evaluate. He sees no single breakpoint for AGI. We're already on the way, though he doesn't buy a self-improving superintelligence takeoff. Falling prices are dumping, not commoditization, and giving models away at a loss can't last. This rebuild of technology will take 10 to 15 years.
ex: Rebuilding the tech stack is like repaving every road on Earth

n93|445.c: Bolt's edge is running a full development environment in the browser, not being a thin GPT wrapper.
n93|445.e: Products that simply wrap a frontier model tend to vanish when a lab ships the same feature. StackBlitz spent four or five years building WebContainer, an operating system that runs inside the browser using WebAssembly. In a single tab it can install any package and toolchain, connect a backend and deploy, with no server costs or lag. Claude Artifacts works well for simple interfaces and charts, but it can't install packages or connect to a backend like Supabase. Bolt was built for exactly that gap.
ex: About 3 million developers use StackBlitz each month
Nearly 200,000 "software composers" used Bolt last week

d.verdict: Complex full-stack apps need a real runtime

n93|445.c: Open-sourcing the prompts costs little, because the real advantage is the end-to-end experience and the community.
n93|445.e: He open-sourced Bolt and its system prompt. Someone would extract the prompt anyway, and open source drives innovation, much as you can view a web page's source code but can't copy the whole business. AI tools have high churn because users must learn to instruct an unpredictable model, and every message costs money. On Discord, Twitter and livestreams, power users understand prompting better than the company does, and their lessons flow back into the product, much like Midjourney. The open-source version has also become the de facto benchmark for testing new coding models.
ex: AI apps that skip user education can see 60–70% churn
The open-source version became a benchmark for new coding models

n93|445.c: Bolt cuts the cost of outsourced app building by about 99%, letting agencies pocket the difference.
n93|445.e: About two months after launch, people were already charging customers through Stripe for products built on Bolt. A product manager in Thailand built Viralhooks on the side. Agencies quoted about $5,000 and two to three months, and she finished in two weeks on a $50 plan. A veteran web builder made a CRM with calendar, contacts and AI chat in a month, against a quote of about $30,000. Agencies can deliver faster while charging the same price. Non-technical people use it too: one parent built a site to find donors for a daughter's medical needs.
ex: Viralhooks: quoted $5,000, built in two weeks on a $50 plan
Chilled CRM: quoted about $30,000, built in one month

n93|445.c: Because AI writes standard framework code, no-code is no longer a lock-in dead end.
n93|445.e: He used to be skeptical of traditional no-code: visual builders, closed ecosystems, easy to get locked in. No-code existed because someone had to translate ideas into code. Now AI writes standard code in frameworks like Next.js, Remix, Astro and Vite, so a professional can take the project over, and it can move back and forth between Bolt and Cursor. The turning point was code generation crossing a reliability threshold. The team had tried to build Bolt earlier and shelved it. It only became possible with Claude 3.5 Sonnet.
ex: Claude 3.5 Sonnet revived a shelved project

items.d: Visual, easy to get locked in

n93|445.c: Coding will shift from autocomplete to delegation, and progress will be fast because code is verifiable.
n93|445.e: Coding AI will move from tab completion and line-by-line suggestions to agentic workflows, where engineers hand off higher-level tasks. Managing an AI is a lot like managing human developers. He expects "software composer" to become a common term, and the user base to grow from about 25 million developers to 100 million people or more. Code generation will improve fast because results are verifiable: it either runs or it doesn't, unlike many AI fields. He expects big gains in the next 6 to 12 months and sees no ceiling yet.
ex: About 25 million developers worldwide, with a goal of 100 million users

n94|449.c: Bonding different materials at the atomic level can deliver far more than the sum of the parts.
n94|449.e: During his PhD at Cornell he worked on combining optics with silicon, which gave him a one-plus-one-equals-ten philosophy. He brought it to Akash when he founded the company with Ty in 2017. Akash grows diamond in the lab from seed crystals using chemical vapor deposition, then bonds it to semiconductors like silicon and gallium nitride. The real differentiator isn't growing diamond but the atomic-level bonding process, which takes years to master. The company started with satellite radio-frequency hardware and, he says, built the fastest satellite radio.
ex: Lab-grown CVD diamond bonded to gallium nitride

n94|449.c: Heat is the root problem for AI compute, behind its reliability, performance and power troubles.
n94|449.e: He compares today's approach to whack-a-mole: fix one symptom and the problem pops up somewhere else. Overheating makes servers fail early, and above roughly 80–90°C chips throttle, slowing down inference. Space hardware runs at far higher power density than the roughly 200 watts per square centimeter of server chips, so once you solve space, servers are much easier. Without solving heat at the level of physics and chemistry, he argues, the AI data center buildout will strain the grid and push up electricity prices.
ex: Chips throttle above roughly 80–90°C
Server chips run at about 200 watts per square centimeter

root.d: The root problem for AI compute

n94|449.c: Diamond could break the thermal crosstalk limit, compressing six or seven years of progress into two.
n94|449.e: How densely you can pack transistors is limited by thermal crosstalk, heat passing between neighboring devices. He ventures a prediction that diamond can lift this ceiling, delivering in about two years the gains that usually take six or seven. This is his speculation, and the episode offered no independent data. The nearer-term payoff is headroom: cooler chips can run at higher frequency or higher density.

d.verdict: His bold guess, no independent data yet

n94|449.c: Demand for data sovereignty will go global, and the U.S. should truly lead the AI chip supply chain.
n94|449.e: An early customer is NextGen, India's largest sovereign cloud provider, which values keeping data in the country, regional leadership and the ability to scale fast. He expects more and more countries to require data to stay at home. He says the U.S. is doing too little in AI chip manufacturing. It should lead across the whole value chain and give federal funding to small companies. Outsourcing manufacturing to please quarterly earnings creates national security risk. AI-powered factories can greatly raise output per worker, so the U.S. doesn't need to compete with China on cheap labor.
ex: NextGen, India's sovereign cloud provider, is an early customer

n94|450.c: A materials breakthrough won't sell by itself, so you must prove its value in a full system.
n94|450.e: He calls himself the silicon carbide guy. Selling silicon carbide power devices years ago, he found that telling automakers a part could add about 40% to an EV's range didn't land. It had to be proven in a complete system. So Akash doesn't just sell materials or chips. It builds boards, modules and even whole servers. The company buys GPUs itself, cools and packages them, then sells to inference providers, model trainers, data centers and cloud companies.
ex: He once pitched silicon carbide parts on about 40% more EV range
Delivering Nvidia servers with liquid cooling plus diamond cooling

n94|450.c: Diamond cooling stacks on top of liquid cooling and other methods, and lower temperatures buy performance.
n94|450.e: In the air-versus-liquid cooling debate, he stresses that diamond works alongside fans, liquid cooling, more efficient chips, fan-out packaging and stacked HBM memory. It adds one more layer on top of existing cooling. Lower temperatures create headroom to raise clock speed or density. The company says it can cut temperatures by about 10°C at first and aims for 20–40°C within a year. In space applications it has achieved 80–90°C. He also notes that overheating delayed the rollout of new products like Nvidia's Blackwell.
ex: About 10°C cooler at first, aiming for 20–40°C within a year
Space applications have seen 80–90°C drops

n94|450.c: The CHIPS Act and defense needs make U.S. manufacturing essential, and AI will speed up materials research.
n94|450.e: Akash received CHIPS Act funding, works with Raytheon, and plans factories in California and Texas. The chip shortage during COVID showed the supply chain must be strengthened. He compares today's AI to radar in World War II, which changed the course of the war. Conflicts today are increasingly decided by the radio-frequency spectrum. In research, AI is already a great assistant, especially for searching the literature, and old ideas that failed for lack of compute are worth trying again.
ex: CHIPS Act funding and a partnership with Raytheon
Plans to build factories in California and Texas

items.d: Changed the course of the war

n95|453.c: B2B companies know how to build and sell products, but not how to care for customers at scale.
n95|453.e: In his view, startups have figured out building products, raising money, hiring and selling. The hard part is serving customers once there are many of them. At HubSpot he saw customers grow from 20 to 5,000, and he could no longer serve each one personally. At Drift, about 250 of 800 employees worked in customer-facing teams, and he thinks that approach of adding headcount failed. His conclusion: only AI can keep relationships one-on-one after a company scales.
ex: HubSpot grew from 20 customers to 5,000
HubSpot revenue grew from $30 million to $130 million

n95|453.c: Customer success shouldn't be a category of its own. What matters is customers feeling truly in control.
n95|453.e: He says customer success is everything, the term itself may be a misnomer, and he pushes back on VCs treating it as a standalone market. He wants customers to have agency and feel in charge, like your relationship with a barber who knows you. The spark came while consulting for Klaviyo, founded by his former colleague Andrew Bialecki, where he saw large models do benchmarking, reports, insights and creative work at scale. All of Agency's customer contact runs through a single founder inbox.
ex: Built the first AI SDR at Drift in 2019
All customer contact goes through one founder inbox

n95|453.c: Good software quietly gets things done for you, and CRMs that bolt AI columns onto spreadsheets will die.
n95|453.e: He imagines that in five years software will work in the background, for example reading your calendar and travel plans, setting up meetings and following up on time. He thinks most software today is bad. Salesforce is expensive, complex and needs consultants, and the data companies work hard to enter rarely gets used. CEOs would do better to throw out their instance. Uber is good software because it just gets the job done. Many new CRMs merely add AI fields to old spreadsheets. Without rebuilding from first principles they will die, though the underlying data store will still be needed.
ex: Uber: it just gets the job done
Salesforce: expensive, complex, needs consultants

n95|453.c: "Do things that don't scale" is outdated advice, so build for scale from day one.
n95|453.e: He wants to challenge Paul Graham's famous advice. Manual workarounds break after about a year, he says, so you should only do things that scale and build the basics to scale from the start: customer insight, communication, pricing and customer relationships. His goal is $1 billion in revenue, and he wants to question everything the way Elon Musk does. There are two ways to reach a billion: sell cheaply to lots of small businesses, or sell at high prices to large enterprises. He chose the latter, taking on big, hard problems.
ex: Goal: $1 billion in revenue

n95|453.c: Large models solve only a small piece, while change management and trust are the hardest parts.
n95|453.e: Most companies don't realize that change management is the hardest part to get through, he says. Large enterprises rarely replace all their systems at once, organizations are often messy, and someone has to understand the customer and migrate step by step. Trust is another big barrier. A customer success manager will scrutinize every word of an AI-drafted email to a million-dollar account, yet never question their own writing that way. No model solves that alone.
