In hiring, he no longer trusts candidates' self-promotion and asks for a paid one- to two-week trial project first.
ex: Candidates first do a paid one- to two-week trial project

items.d: The hardest part to get through
AI emails reviewed word by word
Replace old systems step by step

n97|462.c: Cloud development should give instant feedback like a laptop, and Docker and Kubernetes can't deliver that.
n97|462.e: He spent seven years building recommendation systems at Spotify, then served as CTO of Better.com, and always felt the cloud was powerful but painful to use. He wanted cloud development to have the same tight loop as local work, where you see results right after a change. Off-the-shelf Docker and Kubernetes start slowly and carry a lot of cognitive overhead. So Modal spent its first two years building its own file system, scheduler and container runtime, letting an ordinary Python function spin up in seconds as a serverless job.
ex: Built Luigi and Annoy at Spotify, which he jokes few people use now
About two years spent on the file system, scheduler and runtime

n97|462.c: Startups should get GPUs on demand, not lock up compute with long-term contracts.
n97|462.e: The GPU shortage got the industry used to signing long-term contracts to reserve capacity, which he thinks defeats the cloud's promise of instant availability. Modal runs a multi-tenant pool of thousands of GPUs and CPUs. A customer asking for 100 GPUs usually gets them in seconds and pays only for the time containers actually run. Inference load is spiky and hard to predict, so a single company either pays for idle GPUs or lets service degrade. Pooling bursts of demand from many customers lets the pool absorb the swings.
ex: Ask for 100 GPUs and usually get them in seconds
Billed only for container run time, no reservations

items: Lock in compute with long contracts
Short at peaks, idle in troughs
Scale to hundreds of GPUs in seconds

d.verdict: Spiky inference makes a big shared pool cheapest

n97|462.c: Audio, video and image products mostly need custom-trained models, so the platform must cover the whole pipeline.
n97|462.e: If model quality is the core of your product, he argues, using the same off-the-shelf model as everyone else makes it hard to defend. A clearly better proprietary model is itself the advantage, especially in audio, video and images. So Modal targets high-code engineers who write their own models, and the platform must cover preprocessing, training, inference, feedback loops and batch jobs. Huge, long training runs are a separate market, but short, experimental training fits elastic compute well, so adding a training product makes a lot of sense to him.
ex: A video-model customer processes petabytes on Modal, trains elsewhere, then returns for inference
Stable Diffusion kicked off early inference demand
Suno: AI music still has an uncanny valley, but each version improves

n97|462.c: Enterprise data stuck in the big three clouds is a real obstacle, but it won't stop multi-tenant clouds.
n97|462.e: Elad pushes back: enterprises have their data, committed spend and security approvals on AWS, Azure and GCP, and moving out is expensive. Erik agrees it's a real problem but points to his own past misjudgments. In 2008 he couldn't see why anyone would run compute on someone else's machines, and around 2012 he thought Snowflake's model was crazy. He expects security boundaries to move from the network to the application layer, bandwidth to get cheaper, and zero-egress storage to appear. Add the capacity advantage of slicing a big pool dynamically, and data gravity weakens.
ex: He once thought Snowflake's model was crazy, and it became a major public company
Zero egress fees on R2 are one tailwind he cites

n97|462.c: AI coding is just another productivity leap, unlocking latent demand and leading to more engineers.
n97|462.e: He places AI coding in a 40-year sequence: compilers, high-level languages, databases, cloud tools. Each step made engineers more productive, by roughly 10x per decade in his estimate. But demand for software is latent and far from saturated, so efficiency gains unlock more demand, and the total number of engineers has kept rising. That's why he disagrees with the view that demand is fixed and AI will take programmers' jobs, and he stays optimistic about software engineering careers.
ex: He estimates engineer productivity rises about 10x per decade

n98|465.c: Support is the ideal job for agents: you can roll out gradually and see the ROI immediately.
n98|465.e: After selling his first company to Niantic, he and his co-founder decided to theorize less and talk to customers more, and that pointed to support. Support volume grows linearly with users, and AI can absorb the growth directly. Customers can benchmark it against human agents, start with about 1% of traffic, then ramp up. The metrics are clear: automation rate, headcount saved, CSAT or NPS, and accuracy. The bigger prize is giving every user a 24/7, multilingual personal concierge.
ex: Bilt froze support hiring a month in and, nearly a year later, counted about 65 agents saved
Customers include Rippling, Notion, Duolingo and Substack

items.d: Absorb volume that grows with users

n98|465.c: Everyone can use the same models, so the real advantage is the software layer on top.
n98|465.e: Anyone can call frontier models like GPT-4o or Claude, so Decagon sees itself as a software company. The differentiation comes from orchestration: evaluating which model to use for each subtask, how to combine them, and how to fit each customer's business logic. Add transparency tools that show customers what data the agent looked up and what steps it took, and let them give feedback to correct it. Decagon also uses LLMs to read every conversation, spot knowledge gaps, categorize requests and report on performance. He credits the company's results to being observable, explainable and controllable.

items.d: See data and steps, give feedback
Pick models per task, fit business logic

n98|465.c: For support, strictly following an SOP matters more than gains in math reasoning.
n98|465.e: Recent progress in models like o1 and Sonnet has centered on math, coding and quantitative reasoning. He finds that helpful, but it isn't the bottleneck for support. What really matters is whether a model given a procedure or policy will follow it exactly, especially in regulated industries. So even if talk of slowing model progress holds for reasoning, it may not apply to the abilities he cares about. He hopes labs focus on instruction following next year.

d.verdict: Labs should prioritize instruction following

n98|465.c: The channel doesn't matter: voice is just another way into the same problem, and latency is the challenge.
n98|465.e: Customers care whether their problem is solved, not whether it happens over chat, email, SMS or phone. Decagon started with text because it's easier to build and evaluate, and customers are now testing voice with ElevenLabs, OpenAI, Cartesia and others. Speech-to-speech is fast but struggles with production work like looking up data and calling models several times. Transcribing to text, reasoning, then synthesizing speech is more capable but slower. Mitigations include streaming and filler phrases like "let me look that up for you," and the right trade-off varies by customer.
ex: Voice vendors: ElevenLabs, OpenAI, Cartesia

marks.d: Fast, but hard to look up data

n98|465.c: Most agent categories won't commercialize soon, except those that can roll out gradually with measurable ROI.
n98|465.e: He says he's more pessimistic than industry demos suggest: with today's models, most use cases won't actually get bought yet. A viable category needs two things. It must deliver partial value even when imperfect, then expand, and its ROI must be easy to quantify. Coding agents qualify. Security demands catching every tiny anomaly, while generative models are nondeterministic, so enterprise adoption will be very slow. Text-to-SQL still needs a human checking and fixing it, making it a copilot in practice and hard to justify as a big contract. People's role will shift to supervising and correcting agents.
ex: He thinks Anthropic's computer use demo isn't ready for production

items.d: Security agents need zero misses, so they fail

n99|467.c: Wildfire is mostly a solvable management problem: a century of total suppression made forests three times denser.
n99|467.e: Climate change has lengthened the hot, dry season, but he thinks the recent surge in destruction is largely self-inflicted, rooted in how we manage forests and build the grid. Starting in the 1930s, the Forest Service pursued maximum suppression, requiring fires to be out by the next morning. Frequent low-intensity natural fires disappeared, fuel piled up on the forest floor, and forests became about three times as dense as around 1900. These causes can be fixed faster than climate, yet funding is heavily skewed toward cutting emissions.
ex: About 98% of climate capital goes to emissions cuts, about 2% to resilience and adaptation
The "10 a.m. rule": fires had to be out by the next morning

n99|467.c: Prescribed burns and thinning work best, but permitting and public attitudes block them.
n99|467.e: Prescribed burns and mechanical thinning are the highest-leverage prevention tools. But residents hate smoke, and a burn boss whose fire escapes loses their career, so the incentives are completely lopsided. Treating his own 170 acres of forest took three years, and biologists came six times to check for northern spotted owls. Florida burns two to three million acres a year, while California may have missed even its 100,000-acre goal, and the difference is mostly cultural. Opposition crosses party lines, and he supports the bipartisan Fix Our Forests Act.
ex: Florida burns 2–3 million acres a year, California targets only 100,000
Treating his own 170 acres took three years

d.verdict: The gap is culture and permits, not technology

n99|467.c: Once fire reaches a neighborhood it becomes an urban fire, so homes need layered defenses.
n99|467.e: Since 1980, housing in the wildland-urban interface has grown about 46%, so a fire of the same size now destroys far more homes. Once fire gets past the perimeter, houses ignite one another, as in the great Chicago and San Francisco fires, and it becomes extremely hard to stop. So defense has to be layered: clear vegetation, use noncombustible roofs and materials, tempered glass and sprinklers, keep a reliable water source, make driveways wide enough for a fire truck to turn around, and keep a five-foot zero zone around the house free of anything flammable.
ex: Clear the zero zone and secure water, and you're in the top quarter for protection
He keeps about 20 gallons of fire-blocking gel in Mendocino
He expects pre-positioned drones to put out new fires within 5–10 years

n99|467.c: Utilities start 11% of fires but cause half the damage, and regulation blocks the fix.
n99|467.e: The high winds behind extreme fires also knock down lines and damage equipment, so utility fires are rare but the deadliest. Cutting them would eliminate about half the damage. Tools include tree trimming, more sensitive circuit breakers and preemptive shutoffs before red-flag weather. Burying lines costs $3–4 million per mile and raises rates. He says regulated utilities earn about a 15% return on capital spending and would love to spend it. The holdup is regulators and ratepayer advocates. California rates don't reflect wildfire risk, so bills in high-risk areas may have to rise.
ex: Burying lines costs about $3–4 million per mile
Portfolio company Overstory helps utilities prioritize tree trimming

n99|467.c: California's insurance market was broken by rate suppression, not insurer greed.
n99|467.e: In the regulated admitted market, rates couldn't include reinsurance costs and had to rely on 30 years of historical data rather than forward-looking catastrophe models. Meanwhile reinsurance costs at least doubled over five to ten years. Insurers concluded this simply wasn't a business and stopped writing policies in large numbers. The FAIR Plan assesses insurers by market share, so every policy they write adds to their share of the backstop risk. Regulators only recently allowed reinsurance costs and forward-looking models, with limits. His own company, Stand, writes non-admitted policies that aren't subject to rate controls.

items.d: Backstop risk spread across the industry

n100|471.c: The fire may have been unstoppable, but better preparation could have greatly reduced the damage.
n100|471.e: He grants that climate change played a role, but not the whole story. Brush uncleared for about 40 years provided fuel. A fire had broken out nearby in Malibu three weeks earlier, and high winds were forecast, so reservoirs should have been filled and crews put on full alert. He rejects the claim that burning homes drained the water through their pipes. The system runs on gravity, so full reservoirs set the pressure, yet a reservoir had been drained for repairs and the largest one was empty. With years of fire underfunding and new budget cuts, he calls it a failure of planning and leadership.
ex: The burned area was about the size of two Manhattans
One reservoir had been drained for repairs

n100|471.c: Noncombustible design plus layers of private preparation let Palisades Village survive the fire.
n100|471.e: His Palisades Village shopping district uses no combustible materials at all. Surfaces that look like wood are actually formed concrete. On top of that sit fire-retardant spray crews, backup water, rapid-deployment teams and private firefighters. The plan grew out of a wildfire near the Rosewood Miramar hotel in the Montecito area about six years earlier. The village and eight nearby homes survived, saving thousands of jobs. He stresses that private resources must not divert public firefighters who should be protecting homes.
ex: The plan came from a fire near the Rosewood Miramar about six years ago

n100|471.c: Rebuild zone by zone with many contractors working at once, so residents can start within a year.
n100|471.e: He opposes using a single general contractor in a sequential process: clear the debris, then rebuild infrastructure, then build homes. Instead, split the burn area into zones, have multiple contractors work in parallel, and reward speed and quality. Hazardous cleanup takes about three to four months. Permits should be simplified and fees waived for now, with the goal of residents breaking ground within a year and each house taking about another year. If someone has a six-month plan, he's all for it. He praises the governor for suspending Coastal Commission requirements and speeding up permits.
ex: Hazardous cleanup is estimated at 3–4 months
The governor suspended Coastal Commission approval requirements

n100|471.c: Rebuilding should upgrade infrastructure along the way, because prevention is the best investment.
n100|471.e: If you're rebuilding in a high fire-risk area anyway, don't copy the system that failed. Bury power lines, upgrade water systems, hydrants, reservoirs and communications, and add a modern recreation center, bigger parks and recycled-water irrigation. These can run in parallel with cleanup without slowing home construction. He cites estimates that losses could reach hundreds of billions of dollars and sees prevention infrastructure as the best investment. He also questions how California went from a big surplus to a deficit without explaining where the money went, and backs Elad's idea of a Norway-style sovereign wealth fund.
ex: His priorities: broadband, the grid, vegetation management, water, schools

n100|471.c: Crime rose because laws went unenforced, and strict enforcement and real second chances should go together.
n100|471.e: He believes rising crime largely reflects existing laws going unenforced and limits on proactive policing, though enforcement must stay legal and constitutional. His fixes: hire more officers, add community liaison officers and bring back foot patrols, drawing on his work with Bill Bratton about 20 years ago. Repeat offenders should face consequences, and people who want to change should get a real path forward. The two don't conflict. Los Angeles has spent billions on homelessness, yet the number of people on the street keeps growing, and open-air drug dealing has to be confronted directly.
ex: He's optimistic about new DA Nathan Hochman and the new police chief
He says a fire station near MacArthur Park is the nation's busiest due to overdoses

d.verdict: Both at once, no contradiction

n101|144.c: DeepSeek is real progress but still on trend, and Nvidia's sell-off was somewhat overdone.
n101|144.e: Elad sees DeepSeek's model as the most advanced Chinese open-source reasoning model, one that thinks before answering, and other labs have already borrowed its new reinforcement learning tricks. But falling costs were expected. The widely cited $5.5 million covers only the final training run, and comparable final runs already cost $5–10 million. Add tooling, data and lots of experiments, and he estimates the total at hundreds of millions of dollars. So Nvidia's roughly 20% drop struck him as a bit irrational, and the DeepSeek app's brief run at the top of the charts was mostly curiosity.
ex: Nvidia's stock fell as much as about 20%

items.d: About $5.5 million, the widely cited figure
Hundreds of millions, by his estimate

n101|144.c: Inference for GPT-4-level models got 180x cheaper in 18 months, and models are converging.
n101|144.e: His team estimates that the per-token cost of running a GPT-4-level model fell about 180x in 18 months: 180 times, not 180%. Independent benchmarks from Artificial Analysis show models converging on reasoning, knowledge, math, coding, multilingual ability and cost, so a breakthrough buys only a brief lead. Frontier leaders still get market share, lock-in from prompts and tool integrations, and a strong model that can generate synthetic data and write code for the next generation. Whether that lets a leader take off, he has reservations.
ex: Artificial Analysis independently reruns each lab's benchmarks

items: Synthetic data for the next model

d.verdict: Converging overall; whether leaders take off is unclear

n101|144.c: Big compute bets reflect uncertainty, not measurable risk, and no lab would turn down a giant cluster.
n101|144.e: On infrastructure bets like Stargate, Elad argues that algorithmic efficiency, synthetic data and test-time scaling, giving models more compute while they answer, make progress hard to predict. That makes it uncertainty rather than a risk you can put numbers on. He can't imagine any lab pursuing AGI turning down a giant cluster that comes free or that it can raise money for. He expects pre-training to keep paying off, just less efficiently. How deep capital markets can go, and whether sovereign wealth funds step in, he treats as open questions.

items.d: May get around the data bottleneck
More compute while the model answers

n101|144.c: 2025 is the year of vertical AI: industry-specific apps scale up, and some gradually become agents.
n101|144.e: Elad predicts partial consolidation among foundation models for images, video and voice, faster if regulation loosens, while physics, biology and materials kick off a new model race. The biggest opportunity in applications is vertical AI: companies like Harvey, Decagon, Sierra and Abridge will scale, and some will gradually add agent capabilities, AI that takes actions on its own. In self-driving, attention will center on Tesla and Waymo, with Applied Intuition as the dark horse. Consumer AI will make a comeback, while agents and robotics will show only early glimmers.
ex: Vertical AI app examples: Harvey, Decagon, Sierra and Abridge
Self-driving dark horse: Applied Intuition

marks.d: A comeback, but it takes time

n101|143.c: R1 is what rattled markets, because it broke the story of America's tech lead over China.
n101|143.e: Sarah points out that V3, released in December, didn't move Nvidia. The reaction came with R1, a reasoning model meant to rival OpenAI's o1, and it was post-training, the refinement after the base model is built, that made it genuinely useful. It was a narrative violation: a Chinese lab catching up this fast challenged two decades of US tech leadership. Even if total spend was many times $6 million, that's far below the billions, or Stargate-scale sums, it was assumed to take to compete. That's what unsettled markets.
ex: Markets barely reacted when V3 came out in December

items.d: Huge entry costs called into question

n101|143.c: Deep Research is great for mapping an unfamiliar field, but its implicit rankings must be audited.
n101|143.e: Sarah finds Deep Research, an AI tool that searches the web and writes up reports, great for quickly mapping an unfamiliar field, getting the big picture, and finding the relevant experts. Elad adds that it instantly raised the bar for knowledge work. But in areas where she has deep expertise, its choices about which sources and claims to prioritize are often off. So you can't take its conclusions at face value. You have to audit the outputs.

items: Can't be taken at face value

d.verdict: Start with it, but audit the outputs

n101|143.c: One AI that merges search, social and news invites censorship; the defense is many players plus open source.
n101|143.e: If search, social networks and media all flow into one device you ask questions of, the risk of it being used for propaganda and censorship is high. Sarah thinks the counterweight is a market with many companies and many AIs, plus open-source models anyone can use, and she frames this as a matter of civil liberties. She also argues that once high-quality base models are widely available, many players can improve their own models with synthetic data. That has a leveling effect, weakening any frontier leader's chance to take off.

n101|143.c: Agents are the natural next step for copilots; robotics will see technical breakthroughs this year, not deployment.
n101|143.e: Sarah defines an agent as a system that completes multi-step tasks, manages state, and takes actions rather than just generating content. Examples already exist in security, customer support, SRE (site reliability engineering) and coding, and copilots will naturally evolve into agents as they take on more of the work. Small, low-latency models could deliver free consumer experiences on the device or in the browser, but on-device compute only matters if users don't notice it. In robotics, she expects technical proof of generalization this year, not large-scale deployment.
ex: Agents already exist in security, customer support, SRE and coding

items.d: Helps a person do the work
Multi-step tasks, manages state, takes action

n102|476.c: GPT-3 could already handle expensive professional work, and the real bet was on where capability was heading.
n102|476.e: He used his own legal background as a test. He took about 100 landlord-tenant questions from Reddit's legal forum, had GPT-3 answer them with step-by-step prompting, and gave the answers to three tenant lawyers for blind review. They judged 86 ready to send with no edits. He didn't think GPT-3 could solve complex legal problems in one shot. He bet that models, context, evals and application engineering would improve together. Friends gave up after one imperfect try, while he kept probing the model's limits. When GPT-4 came out, he spent about 24 hours retesting every task he had hacked together before.
ex: Lawyers judged 86 of 100 answers ready to send
A cold email to OpenAI's general counsel led to meeting its leadership

n102|476.c: Build many specialized workflows first, then collapse them into one minimal interface.
n102|476.e: He says anyone who can't imagine AI transforming the whole industry isn't ambitious enough. Models can't yet handle the hardest tasks in one shot, so Harvey keeps expanding specialized features and agentic workflows underneath, then collapses them into a simple interface so it doesn't become a sprawling octopus of menus. Underneath are about 30 to 50 reusable AI patterns. Case law research, for example, serves many litigation tasks such as summary judgment motions. Orchestration makes a complex system feel simple to users, and in professional services the interface ultimately is just email.
ex: An antitrust workflow determines which of 72 countries require filings
Upload a stock purchase agreement and get about 7 suggested actions

items.d: In the end, it's just email

n102|476.c: General tools can tolerate errors if they show their work, but specialized workflows must be reliable end to end.
n102|476.e: Law firms already have layers of review, so the minimum quality bar for general tools can be lower. What matters is showing the reasoning, citing sources and linking each citation to the exact sentence in the original, so checking is cheap and even partially correct work saves time. Specialized workflows aim to produce the final deliverable, so the bar is higher, but the scope is narrow enough to test each step and then the whole. He thinks general benchmarks are completely useless for Harvey. Senior lawyers must design the tasks, define the outputs and do the final grading.

items: Cheap to verify, still saves time
Test each step, then the whole

d.verdict: Benchmarks are useless, senior lawyers must evaluate

n102|476.c: Transforming an industry takes institutional trust, so win the most conservative top clients first.
n102|476.e: The usual software playbook starts with small and mid-sized customers, and Harvey did try self-serve, product-led growth. But he concluded that transforming the whole industry ultimately requires endorsement from the most demanding buyers. So Harvey partnered first with old, deeply conservative institutions like A&O Sherman and PwC. Investor Lexis brought credibility, trust and data products to integrate with. He also found that the people most afraid of automation were usually those who had never used the product.
ex: Over 250 customers and about $50 million in ARR, per the hosts
Early users stalled, turned around in 6–7 months with follow-up questions and domain profiles

items.d: More law firms and professional services

n102|476.c: AI displaces tasks, not jobs, and it will shorten the apprenticeship of young lawyers.
n102|476.e: Legal work is too messy to solve by feeding all legal data into a model, he argues, so lawyers will be collaborators. What gets replaced are repetitive tasks like discovery and data room review. Junior lawyers used to wait ten years, five if lucky, before touching strategy, and AI lets them work with clients sooner. On billing, repetitive work that can be checked will move to fixed fees, while senior advice stays hourly and may get pricier. Firms can also encode their expertise into Harvey and sell it as software.
ex: He guesses top pharma M&A experts could bill about 10x a junior's rate, not 3x

items.d: Years of review, a decade to strategy
Discovery and data room review automated

n102|476.c: Pick markets by how expensive each token is, so after law come tax, audit and transactions.
n102|476.e: His test for an application opportunity is how expensive it is to produce a token. Legal documents often run 50 pages and are extremely costly to produce, which makes law a great target. Legal and tax due diligence are basically the same job: applying complex rules to a pile of documents. So Harvey's model can extend to tax, audit and transactions. As inference costs fell, he spent the savings on quality rather than margin. On management, he admits he learned to delegate too late. When hiring, he values initiative, respect for the industry's complexity, and willingness to ship and make mistakes.
ex: The antitrust workflow could expand from where to file to preparing the filings

n103|478.c: Tesla wins on business model: profitable car sales fund its R&D, so it never runs out of runway.
n103|478.e: He grants that Musk got the business model right. Tesla pays for autonomy research with profits from selling cars, while rivals burn billions chasing the same goal: cheap, general-purpose sensors that can drive anywhere. So the claim that it will drive itself most of the time but never become fully autonomous is almost certainly wrong on a long enough timeline. The only risk is customers losing patience. He has also changed his technical view. Camera-only wasn't feasible in 2013, 2015 or even 2018, but generative models and monocular depth now make many cheap cameras the way forward.
ex: Remaining bottlenecks: heat-tolerant automotive compute and reliable connectivity, like Starlink backup

d.verdict: Given enough time, full autonomy is nearly certain

n103|478.c: Remote operation is an economic bridge: one person per four cars already cuts most labor costs.
n103|478.e: Based on videos online, he infers that Chinese robotaxis rely heavily on remote operation, and he thinks that's reasonable. Even Tesla may start close to one person per car. The math is simple: cut remote assistance to 25% and you save 75% of labor costs. A fleet of 1,000 cars with 250 monitors isn't elegant but pays off, and with today's technology a 1:4 ratio is easy. Pushing to 20:1 or 50:1 adds only single-digit points of margin. The real threshold is getting below one person per car. He thinks China is still a few years behind the best U.S. companies.
ex: 1,000 cars with 250 remote monitors

items.d: Early stage, speeds deployment and data

n103|478.c: Chores make people work like robots, and home robots will become as common as washing machines.
n103|478.e: After eight hours of sleep and eight to ten hours of work, people have little time left, yet they still make beds, wash dishes, fold laundry and pick up toys, working like robots in a way he finds dehumanizing. The last big change in home technology was running water and electricity in the early 1900s, then the appliance wave of the 1950s and 60s. Nothing comparable has happened since. Imitation learning, end-to-end models, reinforcement learning, human demonstrations and web video now let robots handle homes whose layouts and routines change daily. He expects affordable robots to be as ordinary as a sink in 5 to 10 years, though it could be 1 to 20.
ex: At 39, he feels he has at least one more company in him

items.d: As ordinary as a sink, he estimates

n103|478.c: Home robots needn't wait for perfection, and their form should match today's abilities rather than mimic humans.
n103|478.e: A robotaxi isn't a product at all until it's safer than a human, because a child could run into the street at any moment. In the home you can constrain the tasks and the environment, so partially useful products can ship sooner. At one end of the market are fully teleoperated humanoids at about $50,000 plus $1,000 a month, a tiny market. At the other are incremental appliances like a robot vacuum that can move socks out of the way. A humanoid form implies human-level ability, which in 2025 is a leap of faith. He'd rather exceed expectations and surprise users.
ex: After one robotaxi ride, skeptics drop from about 75–80% to 20–30%

marks.d: About $50,000 plus monthly fee, small market

n103|478.c: Being acquired destroyed Cruise, so his new company stays tiny and will never be sold.
n103|478.e: GM's core business is pickups and SUVs sold to the Midwest, a poor fit for urban robotaxis. Cruise lacked priority inside GM and was eventually abandoned, which completely destroyed it. So he says he'll never sell a company again, though an IPO is possible. Layers of VPs, directors and managers, with spans of eight reports per manager, brought bureaucracy and broken information flow. Now, with coding assistants and deep research tools, a few strong engineers can write everything from an iOS app to Rust motor drivers. He wants a very small team doing very big things.
ex: He proposes separate mature and innovation tracks for regulation, opened up by milestones

items.d: Core business is pickups and SUVs

n104|481.c: Tahoe-100 may be the first dataset that makes machine learning truly usable in this field.
n104|481.e: He describes Tahoe-100 as the largest known single-cell RNA sequencing dataset: about 100 million cells from 50 cancer models derived from different patients, treated with 1,200 drugs, covering about 60,000 drug-cell interactions. Earlier public perturbation data was scattered, poorly labeled and riddled with batch effects, so it simply couldn't support large-scale machine learning. That's why he thinks Tahoe-100 will be the first dataset that's truly usable.

n104|481.c: Mixing many patient models into one tumor allows parallel drug screening, with AI-designed drugs as the long-term goal.
n104|481.e: The Mosaic platform mixes models derived from multiple patients, with lung, pancreatic and other cancers, into a single "mosaic tumor," then screens hundreds or thousands of drugs at once. Many models get tested in one go instead of one by one. The patient samples cover the most common cancers, with plans to expand to rare diseases. His long-term vision is a virtual cell model that directly generates a drug that returns diseased cells to health, but he stresses this is a vision, not a current capability.

n104|482.c: Virtual cells must speak the language of systems biology, where diverse contexts matter more than raw data volume.
n104|482.e: Protein language models learn structural biology: how proteins fold and bind. A virtual cell has to understand systems biology, meaning what a target does within the cell, the tumor, the immune environment and the whole organism. An early single-cell foundation model used about 60 million cells, and downsampling that data by 99% barely changed performance. Public data is highly redundant and low in information, so diverse biological contexts matter more than sheer numbers. He estimates 100 million cells equal roughly 200 to 300 billion tokens.
ex: Downsampling about 60 million cells by 99% barely changed model performance

n104|482.c: Open-sourcing Tahoe-100 set a new benchmark and lets a three- or four-person team draw on the whole field.
n104|482.e: He says the decision to open-source came within hours of seeing the opportunity. First, it sets a new benchmark for scale in the field. Second, only three or four people work on this inside the company, and open-sourcing draws outside researchers to test and critique it. Vevo can generate about 50 times the perturbation data publicly recorded over the past decade in just five weeks. So it doesn't have to start from narrow hypotheses and can explore broadly across chemical space and patient space.
ex: Five weeks yield about 50x the last decade's public perturbation data

n104|482.c: It's early morning for biology: build now with a small elite team instead of promising results in years.
n104|482.e: He calls this moment the early morning of biology. Rather than promise results in three to five years, build now, with small teams of top talent. Every reason domain experts give for why machine learning from outside won't work should be challenged one by one. It may work or not, but you never know unless you try. Platform companies can test competing hypotheses, while single-hypothesis companies sometimes advance a drug after testing just three patient samples. On competition from China, he favors bringing rivals into the ecosystem and changing business models rather than blocking them with regulation.
ex: Single-hypothesis companies sometimes advance drugs on just three patient samples

items.d: Test every reason it won't work

n104|483.c: Virtual cells must be accurate enough, because a model that's 10% accurate is just simulating noise.
n104|483.e: Biology experiments run in real time. In his aging research, a single experiment meant waiting two years for animals to age, so running experiments in parallel on a computer would be transformative. But the models must truly be accurate. At 10% accuracy you're just simulating noise. About 90% of drugs fail in clinical trials, sometimes because of the molecule's potency, toxicity or pharmacokinetics, and sometimes because the target was wrong. Virtual cells could narrow down targets before expensive chemistry work begins. The transcriptome layer is already rich enough, so there's no need to simulate every molecule.
ex: About 90% of drugs fail in clinical trials
One aging experiment means waiting two years for animals to age

items.d: Narrow down on the computer first

n104|483.c: China's biotech cost and speed are healthy pressure, and the industry should take a lean middle path.
n104|483.e: He sees Chinese drug companies as highly competitive on cost, pipeline speed, safety studies, IND filing packages and antibody production. That pressure is good for patients, investors and the industry, since everyone wants effective molecules faster and cheaper. On business models, a virtual biotech that chains together contractors is too slow, and full vertical integration is too expensive. He favors a middle path of strong suppliers plus a lean company. As for maturity, he thinks cell models are closer to GPT-2.

n104|484.c: Tahoe-100 could become the ImageNet of systems biology.
n104|484.e: He compares it to ImageNet in 2009. Neural networks also once looked useless, until compute, data and architectures came together. Now single-cell resolution, scalable perturbations and modern training methods may be coming together too. He uses a computer analogy: DNA is like ROM and RNA is like RAM. A virtual cell model must infer a nominal CPU that maps a gene edit or drug to a transcriptome response, then work backward to find the perturbation that returns a diseased cell to health. He stresses this is a goal, not yet reality.
ex: He hopes perturbation data does what PDB and CASP did for AlphaFold

n104|484.c: Cell models are limited by data, not compute, and today's best models score only around 10%.
n104|484.e: DNA models are increasingly limited by compute and context length, while cell models are limited by data, because single-cell sequencing itself is new. A Tahoe-100-sized dataset is about 200 to 300 billion tokens, versus about 500 billion for GPT-3 and 700 billion for ESM-3, but scaling laws for cells won't be known until someone gets there. The best current models predict differentially expressed genes at only about a 10% level, and there's no accepted benchmark. He suspects data quality, not architecture, is the main bottleneck.
ex: Arc used agents to crawl public data into a library of about 230 million cells
Evo 2, trained on 9.3 trillion nucleotides, classifies BRCA1 variants zero-shot

n104|485.c: Perturbation data turns correlation into causation, and it must span many cell types and disease states.
n104|485.e: Observational samples only reveal associations. A genetic or chemical intervention creates a before and an after, exposing what drives changes in cell state. Most earlier public data came from observing healthy tissue. To model the heart, brain, liver or bone, and to understand how the underlying manifold shifts in disease, you need to cover many cells, tissues and disease states rather than repeatedly sampling the same region. Pathways conserved in cancer may also carry over to neuroscience and immune cell development.

n104|485.c: Environmental effects all pass through cells, so single-cell models may be able to infer tissue-level effects.
n104|485.e: He believes outside influences on cells are ultimately filtered through the cell. If you observe enough contexts at single-cell resolution, a model may be able to infer tissue-level effects. The team also uses ex vivo models and humanized mice to add in vivo context. On maturity he is more conservative than his peers: protein models have passed GPT-3 level, but virtual cells are closer to GPT-1 than GPT-2.

items.d: Hani: virtual cells are closer to here

n105|491.c: Founding companies can be a repeatable profession done in parallel, and breakthroughs are grown, not planned.
n105|491.e: When he started his first company at 24, the process felt like improvisation. Investors and lawyers work many deals at once, so he thinks founders can too. That's how you learn faster and see what can be repeated and what must be unique. New things come from variation, selection and iteration: Nvidia's AI opportunity wasn't in any five-year plan, it grew out of gaming. Successful founders' tales of "vision" are usually simplified, and in private they admit luck. So Flagship builds the conditions for breakthroughs to emerge instead of pretending to design the outcome.
ex: Nvidia's AI opportunity grew out of gaming, not a five-year plan
His HBR article with Gary Pisano came out after 23 years of practice

n105|491.c: Far from the known, you face uncertainty, not risk, and Flagship's skill is underwriting that uncertainty.
n105|491.e: Innovation close to the existing frontier carries risks you can estimate, but startups, labs and big companies all crowd in there and end up looking alike. Go further out and neither the odds nor the payoff can be measured. That's uncertainty, not "very high risk," so Wall Street-style risk matrices and "take more shots on goal" thinking don't apply. He says Flagship's people aren't smarter, harder-working or better connected. Their skill is using experiments to turn the unknown into manageable risk. When Moderna started, no mRNA drug had ever been approved.
ex: Moderna was the 18th company Flagship incubated

marks.d: Everyone is doing it, so things look alike

n105|491.c: Technical feasibility isn't commercial success; the market must be willing to pay extra for innovation.
n105|491.e: Around 2008, Flagship's company Joule engineered photosynthetic bacteria to take in carbon dioxide and secrete diesel, using cheap reactors. Scientifically, it worked. But carbon prices fell from $50 a ton to $5, and U.S. energy went from scarce to abundant. The renewable diesel could only sell at the price of ordinary diesel, so the industry couldn't pay a premium for the innovation. His takeaway: feasibility is necessary but not sufficient, and not every field needs a scientific leap.
ex: Carbon prices fell from $50 a ton to $5

n105|491.c: AI's unique value lies in scientific discovery, not document automation, and next comes self-running experiment loops.
n105|491.e: Writing and summarizing are just table stakes, in his view. About six or seven years ago, Flagship's "What If" project asked: could you computationally design a protein with any function, without predicting its structure, just by pairing enough functions with DNA sequences? The genome has no instruction manual, but the information is encoded in it. That question led to Generate Biomedicines. The next step is an autonomous loop where AI forms hypotheses, designs and runs experiments, interprets the results and iterates.
ex: Generate has 15+ computationally designed antibody programs, some already in the clinic
Affinnova was using evolutionary algorithms as early as 2001

items.d: Learn function from sequence to design proteins

n105|491.c: Clinical validation is the real bottleneck, so diseases should be split into tens of thousands of "biological stages."
n105|491.e: Better drug candidates aren't enough. A Phase 3 trial still costs hundreds of millions of dollars to prove a drug works significantly better and isn't toxic. He proposes splitting cancer's crude four stages into as many as 75,000 molecular "biological stages," then running smaller trials on matched patients, winning a narrow approval first and expanding later. That helps small companies most, since they can't afford to wait. Platforms work like expensive insurance: one drug can fail for reasons unrelated to the core technology, and multiple programs de-risk each other. Right now, he says, single-asset companies face a "mass extinction."
ex: COVID vaccines took three or four months because everyone agreed the goal was a solution
Flagship has started about 100 companies in roughly 25 years, all platforms

n106|495.c: AI safety is mostly a national governance problem, and alignment is only a small piece of it.
n106|495.e: Labs can refuse requests like "help me build a virus," cutting some terrorism and accident risk. But competition locks them into a race, since dropping out means losing their say, so geopolitics mostly decides how this ends. Even if AI reliably obeys the U.S. or China, great-power rivalry will push militaries to adopt AI hastily, tolerate more risk and concentrate power. The labor shock from automating digital work can't be fixed by tweaking refusal data either. And he thinks policymakers still treat AI as hype.

items.d: Obeying its principal, just one small piece

n106|495.c: AI virology skills are already a national security issue, so expert-level access should be enterprise-only.
n106|495.e: He thinks AI can't yet help bad actors launch a devastating attack on the power grid, though that could change within a year. Virology is already a national security issue: reasoning models know the literature at near-expert level and may even help with hands-on wet-lab work. Non-state actors worry him most. He wants expert-level virology placed behind enterprise verification, with unknown accounts refused, which costs legitimate biotech users almost nothing.
ex: Locating hardened missile silos or nuclear subs could undermine second-strike capability
He wants the U.S. to invest more in drone manufacturing

items.d: Not yet, but could change within a year
From states and non-state actors alike
Finding nuclear subs threatens second strike

n106|495.c: Voluntary pauses and a U.S. sprint both fail; what's needed is MAIM-style deterrence.
n106|495.e: Without verification or the threat of force, slowing down voluntarily just weakens whoever follows the rules. The case for a U.S. sprint to superintelligence assumes no infiltration. Yet at some top AI companies more than 30% of staff are Chinese nationals: expel them and talent flows to China, keep them and security gaps remain. China also won't sit by while a trillion-dollar cluster built to dominate it goes up. More realistic is "Mutual Assured AI Malfunction": each side can sabotage the other's data centers through cyberattacks or infiltration, which deters superweapon projects.
ex: At some top AI companies, over 30% of employees are Chinese nationals
He rejects Leopold Aschenbrenner's race-ahead argument

d.verdict: Shift to MAIM: deterrence through mutual sabotage

n106|495.c: Chips should be licensed and tracked like nuclear material, and what's missing is enforcement.
n106|495.e: His policy package: a CIA team watching foreign AI projects, and Cyber Command holding options to disable data centers abroad. Chips would be licensed and tracked like fissile material, starting with end-use checks. He asks whether anyone has actually gone to Singapore to see where that 10% of Nvidia chips ended up. DeepSeek's efficiency shows you can't fully cut off a major power, so controls should mainly stop rogue actors like Iran. Maxing out pressure on China could even raise its incentive to attack Taiwan.
ex: Has anyone checked in Singapore where that 10% of Nvidia chips went?

n106|495.c: Humanity's Last Exam closes out exam-style benchmarks, while agent capabilities remain near the floor.
n106|495.e: After MMLU and MATH, he led Humanity's Last Exam, which crowdsourced extremely hard questions with objective answers from professors and researchers worldwide. It's meant to be the last closed-ended academic benchmark. A near-perfect score would mean superhuman ability in some math and science fields, but not open-ended capability. Next come evals of digital tasks that run for hours. Today's models are extremely weak as agents, though that could change overnight. Capabilities are jagged: a model can solve hard physics but can't book a flight. The mood will truly shift once reliable agents arrive.
ex: He previously built the MMLU and MATH datasets and ImageNet-C

n107|498.c: Copilot is moving from pair programmer to peer programmer, but humans stay in charge.
n107|498.e: In VS Code, agent mode can implement features and propose terminal commands, but the developer approves every step, because today's agents still need a human in the loop. Project Padawan goes further: assign a well-defined GitHub issue to Copilot and it writes a plan, opens a draft pull request, commits in steps and responds to review comments, like a colleague. Pull requests and commit history make an agent's changes reviewable and easy to roll back.
ex: A PM who barely codes used the agent to produce a PR that got merged
A demo that took 15 minutes two years ago now takes one

items.d: Takes issues, opens PRs, handles reviews

n107|498.c: For broad adoption, agents must be predictable, steerable, verifiable and tolerable.
n107|498.e: Predictable means you know whether the agent can handle the task. Steerable means you can correct it and it asks questions. Verifiable means you can check the result. Tolerable means it doesn't waste time and compute, because every failed run makes developers less willing to try again. The first hurdle is the model: he expects the full o3's reasoning to push SWE-bench close to 100%. The second is the interface, which should help people judge whether an issue suits an agent and sharpen vague requirements.
ex: SWE-bench contains about 2,200 issue–pull request pairs

items.d: Know if it can do the task

n107|498.c: Writing code is a small share of a developer's day; more value lies in review, fixes and backlogs.
n107|498.e: He estimates developers write code for two or three hours a day and spend about as long reviewing colleagues' code. AI review gives instant feedback across time zones, though a human still signs off before merging. Cloud workspaces let people test suggestions without cloning, installing dependencies or switching branches. Code scanning should fix vulnerabilities outright, and lint and formatting warnings should clear themselves. The bigger opportunity is years of deferred security, accessibility, legacy-system and EU compliance work, always pushed aside by sales and urgent requests.

items.d: About as much time as writing

n107|498.c: Natural language is ambiguous, so programming languages remain the precise layer for checking correctness.
n107|498.e: He doesn't buy that AI will write all code. Human language is non-deterministic, and programming languages remain the deterministic layer where engineers verify correctness and cost. Legacy COBOL and PHP systems won't turn into cloud software on their own, and developers will maintain them for at least another decade. Waymo already runs in San Francisco but doesn't yet go from the airport to San Jose: scope expands step by step, with no fixed switchover date. On thousand-person teams, the bottleneck is knowing what you actually want, so PMs, designers and engineers will all converge on writing precise specs.
ex: Copilot Workspace's spec agent describes before-and-after changes in plain language

d.verdict: Both layers coexist; writing specs becomes the core skill

n107|498.c: Agents will be priced by compute, not by the labor they replace, because their supply is nearly unlimited.
n107|498.e: At $20 per user per month, Copilot costs about 0.1% of an average U.S. developer's salary. He cites productivity gains of 25–28% end to end and over 55% on coding tasks, so the ROI is clear. When Elad asks whether agents could charge based on the salaries they replace, he says no. Human developers are expensive because supply is limited, while agents' supply is nearly unlimited, bounded only by GPUs. Nobody prices a dishwasher at the cost of hiring someone to wash dishes. Still, OpenAI's $200 tier shows high-value products can command high prices.
ex: Recently disclosed: 77,000 organizations and 1.8 million paid users
Copilot is $20 a month; GitHub Enterprise is $21

n107|498.c: Models will converge, pushing differentiation up to workflows, and like Minecraft, software has no endgame.
n107|498.e: He grants that base models may converge but can't say when: after ten years, his Tesla still can't make the left turn into his neighborhood. Differentiation moves up to workflow, less frustration and shipping speed, so GitHub lets teams mix and match models, agents, editors and clouds. Copilot offers Claude, Gemini, GPT-4o, o1 and more. Competition is fiercer than ever, which he compares to F1: stronger rivals make a better race, and roadmaps only hold for a month or two. Software is like Minecraft, with temporary wins and no endgame.
ex: He expects everyone to build personal software in natural language within five years

n108|502.c: The goal is one general model that controls any robot for any task, pooling data across robot types.
n108|502.e: Early on she could teach a robot arm to twist off a bottle cap, use a spatula or hang clothes, but each skill barely transferred to a new setting or object. Companies that start with one application often get stuck in a niche. Robots differ in joints and arms, but data transfers across embodiments, so pooled data doesn't become obsolete with each hardware upgrade, whereas policies used to break every generation. With RT-X, several labs trained one model on a shared data format, and a checkpoint shipped to another lab often beat that lab's own tuned model.
ex: RT-X: a model trained on pooled lab data often beat locally tuned models

items.d: Fails with new settings or objects

n108|502.c: The biggest bottleneck is diverse real-world robot data, not just more data.
n108|502.e: The most important, and most boring, work, she says, is increasing data diversity: more buildings, settings, objects and tasks. Last October PI released laundry folding, table bussing and box folding that handled unseen shirts and shorts, but the data came from only three buildings, so generalization to new environments was very limited and prompting was basic. Vision-language models pretrained on the web widen what a robot understands, but its actions still have to be grounded in its own experience.
ex: Last October's release used data from only three buildings
RT-2 recognized Taylor Swift, who never appeared in its robot data

n108|502.c: Watching human videos can't teach motor control; robots need their own embodied experience.
n108|502.e: Watching videos of Olympic swimmers or tennis pros doesn't give you their muscle control, and the same goes for robots. Human video and web data help, but they can only supplement, not replace, a robot's own motor commands and camera experience. ALOHA-style teleoperation is like puppeteering: it records commands and images together, turning them into the robot's own experience. Later, as with language models, autonomous experience and reinforcement learning can bootstrap from there. She also thinks motor control itself demands a lot of intelligence, so embodied intelligence may be underrated.
ex: ALOHA and Mobile ALOHA showed teleoperation can handle dexterous manipulation

result.d: Built mainly on its own experience

n108|502.c: A general assistant needs one layer to understand intent and another to act; memory is next.
n108|502.e: Predicting motor commands directly for tasks lasting several minutes doesn't work well, and a training label like "fold the shirt" can't capture preferences or mid-task interruptions. In Hi Robot, a high-level model reads the user's prompt and reasons out the next subtask, and a low-level model turns commands like "pick up the tomato" into about half a second of motion. So the robot can handle "I'm vegetarian," "I'm allergic to pickles" or "hold the tomatoes." Cameras already go a long way for sensing. What she most wants to add is memory: today's policies can't recall half a second ago.
ex: Demos: vegetarian and ham-and-cheese sandwiches, grocery shopping, clearing a table

n108|502.c: Humanoids are a bit overrated; manipulation is both harder and easier than driving, so start narrow and forgiving.
n108|502.e: Humanoids are cool, and her lab has one, but she finds them a bit overrated. A human-like body doesn't make imitation easier and is harder to teleoperate than fixed or wheeled arms, so PI picks cheap robots that make data collection easy. Robots act on their own with no one reviewing each move, so early deployments should be failure-tolerant or human-in-the-loop. She won't give a commercialization timeline, noting self-driving may have started too early and robotics might be too early too. Long term, shared intelligence will spark a Cambrian explosion of hardware.
ex: A static two-arm robot has 14 dimensions, seven per arm

d.verdict: Start with narrow, failure-tolerant use cases

n109|505.c: The doctor-patient conversation is healthcare's first signal, and automating notes is the wedge into everything else.
n109|505.e: He believes doctors and nurses won't be fully automated in the next decade, but the conversation happens before orders, notes, billing and clinical trials, so it is the source of everything downstream. That's why Abridge started with the most painful, most frequent paperwork and then followed the conversation into other steps. In the U.S., payment depends on documented care, so the note is effectively the bill, and its accuracy affects both patient safety and hospital revenue.
ex: A JAMA article: about two in five doctors may leave within two or three years
About 27% of nurses may leave within 12 months
He estimates replacing a clinician costs close to $1 million

items.d: Ready in seconds, doubles as the bill
Real-time trial enrollment and diagnostic prompts

n109|505.c: Abridge deliberately chose the hardest customers, large health systems, and the high bar screened out rivals.
n109|505.e: Compared with independent clinics, large health systems set a much higher bar for good enough: one product must cover every specialty, outpatient, inpatient and emergency care, plus multiple languages. That forced deeper research and left essentially one other competitor. CIOs and CMIOs at academic medical centers talk to each other constantly, so a success spreads through the network, while one or two failures can close the market for years. Trust is the hard currency of healthcare.
ex: Wins at University of Kansas Health System, Emory and Yale spread by word of mouth
Live at 110+ health systems, including Kaiser and Sutter
Often runs 3–4 week bake-offs with Microsoft and says it hasn't lost lately

d.verdict: Pick the hard market and face less competition

n109|505.c: Medical speech recognition is far from solved; a 3–5% error rate is clinically unacceptable.
n109|505.e: Some say speech recognition is a commodity with off-the-shelf APIs. He disagrees. Symptoms, procedure names and newly approved drugs are exactly the words most often misheard and the ones that matter most. Doctors even pronounce new cancer drugs differently, so the system must learn each doctor's pronunciation and keep updating its vocabulary. Traditional dictation means reconstructing visits from scattered notes after hours, which mixes up details between similar patients and is bad for doctors, patients and billing.
ex: In California, many Vietnamese and Haitian Creole conversations become English notes directly
Portuguese and Spanish in Boston, Punjabi in Indiana

marks.d: Learns pronunciation, tracks new drug names

n109|505.c: Huge volumes of doctor edits create a flywheel; the goal isn't perfection but steadily less imperfection.
n109|505.e: Abridge processes millions of conversations every few days. A contextual reasoning engine combines each conversation with the problem list, medical history, insurance data and medical textbooks in a specific order to produce a draft note. Doctors still edit the drafts, and he doesn't claim the output is perfect. Instead, those edits feed preference tuning, DPO, reward models and reinforcement learning. He believes this is the first time healthcare technology has measurably reduced doctors' burden.
ex: Validated scales: cognitive load fell about 60% within six weeks
Stanford survey: burnout sometimes fell about 50% in the first months

n109|505.c: High-frequency work that a human reviews goes first; high-risk automation will arrive slowly.
n109|505.e: He sees healthcare automation on two axes, risk and frequency. Tasks that are both frequent and high-risk will be slow to arrive. Clinical notes are frequent, but a doctor reviews every one, so the risk is manageable and that window opened first. In early 2023 Abridge met only the CMIO's need for specialty coverage and the CIO's need for integration. The CFO's ROI was proven later, but two out of three was enough to get in. Long term, seriously ill patients will still want a human doctor who uses AI tools.
ex: On call, GPT or Claude often takes three or four rounds to reach the right plan
In the ER, scattered conversations across rooms must be stitched into one visit

cells.d: Like autonomous care, slow to arrive

n110|144.c: Image generation leaps forward every year or two, and vertical professional tools come next.
n110|144.e: He sees image quality improving in waves: GAN artwork sold at auction around 2018, early Midjourney and Stable Diffusion images often had seven fingers, and today's models produce consistent Ghibli-style images. He expects a jump of similar size in about a year. Current tools are horizontal, general-purpose versions. Next come vertical products that can do commercial work like graphic design end to end.
ex: Recraft is building a vertical version

n110|144.c: Macro turmoil barely affects tech startups, and tariffs should be judged case by case.
n110|144.e: Low consumer confidence and a falling Nasdaq don't worry him much. Short of an existential shock, tech companies keep selling and keep raising. The macro only hurts marginal startups when it drains venture capital and pushes valuations down, though hardware companies feel tariffs more directly. He recalls Sequoia's 2008 warning session, where even the partners admitted a six-person company needn't worry, and big tech went on to grow 10 to 20 times. Some tariffs are useful protection, some are bargaining chips and some are pure cost.
ex: Sequoia's 2008 "RIP Good Times" presentation
Today's largest tech companies are 10–20 times their size back then

items: Sequoia told founders to tighten up

d.verdict: Short of an existential shock, tech carries on

n110|144.c: Models are converging in both capability and product shape, so competition shifts to distribution.
n110|144.e: He sees convergence not just in benchmark scores but at the product layer too: search, research and reasoning are now standard everywhere. That makes distribution, and how much consumer surplus you can give users, the core question. On benchmarks the models cluster together, with spikes only in coding or reasoning and a long tail of weaker models behind. Still, dark horses will keep appearing.
ex: xAI built a near state-of-the-art model in about nine months

n110|144.c: Specialized models have openings in neglected sciences and in genuine technical wedges.
n110|144.e: Bio models appear almost weekly and are hot, but post-training for physics, materials, robotics and health has big markets with few players, because research interest and funding often don't track commercial value. Credible technical wedges, in his view, include state space models that are more efficient on compressible data, translating math and code into Lean for formal reasoning, and reinforcement learning environments that let agents operate software and websites reliably. That last one still lacks a generalizable solution.
ex: Cartesia: state space models
Slow, expensive models suit analyzing a hundred-page Supreme Court brief

root.d: Must be a real research problem, not a wrapper

n110|144.c: AI has entered a business-as-usual phase, but that clarity could be upended within a year.
n110|144.e: He thinks the stack has become legible. RAG has gone from novelty to standard infrastructure, eval practices are solidifying, and some verticals are producing winners. Consumer is still early, with ChatGPT, Perplexity and Midjourney as first attempts. Anthropic's MCP defines how models connect to documents, logs, business tools and IDEs, and OpenAI has said it will support it. It's incomplete but will speed up agent development. He also warns that the more you know this market, the more confused you get, and today's calm may not survive the next launch.
ex: Consolidation in evals, such as Braintrust
MCP: an open interface connecting models to docs, logs, business tools and IDEs

n110|143.c: Image and video still have lots of room to improve, and the key is control and responsiveness to intent.
n110|143.e: She thinks users know exactly where quality and controllability stand today, and image, video, text and logo design all have a long way to go. The public's love of anime, cuteness and beauty shows the underlying demand is simple. Good tools need real-time editing and natural language understanding, so a few words can set the tone of an entire video.
ex: Krea's real-time editing
HeyGen controls voice style with a few words like whisper or ASMR

terms.d: Still lots of room to improve
A few words set the style

result.d: Meet a simple love of beauty

n110|143.c: Strong early-stage companies have plenty of money; the pressure falls on crossover and pre-IPO investors.
n110|143.e: She lays out the stress first: consumer confidence at a multi-year low, the Nasdaq down 8%, and tariffs on Chinese goods and cars. But she judges the impact on early-stage investing to be small. High-quality companies are well funded, and more capital is willing to back expensive foundation model companies than she expected. The real pressure is on crossover and pre-IPO investors after years of tight liquidity, which a pickup in M&A and companies preparing to go public could ease.
ex: The Nasdaq fell 8%

n110|143.c: Protective tariffs only make sense alongside active industrial policy.
n110|143.e: She thinks strategic industries deserve protection. Europe, facing increasingly competitive Chinese cars, may need to protect its domestic auto industry. But tariffs alone aren't enough: you also have to invest in skills, become cost-competitive and rebuild capacity in defense components and auto manufacturing. She points out that the U.S. has already fallen behind in many areas too.
ex: European automakers facing Chinese carmakers

n110|143.c: Specialized model companies live or die by their data engine, and physical-world data must come from experiments.
n110|143.e: Capability charts show frontier models converging clearly over the past year or two, and Google's latest Gemini shows it's still a strong contender. On whether one model will win everything, she thinks the key is how specialized companies collect data. For robotics, chemistry and biology the data often doesn't exist yet and has to be generated through physical experiments. Building physical labs is a much bigger stretch for general labs than setting up reinforcement learning environments for code, which leaves room for specialists.
ex: ArtificialAnalysis.ai's chart of converging capabilities
Code has ready-made data and a clear utility function

items: Hard for general labs to enter

d.verdict: The data engine decides whether specialists survive

n110|143.c: AI is around the third inning: standards are emerging, and consumer agents will show up this year.
n110|143.e: She finds investing more comfortable now, like the third inning rather than the first. Some useful standardization is emerging, and many companies are building MCP servers for enterprise data sources. She lists the most sought-after talent: researchers, inference efficiency experts, hardware-software co-design for sparse and large mixture-of-experts models, product engineers with domain knowledge, and people working on evals, RL environments and agent orchestration. It's unclear which consumer agents beyond search and research will break out, but she expects to see examples this year.

root.d: Key investments for the third inning

items.d: Testing and training grounds for models

n111|510.c: Evals sit upstream of every model capability, and human data demand has shifted to top experts.
n111|510.e: Reinforcement learning can only improve capabilities that already have evals, so whatever skill a foundation model company invests in, from consulting to software engineering, evals come first. The human data market has shifted with it: from crowdsourcing low- and mid-skill labelers to vetting top experts who can work directly with frontier researchers. Mercor started as a way to match talent that traditional hiring overlooked, then discovered how big this demand was.
ex: Top AI labs hire thousands of people through Mercor to train models
Founded in 2023, it has passed $100 million in annualized revenue

n111|510.c: Models already predict job performance better than most hiring managers, especially for power-law roles.
n111|510.e: Mercor's models beat human hiring managers on most internal evals, and he thinks ignoring a model's recommendation will soon look almost irrational, even if the law still requires a human sign-off. The more a role follows a power law, the bigger the payoff from finding the very best. Text interviews get automated first, while passion and persuasiveness still need multimodal signals. The best test is doing the real work, like a scaled-down MVP. Proxy metrics are only needed for outcomes that take a long time to show.
ex: GitHub, blogs and portfolios hold signals managers have no time to read
Repeated hiring for the same role makes performance easier to attribute

marks.d: Top people are worth a lot

n111|510.c: Verifiable domains fall first, and the displacement of knowledge jobs will be fast and painful.
n111|510.e: Math, and soon code, are advancing fastest because answers can be verified. Skills with sparse feedback, like a founder's taste, are harder to learn. He thinks displacement of many knowledge jobs will be quick and painful and could become a major populist issue, with early signs already in customer support and recruiting. The physical world lacks the fast, self-reinforcing improvement loops of digital domains, so automation there will be slower, and work will shift toward robot data collection, hospitality and therapy. For kids, he values versatility and fast learning over betting on coding.
ex: Customer support and recruiting already show signs of displacement

n111|510.c: Writing evals may become the most common knowledge work, paired with reinforcement fine-tuning to teach agents.
n111|510.e: Academic benchmarks are like zero-shot exam questions, but real work is end to end: understanding requirements, coordinating a team, using tools. A high SWE-bench score is a long way from replacing engineers, and building evals industry by industry will take years. When employees write down what good work looks like as evals, the variable cost of doing a task over and over becomes a one-time cost of teaching an agent. Supervised fine-tuning needs too much data to have caught on. Reinforcement fine-tuning just defines the outcome and rewards hitting it, so a few hundred to a few thousand examples may suffice.
ex: Customer support has standard interfaces and few tools, so it's easiest to start
A host worried expert feedback hurts models; he says models should learn to sift it

d.verdict: Reinforcement fine-tuning is extremely data-efficient

n111|510.c: A performance-data flywheel matters more than marketplace network effects; the endgame is one human-AI labor market.
n111|510.e: In a typical labor market, supply outnumbers demand about 50 to 1. Mercor offers free mock interviews and career advice so candidates who aren't hired still get value, while companies pay. He thinks performance data from customers matters more than two-sided network effects: knowing who succeeded and why makes the next pick more accurate. Platforms like Hired couldn't record and analyze interviews at scale, and LLMs make that possible. The endgame is a single global labor market that matches each problem with the right mix of people and AI agents.
ex: Labor market supply outnumbers demand about 50 to 1
Early startups prioritize talent density, then use data to set standards at scale

n112|512.c: What's scarce isn't the metal itself but information about where the deposits are.
n112|512.e: Copper and lithium make up only tens of parts per million of the Earth's crust, and geology has to concentrate them to roughly 1% or more to form an ore deposit. Such places are rare, so the real scarcity is knowing where they are. The easy deposits at the surface have been found, the rest are buried, and exploration efficiency has fallen about tenfold over 30 years. Exploration is like venture capital: a few million dollars can return 100x or 1,000x, if you can raise the hit rate. That's where technology helps most.
ex: About $1 billion once found eight quality deposits; now it finds less than one
KoBold's goal: one discovery per $50–100 million
More copper must be mined in the next 25 years than in all history

n112|512.c: The value comes from integrating fragmented, multi-scale data and updating it through active learning.
n112|512.e: Relevant evidence ranges from continental tectonics, satellites and airborne surveys down to field samples. Much of it is public but scattered across tens of thousands of databases, mostly as unstructured reports and maps. KoBold built three layers: its own sensors, a unified data system and dozens of multi-scale models that express underground rock types and metal content as probability distributions. The team deliberately samples where the models are least certain, retrains them daily and sends new predictions back to the field. Geologists and technologists work together, and the AI can't be separated from the human intelligence.
ex: A Zambian map hand-drawn on linen nearly a century ago still works, since rocks don't move
Built an airborne hyperspectral system capturing 600 colors within a year

n112|512.c: Ore grade drives profit and environmental footprint, and high-grade ore shrinks the operation about tenfold.
n112|512.e: Mingomba's core zone has copper grades above 5%, versus about 0.6% at operating mines. For the same output, ten times the grade means roughly a tenth of the rock moved, the waste and the processing plant, so capital spending, operating costs and the environmental footprint all fall. Copper sells at one global price, so low cost and high margins are the competitive edge. He also says a mine is easier to value than most software companies: throughput, grade, price, cost and recovery can all be estimated.
ex: Recovery is modeled at 90%, with 92% and 88% as upside and downside
Mines are usually underwritten for about 20 years but often run 50–70

n112|512.c: The bottleneck is good deposits, not capital, and good projects never struggle to raise money.
n112|512.e: A host suggests ESG concerns have held back Western capital. He disagrees: quality assets always attract buyers, and what's missing is high-grade, low-cost, developable projects. He partly agrees regulation matters, since property rights, stable taxes and royalties for decades, and community consent all affect success. But screening targets on those too early means missing good deposits. Rare earths aren't actually rare. The problem is China's dominance of refining: processors can bid for feedstock on thin margins, scare off unsubsidized newcomers and pull downstream manufacturing toward them.
ex: Works with about 50 Zambian chiefdoms, among other parties
Neodymium and dysprosium are key elements in permanent magnets

items: Rare earths: refining is too concentrated

n112|512.c: Hold several hypotheses at once and write falsifiable predictions in advance to fight confirmation bias.
n112|512.e: Sparse data can fit many different underground structures, and the industry habit of picking a single best model is, in his view, a weakness. KoBold keeps several competing hypotheses alive, and data is valued by how well it can tell them apart. Its internal exploration epistemology requires writing down falsifiable predictions and kill criteria before new data arrives, so no one patches a hypothesis just to keep spending. And at least one hypothesis must make economic sense, because this is a business, not a research project.
ex: The company has a chief philosopher, author of The Knowledge Machine
The science of how lithium deposits form is young, so small insights matter

items.d: Don't rush to one best model

n113|515.c: Start with read-only research synthesis, not transactional agents that order food or flowers.
n113|515.e: The project grew out of reinforcement learning progress in math, science and coding, and she wanted to see if the same approach could work for everyday browsing. Many browsing agent demos at the time were ordering takeout or flowers. She picked a bigger target: synthesizing many sources, since that's what a lot of knowledge work involves every day. Writing a good literature review is a prerequisite for new research, and read-only tasks keep safety issues more contained.
ex: Target outputs: ranking products by Reddit reviews, writing literature reviews

n113|515.c: With reinforcement learning, experts define the task and outcome, and the model learns the research path itself.
n113|515.e: The first prototype was just a prompt plus an interface showing the vision, with no training at all. Turning it into a product took new data, graders and browsing tools, plus close work with the reinforcement learning team. Browsing has no ground-truth answers the way math does, so they built data backward from the product outcomes they wanted. Human expert data was key, along with lots of synthetic data. Every new tool needs training data that teaches the model to choose, backtrack and correct itself. Simply exposing an API isn't enough.
ex: Eval question: find every paper Liam Fedus and Barret Zoph co-authored
Tools: a text browser that reads PDFs and images, plus Python

n113|515.c: Reinforcement fine-tuning is worth it only for out-of-distribution tasks or when 10% more accuracy is decisive.
n113|515.e: She offers two tests. First, the task is far from the model's training distribution, and repeated prompt tweaks still fail, as with a specialized genomic sequencing task. Second, an extra 10–15% accuracy is critical to a core business process. Conversely, if each new base model naturally gets better at the task, custom training may be wasted. Training in one domain also transfers to others: reasoning models trained mainly on math and code write well too.
ex: A specialized genomic sequencing task

items.d: Only then is RFT worth it

n113|515.c: The more thorough the report, the more users trust it, so citations and confirmations are essential.
n113|515.e: She says Deep Research hallucinates less than any previous OpenAI model, but it can still draw wrong conclusions from real sources. Longer, more comprehensive reports earn more trust, which raises the cost of mistakes, so citations serve as an audit trail for checking the reasoning. For future agents that take actions, capability and safety merge: finishing the task but sending an embarrassing email doesn't count as success. She favors confirming each action at first, then granting more autonomy as trust builds.
ex: Modeled on Operator's confirmations before write actions

n113|515.c: The endgame is a general agent that works like a remote coworker and decides how long to think.
