n113|515.e: Today Deep Research runs for 5 to 30 minutes and does the equivalent of several hours of expert work. She imagines an hour doing days of work, and a day doing weeks of work or even paper-level projects. The obstacles: secure access to private data and passwords, managing context over very long tasks, and the heavy human effort of building data and tools. Training always used the longest thinking time, but making users pick a setting is a bad experience, so the model should decide. Within a year, the goal is one agent that can both open a code PR and book a trip to Korea.
ex: 5–30 minutes equals several hours of expert work
You can interrupt or take over anytime in VS Code or Cursor

n114|520.c: Reinforcement learning is the biggest difference between reasoning models and traditional pretrained models.
n114|520.e: Traditional models learn to predict the next word over huge amounts of text. The o-series adds reinforcement learning on top, training toward solving hard problems and letting the model think as long as it needs. Tools let the model hand off things it's bad at, like exact calculation, to software, and use code to check results and cut wasted attempts. He also sees recursive improvement as the core logic: each generation helps build a better, faster, cheaper next one.

terms.d: Hand computing and checking to code

n114|520.c: The model picker confuses users, and routing should move inside the model.
n114|520.e: ChatGPT's model switcher is complicated. Each task may have a best model, but users can't tell which to pick. He wants the model to make that call based on the task's context. Developers also need control, since not every request can take ten minutes to think, so a smart model should understand constraints like latency, even though judging the right tradeoff itself takes reasoning. Deep Research is a good testbed for long-horizon reinforcement learning, but report length and run time are product decisions in their own right.
ex: Deep Research: will users wait 30 minutes? One page or several?

items.d: No need to pick a model
How long to think, which tools

n114|520.c: Task difficulty depends on how much outside uncertainty must be resolved and whether the environment can be simulated.
n114|520.e: He measures difficulty along two axes: how much external uncertainty has to be resolved, and whether the environment can be simulated rather than bottlenecked by real-world time. Recalling facts happens entirely inside the model. Coding requires running and testing, but that can be simulated quickly. Physical-world work requires experiments whose results and timing can't be memorized. In principle, he sees no reason robotics should be a separate kind of model.
ex: Recalling facts, then coding, then physical experiments: increasingly hard

items.d: Run and test, quick to simulate
Results and timing can't be memorized

n114|520.c: Uncontaminated evals are the scarcest resource, and running a prompt several times catches the best result.
n114|520.e: He thinks the most underrated thing is rigorous evals kept strictly separate from training data. The stronger models get, the faster existing tests are used up, so such evals become more valuable. o3's best run can be stunning while another misses the magic moment, so it's worth running the same prompt several times. Next, he's excited about multi-agent reinforcement learning: first training models to collaborate with each other, then with humans, who are slow and unpredictable, a very expensive tool call.
ex: Labs do both targeted data work and algorithmic gains that lift all capabilities

items.d: Run the same prompt several times

n114|521.c: Tools make long reasoning truly useful; without them, models spin in circles.
n114|521.e: Even a very smart model hits a ceiling with stale information or inefficient arithmetic. Because o3 can browse and run code, it can gather evidence, compute, check results and change course. On some visual tasks, a model without tools realizes it can't make out details and goes in circles in its chain of thought. Once it can crop and manipulate images, it uses tokens more effectively, and its test-time scaling curve looks clearly different. He adds that a model should answer right away when it knows, spending more time only when the problem needs it.
ex: One sentence asks it to do due diligence on a company, forecast and summarize

d.verdict: Hand deterministic work to code

n114|521.c: Coding and research have crossed the usefulness bar, so models can serve as a background task queue.
n114|521.e: The latest models can track down problems in complex internal codebases and save him hours, and he now asks for help several times a day, which never happened before. AI research itself breaks into parts like hardware, training and evals, and each can become an optimization target, leaving lots of room to improve. He treats the model as a background work queue and sends off even coding tasks with low odds of success. Sometimes he's disappointed, but each success saves a lot of time. When retries are cheap, variance actually helps.

n114|521.c: Model vision is learned from static images; closing the perception-action loop would let it correct itself.
n114|521.e: Human vision evolved through interacting with the world, while model vision is learned from static images, a completely different process. Ask a model to read an analog clock and it strongly favors 10:10, because most clock images online show that time. If the loop between perception and action could be closed, he thinks models could resolve this kind of uncertainty by acting, not just by more internal reasoning.
ex: He estimates about 90% of clock images online show 10:10

n114|521.c: RL progress needn't stop at math and code; what's most needed is data for frontier tasks.
n114|521.e: Some argue that because labs pick only a few domains for reinforcement learning, progress will be spiky and stall at math and code. He finds the premise reasonable but disagrees with the conclusion, pointing to creative writing as an example. o3 and o4-mini have already mastered basic tool use. The most valuable training data now sits at the next capability frontier: million-line codebases and two-week feature builds spanning multiple PRs, with dense supervision throughout.
ex: Million-line codebases, two-week feature builds, multiple PRs

items.d: Already mastered by o3 and o4-mini

n115|524.c: The hardest part of learning is getting people to keep doing it, not finding the best method.
n115|524.e: He thinks arguing over which app, book or teacher is best misses the point. Methods differ, but what matters most is actually doing the work, and most people lack strong motivation for anything. Neither he nor his co-founder is a language enthusiast, so they design for ordinary people. Cutting a lesson from 30 minutes to two lowers the barrier to starting, and users often end up studying for half an hour. Streaks also turned out to be more powerful than expected.
ex: About 10 million active users have streaks longer than 365 days
A day-five notification saying reminders seemed useless, so they'd stop, brought people back

n115|524.c: What matters most is accumulated study time; flow is a secondary variable.
n115|524.e: Native English speakers need about 500 hours to get good at Spanish and about 2,000 for Chinese. He grants that flow might turn that into 400 or 600 hours, but the main goal is still accumulating time. The system predicts whether a user will get each question right and picks ones they'll answer correctly about 83% of the time. Drilling only weaknesses makes lessons miserable, all-correct is too easy, and 50-50 is too hard. Duolingo has run 16,000 A/B tests, down to when animations appear.
ex: Target success rate: about 83%
16,000 A/B tests run so far

items.d: For native English speakers to get good

n115|524.c: LLMs removed the content bottleneck, so courses can serve speakers of every native language.
n115|524.e: Course content went from part manual, part automated to almost entirely AI-made, with little or no human involvement. The 40 languages used to be taught mainly to English speakers. Now they can be taught to speakers of any native language. AI conversation practice removes the embarrassment of showing your weaknesses to a real person, and usage is strong. In math, human tutors work but are boring, so the goal is 90% of a tutor's effectiveness with 90% of a game's fun.
ex: 40 languages for speakers of every native language
Goal: 90% of a tutor's results plus 90% of Candy Crush's fun

n115|524.c: A new subject needs hundreds of millions of potential learners and hundreds of hours to master.
n115|524.e: He lays out the bar for new subjects. There must be hundreds of millions of potential learners, because revenue is about $10 per user and niche subjects don't pay. It must take hundreds of hours to master, since anything learnable in two hours is better as a YouTube video. It also has to suit a phone, be good for the world and have an internal champion who truly loves it. Math, music and the upcoming chess course were all chosen this way, while subjects like history fit video better.
ex: Revenue is about $10 per user
Math, music, chess

items.d: Works on mobile, good for the world

n115|524.c: AI is a platform shift, but education changes slowly and will reshape schools over about 20 years.
n115|524.e: He sees AI as a platform shift with no clear endpoint. If AI can generate personal movies, that threatens Netflix, and a similar interface change could threaten Duolingo. But with its distribution, proprietary learning data and brand, he isn't too worried. Education will probably change within 20 years, because AI can personalize in a way one teacher with 30 students can't. Teachers and schools won't disappear, since schools also provide childcare. Regulated systems change slowly, so private schools and some countries may move first.
ex: Elite private schools charging about $50,000 face questions about why anyone should pay

marks.d: Held back by regulation and bureaucracy

n116|528.c: Enterprise search finally works because language models grasp meaning, helped by SaaS and the cloud.
n116|528.e: For decades, search meant matching keywords. Large language models understand both the question and the documents, so they can match on concepts and answer directly. Early enterprise search failed because data sat in each company's private data centers, and vendors could never connect to all of it. SaaS put everyone on the same version and opened content through APIs, and the cloud removed the pain of building distributed systems yourself. Companies also lack the huge stream of user behavior that web search relies on, so understanding meaning matters even more.
ex: Rubrik, which he co-founded, had internal information spread across about 300 SaaS systems
One of Glean's largest customers has over 1 billion documents, about the whole 2004 internet

terms.d: No need to build distributed systems

n116|528.c: Even huge context windows can't replace retrieval, because information still needs filtering and ranking.
n116|528.e: Embeddings, which turn text into numbers so similar meanings can be matched, are only part of the job. Good enterprise search also has to pick content that is still correct, current and from an authoritative source, since older companies pile up outdated documents. Some argue that a big enough context window makes retrieval unnecessary. He disagrees. Even a model with excellent memory and speed would struggle with a million documents from different years and sources. Like people, models reason better when the evidence is organized first.
ex: The first version in 2019 used Google's open-source BERT plus customer-specific embeddings

items.d: Hundreds of systems, decades of history
Then handed to the model to reason

n116|528.c: Search got so good it exposed permission gaps, which turned Glean into a security product.
n116|528.e: About 90% of a company's knowledge is private in some way, so you can't put everything into one model and open it to everyone. Glean records who can see each document and each Slack message, and enforces that for whoever is logged in. But good search exposed governance gaps companies already had, and some customers hesitated to buy because the product worked too well. So Glean added another check: who is asking, what they are asking, and whether the result is appropriate to show. That helps companies get AI-ready.
ex: An employee finds a colleague's salary
A customer's employee sees files on an unfinished acquisition

items.d: Because the product is too good
Check who is asking, and what

n116|528.c: AI is very unintuitive, so companies should invest in their employees' AI skills now.
n116|528.e: He assumed a product with a single text box needed no training. That held for search but not for the assistant. Most people still type one or two keywords, and some ask how they should live their life. So capabilities have to be shown gradually inside daily work, like pushing an engineer a two-page tutorial on an unfamiliar technology. He thinks fixating on short-term ROI and efficiency is a mistake. Companies should build an AI-first team for three years from now, people who know AI is imperfect, makes mistakes and hallucinates, yet is very powerful.
ex: A user asks the assistant how they should live their life

items: Assume one text box needs no teaching
Build the team for three years out

n116|528.c: Glean has moved from search to assistants and agents, but it is still far from the vision.
n116|528.e: Glean started as Google for work. Today's assistant is closer to ChatGPT, combining world knowledge with internal material while respecting each person's permissions. Teams like HR want answers drawn only from approved content and in a set tone. These were first called apps, and once they could take actions inside systems, they became agents. The vision is to ask any question and hand off any task. He admits they're still far away, and the biggest problem isn't hallucination. It's not finding the information, finding an outdated version, or information that was never written down.
ex: Companies had no search budget, seeing it as a vitamin rather than a painkiller
Long-term vision: everyone gets a team of AI assistants, coworkers and coaches

items.d: Custom content and tone for HR and others

n117|144.c: Leaders for the next two or three years are emerging in many AI categories, though some remain open.
n117|144.e: AI was the one market in his career he understood less the more he studied it, but uncertainty has eased a lot in recent months. In many categories you can now name the likely leaders for the next two to three years, though not for five. Foundation models, medical records, coding and customer success have front-runners. Sales productivity, financial analysis and accounting are still open, either because the product approach is wrong or the models aren't good enough yet. Two years ago coding had a dozen possible ways to win. Now the openings have narrowed.
ex: Customer success: Sierra and Decagon
Coding: Cursor, Windsurf, Cognition and Microsoft Copilot

d.verdict: Leaders visible for two or three years, not five

n117|144.c: When two startups lead a market, they should consider merging to focus on fighting the incumbents.
n117|144.e: If a market has mainly two startups, the real threat is usually three or four big incumbents, and merging ends the infighting. X.com and PayPal is a successful precedent, while Uber and Lyft wore each other down for years. The obstacles are mostly ego, too much worry about blending cultures, and private-company valuations. He suggests splitting equity by one shared metric, like users or revenue. If both sides win, a few percentage points don't matter. Not every market needs a merger, though. Payments has room for several players.
ex: X.com merging with PayPal
Payments: Adyen, Stripe, PayPal and others coexist

n117|144.c: Fertility, anti-aging and aesthetics are huge biology markets that almost nobody is seriously pursuing.
n117|144.e: He points to Japanese research showing adult cells can be reprogrammed into sperm or eggs. Mice with two fathers already exist, and in the long run any two adults might have children together. Yet only one company works on this, and he warns the ethical implications are startling. Today there's no way to mature and retrieve many eggs over a woman's lifetime. He calls Botox roughly a $40 billion business, yet skin aging, baldness, gray hair, aging eyesight, hearing loss and tooth regrowth get almost no serious effort.
ex: Oocytes, or immature eggs: about 1–2 million at birth, about 300,000 by puberty
The USAG-1 gene can promote tooth regrowth in some animal models

items.d: Retrieve more eggs over a lifetime

n117|144.c: Biotech funding is built around selling startups to big pharma, which keeps new giants from emerging.
n117|144.e: Setting aside Moderna, which COVID lifted, he thinks the last biotech built from scratch to over $50 billion was probably Regeneron, back in the 1980s. It's as if tech had only IBM and HP and no young challengers. Biotech funds often put in about $40 million to incubate a company for roughly 40% ownership, push it to a crossover round, then sell it to pharma. So startups cluster in cancer, cardiovascular and neuroscience. Add regulatory requirements and a culture where scientists see commercial problems as lowbrow, and a lot of valuable biology sits unused.
ex: Incubation: about $40 million for roughly 40% ownership
Regeneron may be the last to go from zero to over $50 billion

n117|144.c: Copying human demos is brittle, and the real challenge is building realistic environments for reinforcement learning.
n117|144.e: Scaling language models brought broad knowledge and pattern recognition. But broader intelligence also means planning, reasoning over documents, using tools, taking feedback, exploring different paths and checking its own work, and world models may be one conceptual path to AGI. Behavior cloning from human demonstrations is like tracing someone else's drawing: step off the demonstrated path and it breaks. Reinforcement learning, where a model improves by trial and reward, works in games with clear rules. Real tasks lack rules and rewards. Environments need to be realistic, cheap and varied, and he admits he doesn't know how to build them.
ex: He's skeptical of near-term uses like generated games, game assets and robot training data

items.d: Copies demos, fails off the path

n117|143.c: AI app winners combine a valuable vertical workflow, proprietary data and distribution.
n117|143.e: She feels she now sees the market's provisional physics more clearly. Winners capture a valuable vertical workflow, own proprietary data that can be retrieved, and have distribution. Users must also be able to create, derive or extend knowledge on top of that data. Abridge and OpenEvidence, both in healthcare AI, fit this pattern. Sales has always been fragmented, so how to win there is still unclear. She also counts pharma as an open category and expects new entrants in document-heavy industries.
ex: Abridge and OpenEvidence fit the pattern

n117|143.c: Coding is splitting into real-time IDE tools and background cloud agents, and both can thrive.
n117|143.e: She thinks open and small models like Codestral are getting better at real coding tasks, and if quality keeps rising, specialized engineering workflows could win distribution. Microsoft open-sourcing Copilot looks aimed at containing Cursor, which is built on an open-source fork of VS Code, though the effect is unclear. The market is splitting into synchronous work inside the IDE and asynchronous cloud agents that work in the background. OpenAI betting on asynchronous Codex while buying the IDE product Windsurf shows both paths are credible.
ex: OpenAI bets on asynchronous work with Codex while also acquiring Windsurf

marks.d: Built on a VS Code fork

n117|143.c: Merging is often seen as giving up, but it's really a concession made in order to win.
n117|143.e: In markets where two startups mostly compete with each other, the real rival is usually a big incumbent. She sees founders, boards and investors treat even discussing a merger as admitting defeat. That mindset keeps companies that should join forces stuck fighting each other. Her reframe: it is a concession, but one made in service of winning.

n117|143.c: Searching without constraints, as AlphaGo did, could find solutions humans would never think of.
n117|143.e: Go-playing AI had a clear goal and almost no other constraints, so it found moves humans hadn't imagined and that players later adopted. She imagines similar unconstrained approaches producing weird but better code. She compares it to molecular evolution experiments, where evolved catalysts or binding proteins often work in unexpected ways. Elad agrees that models will explore problem spaces humans never learned to search.
ex: Human players studied and absorbed AlphaGo's new moves
Catalysts and binding proteins found through molecular evolution

items.d: Defines only what counts as good

n118|249.c: AI without spatial intelligence is incomplete, and 3D world models are the missing layer.
n118|249.e: She defines spatial intelligence as the ability to understand, reason about, interact with and generate the 3D world. People and animals gather light through their eyes and build a 3D model in their heads to move around and handle things. That ability is woven into evolution, so it's more than just another media format. Language is largely solved, and 3D is just as important and just as hard. World Labs is the first company she knows of building generative foundation models for 3D. The worlds can be fantastical, but their geometry and physics must hold together.
ex: Even with eyes closed, people struggle to picture a detailed 3D model of their surroundings

items.d: Just as crucial and just as hard
She isn't sure where to start

n118|249.c: Creative tools and XR content are the first markets for spatial intelligence.
n118|249.e: She expects designers, 3D and visual effects artists, marketers and game developers to work alongside generative models, the way programmers use Cursor and Windsurf, because 3D is hard even for professionals. What the metaverse and AR/VR lack isn't hardware but content, and generative spatial models can fill that gap. Design aims for both beauty and efficiency, which also suits optimization with reinforcement-learning-style methods.
ex: Like developers using Cursor and Windsurf

n118|249.c: Robots needn't be humanoid, and training them takes a pyramid of data from many sources.
n118|249.e: She believes people will live alongside robots, but a robot's shape should follow its task. Her lab's research on morphological intelligence shows body shape can change as it is optimized for a task: underwater robots end up more like fish, and flying favors non-human forms. Training data should mix video, simulation and synthetic data, teleoperation, and embodied data, and simulation is underrated. Touch is even more underrated. For manipulation it must be fused with vision and spatial perception, though plain navigation may not need it.
ex: Underwater robots look like fish, and airplanes are becoming more robotic

n118|249.c: 3D data is scarce and the products are awkward, because 3D demands active exploration, not passive viewing.
n118|249.e: Images and video are plentiful, but structured 3D world data is scarce. She envies colleagues building language models, since World Labs must invest much more in data collection, processing, engineering and synthesis. Everyone lives in 3D every moment, yet putting it in users' hands is far harder than language. 3D requires active exploration, and nobody wakes up wanting to sit and watch 3D. The experiences she dreams of include diving into the microscopic world, seeing inside a running engine and standing inside a dishwasher.
ex: Imagine shrinking to microscopic scale, seeing inside an engine, standing in a dishwasher

d.verdict: 3D is harder in both data and product

n118|249.c: Good research takes fearlessness, somewhere between a little delusional and rationally bold.
n118|249.e: Around 2003, object recognition had only tiny datasets and no scaling laws, the pattern that more data and compute make better models. She was convinced models needed enough data to generalize. Her advisor suggested 100 categories, she did 101, and her mother helped clean images. The later ImageNet was doubted early on, and she was warned it might cost her tenure, until AlexNet won and proved a hypothesis nobody believed. Her advice is to be fearless. Too rational and you pick problems that are too small, but pure recklessness means too many mistakes.
ex: Categories came from illustrations in an English learner's dictionary
The crowdsourcing platform Mechanical Turk solved the labeling problem

marks.d: A bit delusional, yet rationally bold

n119|544.c: Claude 4's key progress is behavioral: fewer unrequested edits and less reward hacking.
n119|544.e: He says Claude 4 beats older models by a wide margin on benchmarks, but for professional engineers the bigger deal is behavior. It makes fewer changes nobody asked for, is less overeager and does less reward hacking, so engineers no longer waste time undoing extra edits. The other signature ability is long-horizon agentic work: customers let coding agents run unattended for hours on large refactors.
ex: Older models deleted code to pass tests or wrote placeholder tests that always pass
Manus turns videos into slides using FFmpeg, keyframe detection and speech-to-text APIs

n119|544.c: Agent costs should be weighed against the cost of people, not against token spend.
n119|544.e: If an expensive agent run makes a scarce engineer two or three times more productive, it's worth it. In Claude Code, Opus can hand codebase searches to Sonnet subagents, cutting latency and cost and keeping search results from crowding its main context. Anthropic currently offers just two models on the cost-performance frontier, and he would prefer an automatic routing layer so users don't have to decide how much to spend on each task. Memory, he thinks, is too fundamental to outsource to a separate model.
ex: Claude Code was built to get close to users and feel the model's weaknesses firsthand

items.d: Picks the model for the user

n119|544.c: Superhuman AI around 2028 is quite likely, and the bar is an economic Turing test.
n119|544.e: He takes the recursive self-improvement scenario in AI 2027 seriously. Its median forecast is superhuman AI in most fields by 2028, which he finds quite plausible, though confident ranges are hard to give. His bar is an economic Turing test: an agent works for a month on a basket of jobs making up half of economic value, and hiring managers would rather pick it than a person. AI is already speeding up AI research, from systems engineering to monitoring experiments and analyzing data, and it can write reinforcement learning environments that used to be expensive.
ex: AI 2027's median forecast: 2028
Interviews are a poor proxy, since models already ace them

items.d: Monitor experiments, read logs, analyze data
Models help build the next generation
A month on half the economy's work

n119|544.c: As expert feedback grows scarce, the answer is constitutional AI, trusted experts and, ultimately, empiricism.
n119|544.e: In 2021 ordinary people could easily tell which of two answers was better. Now non-experts can't reliably judge expert-level work. Constitutional AI has the model critique and revise itself against written principles and learn from that. He also suggests a few trusted experts dig deep, sometimes teaming with models as centaurs, with their judgments pooled into a preference model. But correct principles don't guarantee correct facts. Below that, it has to come down to empiricism, like his doctor father testing three treatments on different areas of a face and leaving one as a control.
ex: Novo Nordisk cut a cancer treatment report from about 12 weeks to about 10 minutes

items.d: Deep judgments pooled into a preference model
Controlled tests settle right and wrong

n119|544.c: Biological risk is the safety priority, and computer use works but isn't yet safe enough to ship.
n119|544.e: The Responsible Scaling Policy originally covered chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear risks. It now centers on biology, because nuclear harm likely needs nation-state resources while small groups might obtain biological materials. Opus 4 was rated ASL-3 mainly because tests showed it helps novices far more than Google search does. Computer use can already read screens and click, and it's used for sandboxed software testing. But browser access risks irreversible actions, prompt injection and leaked credentials, so it hasn't launched to consumers. On whether some safety research shouldn't be done, he thinks studying deception is necessary. Lines exist but are hard to draw.
ex: Alignment Faking study: deception persisted even after alignment training

n120|548.c: Applied is following a Microsoft-like path: tools first, then an operating system, then applications.
n120|548.e: He compares the company's path to Microsoft's: tools, then an operating system, then applications. The difference is that its partners build cars, trucks, tanks and jets. Self-driving at scale needs the automakers, so Applied sells them the whole software stack, roughly a Tesla-style stack minus the hardware. He also sees value in keeping a low profile. If you publicly claim to do just one thing, you're stuck with it after it stops working.
ex: An automaker CTO urged him: don't be timid, go on offense
Public customer Porsche also feels software pressure from Tesla and Chinese automakers

n120|548.c: Traditional cars have embedded software, not intelligence, and centralizing compute saves thousands in hardware.
n120|548.e: He thinks calling traditional cars intelligent is an exaggeration. They just have embedded software. Many parts are simple inputs and outputs, like a seat-heater switch, yet each gets its own controller and software stack, duplicated layer after layer. Routing those signals into one central computer removes redundant controllers and wiring, saving thousands of dollars per vehicle while enabling richer features.
ex: Simple inputs and outputs like a seat-heater switch

terms.d: Simple I/O no longer gets its own
Signals go to a central computer

n120|548.c: China has the world's most dynamic auto ecosystem, and it will consolidate sharply within five to ten years.
n120|548.e: Tesla's weak sales in China make sense, he says, because the local cars are genuinely good. He sees a path running from Japan to Korea to China, with Vietnam or India possibly next. China has EV architectures built from scratch, many brands and subsidies, and treats cars as national infrastructure and a jobs program. He expects heavy consolidation within five to ten years. Huawei's car platform and reference vehicles, which let automakers focus on manufacturing, brand, sales channels and customer experience, may become the model.
ex: Huawei's car platform and reference vehicles
He thinks Europe has been a bit asleep at protecting manufacturing

items.d: Subsidies, many brands, new EV designs

n120|548.c: Self-driving has no secret sauce left, and winning means surviving until mass-production economics work.
n120|548.e: Data for L4 trucks (mainly in Japan), aircraft, drones, ships and defense is far harder to collect than road data, so synthetic data is central. Their synthetic data stack has shifted from heavy graphics rendering to Gaussian splatting and diffusion models, which also revives old data that was unusable years ago. Four years ago the end-to-end approach was hotly debated. Tesla FSD V13 and the leading Chinese systems show the field has converged. Everyone knows how to do it, he says. Applied has no paper-publishing research group and does no systems integration. The key is surviving until production economics work.
ex: Synthetic data: from graphics rendering to Gaussian splatting and diffusion models
Tesla FSD V13 and leading Chinese systems proved the approach

n120|548.c: Waymo leads safety by far, and within five years FSD-like features will be as common as navigation.
n120|548.e: Waymo averages about 30,000 miles between interventions, far ahead of anyone else, and many L2+ driver-assist systems are already safer than human drivers. Yet business decisions are still driven by liability. The media keeps revisiting the Uber ATG crash from years ago while ignoring everyday fatal crashes by human drivers. The adoption window once expected for 2015–2020 is really 2025–2030, and Waymo will reach about 40 cities in two or three years. Within five years, features like Tesla's FSD will be as common as navigation.
ex: Waymo averages about 30,000 miles per intervention
Waymo expands to about 40 cities within two or three years

items.d: FSD-like features as common as navigation

n120|548.c: Self-driving's impact rivals large language models, but it could become a commodity before it makes money.
n120|548.e: Cars shaped hospitals, supermarket size, parking and the shape of cities, so he puts self-driving on par with the LLM revolution. Anyone who rides in a Waymo asks why their own car can't do that. But by 2030–2035 price pressure will be intense, and autonomy may become a nearly free standard feature. Spending $12–15 billion only to be commoditized before monetizing is terrifying, and Waymo's business model is the key test. He disagrees that there will be fewer cars. People fly more and more, and miles driven could grow by an order of magnitude.
ex: Mining equipment and defense drone swarms also need embedded intelligence

items: Riders want it in their own cars

d.verdict: Waymo's business model is the key test

n120|549.c: A vehicle operating system is a full embedded stack, from the bootloader up to the applications.
n120|549.e: He defines the operating system as the complete embedded stack. At the bottom is a bootloader that guarantees reliable updates. Above it sits the operating system itself, then middleware that handles data transport and abstraction, and finally the applications that control the vehicle or display information inside and outside it. Applied's path was to build engineering tools first, then applications to make the tools better, then the operating system to host those applications.

items.d: Control the vehicle or show information

n120|549.c: Android won on compatibility, and cars need the same kind of compatibility layer.
n120|549.e: Android won because apps run consistently across thousands of devices, backed by a compatibility test suite that now has millions of tests. He wants vehicles to have a similar compatibility layer, and Applied borrows this approach to cope with many vehicle models and chipsets. That way the same software can be reused across models and chips.
ex: Android's compatibility test suite now has millions of tests

n120|549.c: Silicon Valley software habits don't transfer to cars, where safety, lifespan and cost set the limits.
n120|549.e: Safety-critical hardware stays in service for many years, embedded systems are extremely cost-sensitive, and the auto supply chain spans a huge number of suppliers. Because Applied doesn't sell chips, cloud or wiring harnesses, it can recommend new architectures without protecting a product line of its own. Coding assistants must come to automotive engineering too, but they only help if safety, cost and system constraints are built in. He sees having both AI skills and domain knowledge as the company's edge.
ex: About 82% of staff are software engineers, with over 100 open roles

n120|549.c: Trade reciprocity makes sense, and products made in the same place end up with similar costs.
n120|549.e: GM and Volkswagen once made huge profits in China, so some degree of trade reciprocity is understandable. Once imports grow large, countries usually require local production. And products built in the same place tend to converge on cost, whatever country the brand comes from. He also sees Tesla as an American champion, and worries that Europe's open door to Chinese automakers threatens its domestic industry.
ex: GM and Volkswagen once earned rich profits in China

n120|549.c: Self-driving will be clearly and provably safer than humans, but it can never be perfect.
n120|549.e: He believes autonomous systems will be significantly better than human drivers, and that verification and validation tools can prove it, which is part of Applied's business. But they'll never be perfect, because you can always construct a traffic scenario where the vehicle does nothing wrong and still gets hit. So the goal is to be provably better than humans, not zero accidents.

n121|555.c: If AlphaGo could find brilliant moves in a vast game space, algorithms can be searched the same way.
n121|555.e: He traces AlphaEvolve's roots to AlphaGo's famous Move 37. If a neural network can find moves humans never imagined among an astronomical number of positions, the same idea can be used to search for algorithms. AlphaTensor focused on matrix multiplication, FunSearch used large language models to search over programs, and AlphaEvolve generalizes that into a general-purpose coding agent. The matrix multiplication breakthrough convinced him there is a region of superhuman algorithms humans haven't reached.
ex: Strassen's matrix multiplication improvement stood for 50+ years until AlphaTensor
He calls FunSearch the first scientific discovery made with an LLM

n121|555.c: Users define what they want with an evaluation function, and AlphaEvolve searches for how to do it.
n121|555.e: Users only need to supply an evaluation function that can score results, such as an existing simulator for scheduling jobs in a data center. Search can start from scratch or from a solution that's already highly optimized. Gemini proposes code changes, the evaluator weeds out failures, and an evolutionary algorithm keeps a diverse population so it doesn't commit too early to one kind of solution. Offspring then combine ideas from strong candidates. Easy problems are solved almost instantly, while problems open for decades take much longer.
ex: Data center job scheduling: an existing simulator scores the scheduling algorithm

items.d: Blend good ideas into new solutions

n121|555.c: With an evaluator in place, model hallucination turns from a flaw into useful exploration.
n121|555.e: The trouble with ordinary coding agents is that requirements are written in incomplete natural language, and when the model errs, users struggle to tell whether the result is right. AlphaEvolve treats every surprising proposal as a candidate to be tested and lets the evaluator decide, so hallucinations become a source of novel ideas. The key trade-off is how hard to test: screen cheaply on a few instances first, then validate thoroughly on a thousand or so before deciding which ideas shape the next generation.
ex: Promising ideas get tested on a few instances, then about a thousand

items: Hard to tell right from wrong

d.verdict: Verifiability turns hallucination into creativity

n121|555.c: The evaluator isn't a hard limit, since imperfect simulators and LLM judges can also guide the search.
n121|555.e: A strict evaluation function is just the easiest place to start. Even an imperfect simulator can guide evolution, as long as it correlates with the real signal. LLM judges of natural-language proposals and proof agents can extend the framework further. He cites AI co-scientist, where multiple LLMs rate one another's hypotheses for novelty and importance and do far better than a base model answering alone. But simulators only cover certain distributions, so universal guarantees may still require proofs.
ex: AI co-scientist: agents peer-review hypotheses, far outperforming the base model

marks.d: Enough if it tracks the real signal

n121|555.c: Science is fundamentally search: humans write the goals and hard constraints, and AI produces reviewable code.
n121|555.e: He sees much of science as searching a huge space for the right idea, structure or drug candidate, and systematic evaluation can become a scientist's superpower. Humans must spell out goals and constraints: a drug has to work, side effects must be manageable, it must be deliverable, and at the most basic level it can't kill the patient. AlphaEvolve outputs readable code that engineers can review line by line before deployment, which is a whole different level from trusting an opaque neural network.
ex: Drug constraints: efficacy, side effects, delivery, and not killing the patient

terms.d: Hard constraints like efficacy and side effects

n121|556.c: They target problems top researchers have worked on for years, where good solutions are counterintuitive, not neglected.
n121|556.e: He rejects the idea that earlier researchers just didn't try hard enough. The team deliberately picks problems the best people have studied for years, like matrix multiplication, and infrastructure components Google has already optimized again and again. Improvements there are the strongest evidence of novelty. Humans went so long without better solutions because the search space is enormous and good solutions are often counterintuitive.
ex: Matrix multiplication, plus Google infrastructure components that were already heavily optimized

items.d: Ones you can write an evaluator for
Studied by leading researchers for years

n121|556.c: Evaluation is nearly free in math and computing, and simulators can carry the approach into biology and chemistry.
n121|556.e: Math and computer science benefit first because automatic evaluation is often readily available there. In biology and chemistry, the same architecture transfers as long as a simulator or predictive model can score candidate molecules. He thinks the evaluation requirement can be relaxed further: LLM-based judges and approximate simulators that correlate with the real signal can both guide evolution, though it may take more rounds.
ex: Score candidate molecules with a simulator or predictive model

n121|556.c: Speeding up Gemini's training is an early sign of self-improvement, but each loop takes months.
n121|556.e: Optimizations found by AlphaEvolve are already used to speed up Gemini's training, which he calls without doubt a first sign of self-improvement. For now the feedback loop is long, though. It takes a few months from deploying an improvement to the next model benefiting. The truly open question is whether such gains are one-off, level off toward a ceiling, or keep compounding. The team admits it can't answer that yet.

n121|556.c: The algorithm that produces an answer can matter more than the answer, revealing structure mathematicians missed.
n121|556.e: He says using it is surprisingly collaborative. Mathematicians get not just a better number but code that reads as if a person wrote it, and understanding how the parts fit together reveals the thinking behind it. On the cap set problem, a classic puzzle in combinatorics, worked on with Jordan Ellenberg, the generated program revealed symmetries mathematicians hadn't known about. So sometimes the solution itself matters less.
ex: Cap set problem: the program revealed symmetries mathematicians didn't know

n122|560.c: AI drug discovery is moving from research idea to buildable product, with a one-to-two-year window to start.
n122|560.e: He judged that AI drug discovery had just reached the tipping point from academic idea to practical product. Too early means a ten-year slog, too late means missing the build-out. He bet that structure prediction would extend from folding single proteins to how molecules interact, while diffusion and language-model methods could produce diverse outputs. He faults the previous generation of AI biotechs for tying themselves too tightly to their own labs. Chai still runs experiments, but it is building a general platform reusable across hundreds or thousands of programs.
ex: Open-sourcing Chai-1 first proved the platform was general

n122|560.c: Antibody design hit rates leapt from about 0.1% to nearly 20%, far beyond the internal 1% goal.
n122|560.e: Antibodies make up nearly half of recently approved new drugs. Traditional discovery screens huge numbers of candidates from yeast or phage libraries or immunized animals. Earlier computational methods succeeded about 0.1% of the time or less, and the team had set an annual goal of just 1%. Chai-2 designs only about 20 antibodies per target, which fit on one 24-well plate. After two weeks of experiments, nearly 20% bind as intended, and about half the targets get at least one hit.
ex: Seven of the ten best-selling drugs are antibodies
About 20 designs per target, validated in about two weeks

n122|560.c: Testing 50+ targets and removing look-alikes showed the model works on unfamiliar targets too.
n122|560.e: Most AI design papers test only one to three targets, which he likens to claiming a model won a whole competition based on one problem. The team picked more than 50 targets from vendors' off-the-shelf catalogs and removed any with over 70% sequence similarity to known antibody structures. Even at a 25% similarity cutoff, the success rate barely changed. He admits the team still doesn't fully understand why the model generalizes, and guesses it has learned real rules of protein interaction.
ex: Targets over 70% similar to entries in SAbDab were removed

items.d: Orderable from vendor catalogs in one go

n122|560.c: Structure prediction reveals the lock, while Chai-2 is generative design that builds the key.
n122|560.e: Structure prediction takes a protein sequence and outputs the 3D position of each atom, which is close to a classification task. Chai-2 instead generates both a new sequence and a structure that binds a chosen site, like a Midjourney for molecules. The model reasons by placing atoms one by one, and its overall error is sometimes smaller than the width of an atom. Because generation is probabilistic, making ten or a hundred times more designs can turn up better molecules.
ex: Error is sometimes smaller than the width of one atom

d.verdict: From atomic microscope to Midjourney for molecules

n122|560.c: The output is hit molecules, not drugs, and capital, clinical trials and manufacturing remain most of the iceberg.
n122|560.e: He stresses that the model only produces hits, molecules that bind the target, not drugs. The next step is to characterize drug-like properties such as manufacturability and stability, and eventually to design complete drug candidates zero-shot. To the objection that pharma's bottleneck is clinical trials rather than discovery, he concedes capital markets, clinical failures and manufacturing are still most of the iceberg. But lowering discovery risk still matters, especially for targets traditional methods can't reach.
ex: 1 of 14 designs hit both species, after a partner's 5–10 people failed for years

items.d: Tip of the iceberg, which AI is tackling

n122|561.c: Once designing molecules with atomic precision becomes possible, it's hard to work on anything else.
n122|561.e: Seeing Meier's research progress convinced him that designing molecules with atomic precision was within reach, and once he glimpsed that future he couldn't forget it. He thinks Chai matters not just because it makes drugs faster and cheaper, but because it unlocks new classes of targets and molecules. Even though the XBI biotech index has been depressed for five years, he believes the industry is going through a platform shift.
ex: Amid XBI's five-year slump, Chai's hit rate jumped from <0.1% to nearly 20% in a year

terms.d: Out of reach for traditional methods

n122|561.c: Drug discovery is too big for any one company, so Chai opened access to academia and industry.
n122|561.e: The space of drug discovery is so large that no single company can cover every target, so Chai-2 is open to academic and industry partners. Within hours of launch, hundreds of applications arrived, and the team of about ten has had to prioritize. Some in the industry ask: companies can already discover drugs, so what does faster change? Their answer is that it restarts stalled programs and makes AI a must-have tool for keeping up with peers.
ex: Hundreds of partnership applications arrived within hours of launch

items.d: A team of about ten makes choices

n122|561.c: Mini-protein designs now succeed nearly 70% of the time, and biology will get its own CAD software.
n122|561.e: For mini-proteins, all five targets got hits, design success approached 70%, and binding affinity reached the picomolar range, meaning very tight binding. He guesses other molecule types could pass 50% within a few years, but admits that is speculation. Long term, he wants Chai to be the computer-aided design suite for biology, the way engineers use SolidWorks and designers use Photoshop, while also accounting for manufacturability and stability.
ex: Mini-proteins: all 5 targets hit, with picomolar affinity
Think SolidWorks or Photoshop

n122|561.c: Prompts can ask for cross-species binding or for avoiding a given protein, reducing the need for surrogate antibodies.
n122|561.e: Design intent can go straight into the prompt: bind two targets at once, bind in both humans and monkeys, or bind one protein while avoiding another. Animal studies can then use the same molecule instead of a separate surrogate antibody, which also reduces mismatches between animal and human data. He thinks prompt decisions like choosing the epitope, the exact spot to bind, will become a high-leverage skill, and antibody experts remain key partners.
ex: Cross-species: binding both the human and cynomolgus monkey versions of a protein

n122|561.c: Researchers must also be strong engineers, and research code needs unit tests too.
n122|561.e: Chai's team of about ten spans chemistry, physics, biology and AI, and many have no computer science degree, but everyone works toward one goal rather than personal research projects. He expects researchers to be strong engineers too, and someone must be able to hold the whole system architecture in their head, keeping it simple and modular. Deep learning bugs can lurk for weeks. They once used git bisect, rerunning training jobs to pin down a regression, and it cost tens of thousands of dollars. So research code gets tests too.
ex: Using git bisect with training runs to find a regression cost tens of thousands of dollars

items.d: Someone holds it all, keeps it simple

n123|566.c: Failure isn't that educational, and Zenefits, his first company, failed for really dumb reasons.
n123|566.e: He doubts Silicon Valley's idea that failure makes you grow. Companies die for all kinds of stupid reasons, and you learn more by watching a successful company up close. Zenefits left him just two concrete lessons: be extremely careful about compliance, and don't lean too hard on manual operations, a point where Rippling may now overcorrect. He started again because his reputation was ruined and no one would hire him, and Rippling was the only way to rewrite the public story.
ex: His advice to would-be founders is almost always: don't

n123|566.c: Platforms share permissions, reporting and approvals across products, returning $35 for every $1 invested.
n123|566.e: From day one, Rippling built a connected suite of HR, IT and finance products rather than one polished point solution. Permissions, reporting and analytics, workflow automation and approvals show up in every kind of business software. A suite can invest deeply in them once and reuse them across every app, which point-solution vendors can't afford. Cloud migration, internet distribution and the pre-2022 bull market let point solutions hit quick singles, but that window is closing as cloud suites absorb the basic categories.
ex: Same lineage: Oracle, SAP, Salesforce, Microsoft
Over 80% of engineers work on existing products, and new ones start with 4–5 squads

items.d: HR, IT, finance and other products

n123|566.c: Good leaders work backward from what the market demands, not from what fits in a quarter.
n123|566.e: Rippling separates platform teams that build shared capabilities from application teams that assemble products. The scarcest people are those who can own the roadmap, marketing, sales and competition end to end. A weak leader lists what can be done in a quarter and leaves the gap to the CEO. A strong leader faces seemingly impossible constraints and asks how to reach the end state the market requires. He often asks: does having both A and B violate the second law of thermodynamics? Great organizations differ by an order of magnitude, not 20%.
ex: The Apollo moon landing took 4 years, while San Francisco's Van Ness bus project took 12

marks.d: Leaves the gap to the CEO

n123|566.c: AI won't shrink engineering teams, because cheaper software gets absorbed by more demand.
n123|566.e: He's very skeptical that AI will save jobs. Coding assistants help in places, but neither Rippling nor the late-stage companies he talks to have seen huge productivity gains, though maybe they're just not using the tools well. Even if production gets cheaper, demand expands. AI customer support, for instance, cut tickets but made the product easier to use, so usage jumped. Cheaper app development lets a horizontal platform build something like Rippling for ophthalmology clinics. Competitors copy faster and prices fall, so engineering and sales investment stays essential.
ex: AI support cut tickets but drove a big jump in usage
Imagine a Rippling for ophthalmology clinics

n123|566.c: Payroll must be exactly right every time, and AI agents should inherit the permissions of the person they serve.
n123|566.e: Zenefits tried to win the market with manual operations first and automate later, but requirements grew harder to capture fully, and the automation kept being promised but never arrived. So he would rather automate first and serve fewer customers. Payroll has a long tail of edge cases yet must be right every time, and a rules engine can't tolerate the entropy that probabilistic AI introduces. The durable value lies in data pipelines, permissions and identity. An AI agent should inherit the permissions of the person it helps, not use a broad service account.

n124|571.c: Engineers spend 80% of their time understanding and collaborating, yet the industry bets 80% on "doing."
n124|571.e: He observes that no single engineer at a large company holds the whole system in their head. Knowledge is scattered across the codebase, chat logs, project-management tools, and people's memories. That is why coding agents sometimes deliver negligible or even negative productivity gains, which matches what engineering leaders tell him. He estimates that "doing" is only 20% of the problem, and it is largely solved already. Asimov is meant to be an all-knowing answerer for the whole organization, like a principal engineer who understands everything.
ex: He cites the METR report: enterprise coding gains are often tiny or negative

items.d: How real work time is spent

n124|571.c: Evals should come from customer behavior; the goal is cutting onboarding from months to weeks.
n124|571.e: His reasoning: at a big lab, one researcher is a single entry among hundreds of evals, so attention gets spread thin. A startup can turn customer pain points directly into tests while tuning the product, the agent, and model training together. Architecturally, a small long-context model does "neural retrieval" over the codebase, using the model itself rather than keywords to find relevant code, and an agent on top handles search, tools like Jira, and multi-hop reasoning. The concrete target is onboarding: at big companies it takes an engineer months to learn a giant codebase, and they want that down to weeks.
ex: A single codebase can run to about 100 million tokens
Grok 4 raised its HLE score through tool training, but that may not map to user value

n124|571.c: Team memory should be versioned like Git, with component owners approving changes.
n124|571.e: He says Asimov's value is not in answering questions about the current file but in semantic questions where you know the symptom and not which function to look at. His example: a job suddenly runs five times slower because two reasonable changes from two teams combined into something like a race condition, and tracking it down could eat several engineers' days. Letting teams teach the model local terminology raises the question of who has authority. He imagines memory edits working like pull requests, approved by the current owner, which amounts to building a new Git from scratch.
ex: A job 5x slower: two individually reasonable PRs combined into a race-like bug

items.d: What a team's terms mean, for example
Like a component owner reviewing a PR

n124|571.c: Reinforcement learning is limited by rewards, not compute; a universal verifier would itself be superintelligence.
n124|571.e: He argues that with an accurate reward for any task, even simple existing RL algorithms can extract a great deal of capability, with exploration as the main limit. The hard part is where rewards come from. Using a large model as a judge with a rubric partly works, but noisy rewards eventually get gamed, while ground-truth rewards are clean but scarce. A neural verifier that could accurately check every outcome, he reasons, would probably be superintelligence itself. On top of that, current algorithms lack fine-grained credit assignment, so reasoning chains often take the long way around.
ex: Open-source base models suffice: RL compute is roughly two orders of magnitude below pretraining

n124|571.c: Superintelligence will be jagged, arriving first in specific jobs where data is plentiful.
n124|571.e: He deliberately makes a provocative claim: what we call generalization is largely a matter of getting the test distribution into the training set. That is why he likes building synthetic environments for products like Airbnb, Salesforce, and Excel. Meaningful superintelligence could appear within a few years, but only in patches of work, such as front-end development where data is abundant. Other fields depend on the cost of data versus the payoff. The real threshold, in his view, is every engineer getting a double-digit percentage productivity gain.
ex: Atari, AlphaGo, Dota, and AlphaStar are the blueprint for narrow superhuman skill

marks.d: Depends on data cost and payoff
Could reach the top within a year
Plenty of web and synthetic data

n124|571.c: Frontier labs are integrating vertically; startups need their own models or deep roots in customers.
n124|571.e: He reads the collapsed Windsurf acquisition as one step in frontier labs integrating vertically: first ChatGPT went into search, now coding. The driver, he thinks, is funding frontier research more than any economic calculation. But buying a product does not close the gap between research and users. Claude Code is the real success story of a model and product tightly coupled. A startup running on a vendor's model has to pay that vendor's margin, while the big labs can heavily subsidize their own products.
ex: Claude Code: a successful case of vertical integration

d.verdict: Own the model or embed deeply with customers

n125|572.c: If you're profitable you don't need to raise; solve a real problem instead of raising for headlines.
n125|572.e: Surge has been profitable since it started in 2020, so money was never the constraint, and raising would only have meant giving up control. He criticizes Silicon Valley founders who raise $10 million for the headlines and validation before they've even found a real problem. His advice is to build what you want to build and raise only when you actually hit a funding constraint. He also doesn't favor hiring data scientists or product managers early. They optimize for 2–5% gains, while a startup needs 10x to 100x changes.
ex: Just over 100 employees and more than $1 billion in revenue last year

items: Raise first, find a problem later
Profitable, so no outside money needed

n125|572.c: Generative data has no quality ceiling; judging by credentials and checklists just scales mediocrity.
n125|572.e: For a task like drawing boxes around objects in images, a grade-schooler and a novelist do about equally well, so the quality ceiling is low. Writing poems, proofs or slide decks has almost no ceiling. A checklist asking "Is it a poem? Eight lines? Mentions the moon?" lets mediocre poems through. An English PhD isn't a poet, and an MIT grad can't necessarily code. So Surge measures quality the way search engines rank pages, feeding many signals about annotators and their work into internal models.
ex: An eight-line poem about the moon: a checklist can't screen out mediocrity
He describes rivals as staffing shops that just supply headcount

n125|572.c: Realistic RL environments are extremely hard to build, so future training will mix many reward signals.
n125|572.e: Reinforcement learning needs a simulated world where a model can practice. He describes one for a salesperson: Salesforce, Gmail, Slack, Excel, docs and a calendar, with time passing and outside events happening, like a car crash that throws off a trip to see a client, while thousands of messages stay consistent. He thinks there's no ceiling on how realistic an environment can be, and synthetic environments without coherent events and creativity are doomed. Over the next five to ten years, expert reasoning, environments and verifiers will all coexist, because a single reward at the end can't capture complex, long-horizon tasks.
ex: A salesperson world: a car crash reroutes a meeting, and thousands of messages must agree

items.d: How humans actually think it through

n125|572.c: Human feedback will never run out; a thousand curated examples beat ten million synthetic ones.
n125|572.e: Models need an external target to optimize toward, and they don't reliably know when they're wrong. One customer spent six months generating 10–20 million synthetic examples, then found most were useless and could salvage only about 5%. He says a leading model, in roughly 10% of his own use, slips random Hindi or Russian characters into answers about Trump or Obama, and the model never notices. The division of labor is also shifting: the model writes a first draft, and humans make the creative edits.
ex: One customer's 10–20 million synthetic examples: about 99% useless
A top model slipped random Hindi or Russian characters into about 10% of answers

n125|572.c: LMArena rewards clickbait, and chasing it makes models worse at facts and following instructions.
n125|572.e: On LMArena, raters spend five to ten seconds picking whichever answer looks better. That rewards formatting, bold text, emojis and length. Nobody checks the facts or whether the instructions were followed, so the easiest way to climb is to write longer answers. He says one researcher told him leadership would accept worse factuality to move up the rankings. Academic benchmarks like IFEval, meanwhile, are disconnected from the real world. He favors slower, more expensive expert evaluations, and Surge plans to publish research and run independent model evaluations.
ex: An IFEval prompt: capitalize a certain letter every time Lincoln is mentioned

n126|117.c: DeepSeek was a starting gun that showed America's AI lead is actually very thin.
n126|117.e: DeepSeek came out the weekend before he started at the White House. He sees the "frontier model for a few million dollars" story as a media framing, since the paper reported only the final training run, not the experiments before it. But DeepSeek's innovations on weaker hardware were real, in KV caching, MLA (tricks that save memory and speed things up) and reasoning. He rates DeepSeek and Alibaba's Qwen as the best open-source models today. Gains in productivity, drugs and materials will compound and spill over into the military, so this is a race America must win.
ex: DeepSeek's efficiency advances like MLA were achieved on weaker hardware

n126|117.c: The scoreboard is how much of the world's AI inference runs on American chips and models.
n126|117.e: He thinks of the American stack as one package: Nvidia and AMD GPUs at the bottom, models from OpenAI, Grok, Gemini and others in the middle, and a huge app ecosystem on top. Winning is measured by America's share of the world's inference tokens, the units of text models process when they answer. He also thinks models export culture the way movies and social media do. At Twitter he saw how algorithms shape public opinion, so he wants models the government buys to be "truth-seeking," with no undisclosed ideological bias.
ex: Google reported roughly a quadrillion tokens, per month or quarter; he couldn't recall which

items.d: GPUs from Nvidia, AMD and others

n126|117.c: Building compute is stuck on the grid and permits; restart nuclear and find more blue-collar workers.
n126|117.e: The plan's first pillar is "build, build, build," starting with simpler permits for data centers on federal land. For decades US electricity demand grew only 1–2% a year, so power plants, utilities and the grid have never been tested by fast growth. Rules on water, emissions and construction have piled up into a mess. He thinks nuclear power has long been blocked by climate lobbying and doomers, and that it should be built again. Construction also needs lots of electricians, technicians and construction workers, not just engineers.
ex: For decades, US power demand grew only about 1–2% a year

n126|117.c: Open weights are a strategic asset; many eyes catch more problems than a few safety teams.
n126|117.e: He argues that California's SB 1047, had it passed, would have nearly ended American open source, and that one state's rules would have become national law in practice. So AI regulation should be unified at the federal level. He grants that cyber and bio risks need monitoring, but cites Linus's law: thousands of students and researchers studying an open model may catch more problems than one lab's small safety team. To him, the real danger is Chinese models embedded in every robot, camera, car and device.
ex: California's SB 1047, which he believes nearly killed American open source

items: A few safety teams as gatekeepers

d.verdict: Without open source, Chinese models end up in every device

n126|117.c: Export American GPUs and the full stack to allies; robotics is what matters over the next two years.
n126|117.e: He criticizes the Biden-era diffusion rule, 200 pages of limits on AI chip exports, for making GPUs hard to buy even for eager allies. The new policy reverses course, exporting American chips through arrangements like an AI Acceleration Partnership with Gulf states, so the installed base pulls American models and standards along. He thinks robotics becomes critical in the next 18–24 months. Many startups already use distilled versions of DeepSeek and Qwen, so America needs competitive open-source models to carry its own products and standards.
ex: Three executive orders signed so far: infrastructure, exports and ideological bias

items.d: Even allies struggled to buy GPUs
American models and standards come along

n127|576.c: As AI replaces search as the front door, the old deal of content for traffic is collapsing.
n127|576.e: He sees three rewards for creators: selling products or subscriptions, selling ads, and earning recognition, which is mostly what drives Wikipedia. Search ruled for about 30 years. Now AI is becoming the new front door, even inside Google, and users increasingly read derivative content instead of the original. Cloudflare's data shows the same content is 10x less likely to get a click from Google than a decade ago. If creators stop getting rewarded, the models that depend on their content will eventually starve too.
ex: Versus old Google, referrals are 750x harder from OpenAI and 30,000x harder from Anthropic

n127|576.c: Without scarcity there's no market, and blocking AI crawlers by default creates that scarcity.
n127|576.e: Copyright law won't help. The more thoroughly an AI rewrites content, the more likely it counts as fair use, and that is exactly what leaves the original unread. Two California rulings in one week even reached opposite conclusions. AI companies agree in principle that they should pay for content, but no one wants to pay while rivals, especially Google, get it free. So starting July 1, Cloudflare blocks AI training crawlers by default for all customers and pushes finer-grained rules, like free for humans and paid for bots.
ex: July 1, "Content Independence Day": AI training crawlers blocked by default
robots.txt is too crude and relies on voluntary compliance

items.d: AI can't take it free anymore

n127|576.c: A good content market should reward filling gaps in knowledge, not stirring up outrage.
n127|576.e: He says Google taught creators to treat traffic as value, so Huffington Post-style headline testing, Demand Media and BuzzFeed chased outrage and cookie-cutter articles. Models approximate human knowledge. The well-covered parts get pruned, and what's left, the holes in the Swiss cheese, is the most valuable, so a market should pay to fill them. Spotify shows how: it tells musicians what people search for but can't find, and some write songs for exactly those searches, earning tens of millions of dollars a year.
ex: Music was about $8–9 billion before iTunes; Spotify now pays out over $10 billion yearly

n127|576.c: One-time buyouts are naive deals; Google should license search indexing separately from AI answers.
n127|576.e: He calls paying $20 million once for a publisher's entire archive an extremely naive deal. It's better to share in AI subscription or ad revenue so creators benefit from growth. Google's old deal was indexing in exchange for traffic. Now it takes the same content but sends back only about a tenth of the traffic, so it shouldn't get special treatment, and search indexing should be licensed separately from AI Overviews and Gemini. Big publishers can negotiate directly, while Cloudflare offers collective licensing or micropayments for the long tail of creators.
ex: Blocking Google was unthinkable a decade ago and is now seriously discussed

n127|576.c: Inference will move to devices and the edge; power is a hard limit, but high usage isn't inevitable.
n127|576.e: When Cloudflare and Nvidia put GPUs at the network edge in 2020, almost nobody cared. Four years later a nearly identical launch was a hit. He expects much inference to run on devices, with bigger models at the nearest edge location, since decisions like a self-driving car braking can't wait on the network. Edge sites lack a big data center's power, but he thinks GPUs will retrace the CPU's thirty-year path of efficiency gains in 5–10 years. A 100x efficiency gain would be good news for Cloudflare, which charges by usage.
ex: Around 2010 he told Intel he only cared about cores per watt
A 100x efficiency gain helps Cloudflare and hurts clouds renting out whole GPUs

items.d: Phones and cars run models locally
Plenty of power, but far away

n128|580.c: Single-node inference tricks will commoditize, but orchestrating many nodes together remains hard.
n128|580.e: He expects OpenAI's open-source model to be the first best-in-class American open model since Llama 3.1 405B, leaning toward reasoning and code, with OpenAI preparing custom kernels with partners ahead of launch. Sarah thinks model-level optimizations will eventually be open-sourced and commoditized. He agrees for a single node, but large-scale distributed orchestration still separates winners from the rest. Inference providers running only off-the-shelf software have no market at all, and Together and Fireworks beat their peers through low-level implementation work.
ex: One DeepSeek inference replica needs about 160 GPUs, over $10 million in hardware

d.verdict: The edge stays in system orchestration

n128|580.c: About 200 neoclouds, the new GPU-rental clouds, will split sharply, with only four ways out.
n128|580.e: SemiAnalysis tracks about 200 neoclouds, and their fortunes vary wildly: some have poor utilization, others are booked solid on four-to-six-year contracts. Commercial real estate investors accept 10–15% returns on equity, venture capitalists don't, and GPUs depreciate fast. Some operators without enough cash flow to service their debt are dumping compute at low prices and will likely go under. His ClusterMAX ratings show a few neoclouds beating the big three clouds, but today's top tier will soon become the baseline.
ex: Together and Nebius are moving up into selling inference APIs

n128|580.c: Nvidia is a three-headed dragon, and a chip startup's 2–4x paper advantage gets eaten away layer by layer.
n128|580.e: He says Nvidia combines top GPU engineering, networking and a software ecosystem far ahead of rivals, built over more than twenty years. Google's TPU, Amazon's Trainium and Meta's MTIA copy its architecture and mainly win by avoiding Nvidia's margins. Independent startups lose everywhere: 20–30% behind on cost, performance and power from the manufacturing process, about a year late on memory, and behind on networking and supply chain. Slip six months and the advantage is gone. He sees AMD GPUs and Trainium as the likeliest second choices.
ex: Amazon blamed the slow Trainium ramp on rack integration yields

items.d: Networking and supply chain lag too

n128|580.c: Specialized chips bet on the wrong workloads, because models change faster than hardware generations.
n128|580.e: Cerebras, Groq, SambaNova and Graphcore bet on about 10x more on-chip memory than Nvidia, but models kept growing until even Cerebras's giant chip couldn't hold them. The opposite bet failed too. Chips built around big compute units suit dense models like Llama 70B, but DeepSeek-style mixture of experts, which activates only some sub-models at a time, splits big matrix multiplications into many small ones and leaves the hardware idle. Hardware takes two years per generation, and workloads can change in that time, so betting simply on "transformers" is too simplistic.
ex: Nvidia's on-chip memory grew only about 30% from A100 to Blackwell

marks.d: Can't fit models once they grow
MoE's small matrices leave them idle

n128|580.c: Data center bottlenecks keep shifting, and fixing one adds only about 20% more capacity.
n128|580.e: In 2023 the constraint was Nvidia chips, then CoWoS packaging and HBM memory. Now add optics, buildings, substations, transformers, power generation, grid hookups, permits and labor. Meta used tent-like structures to build faster, while GPUs in Ohio were still delayed by grid problems. On-site power runs into multi-year backlogs for gas turbines. Electricians are scarce, wages are rising, and training takes longer than construction. He thinks Microsoft moved too slowly on Stargate, so OpenAI turned to Oracle, CoreWeave and others.
ex: GE gas turbine backlogs run about 4–8 years
Meta used tent-like structures to speed up construction

n128|580.c: Export services and tokens before GPUs, and tightly control chipmaking equipment.
n128|580.e: He wants users worldwide on American models, because models carry a worldview, the way TikTok shaped how kids in Lebanon see America. The export order should be services, then tokens, then infrastructure, with physical GPUs last and chipmaking equipment tightly controlled. Cutting off GPUs entirely invites rare-earth retaliation. Even without equivalent chips, China can make older processes work by using 3x the power and supplying 4x the electricity, subsidize chips as it did solar and EVs, and recoup the value through APIs, services and data.
ex: A brief EDA software ban was reversed after China pushed back with rare earths

items.d: Highest value and margin; sell first

n129|583.c: Scaling isn't the only path, "agentic" is a spectrum, and the hype is running ahead of deployment.
n129|583.e: He thinks scaling has a little juice left but is getting harder to squeeze, and the public fixates on it because a few companies made it the main story. Agentic workflows, multimodality, applications and new techniques are also paths forward, and text diffusion models could be a wildcard. He introduced the word "agentic" to end the debate over what counts as an agent, since autonomy is a spectrum. He didn't expect marketers to slap it on everything. Real adoption is growing fast, but still more slowly than the hype.
ex: An older Llama generates puzzles that help newer models learn faster

n129|583.c: The biggest barrier to deploying agents is talent: teams that know how to run evals and error analysis.
n129|583.e: Computer use works only some of the time, and guardrails and evals are hard too, but he thinks the biggest barrier is talent. Good teams use evals to do error analysis systematically. Weak teams make random changes and improve far more slowly. Take the new generation of RPA, software that automates office workflows: the first run usually has errors, and which ones matter depends on private business context in employees' heads. So human engineers and product managers are still needed for the next year or two. What truly works today are question-answering and coding agents.
ex: A wrong invoice date is minor; repeatedly pinging the CEO for approval is a process problem
Claude Code plans, makes a checklist and executes step by step

n129|583.c: Once writing code gets fast, deciding what to build becomes a startup's new bottleneck.
n129|583.e: He dislikes the term "vibe coding" because it suggests accepting whatever the AI writes. Serious AI-assisted development is intense mental work, which he calls fast engineering. At AI Fund, work that once took six engineers three months can sometimes be done by him or a friend over a weekend. When a prototype takes a day instead of three weeks, waiting a week for user feedback becomes the drag, so teams lean more on data-informed intuition and deep customer empathy to decide quickly.
ex: A six-engineer, three-month project finished in one weekend

n129|583.c: Technical product founders are likelier to win; a startup is more like tennis than calculus.
n129|583.e: Mobile know-how eventually became common knowledge, but the AI frontier keeps moving, so people who truly understand it stay scarce. That makes technical product leaders who get generative AI more likely to succeed than business founders without a feel for the technology. He separates two drives, obsession with beating competitors and obsession with customer success, and values the second. Startup decisions rarely allow time for full analysis. Most are reversible two-way doors, so decide fast and fix mistakes later.
ex: Uber's key insight: GPS made a new kind of service possible
Early Coursera put learners at the center

items: No feel for what AI can do
Understands what AI can and can't do

n129|583.c: People who can't use LLMs lose much of their productivity, so hiring should screen for AI fluency.
n129|583.e: At AI Fund, the legal, finance and front-desk staff all code, not to become engineers but to tell computers more precisely what to do. In many roles, not knowing how to use LLMs is like not knowing web search back in the day. He once hired a new graduate fluent with AI over a full-stack engineer with ten years' experience who barely used AI tools. The strongest are veterans with a decade or more of experience who are also AI experts. He has also turned down a headcount request while approving budget to "hire AI."
