ex: Headcount request denied, but budget to "hire AI" approved

marks.d: In a class of their own

n130|589.c: The rare earth bottleneck is refining, not reserves, and offtake deals with price floors can break it.
n130|589.e: The US relies on China for about 90% of its refined critical minerals and on Taiwan for advanced chips. The US, Canada and India all have rare earth deposits. The real bottleneck is refining. After Made in China 2025, China expanded output and cut prices, driving Western refiners in Tennessee, Arizona, Georgia and elsewhere out of business, leaving it free to raise prices later, a classic monopoly play. His fix is commercial: anchor buyers sign offtake agreements with price floors, and the Defense Department's deal with MP Materials is the template.
ex: The Defense Department's partnership with MP Materials, worth about $750 million

items.d: Charge more once rivals are gone

n130|589.c: Rising capital spending and power demand are early signs the US is becoming a production economy.
n130|589.e: The US economy runs mostly on consumption and services, with manufacturing about a tenth of GDP, but that flat share is a lagging indicator. Leading indicators are rising. Capital spending has passed 2% of GDP and could double next year. One analysis credits AI with about 1 percentage point of GDP growth over the past year, against total growth of roughly 3%. Electricity demand is growing for the first time since 2008. He doesn't think mature economies are destined to turn into service economies. Technology, not demographics or wages, is the deciding factor.
ex: China's share of the world economy: about a third in 1800, about 7.5% in 1913

items.d: Mostly services, manufacturing about a tenth

n130|589.c: AI lets one person do the work of ten, and companies will choose 10x output over layoffs.
n130|589.e: If a job needs only a tenth of the people it once did, a company can either cut staff or expand output about tenfold. He expects expansion to win, because companies that shrink will lose to rivals that grow, and human wants are nearly endless. This is the Jevons paradox: when efficiency jumps and relative costs fall, total demand goes up. So AI is more like giving workers superpowers than replacing them.

d.verdict: Competition and endless demand push companies to expand

n130|589.c: This century's story is the rise of superintelligence, not of the East, bringing a second Great Divergence.
n130|589.e: He thinks early AI adopters will pull away from laggards, echoing the Great Divergence after the Industrial Revolution, and the cheap-labor edge developing countries rely on will erode. Europe is the cautionary tale. He blames its missing the internet, digitization and consumer-app waves, and expects the EU AI Act and digital services taxes to keep it behind. The Middle East is a plot twist: Gulf capital, leadership and cheap energy can make it America's compute partner, as long as China can't get at those clusters.
ex: Europe's share of world GDP: about 65% in the early 1900s, about 15% now
The stack race: Nvidia's ecosystem versus Huawei Ascend plus DeepSeek

items.d: Held back by regulation, losing share

n130|589.c: Scaling energy has to go through nuclear, which needs faster permits, shorter builds and trusted foreign capital.
n130|589.e: He sees cheap energy and economic growth as tightly linked for two centuries. US electricity costs about half what Europe's does, and nuclear is the best path to abundant power. Large nuclear projects cost tens of billions of dollars and take years, so they need faster approvals, shorter build times, and clarity through CFIUS, the foreign-investment review committee, that trusted foreign investors can fund energy infrastructure. Gulf capital can fill the gap. France shows nuclear can scale even under heavy regulation. He also backs natural gas, wanting all of the above.
ex: France gets about 75% of its energy from nuclear

n131|592.c: A clinical decision gives you one shot, and the harm from medical errors is vastly underestimated.
n131|592.e: He separates clinical decision support from AI that writes notes and handles paperwork. A paperwork mistake can be fixed, but with a patient you get one shot to get it right. Medical error is often called the third leading cause of death in the US, and he thinks even that understates the harm: for every death, perhaps 10 to 100 patients get worse without dying. AI adoption cycles have also shrunk from five to ten years to one or two, and OpenEvidence became the de facto standard for clinical knowledge in about 18 months.
ex: He says about 40% of US doctors use it daily
Usage is about 20x that of the next clinical decision platform

d.verdict: The two carry completely different levels of risk

n131|592.c: The whole patient history is the query, and semantic search finds key evidence buried in paper details.
n131|592.e: He gives the case of a 44-year-old woman with moderate-to-severe psoriasis and multiple sclerosis. IL-17 inhibitors may worsen MS, while IL-23 inhibitors are safe and well tolerated, but the latter were approved only in 2019, after many doctors finished training. Keyword search easily misses that distinction. OpenEvidence treats the whole history as the query, searches by meaning, and returns the three to five most relevant trials or guidelines. The key detail may sit in a paper's methods or population section rather than in the abstract.
ex: Search covers about 35 million biomedical publications

n131|592.c: Doctors-only and citations first: it's a search engine, not an answer engine.
n131|592.e: The product is open only to doctors, because a license brings accountability. Just as a Bloomberg terminal user would notice an obviously wrong bond quote, doctors should be able to spot anomalies and check sources. When evidence conflicts, it flags the disagreement and points users to two phase 3 randomized controlled trials with opposite conclusions instead of giving a single verdict. Citations were core to the product long before ChatGPT added references, and he positions it as a search engine in Google's lineage.
ex: Conflicting evidence points to phase 3 trials in both NEJM and JAMA

n131|592.c: Reach doctors directly as consumers, not as appendages of the health system.
n131|592.e: He says he had zero interest in building a healthcare company. He wanted to build a consumer internet product for knowledge workers. Doctors have long been treated as appendages of the health system, even though they make the high-stakes decisions. OpenEvidence went straight onto doctors' own phones as a free app, bypassing institutional procurement. He thinks the transferable lesson is psychological: treat knowledge workers as independent users, and deep-rooted adoption barriers in an industry can start to loosen.
ex: Leaders at Mayo Clinic, Cleveland Clinic, UCSF and others use it

n131|592.c: Medical knowledge doubles every few years, so continuing education must become the core of training.
n131|592.e: Measured by citations, medical knowledge doubled roughly every 50 years as of 1950. He notes a BMJ estimate that it now takes just 73 days, though he finds that method too aggressive. Even counting only the top quarter of peer-reviewed literature, it doubles about every five years, and keeping up with the best work in one specialty would take hours a day. So continuing education has to become the core. He sees AI as an autopilot for the pilot, giving doctors in remote areas an on-demand "curbside consult."
ex: Southwest Georgia: two oncologists within 50 miles, and one of them uses it

n132|598.c: Countries get mispriced more than companies; find the right wave, then be a good surfer.
n132|598.e: He thinks the world doesn't need another multibillion-dollar private equity firm, so Affinity aims to be a partner that helps portfolio companies solve their hardest problems. The governance and reputations of 200-plus countries are priced far less efficiently than tens of thousands of frequently traded companies. Albania is his contrarian example. Friends were skeptical, but he valued its European location and Prime Minister Rama's pro-business reforms, and friends who later visited wanted in too. Singapore is his first reference point for tough policy problems.
ex: Albania: friends were skeptical until they visited, then wanted to invest

result.d: Just be right where you're most confident

n132|598.c: Silicon Valley solves problems well but picks them poorly; BrainCo brings big institutions' problems to engineers.
n132|598.e: He calls AI the biggest technology shift of his lifetime, so Affinity has to rethink the opportunities and weak spots of every portfolio company. But he and his Middle East partners found few AI vendors that actually delivered results. Elad Gil suggested building their own, and BrainCo launched in January 2024. Big institutions hold sandboxes of real problems that top engineers never get to touch. Rather than one-off consulting, BrainCo runs on shared infrastructure and reuses applications across clients and industries.
ex: Early use cases: hospital patient flow, hotel bookings, insurance claims

n132|598.c: A building permit takes 40-plus steps and months of waiting; with AI it should take minutes.
n132|598.e: One government's building permit process had more than 40 steps, and applicants paid consultants and waited three to four months. The team first aimed to get a single step above 90% efficiency. They have now automated 35 steps, each above 90% accuracy, and found more than ten man-made steps that could simply be dropped. Turning architectural drawings into a format models can read was the hard part until a model upgrade solved it. The benefits include lower costs, faster construction and tax revenue, and less backroom dealing.
ex: 35 steps automated so far, each above 90% accuracy

n132|598.c: AI adoption is limited by organizations, not demand: you need hard problems, data and leaders who push change.
n132|598.e: BrainCo skipped the usual path from small businesses to mid-market to enterprise and went straight for global institutions. They wanted proof of value first, so the team did a lot of work up front. The company now has more than 40 people, and growth is limited by hiring, time, project choices and technical quality, not demand. He screens clients on three things: complex problems where AI has big leverage, usable data, and leaders who can push experiments through internal resistance.
ex: A team of 40-plus, with early clients expanding across departments

n132|598.c: Energy is held back by permitting, not capital; America should build a lead before regulating.
n132|598.e: He says the US has about 1,300 gigawatts of generating capacity, yet about 2,000 gigawatts are waiting in line for Federal Energy Regulatory Commission approval. That shows private capital is plentiful and permitting is the bottleneck, even though new capacity can't come online overnight. He backs two things: clearing energy permitting barriers, and holding off on regulating AI capabilities until policymakers really understand AI. He thinks Europe's heavy regulation has stifled AI, and America should attract top talent and build a lead first.
ex: He says he pushed TSMC to build in Arizona during the first term

n132|598.c: Build peace on shared interests, not historical grievances, and let business ties make it real.
n132|598.e: He took on the Middle East from scratch, spending six months to a year consulting all sides and studying past failures, and he was skeptical of Washington's veteran experts. His method was to define an end state everyone could accept, get all parties on the same side of the table, then keep iterating. Conventional wisdom held that Arab-Israeli normalization required solving the Palestinian issue first. He stressed instead shared security interests against Iran and the economics of Israeli technology plus Gulf capital, leading the UAE, Bahrain, Sudan and Morocco to normalize ties with Israel.
ex: Phoenix: bought around $37, now near $120, which he calls nearly a 9x return

d.verdict: The Abraham Accords succeeded through repeated trial and error

n133|465.c: Customer support is the best entry point for enterprise AI, and big companies arrived sooner than expected.
n133|465.e: Support involves huge conversation volumes tied to a clear cost baseline, so buyers can easily do the math. Early digital-native customers like Rippling and Notion helped the product iterate quickly, then banks, airlines and telecoms came looking because they handle the most contacts. Today AI transformation is pushed top-down by boards and executives, and support is often the first stop. The first metric is cost reduction, but if customer satisfaction drops, the efficiency gains don't count as success.
ex: A customer signaled a six-figure contract before Decagon had any revenue
Case studies show contact center or operating costs down 60–70%

items.d: Banks, airlines, telecoms with the most contacts
Top-down AI push, support goes first

n133|465.c: Early on, be greedy about winning deals; once established, you must invest in long-term foundations.
n133|465.e: At the start, what matters most is winning the customers in front of you, not spending a quarter on planning. Once you have a foothold, you can't only do what closes deals right away. If you don't shore up the core product's foundations, every deployment stays expensive, and about six months later you'll regret it, when fixing it is harder. The company is nearing 200 people and building out HR and organizational structure, and it's deliberately carrying its San Francisco culture into its New York and European offices.
ex: Nearly 200 employees, a New York office, and a European office in the works
Looking to Ramp and Databricks as role models

d.verdict: Skip the foundations and you'll regret it in six months

n133|465.c: Model labs will move into apps, but a thick layer of enterprise software protects Decagon.
n133|465.e: Owning the end customer pays more than selling an API, so labs have an incentive to move into applications, and he sees their API business as more of a wedge. They'll probably start with standalone consumer products, with coding first in line, while complex enterprise support comes later. Decagon's defense is a full enterprise software suite around its agents that lets business users build and iterate on agents themselves, while engineers handle only system integrations. He thinks the traditional SaaS model, configuration-heavy and maintained by technical staff, doesn't fit the AI era.
ex: Anthropic launched Claude Code, and OpenAI once tried to buy Windsurf

items.d: Engineers handle APIs and CRM hookups

n133|465.c: Charging per conversation expands the market from software seats to the whole services economy.
n133|465.e: Charging per seat makes little sense for agents that work on their own, and charging per minute rewards dragging out calls. Decagon sells a set volume of conversations over the contract term, and can count only those that don't need a human handoff. Once pricing is tied to output, agents compete for a function's payroll and outsourcing budget, not just its software budget. So he thinks the entire services sector could move into software, and all the agent companies combined are still just a grain of sand.

items.d: Can count only conversations not handed to humans

n133|465.c: Brands will have one conversational front door, and a world of agents talking to agents is nearly here.
n133|465.e: Today a brand's sales, booking and support sit in different teams and budgets, but consumers see a single brand. So the end state is one concierge-style conversational front door, with fewer trips into apps and websites. Personal agents can already order food, and soon they'll go straight to an airline's support agent to rebook a flight. At first agents will talk to each other in natural language so humans can step in, moving to more efficient protocols later. The work will also expand from answering questions to upselling and proactive outreach.
ex: A personal agent talks to an airline's agent to rebook a flight

items.d: Sales, booking and support in one
Personal agents go straight to brand agents

n134|602.c: Kids must love school: two focused hours of academics buy four hours of great activities.
n134|602.e: He sees the school day as a bundle of academics, socializing, sports, childcare and life skills, with lectures eating up too much of it. When fifth graders asked for less school, a deal emerged: about two hours a day of focused learning on apps in exchange for about four hours of meaningful workshops. A traditional high schooler chasing elite colleges sits through six hours of class and four of homework, while Alpha students reach top scores with two or three hours of academics.
ex: He says 96% of students say they love school
40–60% of students say they like school more than vacation

items.d: The elite-track high school he compares

n134|602.c: Teach by knowledge level, not age, and AI can fill students' big gaps.
n134|602.e: Transfer students' real levels often sit far from their grade. Straight-A students may be three years behind, and B students three to seven. A system that promotes by seat time leaves Swiss-cheese gaps, and without fractions you can't learn algebra. With an AI tutor, mastering one subject for one grade takes about 20–30 hours. The system keeps accuracy at 80–85%: higher is boring, lower makes kids give up, and no teacher with 30 students can manage that.
ex: One subject, one grade level: about 20–30 hours
"100 for 100": retaking lower-grade state tests, about $400–500 per student

n134|602.c: Software teaches the knowledge; adults shift to motivation and high standards.
n134|602.e: Once apps handle instruction, "guides" stop lecturing and provide emotional and motivational support, seeking out students who aren't engaged. Guides earn at least $100,000 a year and are measured on kids loving school, learning twice as fast, and life skills. There's no tenure, and students help interview candidates. He thinks parents accept strictness from sports coaches but not in academics, yet high standards are the key to a child's happiness. With academics handled by software, groups can be larger and guides paid more.
ex: Guides earn at least $100,000 a year
Three metrics: love of school, 2x learning, life skills

n134|602.c: External rewards don't kill intrinsic motivation, and giving students their time back is the biggest reward.
n134|602.e: He rejects the idea that prizes and leaderboards crowd out intrinsic motivation. Different kids need different triggers, and what matters is building habits and breaking limiting beliefs about themselves. The strongest reward is time: less class, less homework. From kindergarten, "Alpha bucks" teach kids to earn, save, spend and give. Middle schoolers who reach the national top 1% in a subject earn $1,000 and can invest it in a real account, where losing money is also a lesson.
ex: Reach the top 1% in a subject, earn $1,000
His younger daughter hit the top 1% for the prize and decided effort is enough

n134|602.c: Today's ChatGPT is terrible for education: writing is thinking, and facts must be memorized.
n134|602.e: He agrees most students will use general chatbots to cheat, and says they need to be rebuilt around learning science. He rejects the idea that prompting equals writing, because writing is how you reorganize knowledge. Critical thinking rests on memorized facts. If 7×8 still takes up working memory, complex problems overload it. AI can speed up memorizing facts but can't replace long-term knowledge structures. Most edtech ignores learning science and sells to bureaucracies that don't prioritize results.
ex: Math Academy: about 22–28 hours to master a grade of math

items: If AI can look it up, skip memorizing
Facts are the foundation of thought

d.verdict: AI should speed up mastering facts, not replace thinking

n134|602.c: Education is a huge market, and for-profit schools plus vouchers can scale the model.
n134|602.e: The US private school market tops $50 billion, Texas spends about $100 billion a year on education, and federal legislation could unlock around $200 billion in vouchers. He wants mission and profit together. New-model schools charging $15,000–25,000 can be covered by Texas's roughly $10,000 voucher plus a few hundred dollars a month from parents. He has also packaged the academic system as the TimeBack platform for others to run schools, calls for randomized controlled trials with a million students, and expects public school transformation to take about a decade.
ex: The US private school market tops $50 billion
He says he has put in his first billion

items.d: The academic system, for others' schools
Start with the lowest-performing 10% or so

n135|605.c: Agents will hit harder than generative AI, turning many apps into back-end plumbing.
n135|605.e: For decades, product design has been about building interfaces so people can reach the databases and algorithms behind them. Natural language makes interfaces less valuable, and agents can bypass them entirely. He roughly estimates that about half of the more than 5 million mobile apps just collect input and complete transactions, and they could become APIs or MCP servers that agents call. Ads sell leads, but merchants would rather pay for completed transactions. Thin front ends whose users feel no loyalty to the interface are most at risk.
ex: Over 5 million mobile apps; he estimates about half just take input and transact
Search's challenge isn't capability but monetization

n135|605.c: Enterprises can't tolerate AI making mistakes on its own, so for now it's an assistant, not an employee.
n135|605.e: A consumer who gets a wrong answer can just ask again, but a model that shuts down the wrong server in production creates real liability. So he sees today's AI as a human-in-the-loop assistant, not yet ready to charge for work completed. Coding is the early exception: public code gets models to about 90%, and developers fill in the rest. Genomics, drug discovery and cybersecurity need proprietary data that isn't publicly available.
ex: Coding: public code gets models to about 90%

marks.d: Model does about 90%, humans the rest
Where it goes as accuracy improves

n135|605.c: Big models are like smart new hires; the lasting advantage is in systems of record and workflows.
n135|605.e: A frontier model is like the smartest PhD from a top school: it still has to be taught the company's context, and swapping model versions is like replacing an employee. Wrappers that only add guardrails or a presentation layer will get absorbed by the models. Durable applications own the workflow and the authoritative data, such as payroll, equity or clinical trial records. Companies should buy rather than build common functions like legal review or accounts payable, but sensitive data such as source code must be isolated and never used to train others' models.

items.d: Rebuilt end to end around AI

n135|605.c: You can't stop what you can't see, so security needs a platform that correlates all the data.
n135|605.e: Security starts with sensors on every endpoint and at every perimeter, blocking known threats while collecting data to find unknown ones. Standalone point tools see only their own data. An email security tool sees someone click a phishing link but not the firewall traffic that follows, so it can only produce a long list of things to check. Data needs to be correlated as it comes in and investigated automatically, and he sees many SOC startups as wrappers that platforms will absorb. He admits big companies have sprawling tools, and consolidating takes two to three years.
ex: A host's example: one security chief with 118 identity tools
Products grew from 4 to 24, consolidated into 3 platforms

d.verdict: Once a capability matures, it belongs in the platform

n135|605.c: Attacks now take minutes, so response times must shrink to under an hour.
n135|605.e: Attackers can also use agents to find holes inside a company and exfiltrate data. Seven years ago, going from targeting to exfiltration took about three or four days. The fastest case the company has seen took 23 minutes, while average response is still measured in days, so response must come in under an hour. The company pen-tests around the clock, and he says about half of enterprises don't test seriously because they fear the results. Credential theft is the main way in, and deepfakes weaken two-factor authentication, so defenses should shift to just-in-time authorization and behavioral anomaly detection.
ex: Seven years ago an attack took 3–4 days; the fastest now takes 23 minutes
Behavioral signals such as changes in someone's typing patterns

items.d: As fast as 23 minutes; response takes days

n135|605.c: Customer support exists because products are bad; back-office work is AI's biggest efficiency win.
n135|605.e: He's cautious about AI in sales. It can draft proposals and outreach, but convincing a CIO still takes a trusted person, and automated outreach runs into automated filters. The bigger lever is repetitive back-office work, which he estimates could yield 200–400 basis points of efficiency, more at bigger companies. Support should shrink 80–90% within two to five years through better onboarding, fewer bugs and faster diagnosis, and the company now puts product-driven support issues ahead of new features.
ex: Goal: eliminate 80–90% of support volume in 2–5 years
An agent cut 500 lines of code down to 75

items.d: About 200–400 basis points, more at scale
Fix the product, don't add staff

n135|605.c: Acquisitions are distributed R&D: buy a top-two player in each niche and keep its founders leading.
n135|605.e: Companies under $1 billion in revenue spend more than half their costs on sales, marketing and support, while the largest vendors spend about 30%. So selling more products to customers who already trust you is far cheaper than winning new ones. Palo Alto has made 27 acquisitions, buying only companies ranked first or second in their niche, and often keeps the founders running the business. Buying Protect AI added model scanning and continuous red-teaming.
ex: 27 acquisitions in total
R&D runs about 12–16%, and G&A about 4–8%

n136|608.c: Reasoning can be trained through a model's own iterative self-improvement, not just coaxed out by prompts.
n136|608.e: Around 2021, models weren't smart enough, and chain-of-thought prompting gave only small gains, so he prioritized capability. STaR has the model generate its own solutions, learn only from the ones it gets right, then take on harder problems, over and over. On multi-digit arithmetic, each round pushed up the number of digits it could solve, with no obvious plateau, which convinced him the method could scale. Learning only from correct samples can get stuck in a local optimum, so the model can also write rationales for problems it missed and train on those.
ex: n-digit addition and multiplication: solvable digits rise with each round
The original had no baseline; he compares it with REINFORCE

items.d: The model writes its own reasoning

n136|608.c: Extending reasoning training to any text hinges on online learning and weighting by difficulty.
n136|608.e: Quiet-STaR aims to take the same recipe from question-answer problems to ordinary text at pretraining scale, learning more general reasoning through next-word prediction. He sees two often-overlooked ingredients: online training, and a difficulty-aware baseline that learns more from hard problems and less from easy ones. He thinks recent work on RL pretraining is similar, and the scaling dimensions for boosting intelligence are far from used up.

terms.d: More from hard problems, less from easy

result.d: Learns to think on ordinary text

n136|608.c: Frontier models are unevenly smart, and the easier a task is to verify, the better they do.
n136|608.e: Models can solve some Humanity's Last Exam problems that aren't easy even for PhDs, yet still fall into traps set by a question's unstated assumptions. His advice is to give as much context as possible and pick questions with closed-form answers or easy checks. Coding agents fail partly because of latency limits, which is why background Codex can think longer than interactive Cursor. They also fail when tasks fall outside their RL training distribution, and since labs don't publish their RL data, diagnosing this precisely is hard.
ex: Background Codex can think longer than interactive Cursor

marks.d: Limited by latency and training data

n136|608.c: Chasing autonomy time alone erodes human agency; grow the pie instead of slicing it up.
n136|608.e: The industry increasingly measures progress by how long a model can work without human intervention, and he's skeptical of those numbers. An agent that runs for eight hours and returns something roughly right leaves people with less control over, and understanding of, what they've built, like a 100,000-line auto-generated pull request. The mainstream approach slices global GDP into automatable markets and replaces them one by one. He wants models that understand people's goals and help them explore out-of-distribution directions, growing the pie and producing more real innovation.
ex: METR-style measures rose from about 2 hours to about 2.5
A 100,000-line auto-generated pull request

d.verdict: Models should help people grow the pie

n136|608.c: Optimizing turn by turn makes models sycophantic; train them to understand and remember people over time.
n136|608.e: Easy-to-quantify benchmarks make it simple to assign credit inside an organization and to run RL, but they can't measure how long-term interaction affects someone's life. Treat each turn as an isolated contest, and the model crams everything into one answer. It doesn't ask follow-ups, clarify or express uncertainty, which leads to sycophancy. Memory is underinvested because single-task training rarely rewards information carried across conversations. He admits a personal model will never be perfect, but aiming to learn the person goes a long way.
ex: In his PhD, he used models to simulate different students to design better tests
A user followed the model's advice on a bad startup idea and stopped trusting it

n137|611.c: A company that builds, installs and owns home batteries can become a cheaper power company.
n137|611.e: Base designs, builds, installs and owns the batteries, then sells electricity straight to households. When the grid is running normally, the batteries help the grid. During an outage, they power the home. Software pools the scattered batteries into a "distributed power plant" that bids into the electricity market, and that revenue pushes prices down. More scale means lower costs, and savings passed to customers bring more demand. He wants to repeat in energy what Tesla, SpaceX and Anduril did: engineering-led companies taking on incumbents.
ex: He says customers save roughly 10–20% a month on their bills
Operating only in Texas for now

n137|611.c: America isn't short of power. Its grid capacity just sits idle most of the time.
n137|611.e: The US grid is built for peak demand, about 700 gigawatts, but average demand is only around 300 gigawatts, so 300–400 gigawatts sit unused most of the time. Storage plus software can shift power from quiet hours to busy ones and put that idle capacity to work. He agrees more generation still needs to be built and thinks demand-growth forecasts point the right way, maybe even too low. Energy-hungry industries will cluster around cheap power, so Texas and the Gulf region will draw AI computing.
ex: If peak capacity hits about 1 terawatt, nearly 700 gigawatts could sit idle
The Stargate project in Abilene, Texas

items.d: The grid is built for the peak
What's actually used most of the time

n137|611.c: Solar plus storage will dominate the next 50 years, and nuclear must get much cheaper and faster.
n137|611.e: He sees the last 50 years as defined first by coal, then by natural gas. The next era will be set by cost curves, and those favor solar and storage. He agrees Chinese subsidies funded much of the early manufacturing capacity, but stresses that US and European capital invested too, and the cost curve is now locked in. He wants nuclear to succeed, but it has to get much cheaper and faster to build. If solar plus storage scales fast enough, new nuclear may not make economic sense.
ex: Solar is about 20% of Texas's fuel mix and about 30% of California's

items.d: The next era, driven by falling costs

n137|611.c: Batteries move energy through time, so their real competitor is the wires, not power plants.
n137|611.e: The number he watches is the total cost of a kilowatt-hour delivered to the home: generation plus delivery. Over 20 years, solar has slashed generation costs, while transmission and distribution costs keep rising as equipment ages. Regulated utilities earn a fixed return on the capital they spend, so they would rather build more than innovate. Wires move energy across space and batteries move it through time, so Base mainly replaces grid investment. He wants faster permitting and grid hookups, plus rewards for customers who shift use away from peak hours.
ex: Texas runs its own grid, ERCOT, outside the federal regulator FERC's reach

terms.d: Down sharply over 20 years thanks to solar

result.d: The savings are mostly in delivery

n137|611.c: Talent is the tightest constraint, capital is just table stakes, and technology drives 90% of cost cuts.
n137|611.e: The company grew from about 10 people to about 250, demand outstrips production, and it is building its first factory in Austin. Early leaders came from SpaceX, Anduril, Starlink and Tesla's battery team, and they still do hands-on work. The culture is about urgency and focus, with the north-star metric on screens in the office. Base raised about $1.3 billion in roughly 18 months, and cheap capital can lower power prices. But he calls $1 billion just the ante: about 90% of cost cuts come from technology.
ex: Raised about $1.3 billion in roughly 18 months
A co-founder ran manufacturing at SpaceX and Anduril

root.d: Power is a commodity, so cost wins

n138|615.c: Language models have distilled intelligence without consciousness, and they've quietly passed the Turing test.
n138|615.e: Predicting the next word already produces recognizable intelligent behavior, like reasoning, understanding and synthesis, but the mechanism is purely mechanical, and he sees no consciousness in it. It reminds him of the intelligence without awareness in the sci-fi novel Blindsight. He thinks the Turing test, whether a machine can pass as human in conversation, has effectively been passed, yet society barely reacted. He can't propose a better test for consciousness, but guesses that real-time perception and feedback, say in a robot, would make systems seem more conscious.
ex: A friend doing a philosophy PhD finds GPT-5 a better conversation partner than their advisor
A Warp user once insisted the product's AI was sentient

marks.d: Like robots; might seem more conscious

n138|615.c: By owning the terminal itself, Warp becomes an agentic development environment.
n138|615.e: The terminal has barely changed in 40 years: powerful but hard to learn, full of commands nobody remembers, and intimidating. Warp first set out to build a collaboration platform around it, then found demand for coding agents was far stronger and pivoted. Users can type commands or describe a goal in plain English and let an agent write code, set up projects and debug. Owning the whole app lets Warp keep command-line workflows while adding editing and code review, unlike VS Code forks or text-only terminal agents.
ex: Growth picked up sharply three or four months after the coding agent launched
Per the host: nearly 1 million monthly users, adding about $1 million revenue every 7–10 days

items.d: Unchanged for 40 years, hard to learn
Helps with tools like Docker and Git
Commands and plain-English goals side by side

n138|615.c: Coding will move from hand-writing to prompting to partial automation, making senior judgment more valuable for now.
n138|615.e: He expects most developers to build by prompting within a few years, with tickets, user feedback and server errors kicking off background agents. But he'd be surprised if everything became automated. Agents are like junior engineers: without senior people guarding the architecture and reviewing code, they introduce bugs, security holes and code that's hard to maintain. So in the near term, architecture and review skills earn a bigger premium, and developers who stay at a junior level face the most risk. Automated security analysis, verification and languages like Rust will matter more.

n138|615.c: The big labs moving into coding is worrying, but their distribution edge may not hold.
n138|615.e: Anthropic, OpenAI and Microsoft are all pushing hard into coding, and he admits that's a little scary. But he doubts they can repeat classic distribution plays like Microsoft bundling apps into Windows or Google absorbing vertical search. On the consumer side ChatGPT is the default, yet developers still start from a terminal or IDE they download, and GitHub, best placed to own that spot, hasn't executed well. He hopes competition turns intelligence into a commodity, but frontier models keep pricing power for now because the gap with open source is real.
ex: Consumer tools bundle too: Lovable, Bolt and Replit are moving toward helping you start a store

items.d: Anthropic and OpenAI push into coding

n138|615.c: Models already reason well enough, context is the real limit, and automation is easier to price than productivity.
n138|615.e: In Warp's testing, Sonnet 3.7 to 4 was a big jump, but 4 to 4.5 added only a few points on the SWE-bench coding benchmark. GPT-5 was roughly on par, with a different feel and higher latency, and he isn't sure what trend that signals. The current limit is context: the whole codebase, outside information and what the user actually intends. He's most bullish on programmable agents running headless in CI, the automated test-and-deploy pipeline, because automation's value is easier to measure than fuzzy productivity gains.
ex: Research on whether coding assistants pay off in real codebases is still unclear

items: Needs a human at the keyboard

d.verdict: Automation beats productivity tools

n140|121.c: A slow response to AI is an organizational speed problem, and fast iteration beats careful strategy.
n140|121.e: Hypergrowth created deep specialization, with seven to ten layers between engineers and customers. That works when product-market fit is strong, but it's too slow in an AI era that changes every month. His first move was accountability: separate owners for AI and the core data warehouse, wired directly to go-to-market teams, plus cross-functional "war room" teams. Wider behavior change needs internal champions, and co-founder Benoit's enthusiasm for coding agents moved engineers more than any CEO mandate.
ex: During 100%-plus annual growth, 7–10 layers separated engineers from customers
Sales engineers use coding agents and synthetic data to build custom demos

items.d: Fell behind early in the AI wave

n140|121.c: Snowflake gave up building its own models to win on data, and defensibility must be rebuilt daily.
n140|121.e: Snowflake built a respectable model early on but couldn't match the capital of OpenAI and Anthropic, so it pivoted to an "AI data cloud," betting on the data already on its platform. He says about half of eligible Fortune 2000 companies are customers. He sees model companies as empires that haven't yet reached the ocean: they'll keep expanding, so products that are just a prompt wrapped around a model are fragile. Cloud providers have unlimited budgets and patience, so Snowflake must stay ahead or become Intel.
ex: All three big clouds want the data market, yet Snowflake and Databricks endure

items: Used by about half the Fortune 2000
Value stays separate from the model

d.verdict: Stay ahead, or end up like Intel

n140|121.c: Enterprise agents need clear limits: no do-everything platform and no reckless, YOLO-style AI.
n140|121.e: He rejects the platform pitch of any data, any workflow, one agent to rule them all: infinite options leave you not knowing what to build. Snowflake Intelligence focuses on getting value faster from structured and unstructured data. It serves every employee, not just people who write SQL, and doesn't try to replace SAP or Salesforce. Enterprise answers are right or wrong, so every capability needs evals, and swapping models means checking that nothing broke. It's priced by usage, not per seat.
ex: Raven, the internal sales assistant, combines contracts, usage, communications and tickets
Early customers include Cisco, Fanatics and the US bobsled team

n140|121.c: Start enterprise AI with sure-payoff use cases and run many small bets of about $1,000 each.
n140|121.e: He sees three sure payoffs: coding agents, customer support that handles voice and text using institutional knowledge, and easier data access that can replace $50-per-user-per-month licenses. Text-to-SQL, turning questions into database queries, looks simple but is much harder than customers expect. Don't place a big bet up front: Raven went through two or three versions first. Take lots of shots, spend about $1,000 on each, and scale only what proves its value.
ex: Raven's predecessors included sales enablement tools and a Customer 360 app

root.d: Not every workflow needs an agent

items.d: Company knowledge, voice and text, human backup

n140|121.c: Ads will return inside chat but must be transparent, and models should lean on outside tools.
n140|121.e: Ads are here to stay and will be reinvented for chat interfaces. The hard part is that the influence is subtler, like a psychiatrist who secretly favors one drug, so users need to know what the platform gets out of it. More citations and sources are a good sign. PageRank was already running out of steam by 2004–05. Google's real edge was its click-feedback loop, and AI products need the same kind of loop built on evals. He doesn't think models should internalize everything. Calling reliable tools like search or code is the rational choice.
ex: Google search ads could improve within minutes based on feedback

n141|624.c: Biotech is going through a dot-com-style shakeout, and the problem is commercial timing, not the science.
n141|624.e: The post-COVID mRNA boom pulled in generalist tech capital. Then rising rates, tariffs, regulatory uncertainty, competition from China and slow commercialization of new therapies pushed the industry to the bottom. Gene editing, cell and gene therapy and RNA drugs all have approved products, so the science is real, just slower and costlier than expected. In 2021 capital was nearly free, and companies were encouraged to build platforms spanning many diseases. Once investors stopped paying for platforms, the small proof-of-concept programs became the company's entire value.

items.d: Free capital, many diseases at once
Proof-of-concept programs become all the value

n141|624.c: Competition has shifted from novel therapies to speed and cost, and China is now a lasting force.
n141|624.e: He thinks the last decade was about biologics and novel therapies, and the next will be about speed and cost, which is exactly China's strength. Chinese biotechs can push molecules into early clinical trials quickly and cheaply, and big pharma companies like Merck, Pfizer and Eli Lilly have started buying molecules from them. Some in the West find this motivating, while others question China's data and regulatory standards. Either way, he believes China is here to stay as a biotech hub.
ex: Carvykti, from J&J and Legend Biotech, is a commercial success in the US

items: China moves fast into early trials

d.verdict: China will remain a biotech hub

n141|624.c: Drug development struggles because many molecules aren't good enough, so each decision must get faster and cheaper.
n141|624.e: A new drug takes about 10 years and more than $2 billion to reach the market, and many programs fail only after years of work and hundreds of millions of dollars. He agrees that fixating on clinical-trial costs misses the point: the root problem is that many molecules just aren't good enough. You need better molecules and faster feedback from humans. A failed software project costs a year and a few million dollars, while a failed bio program costs four to six years and hundreds of millions. GLP-1s and Keytruda both show insight and conviction decide outcomes.
ex: GLP-1s: about five years ago, obesity programs could barely raise money
Keytruda was nearly licensed away

items.d: About a year, a few million dollars

n141|624.c: AI's near-term value is steadily compressing research workflows, not typing in a disease and getting a drug.
n141|624.e: Benchling places open-source, in-house and customers' own predictive models at the right points in scientists' workflows and connects them to existing data, so wet-lab scientists who don't code can use computational tools. The next step is recommending the next experiment. Deep research agents cut questions that once took weeks or even months down to hours. Much scientific knowledge lives as folklore in people's heads and walks out the door when they leave.
ex: A customer planned 8 months testing 20 mouse models, then found some already done
Prep reports for FDA meetings went from a full day to about five minutes

n141|624.c: Biology has its GPT but no chat yet, and in vertical markets 90% of the work is translation.
n141|624.e: Biology already has powerful models but lacks the kind of interface software engineers use every day. Accuracy, intellectual property, security, legal risk and workflow fit all stand in the way. Big pharma has pilots and copilots, but he hasn't yet seen an R&D organization truly transformed. In regulated verticals, most of the work is earning trust, embedding tools at the right moment, keeping them simple and validating accuracy. The AI that wins is the AI people actually use.
ex: Big pharma's proprietary lab data is an advantage startups can hardly match

items.d: The winning AI is the one people use

n141|624.c: Pure model vendors will struggle, and AI progress is best measured by the share of experiments it touches.
n141|624.e: Bio-model companies living off big upfront payments from a few pharma giants are unattractive, because modeling commoditizes too fast. The ways out: build your own pipeline and become a drug company, distribute through SaaS or pay-per-use, or create a marketplace for standardized research data, including failed experiments. He rejects the vending-machine standard that success requires an AI-discovered drug on the market. A better metric is the share of experiments predicted, simulated or otherwise touched by AI, which he thinks rises every day.
ex: Models like Chai and AlphaFold are already offered inside Benchling's workflows
Eli Lilly's TuneLab: a federated setup trading data for model access

items.d: A shared pool, failed data included

n141|624.c: Founders can use their moral authority to push contested bets, and vertical companies must go deep with customers.
n141|624.e: Co-founder Ashu handed off all his direct reports to work on AI full time, and some customers thought he had left. Customers were cutting staff at the time and employees worried about distraction, but his hands-on experiments won the team over. Sajith thinks breaking existing structures is something only founders can do. He spends about 30–50% of his own time with customers, and five to ten of them usually reveal a shared need. In vertical markets, doing things that don't scale works far better.
ex: He says doing things that don't scale works about 10 times better in vertical markets

terms.d: Ashu works on AI full time

n142|626.c: Robotics has had its GPT moment, but not yet its ChatGPT moment.
n142|626.e: He thinks the field seems to have found a recipe that scales, but hasn't yet turned scale into a great consumer product. The classic sense-plan-act approach needs hand-designed interfaces for every task and environment, so the work never compounds. Learning-based methods scale with data and models. As in other areas of AI, more relevant data should make robots more useful, but nobody knows what the next jump in data will unlock.

items.d: A recipe, not yet a product

n142|626.c: Diffusion Policy and action chunking made imitation learning stable enough for ordinary people to collect data.
n142|626.e: Early imitation learning, where robots learn from human demonstrations, was brittle and needed the same skilled demonstrator every time. Diffusion Policy can hold several reasonable actions for the same observation, so data from many untrained people can be pooled without the model falling apart. ACT's action chunking predicts a short stretch of motion instead of a single step, the way a person glances once and then moves for a while, so movements are smoother. ALOHA's low-latency teleoperation made demonstrating feel like a game, and data that smooth finally let Transformers shine.
ex: Before this, robot learning mostly used shallow MLPs and convolutional networks

terms.d: Predicts a stretch of motion at once

result.d: Data from many people works together

n142|626.c: After about 20 rounds of iteration, glove data now matches teleoperation in quality.
n142|626.e: He first worried that glove data wouldn't match the robot's own body, so it would be worse than teleoperation. Instead, the glove's form let people move more naturally and dexterously, and after a lot of conversion work there's no obvious gap. The company now has about 10 million trajectories collected in the wild from more than 500 people, including navigation and long multi-step tasks. He once feared others would copy the glove, then found the full system far harder to build than expected.
ex: About 10 million long-horizon trajectories from real-world settings
Data from more than 500 people

n142|626.c: Home robots must be cheap and safe and tested in homes first, and demos deserve zero assumptions.
n142|626.e: The goal is to hand chores to robots so people can spend time on family and hobbies. If robots get cheap, safe and capable enough, he imagines them in over a billion homes within ten years. The design is pared down: a cartoonish look, and three fingers that cover most grasps. In 2026 they'll test in selected users' homes, then decide on mass production in 2027 or 2028 based on reliability, capability, safety and price. When watching others' demos, first ask whether the robot was autonomous, and believe only what's clearly shown.
ex: Prototypes cost $6,000–20,000, and could drop below $10,000 at scale

items.d: Depends on reliability, safety and price
Envisioned in over a billion homes

n142|627.c: UMI took data collection out of the lab, and only in-the-wild data lets robots generalize.
n142|627.e: Teleoperation takes hours to set up, so its data stays stuck in the lab. UMI uses a 3D-printed gripper and a GoPro to record what the camera sees and how the hand moves. What matters is paired observations and actions, so no robot is needed at all. Three students collected about 1,500 coffee-serving clips in restaurants in two weeks, and the resulting policy served coffee in unfamiliar spots at Stanford. But it failed in direct sunlight, because every clip was recorded on rainy days.
ex: About 1,500 coffee clips, collected in roughly two weeks
All data came from rainy days, so it failed in direct sunlight

n142|627.c: Imitation learning is more efficient for manipulation, while reinforcement learning suits walking better.
n142|627.e: Walking mostly requires simulating contact between feet and ground, which is fairly tractable. Manipulation means simulating hand deformation, transparent cups, liquids, reflections and forces, which is extremely expensive. On the other hand, manipulation is easy for people to demonstrate. He thinks a perfect simulator could solve any task, so the real question is which route gets there faster.

items: Ground contact is easy to simulate
Reactive behavior is hard to demonstrate
Deformation, glass and liquids are hard to simulate

d.verdict: It comes down to which is faster

n142|627.c: Perception makes up for cheap hardware, so mechanical and learning teams must iterate together.
n142|627.e: Industrial robots can't see, so they rely on rigid, precise parts. With vision, a robot can correct for imprecise hardware, which allows cheap, compliant actuators that are inherently safer. The learning team pushes hardware to its limits and breaks parts often, so putting mechanical and learning teams together means failures feed back into the design quickly. The two big remaining problems are a training recipe that stays robust at scale and hardware reliability.
ex: At larger scale, auto-calibration and failure detection matter more for data quality

n142|627.c: Diverse data enables zero-shot generalization, and the glove makes fine force control possible.
n142|627.e: In about six Airbnbs, with no demonstrations from that particular home, the robot cleared dishes and loaded the dishwasher, handling shiny silverware and glass tabletops. He credits the diversity of data from more than 500 people. In teleoperation the operator's hand is effectively numb and can't feel excess force. A person wearing the glove feels contact, which makes force-sensitive tasks like running an espresso machine or folding socks possible. The table-clearing demo required holding two wine glasses in one hand, and development broke a lot of glasses.
ex: Zero-shot tests in about six Airbnbs
He calls it the industry's first end-to-end sock folding and espresso machine operation

root.d: No demos from that home needed

n143|634.c: Harvey's value is shifting from making individual lawyers faster to running whole firms more profitably.
n143|634.e: When lawyers first got GPT-4, they ran into hallucinations and missing context, and Harvey spent about two years building a "lawyer IDE" around the model. Today a firm handles thousands of client matters at once, so the hard part is orchestration, governance and enterprise requirements, not just smarter models. About a year and a half ago, firms began introducing Harvey to their clients. That brought in corporate legal teams like Walmart and AT&T, private equity funds, and demand for secure collaboration between firms and outside counsel.
ex: Nearly 1,000 customers, about 500 employees, founded about 3.5 years ago
New customers include Walmart, plus AT&T and others

items.d: Secure sharing between firms and clients

n143|634.c: Client matters are a natural environment for agents, and partners' judgment is the reward function.
n143|634.e: A partner sets strategy, and associates research case law, summarize, draft and cite, then hand back a memo. That already looks like an agent. On the first day with GPT-4, co-founder Winston spent 14 hours replicating those tasks. Finding a change-of-control clause is easy to evaluate, but scoring how good a merger agreement is remains one of the hardest problems. The drafts, edits and partner feedback that firms accumulate capture reasoning that public SEC filings lack. The real test of a deal may be no surprise litigation three years later.
ex: A $1 billion fund: an LPA of about 100 pages and about 100 investors

n143|634.c: AI changes junior work first, while senior partners, like distinguished engineers, are hard to replace.
n143|634.e: Senior partners set strategy and abstractions, delegate execution, spot subtle failure modes and manage clients, which he thinks models can't do anytime soon. He cites a Wachtell partner who worked on Dell going private and then public again, relying on technical understanding of complex entity structures, not just relationships. To the worry about how partners get trained with fewer associates, he answers that models can speed up learning: generate a merger agreement, then ask why it's structured that way. The change has to happen one practice area at a time.
ex: Dell's take-private, restructuring and return to public markets
The change starts with fund formation teams and their private equity clients

n143|634.c: Harvey should be the platform that brings AI to every firm, not open its own firm.
n143|634.e: He sees running a law firm and building a tech company as two different businesses, and a company can only do one thing well. Running its own firm would also create conflicts of interest and cap its scale. A single cross-border deal can involve about 100 outside law firms, plus investment banks, tax and HR advisers, and Harvey wants to be the secure collaboration and AI infrastructure connecting them. Forward-deployed engineering is a way to discover the product, and customizations that keep recurring become platform features.
ex: He has talked with about 30 former Atrium employees
Legal is about a $1 trillion market, professional services about $3–5 trillion

d.verdict: A company can only do one thing well

n143|634.c: AI's biggest payoff is reorganizing institutions, not making one person 20% faster.
n143|634.e: Making one person code 20% faster doesn't ship the product 20% sooner. The real gains come from coordinating specialized people with AI systems, not from one superintelligence doing everything. Law firms are already about ten times bigger than before computers and the internet, and a similar expansion could happen again. He also thinks people underrate how much models keep improving: before GPT-4 launched, Harvey found its approach worked on GPT-4 but not on GPT-3.5.
ex: Law firms are about ten times larger than in the pre-computer era
Legal found its AI product shape before coding did

n144|635.c: Dubbing was only the starting point, because voice is the most natural next interface for technology.
n144|635.e: In Poland, foreign films are often dubbed by a single flat narrator reading every role. He found that awful and wanted dubbing to keep the original speaker's voice, emotion and intonation. The bigger bet: people still spend huge amounts of time on keyboards and screens, but speaking is the most natural interface, and future devices, even robots, will rely on voice as a key way in. Early attempts to tune off-the-shelf models sounded too robotic, and the breakthrough came from research led by his co-founder.
ex: Multilingual dubbing of Lex Fridman's interview with Prime Minister Modi
He cites about 350 employees and about $300 million in annual revenue

n144|635.c: Small labs form around specific problems, with research leading and product work running in parallel.
n144|635.e: The first voice lab had about five people and started with narration that sounds human, then built audiobooks, film narration and dubbing on top. The agents lab combines speech-to-text, a language model and text-to-speech, and quickly took on legacy integrations, deployment, testing, monitoring and evals. The music model and creative suite came from customer demand, while dubbing was a conviction bet. The rule: if a research breakthrough looks more than three months away, the product team builds a workaround itself.

n144|635.c: No single benchmark defines a good voice, so choose by brand, language and audience.
n144|635.e: Buyers often can't judge voices, and the same model can rank very differently just by swapping the voice, so existing benchmarks are incomplete. ElevenLabs has voice specialists and a marketplace of celebrity voices that includes Michael Caine. Standard audio labels record what was said, not how it was said, so the company built its own qualitative labels for emotion, accent and tone. He expects voice choice to adapt dynamically to the person, the situation and the time.
ex: A large European company wanted a voice as robotic as possible
In Japan and Korea, lively voices for younger users, slower ones for older users

marks.d: Wanted the most robotic voice possible

n144|635.c: Voice agents are moving from reactive customer support to proactive service and interactive teaching.
n144|635.e: Customer support is the fastest-growing category, and it's expanding from refunds and delivery tracking into product picks, gift ideas and even checkout. With Epic Games, players can talk to Darth Vader in real time inside Fortnite, a model that could extend to the worlds of books and games. He's most excited about education: moving from passively watching lessons to practicing with masters, like rehearsing negotiation with Chris Voss. The company is also working with Ukraine's Ministry of Digital Transformation on what it calls the first agentic government.
ex: Meesho's agent now helps with product picks and gift ideas
Chess.com: learn chess from Nakamura and Carlsen

n144|635.c: Models will commoditize within two to four years, so research buys a lead while product builds the moat.
n144|635.e: He expects foundation models to commoditize in the long run, possibly within two to four years. Open-source narration is already close in quality, though controllability is still hard. Research buys only about a 6–12 month lead. Lasting value sits in the product layer: the voice library, integrations, workflows, distribution and hooks into business processes. Audio progress comes from architectural breakthroughs, not headcount. He estimates there are only 50–100 top audio researchers in the world, and about 10 of them work at ElevenLabs.
ex: For the next year or two, enterprises should use an inspectable STT→LLM→TTS cascade
Scribe v2: latency under 150 milliseconds, by his figures

n145|143.c: Robotics will see a sentiment crash in 2026, then investors will split into winners and losers.
n145|143.e: She expects the technology to keep improving, but not every promised timeline can be met. Small humanoid or semi-humanoid deployments will appear, imperfect performance will trigger overreactions, and investors will sort into winners and losers. Capital, manufacturing, sensors and supply chains all favor big players, so her bet on the winners is Chinese companies, Tesla and maybe one startup.
ex: Tesla's driving models can transfer to Optimus walking, but won't solve manipulation
Google's foundation-model comeback was predictable from its data, capital, chips and talent

items.d: Not every timeline can be met
Humanoids and semi-humanoids go to work
China, Tesla or one startup wins

n145|143.c: Consumer AI needs network effects to reach escape velocity, or it will get copied.
n145|143.e: She agrees consumer agents are opening up some stunning opportunities, but durability has to pass a test. Without network effects or another moat, a big lab or Google can copy a successful feature within two or three years and catch up through distribution. On the flip side, many founders are scared off by the giants, or simply rebuild last-generation products on new models, and that leaves a gap of its own.

items: Copied within two or three years

d.verdict: Consumer hits without a moat don't last

n145|143.c: The "age of research" opens a window for new labs and new architectures.
n145|143.e: She reads Ilya Sutskever's "age of research" as good news for emerging labs. Scale still matters, but many ideas can be tested below the compute threshold, and capital is willing to fund scaled-up tests of architectures that were underinvested before. In her view, more compute-efficient methods may matter more than simply piling on resources.
ex: Architectures like diffusion models and state space models (SSMs)

marks.d: Test ideas below the compute threshold

n145|143.c: Drone systems and defense startups will drive a major reshaping of warfare.
n145|143.e: She sees two forces combining: the current US policy stance, which backs new entrants, and a rising density of defense startups. Together they will make drone-based systems a major overhaul of how wars are fought. The acceleration will spill over into space, communications, energy and mining.

n145|143.c: Market anxiety about AI comes from investor positioning and is largely disconnected from the technology.
n145|143.e: She sees the recurring AI anxiety as mostly about positioning: huge sums are riding on technologies and adoption assumptions that investors don't understand from first principles. So one weak Nvidia quarter can set off a panic that has little to do with the underlying shift. She also thinks adoption is moving astonishingly fast, and boldly predicts that in 2026 someone will make hundreds of millions of dollars trading markets with LLMs.
ex: Prediction: someone makes hundreds of millions trading markets with LLMs

items.d: Riding on tech and adoption assumptions

n145|144.c: The "AI is overhyped" take returns every year, but technologies take about a decade to spread.
n145|144.e: He expects another round of commentary saying AI is overhyped and doesn't work, but it doesn't matter: technology waves usually take about ten years to diffuse, and users are already getting huge value. More telling is that traditionally conservative professions, doctors, lawyers, some accountants and compliance teams, are adopting fast. After coding, medical notes and legal, he expects the next wave of vertical software to consolidate around a few winners in 2026 and reach huge scale.
ex: An Offcall report shows doctors widely using Abridge and OpenEvidence
Harvey in legal

root.d: The backlash doesn't change the picture

n145|144.c: Self-driving took 15 to 17 years, which sets the bar for patience with robotics.
n145|144.e: He sees self-driving as a single-purpose robot, and it took about 15 to 17 years to go from early work to truly usable. In 2026, Waymo, Tesla's robotaxis and self-driving in personal cars will become far more visible. In his experience, incumbents usually win at scale, and Tesla could carry its self-driving work over to Optimus.
ex: Waymo and Tesla are today's self-driving winners

items.d: Incumbents like Tesla more likely to win

n145|144.c: If priced sensibly, the first big AI company IPO will soar and pull others along.
n145|144.e: He starts with the risks: the capex cycle may not have enough demand behind it, credit and pay-on-delivery contracts are passing risk down the chain, and investors are overconcentrated in a few stocks like Nvidia. But retail investors want pure-play AI stocks beyond Nvidia, and the labs need enormous capital. He also describes a hedge fund manager who will have to buy a lab IPO because of benchmark pressure, and admits that isn't an investment he'd make.
ex: A hedge fund manager says he must buy lab IPOs regardless of his view

terms.d: Wants pure AI plays beyond Nvidia

result.d: Sensible pricing means a surge and followers

n145|144.c: AI science breakthroughs will be overhyped in the moment and underrated over the long run.
n145|144.e: He expects physics, materials or math models to produce one or two stunning results, like a new material or a proven conjecture, followed by claims that science has been solved. That overstates any single result while underestimating the long-term trend. He also floats code plus self-improvement as one possible path to a fast takeoff, but is clear that it's speculation and he may be wrong.

d.verdict: Single breakthroughs overhyped, long-term trend underrated

n145|144.c: GLP-1 adoption is unstoppable and still underrated.
n145|144.e: He sees GLP-1 adoption as irreversible, and falling obesity rates will have broad second-order effects. Visible results, plus the realization that how a drug is delivered matters, could open the door for engineered peptides and hormone therapies. He reads biohacking, like off-label GLP-1 use and peptide injections, as an early signal, and wonders whether a "Hims for peptides" will emerge.
ex: Bodybuilders once made creatine popular
Some people fly to Dubai just for injections

n146|129.c: In 2025, reasoning and retrieval made answers accurate, and tokens became truly valuable for the first time.
n146|129.e: He says scaling laws went as expected. The pleasant surprise was progress in grounding, reasoning and web search: routing that decides by confidence whether to look things up sharply cut hallucinations, the industry's biggest credibility problem. Once answers could be trusted, customers started paying real money for tokens, and reasoning token usage is growing along several exponential curves at once.
ex: He's heard secondhand that OpenEvidence has gross margins around 90%
Cursor, Claude and enterprise OpenAI workloads are solidly profitable

items.d: Reasoning usage grows on several exponentials

n146|129.c: Technology replaces tasks, not jobs, so a job should be defined by its purpose.
n146|129.e: He points to radiology. Geoffrey Hinton once predicted AI would transform the field and advised people not to go into it. AI is now in nearly every radiology application, yet there are more radiologists than before. Reading scans is a task, and diagnosing disease is the purpose. Reading faster means serving more patients, so hospitals hire more. The same goes for lawyers and engineers: he'd rather Nvidia engineers write less code and solve more problems. Building AI factories has also sent demand and pay for electricians and plumbers soaring.
ex: Hinton told people to skip radiology, yet radiologists increased
Everyone at Nvidia uses Cursor, and it's still hiring heavily

d.verdict: AI takes tasks; purpose creates more demand

n146|129.c: AI is a five-layer stack, and open models keep every industry from being suffocated.
n146|129.e: He breaks AI into five layers: energy, chips, infrastructure, models and applications. And AI has to understand not only human language but also biology, chemistry, physics, finance and healthcare information. Frontier labs can choose to stay closed, but without open pretrained models, startups, universities and century-old manufacturers and healthcare companies would be strangled before they could apply AI to their own fields. So he urges policymakers not to restrict the open-source layer.
ex: Chip fabs, system plants and AI factories are all being built at once

items.d: Open source is a key foundation

n146|129.c: Doomer and "god AI" narratives do harm, and safety starts with performance.
n146|129.e: He thinks well-known CEOs and researchers who warn governments unfamiliar with the technology about mass unemployment or all-powerful AI are doing something extremely harmful, and companies lobbying to restrict rivals are deeply conflicted. No single system mastering human language, genomes, proteins and physics exists, and none is coming soon. The first step in safety is a system that works reliably as advertised. The cheaper AI gets, the more monitoring AIs can watch over each critical agent.
ex: Synthetic data, cybersecurity and monitoring companies are all working on safety
He compares it to having a police officer on every corner

n146|129.c: Token costs could fall a billionfold in a decade, so leaders can't use capital to escape followers.
n146|129.e: He says hardware alone improves 5 to 10 times a year, far faster than Moore's law's roughly 2x every 18 months, compounding to 100,000 to 1 million times over ten years. Add algorithm and model gains, and a billionfold drop in token costs wouldn't surprise him. Training costs fall more slowly, but a $100 million or $500 million training run may cost about 10 times less a year later. Because hardware, algorithm and architecture advances are shared, teams six months to a year behind can keep pace.
ex: Per the host, GPT-4-level inference costs fell over 100x in 2024
He calls the DeepSeek paper last year's biggest contribution to American AI

result.d: Followers catch up within six months to a year

n146|129.c: The next five years' biggest opportunity is vertical AI, which needs far more reliability than consumer AI.
n146|129.e: Consumer AI can satisfy people at 80–90% accuracy, but industrial settings need something close to 99.99999%. General platforms might reach 99%, and vertical players have to close the rest of the gap, while open source makes going vertical cheaper. He believes everything that moves will become robotic. Self-driving has gone from digital rails to modular systems to end-to-end models and now to reasoning, and he says the industry started too early. Humanoid robots still face physical problems like falling over.
ex: Caterpillar as an example of a vertical player
The risk of a 300-pound humanoid robot falling

n146|129.c: The bubble story is too simple: computing is shifting from CPUs to accelerated computing, and everyone needs capacity.
n146|129.e: He argues that even without OpenAI, Anthropic and Gemini, Nvidia would still be worth hundreds of billions of dollars, because with Moore's law fading, computing itself is moving from general-purpose CPUs to accelerated computing. Working from the outside in: global GDP is about $100 trillion, roughly 2% goes to R&D, and wet labs, quant finance and carmakers are all moving onto supercomputers. He also says OpenAI's revenue roughly tracks its compute growth, and researchers and startups widely can't get enough compute.
ex: Nvidia's self-driving business is approaching $10 billion
Energy is today's hard constraint, met mostly by natural gas for a decade

items.d: The total pie, seen from outside

n147|649.c: Cutting 14 critical technology areas to 6 focuses effort on capabilities every service can use.
n147|649.e: He oversees DARPA, the Defense Innovation Unit, the Strategic Capabilities Office and the Chief AI Office, with about $150 billion a year in technology spending. Too many priorities means nobody remembers them and none get enough resources, like a startup with 14 product lines that no one would fund. So he compressed 14 areas into 6 actionable ones, each with an engineering sprint, choosing only shared capabilities that serve every branch. Needs unique to one service stay with that service's labs.
ex: Applied AI at scale, hypersonics at scale, directed energy at scale
About $150 billion a year in technology spending

items.d: Actionable, each with an engineering sprint
Useful on land, sea, air and space

n147|649.c: Defense shouldn't build its own foundation models but use commercial ones securely.
n147|649.e: The private sector has already poured hundreds of billions of dollars into foundation models, so the department doesn't need to reinvent them. The hard part is getting commercial models onto networks at different classification levels without government data flowing back into training. A roughly 60-day tiger team of former Databricks, Meta and AWS engineers launched Google's Gemini first, then added xAI's Grok. Uses fall into three groups: enterprise efficiency, intelligence analysis, and war-gaming and operational planning.
ex: About 3 million personnel have access; over 1 million unique users in 30 days
Gemini launched first, Grok followed

items.d: Fewer long reports and slide decks

n147|649.c: Uncrewed systems are the new front line and could take 20–30% of the defense budget within a decade.
n147|649.e: The war in Ukraine brought drones and robots back to the front line, and sending robots in first can reduce casualties. Carriers and sea lanes still matter, but the mix of equipment will shift toward autonomous submarines, uncrewed ships, large drones and autonomous aircraft, which are cheaper and pack more firepower. He's also betting on directed energy at scale, because shooting down a drone worth tens of thousands of dollars with a multimillion-dollar missile makes no economic sense.
ex: Israel's Iron Beam laser interceptor
Multimillion-dollar missiles against drones costing tens of thousands

items.d: Only a few countries can build them
Robots return to the front line

n147|649.c: Replace 300-page requirement documents with problem statements, so newcomers no longer have to sue to get in.
n147|649.e: He thinks the defense industrial base isn't ready for today's threats, as a year of operations against Iran, Venezuela and the Houthis showed, while China carries out the largest military buildup in history. Contractors have shrunk from about 50 in the 1980s to about 5, and SpaceX, Anduril and Palantir all had to sue the department to win their first contracts. Now the goal is to cut red tape and open a front door: state the problem and invite solutions, because primes excel at filling out questionnaires while startups bring new answers.
ex: SpaceX, Anduril and Palantir each sued to win a first contract
Visited about 20 companies, six days on the road in two weeks

n147|649.c: Layered capital can bridge the valley of death, but hardware startups must prove they can mass-produce.
n147|649.e: He describes a relay: DIU has about $1 billion for fast contracts, another office helps proven products scale up, and the Office of Strategic Capital has about $200 billion in lending authority at roughly Treasuries plus 100 basis points. He reminds founders that selling to the government is about lives, so they need a plan to build ten thousand units. Rebuilding the supply chain is about survival, which means developing second and third suppliers for weak links like germanium, brushless drone motors and optical fiber.
ex: The Office of Strategic Capital closed 5 critical-minerals deals within months
One nozzle supplier serves about 20 systems

n148|652.c: Software isn't headed to zero. Lasting value goes to companies that change course quickly.
n148|652.e: He grants that after ChatGPT arrived, customers and investors had good reason to question the whole software stack, but the idea that software will be worth nothing is overblown. The internet, mobile, cloud and now AI all followed the same pattern: speed decides everything. Companies that build fast, learn fast and change course in time capture the lasting value. He sees each technology shift as mainly a change-management problem, and the way to prove the bears wrong is to make growth speed up again.
ex: BlackBerry kept selling well for several quarters after the iPhone launched
At ServiceNow, he told engineers that not leaning in was not an option

n148|652.c: A product gets you in the door, but only a platform lasts, and real platforms are very rare.
n148|652.e: He quotes his former boss Frank Slootman: "Tools are for fools." In a disruption, a single product is easy to swap out, while a platform is woven into a customer's systems and chosen after careful thought. He partly agrees with Sarah that a killer wedge product is essential. It can take a company from zero to around $100 million in revenue, but what gets in easily also gets thrown out easily. Reaching billions takes at least two products that work together and connect to the systems around them.
ex: Fewer than ten pure software companies have revenue above $10 billion

items: Gets you in, up to ~$100M revenue
At least two products working together

d.verdict: You need a wedge, but scale comes from a platform

n148|652.c: Vibe coding makes apps faster to build, but it can't get around big companies' hard requirements.
n148|652.e: He rejects the idea that companies will simply generate whatever apps they still need. Building an app faster doesn't give you a sales channel into a bank. It doesn't replace regulatory approval, governance reviews or security audits, or requirements like backup across multiple clouds and fully isolated on-premises deployments. Established enterprises still have lots of room to expand, and each new workload they add roots MongoDB deeper in their infrastructure.
ex: One bank runs about 300 critical apps on MongoDB, out of roughly 9,000 total

items.d: How to sell into a bank
