n148|652.c: The data layer is a must-have in the AI stack, and the AI shift has barely started.
n148|652.e: He looks for two things: a market that will last and a layer that is a must-have. The database market is 50 to 60 years old, and he sees MongoDB, founded in 2007, as its real disruptor. Large models will be around for the foreseeable future, and data always has to live somewhere. Unstructured, fast-changing data only increases the need for databases. Applications, meanwhile, must offer deep industry focus, faster payoff, and things old SaaS couldn't do.
ex: Oracle turns 50 in about a year and a half
Twenty years into cloud computing, companies are still migrating

items.d: Need industry depth and faster payoff
A must-have: data has to live somewhere

n148|652.c: Enterprise AI is uneven: coding assistants have broken through, while office copilots still lack clear value.
n148|652.e: He meets at least 10 customers a week and sees big companies adopting slowly overall. Office copilots still have unclear value. Coding assistants became useful in 2024 and broke through in 2025. Fully AI-run customer service isn't there yet. To replace a system of record, a new product must be cheaper, faster and better, priced on the value it delivers, and aim for transformation rather than small efficiency gains. He stresses that MongoDB's third-quarter results were definitely not driven by AI, which is an addition to the core business.
ex: A European retailer built its own ERP system on MongoDB
A retail CTO didn't know MongoDB offers vector search

n149|657.c: Longevity research is underfunded mainly because aging isn't classed as a disease, not because the tech is hard.
n149|657.e: She thinks the main reason longevity research lacks money is that society doesn't yet classify aging as a disease, so funding it looks illegitimate. Technical barriers matter less. She started the Longevity Fund years ago for the same reason: good projects couldn't get funded. She later chose cryopreservation because it is a zero-to-one problem that is technically fascinating and hugely important for society, and the only one she could picture devoting the next ten years to.

items.d: Society doesn't classify it as one
Why she started the Longevity Fund

n149|657.c: Cryopreservation is a new kind of critical care: pause time until a treatment arrives.
n149|657.e: She positions Until as critical care that pauses biological time. Treatments for some diseases advance so fast that a patient may miss a trial by just a few months. The long-term goal is reversible whole-body medical hibernation. The near-term goal is reversible preservation of single human organs. She thinks the strongest use case is critical illness where the patient would otherwise die. Uses like jumping to the future or going to Mars run into people's unwillingness to leave their social ties behind.
ex: Metastatic melanoma went from under a year to possibly over a decade of survival

n149|657.c: The key is to pass quickly through the danger temperatures so that ice doesn't form.
n149|657.e: Water expands as it freezes and tears tissue apart. Freezing is random: a tiny ice seed forms, then grows, and tuning the speed of each step lowers the odds of ice. Below about minus 130°C, ice no longer forms, so the goal is to get through the danger zone fast. The faster you cool and rewarm, the less cryoprotectant, an antifreeze-like chemical, you need. But large organs can't be cooled instantly, so biology still matters. She notes some teams are betting on tolerating partial ice instead.
ex: Below about minus 130°C, ice stops forming

terms.d: Get through the danger zone quickly
Keep ice from forming while warming

result.d: Lower ice risk and chemical toxicity

n149|657.c: Reversible freezing already works at small scales. The open problem is scaling it to whole organs.
n149|657.e: She points to precedents. Human embryos have been frozen and rewarmed for over 30 years, leading to successful pregnancies. Freezing tissue is routine. Greg Fahy transplanted a frozen-and-rewarmed kidney into a rat, and it worked normally after about a month. The hard parts are perfusing the blood vessels, moving chemicals in and out, material properties, and fast, even rewarming. She sees this as rare in biology: engineering, like better rewarming devices and heat distribution, can partly get around biological limits, and physics tools can model it well.
ex: Human embryos have been reversibly frozen for over 30 years
Greg Fahy's experiment transplanting a cryopreserved kidney into a rat

items.d: The brain is the biggest unknown

n149|657.c: If time stops being a factor, organ transplants will work in a completely different way.
n149|657.e: Donor organs fail quickly. Teams sometimes charter planes to move them, patients wait near transplant centers carrying pagers, and matching happens at the last minute. She relays a view from surgeons she works with: if time weren't a factor, matching and surgery could happen at the best moment for everyone. She also hopes aging and cryopreservation become legitimate fields that top scientists can join without stigma, neither blindly hyped nor dismissed as science fiction.
ex: Patients carry pagers while waiting for a donor organ

items: Time is no longer a factor
Match and operate at the best time

n150|659.c: Once shared 4D simulations mature, video calls will become a lower-quality fallback.
n150|659.e: He says Roblox's business plan from almost 20 years ago already set the goal: a shared, physics-based space where people experience things together. AI just gets there faster, scaling from about 100 people to 10,000 with photorealistic graphics. Human communication has always chased higher fidelity, from murals and letters to phone and video. Once 4D simulation matures, a meeting could mean walking around a shared office and pointing at things. Spatial audio lets voices at a 1,000-person gathering fade naturally with distance.
ex: About 30 milliseconds of lag makes a group singing together sound out of sync

n150|659.c: The real challenge isn't physics but keeping 10,000 people in sync in one shared world.
n150|659.e: He sees the hard part as recording where 10,000 people went and what they did, and how to represent hours of shared memory. The next 5 to 10 years will show whether that works best as video latents, native 3D or a mix. Roblox plans to store its history as vector data that can be replayed from any angle and, where privacy allows, used to reconstruct safety incidents. Because this data captures interaction with the underlying 3D world, it beats video-plus-keyboard data for training embodied NPCs, characters that act in the world.
ex: About 13 billion hours of engagement a month
Roblox has begun training its own compliant NPC models, keeping data in-house

items: No interaction with the world itself

d.verdict: Better for training NPCs that act in the world

n150|659.c: NPCs will go in three steps: playing games, becoming your digital double, then acting for you.
n150|659.e: Step one is a general NPC that can play any Roblox game reasonably well. Step two is an avatar double that, with the user's consent, learns their gestures, gaze, voice and behavior. Step three is that double acting on the person's behalf, like playing with a child for 15 minutes for a busy parent. He gave no launch timeline and said the share of kids forming deep relationships with AI is currently zero. He also admits hand-built games like GTA set a very high bar for character behavior.
ex: Creators can prompt the system to generate a "happy Franklin" style NPC

items.d: Acts for you in the world

n150|659.c: AI amplifies creators rather than replacing them, and cheaper creation doesn't mean easier money.
n150|659.e: He expects more creators within five years, with each team producing far more, so a five-person team can make stunning work. But players' quality expectations will rise just as fast, so the efficiency gains first go into richer products and faster iteration. Roblox Studio can let agents edit code, run tests and send NPCs to playtest during the 24 hours a developer is away. Assets may one day be stored as prompts and generated on the fly at different detail levels for each device.
ex: Dress to Impress and Grow a Garden became hits thanks to their creators
Top creators earn tens of millions of dollars a year

n150|659.c: Hold a 3X goal you can break down and a 10X vision that keeps you up at night.
n150|659.e: He thinks leaders need a 3X goal that can be split by market across teams, plus a long-term 10X vision. The near-term goal is 10% of global gaming content, roughly 300 million daily active users, about three times the current business. On the platform, the 1,000th-ranked creator's average earnings grow faster than the top creator's, and the factors behind recommendations will be made public to fight gaming the system. For hiring, after acquiring Imbellus, Roblox screens tens of thousands of people with its own assessments, ignoring school pedigree.
ex: The goal: about 300 million daily users and 10% of global gaming
The 1,000th creator's income grows faster than the top creator's

items.d: Long-term direction that keeps you up

n151|662.c: Moving to neural networks meant a clean break, scrapping nearly all of the old rule-based system.
n151|662.e: When the R1 launched in late 2021, it used a third-party front camera plus a rule-based planner. He says the team knew at launch this was the wrong path, so in late 2021 or early 2022 they decided to rebuild from scratch. Second-generation hardware arrived in mid-2024, sharing not one line of code with the old system. Then the fleet had to grow before the data flywheel, where more cars bring more data and better models, could spin. He thinks systems stuck in a rules framework have almost no chance of catching up with neural networks.
ex: The second generation shares no code with the old system
An Autonomy Day in late 2025 showed the first results

n151|662.c: Vertical integration plus a fleet training loop is the key asset. At most five players will have it.
n151|662.e: He argues the neural network approach requires owning the cameras, radar and lidar all the way down to the raw signal. The car flags interesting events, stores them locally and uploads them over Wi-Fi, and they go straight into GPU training with no third party in between. Independent self-driving suppliers usually lack fleet scale, and sensor-only companies lack the vehicle architecture. He estimates there are only three or four viable players outside China, including Rivian, Tesla and Waymo, and the rest will keep shrinking.
ex: LTE is too expensive, so large files upload over Wi-Fi
The development fleet grew from hundreds of vehicles to thousands

items.d: New skills go back to the fleet

n151|662.c: Driver assist and full autonomy are converging. The difference lies in rare cases, the fifth to seventh nines.
n151|662.e: Level 2 driver assistance used to rely on cameras, while Level 4 driverless systems used expensive, heavy sensor suites that were overkill for consumer cars. Now sensors and compute are getting cheaper, and the levels are converging. Through the first three or four nines of reliability, every system feels the same. The difference is in rare but potentially fatal edge cases. Rivian builds its own inference chip to cut costs so every car can run advanced autonomy, since the "brain" is the priciest part. By 2030, he expects buying a car that can't drive itself to seem as odd as buying one without airbags.
ex: Nvidia chips work, but they get too expensive at scale

items.d: Rare edge cases make the difference

n151|662.c: Legacy cars' 100-plus control units are a tangle of weeds. Only a software-defined design can keep evolving.
n151|662.e: Legacy cars have 100 to 150 ECUs, small computers that each control one part, each owned by a supplier or even a sub-supplier. A welcome lighting sequence can involve about ten parties, so updates are slow and debugging is hard. It traces back to fuel-injection computers outsourced in the 1960s that grew into a tangle of weeds over decades. Rivian runs a unified operating system on one to three computers and can push changes over the air in minutes to an hour, about once a month. Automakers, he says, must build, buy or shrink, and suppliers' classic ADAS setups don't suit a fleet that keeps learning.
ex: A $5.8 billion Volkswagen deal licenses Rivian's network architecture and ECU layout

d.verdict: Automakers must build, buy or shrink

n151|662.c: The world doesn't need another Model Y. It needs another choice.
n151|662.e: The R1 averages about $90,000, which limits sales. The R2 starts at $45,000, aimed at the roughly $50,000 average price of a new car in the US. He notes there are more than 300 gas model lines under $70,000 but only one or two good EV choices. The Model 3 and Model Y make up about half of EV sales, and EVs are only about 8% of the market. Many rivals copy the Model Y, which leaves buyers with little choice. Most R1 buyers are first-time EV owners, showing a good alternative can pull people away from gas cars.
ex: The R1S sells about twice as many units as the Model X
Drivers can pick a mild, moderate or assertive driving style

n152|143.c: Code got cheap, but "vibe sales" hasn't happened. Getting products adopted is still the bottleneck.
n152|143.e: She sees AI-native companies in her portfolio with hundreds of millions in revenue and fewer than 50 engineers, yet they're growing sales teams to nearly 100 people. A five-person startup writing its own CRM proves little, since it may have used a spreadsheet before. Building enterprise tools for a big bank means security reviews, arguments over process, maintenance and change management across the whole organization. A good demo isn't a complete product, so distribution and competitive advantage still matter.
ex: Hundreds of millions in revenue, under 50 engineers, nearly 100 salespeople

d.verdict: Cheap code doesn't make selling easy

n152|143.c: With code in surplus, the new bottleneck is that nobody truly understands the codebase.
n152|143.e: When agents write code faster than people can read it, nobody deeply understands the whole codebase. Quality and fragility become hard to judge, and vibe-coded junk shows up in production. She sees the opportunity in allocating scarce human attention. She also warns that once hard, high-status work becomes easy, engineers face an identity crisis, and keeping your identity small helps you adapt.
ex: Applied Intuition's founder advises keeping your identity small

root.d: More code than people can read

n152|143.c: Valuation is acquisition currency, so rising AI valuations weaken incumbents.
n152|143.e: She points out that incumbents buy challengers using their own valuation as currency, paying in stock. If AI labs and top apps reach billions in annualized revenue and their valuations keep rising, challengers gain the means to acquire, and traditional vendors' bargaining power shrinks. She also thinks even $1 billion in revenue doesn't lock in category leadership, since the next jump in capability could reset the rankings.
ex: Many companies hit $100M+ annualized revenue faster than their SaaS predecessors

n152|143.c: Inference usage is exploding, but efficiency gains mean revenue grows slower than usage.
n152|143.e: She notes that consumption on inference clouds like Baseten and Fireworks, services that run models for customers, has grown about 1,000-fold. But efficiency keeps improving, so each call gets cheaper and revenue grows more slowly than usage. The human brain runs on only about 12 to 20 watts, which suggests models still have plenty of room to become more energy efficient.
ex: Inference cloud consumption grew about 1,000-fold
The human brain uses about 12–20 watts

result.d: Still lots of room on energy efficiency

n152|144.c: The idea that companies will replace paid software with internal vibe-coded tools is extremely shortsighted.
n152|144.e: He grants the pullback reflects some real long-term shifts, but calls the idea that companies will swap purchased software for tools built over a weekend extremely shortsighted. Take Samsara: its fleet software includes in-vehicle camera hardware, distribution, enterprise sales and support, none of which you can copy in a weekend. Customer-service agents like Decagon and Sierra, priced by usage instead of per seat, will hit the previous generation of software. That doesn't mean all SaaS disappears. Demand for software far exceeds supply, so efficiency gains will mostly go into more products.
ex: Decagon and Sierra charge by usage

n152|144.c: Claims that agents are already buying things on their own are mostly hype.
n152|144.e: He thinks claims that agents are already choosing vendors are exaggerated. Partnerships make software turn on tools like Supabase by default, much as Airtable quietly runs on AWS. That's an old pattern, not an independent buying decision. Real agent commerce would require understanding the buyer's role and needs. He bluntly says much of last month was hype: many posts on one agent forum were probably written by humans or even planted as marketing, yet the media treated the emotional content as proof of autonomous agents.
ex: Like Airtable quietly running on AWS

items: Agent forums acting on their own

d.verdict: Real agent commerce is still ahead

n152|144.c: AI labs went from $1 billion to $10 billion in revenue in about a year.
n152|144.e: Using Capital IQ data, he compares how long companies took to go from $1 billion to $10 billion in revenue: over 20 years for ADP and Adobe, seven or eight for Microsoft, three to five for Google, Meta and AWS, and about one for AI labs. Public forecasts suggest they may reach $100 billion within three to five years, a step that took Microsoft about 27 years. Meanwhile token prices have collapsed: GPT-4-level output fell about 150-fold in 21 months, and o1-level about 88-fold in 11 months.
ex: GPT-4-level pricing fell from about $37 to $0.25 per million tokens

n152|144.c: Tech's share of GDP will keep rising, but value will stay concentrated among top and mid-tier companies.
n152|144.e: He offers reference points: Google was worth about $100 billion in 2005, Apple became the first trillion-dollar company in 2018, and today the top eight tech companies total about $23 trillion, more than half the S&P 500. Big tech's share of US GDP rose from about 4% in 2005 to about 12%, and could reach 15% to 20%, or even 30%, by 2035. Sarah thinks the long tail will capture more. He agrees there will be more $100 billion companies, but expects value to stay concentrated at the top and in the middle.
ex: The top eight tech companies are worth about $23 trillion combined

n152|144.c: Most companies peak in value for about 12 months, so boards should review exit options regularly.
n152|144.e: He looks back at the dot-com era: about 450 companies went public each year in 1999 and 2000, and only 10 or 20 still matter. Lotus quickly reached hundreds of millions in revenue, then lost its market to Excel. He believes most companies have a value peak lasting about 12 months, so boards should assess an exit once or twice a year. Only a very few should never sell. Disruption cycles are compressed, with two years now like ten, and the best defense is a bundle of products covering many steps in one industry.
ex: About 450 companies went public each year in 1999 and 2000
Excel took Lotus's market

result.d: Single products are easy to copy

n153|667.c: CoreWeave wins on scale and reliability, both rooted in its founders' energy asset management background.
n153|667.e: Magnetar first invested in CoreWeave in 2021, when it was moving from Ethereum mining to high-performance computing. It started with visual effects rendering and only began training models for OpenAI in 2023. He thinks CoreWeave wins on two things. Scale depends on access to capital, energy and data centers. Reliability means keeping huge GPU fleets online, which is very hard. The founders' background in managing energy assets and a tech stack built early on were key.
ex: Magnetar runs three businesses: private credit, venture and systematic public markets

items.d: Shifting from mining to high-performance computing

n153|667.c: The real collateral behind GPU debt is cash flow from contracts with investment-grade customers.
n153|667.e: He says hyperscalers' AI capital spending in 2026 is expected at about $660 to $690 billion, and funding it all with equity would cause huge dilution. Instead, GPUs and contracts go into a special purpose vehicle. The main collateral is multi-year take-or-pay contracts with investment-grade buyers like Microsoft, Meta and Nvidia, and the GPUs are only secondary collateral. The equipment pays back in about 2 to 3 years, the debt fully amortizes in 4 to 5, and the residual value then belongs to the cloud provider. Media comparisons of GPUs to used-car collateral miss exactly this.
ex: Hyperscaler AI capital spending in 2026: about $660–690 billion

items.d: Goes to the cloud provider after payoff

n153|667.c: Demand outstrips supply, so "circular financing" is only a problem for speculative capacity.
n153|667.e: He notes the bottleneck in 2023 and 2024 was chip supply. Now it's the people, power and facilities needed to turn chips into revenue. He hasn't seen any idle "dark GPUs," unlike the dark fiber of the early 2000s. Last year's enterprise AI market was about $37 billion, with positive unit economics. Only speculative capacity or pure vendor financing deserves worry, and the ultimate buyers are hyperscalers using compute at massive scale.
ex: Last year's enterprise AI market was about $37 billion
Citing SemiAnalysis, Blackwell is about 30 times more efficient than Hopper

d.verdict: This isn't another dark fiber bubble

n153|667.c: Inference is spreading across many sites, and power will come from smaller units and on-site generation.
n153|667.e: Training clusters usually sit at one site drawing 50 to 150 megawatts. Inference, the computing done when a model answers, will spread across many data centers at 4 to 5 megawatts each. That makes software more important and is the focus of his next financings. Power is the constraint, but it's easier to get in smaller units. Much grid capacity is built for peaks and sits idle most of the year, so reliable flexible scheduling and storage can free it up. Another route is adding solar and gas turbines to a 10-megawatt grid connection to reach 50 to 100 megawatts.
ex: Crusoe got its start using natural gas that would have been flared
Steel, electricians and transformers are all near-term bottlenecks

n153|667.c: The SaaS sell-off went too far. Pick companies one by one instead of dumping the whole sector.
n153|667.e: He grants that usable AI performance jumped in late 2025 and early 2026, which will hit industries that aren't AI-native. But over the past four or five years, SaaS free-cash-flow margins rose sharply while revenue multiples stayed flat or fell. Enterprise software is integrated across systems and hard to copy. He's also more bullish on physical AI. Hardware investments in the 2010s lost Magnetar money, partly because software was an afterthought. Now general-purpose AI makes hardware easier to scale, and investment-grade contracts can support project financing.
ex: He sits on the boards of two robotics companies

items.d: Spans systems, not a single product

n154|671.c: Notion shipped simple features first. Its general agent took three or four tries to become useful.
n154|671.e: After getting early access to GPT-4 in 2022, he and co-founder Ivan decided the time had come and split the work in two: a near-term writing assistant and a long-term general assistant. AI Writer, a single-step task with no retrieval, shipped in two or three months. Workspace Q&A needed a real-time semantic index and serious evals, so it came most of a year later. The agent that works across documents and databases in multi-step tasks looked functional in early versions but wasn't useful, and took three or four attempts.
ex: AI Writer took about two or three months to ship

items.d: Worked on the third or fourth try
Start with zero permissions, granted as needed

n154|671.c: Most companies index poorly. Good retrieval means tuning for each data source one by one.
n154|671.e: He thinks most companies are bad at indexing. Information in Slack and Google Drive looks completely different, no single strategy covers everything, and you have to test empirically with real queries. Embedding-based retrieval spares users from carefully organizing their content, but behind-the-scenes engineering like chunk size and retrieval stages still matters. Because models keep improving, Notion rewrites its AI harness, the code wrapped around the model, about every six months instead of freezing an architecture once it's built.
ex: Connecting Slack and Google Drive took years of engineering
The harness gets rewritten about every six months

n154|671.c: Coding agents raise how far one engineer can go, but that's nothing like vibe coding.
n154|671.e: He breaks the evolution of coding tools into three stages: autocomplete, AI rewriting code, and agents. Notion started using Claude Code around last April. Agents can implement, verify and maintain features end to end, but only if engineers redesign the architecture and verification loops. Otherwise the output is junk. Team size hasn't changed much. What changed is the spread between individuals: the floor stayed put while the ceiling rose sharply, so the best might be 100 or 1,000 times more productive. Agents write almost all PRs, but these still need review and end-to-end tests.
ex: Designers use Design Playground to build deployable high-fidelity prototypes

items.d: Build, verify and maintain end to end

n154|671.c: Coding agents are the core of AGI because they can write code to build missing abilities.
n154|671.e: He wants agents to start from a small core and build what they lack, such as writing and deploying an integration for a service that isn't supported yet. Code provides deterministic logic and is also the channel for connecting new data. Personal agents inherit almost all of a user's permissions, while custom agents start with none, get permissions per task and run in the background. Because the leading model changes every month, Notion aims to be a Switzerland of models, neutral across providers. It also built an enhanced Markdown for agents and exposes databases through SQLite.
ex: Four Chinese open-source models are much cheaper, and Notion plans to support all of them

n154|671.c: People are shifting from writing code to managing agents, and products must help them do that.
n154|671.e: At night he queues tasks in Claude Code or Codex and lets them run overnight, once for 13 days straight, while he mostly does end-to-end verification at the outermost layer. His email agent learned his preferences through an interview and daily corrections. After a few weeks he removed approvals, and it now auto-archives about 95% of his email. Trust is built gradually: prototype, keep approvals and watch closely, then grant autonomy. Notion's role is shifting from helping people do work to helping them manage the agents doing it. A hundred background agents need a dashboard, not 100 chat windows.
ex: His email agent auto-archives about 95% of messages
The HR team is among the heaviest users of custom agents

n155|397.c: He went from hand-writing 80% of his code to delegating 80%. Now token throughput is the bottleneck.
n155|397.e: He says that until late 2025 he wrote about 80% of his code by hand. After December that nearly flipped, and he has barely typed code since. He runs agents in parallel on about 10 repos, and the unit of work has grown from a line or a function to a whole feature. The constraint is no longer compute but how much token throughput he can direct. An idle agent is like an idle GPU, so when one provider's quota runs out he switches to another. When things go wrong he calls it a skill issue: the capability is there, but instructions, memory and task design are lacking.
ex: About 10 repos in parallel, roughly 20 minutes per task

n155|397.c: Many apps shouldn't exist, because software's customers are no longer people.
n155|397.e: A persistent claw runs in a loop in its own sandbox, with richer memory, and can act while its owner is away. He only asked his home agent Dobby to find the speakers. It scanned the local network, reverse-engineered the interfaces, and after about three prompts started playing music. It then took over lighting, climate, shades, the pool and security, replacing six apps. He thinks vendors should just expose APIs and let agents handle the cross-system intelligence. But he hasn't given Dobby access to his email or calendar, since security and privacy remain obstacles.
ex: Dobby replaced six smart-home apps
He expects ordinary people to set this up easily within one to three years

items: A person logs into each one

d.verdict: Disposable, personalized software will become the norm

n155|397.c: AutoResearch means taking yourself out of the loop and letting agents run experiments overnight.
n155|397.e: The principle is to set the goal, metric and boundaries once, then let agents run on their own for a long time. He ran it overnight on a small GPT training project he had hand-tuned for years, and it found improvements he had missed, like adding weight decay to the value embeddings and tuning Adam's betas. The reason is that hyperparameters interact: changing one shifts the best value of another, and no human tries every combination by hand. Extrapolating, labs could run many cheap experiments on small models, scale up the winners, and leave researchers mainly supplying ideas.
ex: It found missed improvements such as weight decay on value embeddings

items.d: Into a branch, occasionally into main

n155|397.c: Even a research organization can be written down and optimized, but what can't be evaluated can't be automated.
n155|397.e: He sees program.md as a rough spec for how an autonomous researcher works. Different instruction files produce different rates of progress, so the research process itself can be measured and optimized. Even an organization's roles, communication and decision rules could be written as text and compared. He imagines a contest: same hardware, whose program.md works best, and then models learning to write better ones. The hard limit is evaluation. Speeding up CUDA kernels is ideal because correctness is fixed and speed is measurable. Without a reliable evaluator, automated research has nothing to go on.
ex: Optimizing CUDA kernels is an ideal, easy-to-evaluate task

n155|397.c: Models are jagged: part genius PhD student, part ten-year-old.
n155|397.e: He describes models as both a brilliant PhD student who can do systems programming and a ten-year-old. They finish long technical tasks yet make absurd mistakes. He blames reinforcement learning: verifiable tasks like passing tests get heavily optimized, while intent, humor and knowing when to ask a question don't, so models still tell the same atom joke from years ago. He agrees progress in code and math transfers to general intelligence, just not enough to be satisfying. He also expects models to specialize, though changing the weights easily damages other abilities.
ex: For years, models have told the same joke about scientists not trusting atoms

n155|397.c: Digital work will be rewritten first, because atoms are much harder than bits.
n155|397.e: He uses US Bureau of Labor Statistics data to see which jobs process digital information, but won't predict whether they'll grow or shrink. He's only sure they'll change, because AI is a third kind of information processor alongside people and traditional computers. Bits copy far faster than atoms move, so a large-scale digital rewrite comes first, followed later by sensors, actuators and broad physical autonomy. He's cautiously optimistic about software engineers: cheaper software could expand demand, per the Jevons paradox, where lower cost leads to more use.
ex: Bank teller jobs didn't shrink after ATMs spread
Self-driving shows robotics progress takes years and lots of capital

items.d: Bits copy fast, so they change first
Maybe a bigger market, but later

n155|397.c: Open models trail closed ones by six-plus months, and this spread-out setup turned out well almost by accident.
n155|397.e: He agrees open models have narrowed the gap from about 18 months to about 6 to 8 months, and expects them to stay a few months behind. He compares this to Linux but notes training models takes far more capital than building an operating system. A possible split: open models handle everyday and local tasks, while closed "oracle" models handle frontier research and big engineering. Full centralization carries systemic risk, so he hopes for more labs. He also notes lab employees face financial incentives and institutional pressure, and says he's considering moving back and forth between working inside and outside labs.
ex: The gap shrank from about 18 months to about 6–8 months

n156|679.c: Science isn't just thinking hard in a room. AI must work in a loop with physical experiments.
n156|679.e: He sees science as running experiments and learning from real results, something models around 2022 were too weak to do. Since then, progress in reasoning, test-time compute, self-correction, tool use and coding agents has made it possible to connect models to the physical world. So the core asset isn't a static materials dataset but a continuous stream of feedback grounded in experiments.
ex: Early on, he worked on sparsity and mixture-of-experts at Google Brain

items.d: Not thinking hard in a room
Experimental feedback becomes the core asset

n156|679.c: Internet literature can't teach physical truth, only the distribution of its noise.
n156|679.e: Periodic borrows the broad prior knowledge open-source models learn from huge amounts of text, and spends almost no effort improving coding models. But the literature doesn't record reliable physical ground truth. One engineer found that reported values for the same material property spanned several orders of magnitude, and a model would only learn that spread. The value comes from an active loop: inspect anomalies in experiments, compare against simulation and literature, then choose the next batch of experiments. In specific, data-rich chemical spaces, this is very sample efficient.
ex: Literature values for one material property differ by several orders of magnitude

items.d: The model picks the next step

n156|679.c: A language model orchestrates, while specialized atomic-scale networks serve as tools and rewards.
n156|679.e: He sees the language model as the natural interface and orchestration layer. It reads papers, takes in multimodal experimental data, directs experiments and calls specialized tools rather than computing everything itself. Neural networks designed for atomic systems are symmetry-aware, low-latency and can be fine-tuned per domain, so they act as tools or reward functions in the system. Models at the quantum-mechanics level generalize across similar atomic and molecular problems, but don't automatically carry over to other scales like fluid dynamics.
ex: They build their own models only where frontier models fall short

n156|679.c: Start as the intelligence layer for advanced manufacturing. A major discovery might follow a biotech model.
n156|679.e: Periodic treats itself as customer zero, reworking research workflows alongside its scientists, and then targets advanced manufacturers where materials and process engineering are the bottleneck. In the near term it aims to be the system of record and control plane for experiments, used to check data, debug equipment, improve recipes and control experiments. At heart that's a software business. He admits a truly major breakthrough could make it look more like a biotech discovery model. In the long run, AI moves from generating text and code to generating matter.
ex: Long term, it will affect semiconductors, aerospace and energy

items.d: System of record and control plane
A big breakthrough could look like biotech
From text and code to materials

n156|679.c: Intelligence is spiky, so every field needs its own data loop.
n156|679.e: He rejects treating intelligence as a single number. A model can be world-class in one area of math and brittle on a neighboring problem, and being good at repo-scale software doesn't mean it understands biology. Software improves itself quickly because unit tests give cheap, instant, verifiable feedback. AI research is much slower, since every experiment needs GPUs, long runs and generalization checks. Once automated, the bottleneck may shift to scientists interpreting data. Advanced robots aren't required, but reliable, dexterous humanoids would greatly speed up building new labs.
ex: Compute is still the main capital expense, and lab equipment has long lead times

marks.d: Unit tests on a few CPUs

n157|681.c: Stablecoins are fully reserved money that makes the dollar more useful, not a replacement for it.
n157|681.e: He's influenced by the Austrian school and sound-money thinking, but expects reserve currencies like the dollar to dominate for another 30 to 50 years. During the Great Depression, the Chicago Plan called for money to be fully backed by government debt. Banks instead won deposit insurance and kept fractional-reserve leverage, which collapsed in the financial crisis at more than 10 and even 30 times leverage. USDC follows a narrow-money approach, redeemable one-to-one, and the GENIUS Act has written this model into law.
ex: Irving Fisher's "100% Money" and the Chicago Plan
Reserves are cash, overnight repos and Treasury bills averaging about 13 days

d.verdict: A safer internet dollar

n157|681.c: AI agents will buy services from each other, and today's payment rails can't support that economy.
n157|681.e: He calls the past three months the biggest jump in capability he's seen in his career. More and more white-collar and service work will go to agents, which will also collaborate and buy specialized output from one another. Today's payment systems aren't globally interoperable or instant, can't be programmed by arbitrary software, and can't handle billions of micropayments worth a few cents each. Agents also need a medium for forming entities, holding value and executing contracts, with a state that can be proven computationally.
ex: One agent pays $0.20 to $1 for another agent's output
A single micropayment might be just 5 to 10 cents
He sees OpenClaw and Moltbook as early forms of AI collaboration

items.d: Agents take on white-collar and service work
Purchasing specialized output from each other

n157|681.c: Blockchains are operating systems, and Arc aims to be a regulated "economic operating system."
n157|681.e: He sees blockchains' value in being tamper-proof and publicly auditable, able to prove inputs, outputs and state, which matters for fiduciary transactions and autonomous machines. Early public chains chased a censorship-resistant parallel universe. He disagrees, because not everyone wants to be their own bank, and intermediaries are still needed. So Arc uses known validators made up of financial infrastructure firms, targets deterministic settlement within a few hundred milliseconds, prices fees in USDC rather than a volatile gas token, and builds in privacy and compliance from day one.
ex: Transfers already cost under a cent, and Arc aims for a millionth of a cent
Zero-knowledge proofs and rollups move computation off-chain and verify it on-chain
He says blockchains are having their "broadband moment"

items.d: Financial firms validate, settlement is final

n157|681.c: Tokenization is reaching every part of the securities chain. What matters is doing things that weren't possible before.
n157|681.e: He says tokenized stocks already exist. According to RWA.xyz, the most active tokenized stock is Circle itself, and USYC and EURC are the largest products of their kind. Registration, custody and clearing, brokers and exchanges are all moving, with SEC guidance about a month ago as a push. Most growth so far comes from overseas investors who can't otherwise buy US stocks. But he thinks the real question isn't copying stocks onto a chain. It's what new things become possible that weren't before.
ex: Computershare, DTCC, Nasdaq and the NYSE are all moving ahead
USDC is the money rail for prediction markets like Polymarket

n157|681.c: AI could bring double-digit growth, but GDP may hide capital crowding out people.
n157|681.e: He won't give a precise forecast, but thinks double-digit GDP growth in some regions in the 2030s is not unrealistic. AI is spreading faster, though bureaucracy, laws and people's appetite for risk will slow it, and places will differ. He worries that if growth mainly means capital capturing more capital at people's expense, GDP stops being a meaningful measure. There will be a lag between disruption and new institutions. On-chain organizations governed by humans and machines together could be extremely efficient, but only if the social contract is renegotiated.
ex: Double-digit growth in some regions in the 2030s is not unrealistic

result.d: Not just a bigger GDP number

n158|684.c: Rebuilding a platform with AI-generated code actually costs more, so the SaaS apocalypse theory doesn't hold.
n158|684.e: He argues AI-generated code looks cheap, but once you count the engineers pulled from other work, GPU infrastructure, the model vendors' margins and token consumption, it's expensive. His team estimates that rebuilding a simple ServiceNow app with a large model costs about 10 times as much. Adding AI on top of a mature platform takes only a small slice of the IT budget and produces more innovation, so starting from scratch doesn't pay off.
ex: Rebuilding a simple app costs about 10 times more

result.d: Compared with using the existing platform

n158|684.c: Large models only give advice. Getting things done takes a deterministic workflow platform.
n158|684.e: Take a payroll dispute. A large model can instantly list the steps to resolve it, but it won't actually close the case. Closing it takes company data and context, plus rounds of coordination among HR, finance, legal, compliance and risk before the employee gets an outcome. Companies forgive people for mistakes but not software, and models are probabilistic and lack decades of company context. So he embraces long-running agents and computer-use models, while ServiceNow remains the layer that executes and owns the result.
ex: A payroll dispute needs HR, finance, legal, compliance and risk working together

items: Coordinates across teams and closes cases

d.verdict: AI thinks, workflow acts

n158|684.c: Single-function departmental software is most at risk. Cross-department systems of record are hard to copy.
n158|684.e: He thinks point tools with limited value that executives don't care about are the easiest for AI to replace, while cross-department products and critical systems of record are hard to copy. People once feared cloud providers would eat software, but they became partners, and ServiceNow customers send them billions of dollars of workloads each year. He positions ServiceNow as an AI control tower connecting clouds, large models, data lakes and systems of record, preserving customer choice and using zero-copy access when data doesn't need to move.
ex: Over 85 billion workflows in flight and 7 trillion transactions on the platform
Integrated with about 800 major systems of record

n158|684.c: Acquisitions fill gaps in the front door, identity and operational security, because cybercrime is enormous.
n158|684.e: He fits three acquisitions together. Moveworks is the agentic front door, where employees go to get things done with AI. Veza manages identities for both humans and non-humans. Armis extends visibility from IT to operational technology like factory controllers, medical devices and buildings. He says all three were integrated within 20 days. To show how urgent security is, he puts cybercrime losses at about $1 trillion a month, equal to the world's third-largest economy.
ex: Three companies integrated in 20 days
Cybercrime losses of about $1 trillion a month

n158|684.c: Agents already handle 90% of support cases, and net new hiring will drop sharply within five years.
n158|684.e: Inside ServiceNow, agents already handle 90% of customer support cases, leaving people the remaining 10%. He calls it a lateral shift: people move from transactional work to judgment and critical thinking. He expects that within five years, even as the company keeps growing, net new hiring will fall sharply. Incremental work that once needed thousands of finance, HR and support roles will go to agents, while engineering innovation and trust-based relationships still need people.
ex: Agents handle 90% of internal support cases
He expects about 2.2 billion agents to join the workforce within a few years

n158|684.c: The faster AI moves, the more human agency is worth, and agency can be learned.
n158|684.e: He says AI is fast, but it will never be this slow again, so leaders shouldn't look for an escape hatch. They should lean in, because facing challenges is how you build capability. He believes agency can be developed through practice, simulation, training, certification and coaching, and says he built his own step by step after starting out as a shy teenager. Buying a deli at 16 taught him that only customers decide whether a business succeeds. A Xerox executive who hired him against the odds taught him to give people a chance.
ex: At 16 he bought a deli with an IOU of about $5,500
Xerox executive Emerson Fullwood made an exception to hire him

n159|688.c: In enterprise AI, innovation is outrunning real business results, and the gap keeps widening.
n159|688.e: SAP has about 400,000 customers and runs finance, HR, supply chain, manufacturing, and procurement, the whole path from order to cash. He calls it a company's "operating system." It was founded in 1972 by former IBM employees who saw that rewriting finance systems for every customer couldn't scale, so they built standard software. SAP survived the shifts to mainframe, client-server, internet, and mobile because customers always judged software by outcomes and return. He thinks AI innovation now runs far ahead of what companies actually get from it, and SAP's job is to close that gap.
ex: About 400,000 customers; founded in 1972 by former IBM employees

n159|688.c: AI will rebuild enterprise software's interface, process, and data layers, much like the move to cloud.
n159|688.e: He thinks the era of pre-designed screens is over. Interfaces will be generated on demand, and proactive agents, AI that acts without being asked, will run checks overnight and flag falling orders or supply chain breaks. In processes, agents can blend structured and unstructured work, moving from rigid standard processes to "service as software." In data, the general ledger, invoices, inventory, and other data need to be unified into one semantic model, because AI is only as good as its data. He compares it to the cloud shift: first host the old software, then rewrite it for multi-tenancy.
ex: Agents check things overnight and flag falling orders or supply chain disruptions

items.d: From standard processes to service as software

n159|688.c: Going from ten documents to thousands is the real challenge, and MCP can't handle 20,000 APIs.
n159|688.e: He says a proof of concept is easy: anyone can build a chatbot over 10 documents. At 100 or 1,000 documents it becomes a serious engineering problem. The same travel policy question should get different answers for an employee in the US and one in Germany, so the system has to tap master data like location, salary, and tax. MCP, a standard way for AI to call outside tools, works well with 10 APIs, but SAP has about 20,000. That blows up the context window and makes orchestration hard. And "order" might mean a repair, sales, or purchase order, so it must be disambiguated.
ex: SAP has about 20,000 APIs
"Order" can mean a repair, sales, or purchase order

items.d: Different answers by location and tax
Context overflows; needs disambiguation and orchestration

n159|688.c: Business agents need to be verifiable like code, and logging their decisions creates a data flywheel.
n159|688.e: Coding agents work well because their output compiles and can be tested. Business software needs the same: expected inputs and outputs, evals, and edge cases. Systems of record provide some verifiability, but not enough for autonomous agents, because much of the context is tribal knowledge in employees' heads. So agents should ask clarifying questions. SAP records these decision traces, which he calls "agent mining." They reveal anomalies or new practices worth spreading, and those findings feed back into better evals.
ex: "Agent mining" is an upgrade of process mining

n159|688.c: LLMs are poor at predictions from tabular data, so SAP built its own relational pretrained model.
n159|688.e: He points out that LLMs generate sequences of tokens, which makes them a poor fit for prediction, classification, and regression, like whether a customer will pay or how many days late. Traditional methods such as XGBoost and AutoML work but are hard to roll out, since a data scientist has to do feature engineering for each model. SAP spent about two years on a relational pretrained transformer, RPT-1, which handles classification, regression, and some time-series tasks even with little data. A three-to-four-point gain in demand forecast accuracy is worth millions to a large customer.
ex: A pharma company in 90 countries needs about 180 models for payment prediction
A 3–4% accuracy gain can be worth millions

items: A separate model per use case

n159|688.c: Pricing will move from per seat to usage-based, then to outcome-based once results are verifiable.
n159|688.e: Most SAP software is still priced per seat, with Concur, Fieldglass, and the business network as exceptions. He expects a move to usage-based pricing and, once verifiability improves, perhaps outcome-based licensing, citing Sierra as an example. For now it's a hybrid, because customers want predictable budgets and controlled costs, and they don't fully trust outcomes yet. He thinks winners will be decided by adoption and the results delivered. Customers don't care about the underlying technology, so SAP invests only where it can differentiate.
ex: He cites Sierra as an example of outcome-based pricing

marks.d: Hybrid: mostly usage, some seats kept

n159|688.c: Fragmented data and security are the main obstacles, and jobs will shift toward supervising agents.
n159|688.e: He sees data fragmentation as the biggest obstacle: years of purchasing decisions and acquisitions leave a patchwork of different systems, and companies that clean up their data early will find AI easier to adopt. Security matters just as much. Open-source agents like OpenClaw are interesting but not ready for production, as the recent LiteLLM vulnerability that leaked keys showed. As for work, chores like gathering data and making slides will be automated. People in finance shared services will work like junior developers, supervising agents, giving feedback, and reviewing output.
ex: A LiteLLM vulnerability leaked keys and credentials

items.d: Mixed systems from purchases and acquisitions
Hard to build a unified experience

n160|319.c: An app company's lasting edge is its workflow data, not the model weights.
n160|319.e: He thinks open-weight models have crossed the capability bar, and reinforcement learning and post-training are now mainstream, so app companies are taking intelligence back into their own hands. What's hard to copy is the user signal embedded in workflows. Frontier labs never see that feedback, but app companies can use it to train specialized long-horizon agents. By volume of inference calls, about 99% comes from AI-native app companies, and most of the market hasn't really started yet.
ex: Abridge: doctors' edits and later EHR actions become reward signals
One support ticket often triggers 10 to 20 actions

items.d: Doctor edits, actions in the EHR

n160|319.c: Find product-market fit with the best model first, then post-train for better, faster, cheaper.
n160|319.e: He says customers first pick the best model that unlocks economic value and only later optimize for cost. Don't post-train before you have product-market fit. Once the value is proven, specialize the model; a customer support model doesn't need frontier-level coding skills. More than 95% of production tokens run on dedicated inference, and almost every customer has done fine-tuning or compiler optimization. Inference also feeds training: live traffic produces data, evals, and reward signals.
ex: Over 95% of tokens run on dedicated inference
Acquired Parea, a customer, to strengthen post-training research

n160|319.c: Chinese open models offer great value, and refusing usable intelligence is penny-wise and pound-foolish.
n160|319.e: He says he could be wrong, but in air-gapped deployments a model can't "magically" cross the network boundary. He also hasn't seen real evidence of agendas planted in models, only early isolated cases that were caught quickly. He estimates DeepSeek costs about 20% of an Anthropic model in production, with similar or better latency and possibly higher reliability. At the same time, he thinks the US needs its own open-source models, and that they will come.
ex: He estimates DeepSeek costs about 20% of an Anthropic model in production

n160|319.c: Compute is the biggest constraint, and while renting GPUs isn't sticky, inference software keeps customers.
n160|319.e: Baseten runs 90 clusters across 18 clouds, with utilization so high it's uncomfortable, and holds a compute allocation meeting at 4 p.m. every day. He says nominal GPU supply overstates what's actually usable: there are about a dozen reliable clouds and only three or four top-tier ones. Getting 1,024 B200s from a good cloud now takes a three-to-five-year contract, possibly with about 20% prepaid. Bare GPU rental is a commodity, but the inference software has kept every one of the top 30 customers, with net revenue retention around 400% a year.
ex: 18 clouds, 90 clusters, and a compute meeting every day at 4 p.m.
The H100 has been out about 4.5 years, and prices are still rising

items: Customers see it as a commodity

d.verdict: Compute plus software is the lasting edge

n160|319.c: Cheaper inference means more usage, and inference is the last market standing even after AGI.
n160|319.e: He thinks that as inference gets cheaper, developers add far more intelligence, agents run longer, and better answers bring more revenue. There's no ceiling where it's "enough." This is the Jevons paradox: when something gets cheaper to use, total use goes up. So even after AGI, inference remains the enduring "last market." In the end state, consumers get personalized healthcare, education, and tools, and there's more software, not fewer engineers. Workflow companies that don't add intelligence will face an "extinction moment."
ex: Workflow companies that don't add intelligence face an "extinction moment"

n161|697.c: One reusable AI platform can deploy across industries, cutting time to results from a year to days.
n161|697.e: Long Lake has made about 30 acquisitions across property management, architecture, HR services, and specialty tax. About 80% of its Nexus platform's infrastructure is shared across industries. One side plugs into swappable models; the other into each business's data, skills, and workflows. The hard part is mapping processes, cleaning data, and integrating systems, which applied AI engineers handle. Early acquisitions took over a year to show measurable AI results. Now new partners can deploy and see impact within days.
ex: About 30 acquisitions, with about 80% of infrastructure reusable

items.d: Each industry's data, skills, and workflows

n161|697.c: AI first saves time, and companies spend that time on growth rather than layoffs.
n161|697.e: The host took this to mean an immediate margin boost. He corrected that what shows up first is time savings, and the freed-up capacity goes into growth and customer experience. Growth in services is capped by headcount: more revenue usually means hiring, training, and managing proportionally more people. When the existing team becomes 30–40% more efficient, it can serve more customers at lower incremental cost, bringing a software-style growth model into labor-heavy industries.
ex: Acquired businesses went from 0–5% growth to over 20%
He calls Long Lake the fastest-growing company in property management

n161|697.c: More productive employees are worth more, so AI will create jobs rather than destroy them.
n161|697.e: He says employees used to spend about 25–30% of each day on drudgery. Removing it lets the company pay more and attract and keep stronger people, making it a talent magnet. Leaving for a competitor without these tools would feel like giving up email. The more productive people are, the more valuable they become, and the more of them you want. Customers benefit too: faster responses, fewer errors in budgets, board reports, and emails, and higher retention.
ex: Drudgery once took 25–30% of an employee's day

n161|697.c: Owning operating businesses drives AI adoption better than selling them software.
n161|697.e: He sees deploying AI as change management at heart: you redesign workflows, not sign another software contract. Owning the business means owning the customer relationship, being directly accountable for results, and being able to reshape the organization as needed. A software vendor that doesn't own the business can't see the same outcomes. Long Lake's engineers are spread across about 20 states, sitting with frontline teams, treating employees as customers, and quickly turning their pain points into Nexus tools.
ex: Early employees came from Palantir, Ramp, and Robinhood
The M&A team came from GTCR, Blackstone, TPG, and H.I.G.

n161|697.c: Be a long-term compounder, not a buyer who sells after a few years.
n161|697.e: He models the company on long-term operators like Danaher and TransDigm. A transformation takes two to five years, so selling a company right after making it best in class makes little sense. Growth in services carries a steep "marginal tax": each new dollar of revenue leaves only about 20 cents after labor, so a 30–40% efficiency gain sharply lifts incremental profit. Business travel was chosen because it's critical, mistakes are costly, trips generate revenue, and the business has built up a century of customer trust.
ex: He estimates AI penetration in real business settings is only about 1%
Amex GBT traces its roots back to 1915

result.d: Preferred by sellers; lower cost of capital

n162|589.c: Economic security has to cover the whole AI supply chain, not just chips.
n162|589.e: He describes Pax Silica as a 14-country economic security alliance that looks at the whole ecosystem. Concentration risk isn't only in chips but in thousands of unglamorous inputs like precision gear reducers, servo motors, rare-earth magnets, and actuators. The first project is a 4,000-acre "forward-deployed industrial base" offered by the Philippines, about a third the size of Manhattan. In phase one the State Department holds it as diplomatic property. Phase two spends two years on tax, investor protections, and legal guarantees. Robotics is a candidate industry.
ex: The Philippine site is 4,000 acres, about a third of Manhattan
The alliance has 14 member countries

items.d: State runs it under embassy rules
Decades-long framework, handed to private operators

n162|589.c: America's strength is its private sector, so companies, not governments, should organize supply chains.
n162|589.e: He grants that the Belt and Road has been quite successful strategically: Chinese state firms built mines, roads, and processing plants abroad and locked in raw materials for factories at home. What he opposes is centrally planned capital allocation, which produces overpriced roads to nowhere and can push a host country's debt from X to 10X, like sinking into quicksand. The US approach makes companies the organizers. Government helps builders set up commercially viable platforms and forms true joint ventures with host countries, sharing risk and reward.
ex: A host country's debt can balloon from X to 10X
AI drives demand for copper, cobalt, data center spending, and electricians

items: Joint ventures share risk and reward

n162|589.c: Reindustrializing doesn't mean reshoring everything: keep chips at home and build allied hubs for the rest.
n162|589.e: He notes the US has about 4% of the world's population but roughly 20–30% of its consumption, so production clearly lags. Closing that gap is itself a massive reindustrialization. With unemployment around 4%, new capacity has to be semi- or fully automated, and Singapore's highly automated ports and factories show it can work. Chipmaking has scarce talent and is extremely capital-intensive, so it should stay in the US. Other inputs follow a hub model built on each ally's minerals, manufacturing base, or regional strengths.
ex: The US has about 4% of the population and 20–30% of consumption
With unemployment near 4%, new capacity must be highly automated

items.d: Regional hubs built on allies' strengths

n162|589.c: The bottleneck in critical minerals is refining, and both supply and pricing must be fixed.
n162|589.e: The host argued rare earths aren't actually rare, just turned into leverage by Chinese subsidies. He adds that deposits are indeed widespread, but whether mining pays off depends on energy and ore grade, and what's truly scarce outside China is refining capacity. The State Department held a critical minerals summit with more than 55 countries, then signed memorandums of understanding with dozens and began funding projects. Funding supply alone isn't enough, because Chinese subsidies would wreck the economics, so the government is negotiating demand-side pricing arrangements.
ex: The February 4 minerals summit drew more than 55 countries
He is very confident pricing can be solved within his tenure

n162|589.c: VCs can judge execution, and technical substitutes may end dependence faster than planning can.
n162|589.e: He thinks venture capitalists can see what government forms can't: whether founders can handle execution risk and scientific risk. Those judgments can help point taxpayer money in the right direction. The bigger upside is technical substitution. Bay Area work on new materials and rare-earth-free magnets could get around dependence like pulling a rabbit out of a hat. He also likens America to a founder who keeps going despite rejection, calling it a nation of underdogs that does best with its back against the wall.
ex: New materials like rare-earth-free magnets could bypass dependence on China

items.d: Points public money in a direction

n163|212.c: Once models became truly useful, waiting became intolerable, and there's no market for slow inference.
n163|212.e: He thinks it wasn't until 2025 that models got good enough for people to rely on daily. Before that, people talked about AI but rarely used it, so speed didn't matter. Once you use it every day, waiting becomes unbearable, just as nobody wants slow search or dial-up. Cerebras says its inference is 15 to 20 times faster than GPUs, for models from about a billion to over a trillion parameters, Chinese and American alike.
ex: Inference about 15–20 times faster than GPUs
Covers models from about 1 billion to 1 trillion parameters

items.d: In 2025 people start using them daily
Nobody wants slow search or dial-up

n163|212.c: New workloads need purpose-built architectures; tweaking GPUs won't deliver a 20x gain.
n163|212.e: He recalls that graphics made Nvidia and mobile made ARM, while well-placed incumbents failed to win those new markets. So AI needed a purpose-built architecture, not a derivative one, which was a deeply contrarian bet. Cerebras built a dinner-plate-sized wafer-scale chip. From mid-2017 to mid-2019 it burned about $8 million a month without getting it to work, telling the board every six weeks that it still didn't work, until yields finally hit the mark in summer 2019.
ex: The chip measures 46,000 square millimeters
He expected the software stack to take 5 years; it took about 10

items.d: Closed in about four and a half weeks

n163|212.c: Deals with G42 and OpenAI proved Cerebras could hold up at real-world scale.
n163|212.e: Early customers were supercomputing centers like Lawrence Livermore and Sandia, then oil and gas and pharma companies. They weren't speed-sensitive and couldn't drive mainstream volume. G42's $1 billion order forced the company to rebuild its supply chain and deploy big clusters, testing it at real scale in a way no internal test lab could. In mid-2025 OpenAI said fast inference mattered, Cerebras clearly led in testing, and the two signed a deal worth over $20 billion. AWS will also put Cerebras systems in its data centers.
ex: G42's order was worth $1 billion
The OpenAI deal is worth over $20 billion

items.d: About 300; third expected in the tens of thousands

n163|212.c: Going public brings broader investors and audited credibility; the biggest risk is diluting the culture.
n163|212.e: He describes an IPO as trading specialist tech investors for a broader investor base, with a slightly lower cost of capital in exchange for strict governance. It's new that a few companies like OpenAI and Anthropic can raise privately at valuations close to public-market levels. Going public brings audited credibility, which big US companies value, and Cerebras was for a time the only pure-play AI public company. With over 800 employees, his biggest fear is diluting the fearless engineering culture by hiring in a rush or settling for less.
ex: About 800–850 employees
Organized employee secondary sales over about 10 years before the IPO

n163|212.c: Speed creates new businesses, not just faster versions of old ones.
n163|212.e: He uses Netflix as an analogy: fast internet turned a DVD-by-mail company into a studio, not just a faster way to deliver envelopes. Inside Cerebras, a few engineers each oversee 8 to 10 agents running around the clock, plus QA agents, and productivity jumps from 10x to 100x. But he admits most people, himself included, are still struggling to adapt. He expects AI to first replace coding, design, and some SaaS tools, then reorganize work the way PCs, cloud, and SaaS did.
ex: Token spend per person rose from under $1,000 to $25,000–30,000 in 8 months
A few engineers manage 8–10 agents at once

items.d: Like Netflix going from DVDs to studio

n164|701.c: Companies can't keep agents out; autonomous ones are now over half, so the shift is to oversight.
n164|701.e: He saw the seed of agents in AutoGPT: the model picks actions, calls tools, and loops. GPT-4 wasn't strong enough then, so it didn't work well, but it signaled that agents would eventually do anything a person does on a computer. Today reasoning models handle long-horizon tasks, and Claude Code, Cowork, and approved OpenClaw deployments have made the market real. Connector-based low-code platforms offer limited productivity, so large enterprises are moving to autonomous agents with less control, because adopting off-the-shelf ones is far easier than building their own.
ex: Autonomous coding agents and assistants make up over 50%
Low-code automation is about 45%; homegrown agents about 2%

n164|701.c: Existing security tools can limit permissions but can't understand what an agent intends.
n164|701.e: The same action can be exactly right or extremely dangerous. Deleting and rebuilding a database might be what the user wanted, or the agent might have drifted off course on another task. Endpoint, API, and identity tools don't know what the agent is thinking. Useful agents also need broad, human-like permissions, which makes identity controls awkward. He also doubts that adding a proxy and writing smarter policies is the answer. Some agents can't technically be proxied, and seeing the traffic doesn't tell you what the agent plans to do or whether to allow it.
ex: Rebuilding a database could be a valid request, or an agent going off track

n164|701.c: Oversight must be selective, with small models deciding when to call in a bigger model.
n164|701.e: He says putting a frontier model in charge of reviewing every running agent would make the security layer cost more than the agents themselves and add unacceptable latency. That doesn't work commercially. Onyx trains small, specialized models that answer one question: is this action worth having a smarter agent investigate? The goal is to miss few real threats without over-escalating. He agrees with the host's speed-chess analogy: play routine moves on instinct and calculate deeply only at critical moments.
ex: Like speed chess: routine moves on instinct, deep calculation when it matters

items.d: Is it worth a closer look?

n164|701.c: AI that finds vulnerabilities automatically arrived suddenly, and the market isn't overreacting.
n164|701.e: He says a decade ago, automated vulnerability research looked 20 to 50 years away, and models like Mythos brought it all at once. His team did a lot of this kind of work in Israeli intelligence. He advises patching known issues fast and shoring up basic controls across identity, firewalls, endpoints, and AI-specific systems. He has no firm view on staged releases of frontier models: giving defenders time is valuable, but if adversaries reach the same capability first, the delay is a big mistake.
ex: He once thought automated vulnerability research was 20–50 years away

items.d: The capability arrives all at once
Patch fast and fill basic control gaps

n164|701.c: Vendors shouldn't certify their own safety, and independent oversight will eventually reach model weights.
n164|701.e: He compares it to a car inspection: you wouldn't trust only the seller's own check, and having labs inspect their own models is the same thing. Basic model mistakes will shrink as vendors improve, but independent judgment that runs against user intent gets harder to remove as capability grows. Companies don't want to hand historical agent behavior to labs hungry for training data, and they use several models at once, so no single vendor can cover it all. He thinks independent oversight will eventually extend to inspecting weights and activations.
ex: He estimates independent oversight is a $100 billion-plus opportunity

items.d: Harder to remove as capability grows
Companies won't hand data to labs

n165|704.c: A real platform is one where the ecosystem creates more value than the platform itself captures.
n165|704.e: He draws on the platform shifts Microsoft has lived through: a platform earns the name when participants create more value on it than the platform owner takes. AI should likewise be an ecosystem, not a single model. Every company, whether AI-native or traditional, should be able to own the intelligence it creates while also using other people's models. He also warns that many open-weight models shine on one or two benchmarks and disappoint in real deployment, which is why clean data lineage matters more.
ex: Many open models only look good on one or two benchmarks

marks.d: Ecosystem value exceeds what the platform captures

n165|704.c: Private evals may be a company's biggest IP, and you're only in control if you can swap models.
n165|704.e: He thinks public benchmarks are nearly saturated, so each company's private evals matter more. The recipe for turning a generalist into a specialist: a model with clean lineage and high-quality data, careful ablations, plus hill-climbing scaffolds, reinforcement learning, and trajectory collection. The test is whether a company can swap model A for model B and keep improving on its own evals without leaking its trajectories. If it can, it's in control; if not, it isn't. Trajectories of people working with agents can also train agents that act like veteran employees.
ex: Land O'Lakes demo: a 5B reasoning model trained on frontier-model trajectories
Accumulated know-how might one day go on the balance sheet

items.d: Swap A for B and keep improving

n165|704.c: SaaS isn't dying; its data models and business logic should be unbundled and rebundled for agents.
n165|704.e: He thinks cheaper interface generation can't replace the whole application stack. The data models and business logic SaaS vendors have refined over decades remain solid, so there's no need to rewrite a general ledger schema or Power BI's semantic measures. The opportunity is to unbundle those assets and repackage them for agents. On pricing, per-user subscriptions will stay because they give budget certainty, heavy agent workloads need usage-based pricing, and outcome-based pricing fits only some cases. Build versus buy depends on whether building and maintaining it in-house costs more than buying.
ex: Work IQ lets agents read meeting notes and propose GitHub code changes
Per-user Copilot pricing didn't anticipate customers running 10,000 agents

items.d: Depends on case; customers resist revenue sharing

n165|704.c: The new job is designing agent systems that do the work, not copying old roles.
n165|704.e: Microsoft's Azure networking team built more capacity in 15 months than in the previous 15 years combined, working with more than 500 fiber operators. They built an agent system called Miles and started asking for tokens instead of headcount. He paraphrases Kevin Scott: making hard things easy is just leverage, and the real ambition is making the impossible possible. He doesn't fully agree that engineering roles will collapse into four types. Specialists still matter, but generalists with broad agency get the highest returns.
ex: Azure networking built more capacity in 15 months than the previous 15 years
LinkedIn created a "full-stack builder" role

items: Design systems that do the work

n165|704.c: Data centers need community permission, and people must see benefits within 12 to 18 months.
n165|704.e: He believes data center buildouts depend on public permission. Communities need proof: residential power prices don't rise, the grid improves over time, water is replenished, and the construction, long-term jobs, training, and tax revenue are real. Deliver that and you get permission; fail and you don't. The benefits must be broad, not captured by one company or by tech workers. He says people need to see concrete gains within 12 to 18 months, like new startups, better local small businesses, or better healthcare. Asking people to just trust you is not acceptable.
ex: He thinks the next big startup could be a new university

result.d: Fall short and there's no permission

n166|707.c: Biohub won't cure diseases directly; it builds tools for the entire scientific community.
n166|707.e: Zuckerberg says Biohub won't cure diseases itself. Instead it builds tools that speed up the whole field. The original San Francisco model, developing tools over the long term across several universities, proved effective, so it expanded to New York and Chicago and became the center of the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative's philanthropy. He now thinks the goal of curing or managing all diseases by the end of the century may even be too conservative.
ex: Expanded from San Francisco to New York and Chicago

n166|707.c: Biological data can't be bought or scraped; you have to invent new ways to generate it.
n166|707.e: He points out that unlike internet text, the data needed to train biology models simply doesn't exist. It can only be produced by inventing new imaging, cell engineering, and sensing methods. That requires frontier biology and frontier AI to advance together, on a 10-to-15-year timeline. It's also what makes Biohub hard to copy: competing AI labs don't have frontier wet labs to match.
ex: New York does cell engineering; Chicago builds devices to measure inflammation

n166|707.c: Biology must be modeled in layers, with proteins, cells, and the whole body each needing different data.
n166|707.e: He thinks you first need to understand how proteins interact before you can understand cells, then the immune system and the whole body. Each layer may be qualitatively different and need its own data and models, so you can't just pile data into one recipe. The immune system is a good entry point: immune cells move around, linking the protein level to whole-body dynamics. Inflammation is also tied to many diseases. Once the system level is understood, other companies can build specific therapies on it.
ex: Inflammation is tied to many diseases, and immune cells link several layers

n166|707.c: Open source spreads faster than commercializing, and progress comes from empowering individuals.
n166|707.e: He grants this work might become a business, but getting models into more scientists' hands quickly matters more, and being a nonprofit that open-sources keeps the strategy simple. Big compute, new methods, large capital, and long timelines all suit a nonprofit structure, while specific therapies are left to biotech companies and academia. His vision isn't a central superintelligence doing all of science, but individuals using tools to try unconventional ideas. Biosecurity still requires trade-offs.

n166|707.c: A small elite team can drive AI progress; the five-year goal is a better layered biology model.
n166|707.e: He thinks 10 to 20 excellent, mission-driven people are enough to make meaningful AI progress; you don't need hundreds or thousands. Having frontier biology labs alongside is Biohub's recruiting advantage. Success in five years means building a clearly better layered world model of biology that makes a distinct intellectual contribution, with new downstream ideas following from it. He says AI's exponential curve has stayed on track, and it's the constant acceleration that makes it feel so astonishing.
ex: Ten to twenty excellent people can drive progress

n166|708.c: Science was held back by siloed work, hard-to-access papers, and a lack of shared tools.
n166|708.e: Priscilla Chan recalls that when they set the goal of curing all diseases a decade ago, some famous Nobel laureates laughed. When they asked scientists what was holding things back, the answers were siloed research, papers that were hard to access, and a lack of shared tools. A tool built by a postdoc often disappeared once that person graduated. So Biohub started by building tools for the whole field.
ex: Tools built by postdocs often vanished after they graduated

n166|708.c: Big datasets plus big models can turn biology from a discovery science into an engineering science.
n166|708.e: Her funding built step by step: first single-cell sequencing methods, then the Human Cell Atlas, then the Cell by Gene annotation tool, which drew outside researchers to contribute data Biohub never funded. Critics at the time dismissed it as mere stamp collecting. She thinks large models that can make sense of massive data answer that critique, and could shift biology from a science of discovery to a science of engineering.
ex: Single-cell sequencing → Human Cell Atlas → Cell by Gene

items.d: Large models make sense of massive data

n166|708.c: AI and the wet lab are one effort, with experiments chosen to connect different biological layers.
