n166|708.e: She says Biohub deliberately made AI and the wet lab a single effort rather than two departments. Experiments are chosen partly to connect different layers of biology. Under Alex's leadership, she says, the teams are walking arm in arm toward the same goal, which is exciting and a little scary.
ex: Spatial transcriptomics, transparent zebrafish imaging, cell communication sensors

n166|708.c: The goal is to treat each person as an individual, not apply results from cohort studies.
n166|708.e: She hopes to start from a person's genes, disease risks, and variants, trace them to proteins and mechanisms, and arrive at a drug or protein designed for that person. Today's approach is close to guesswork. Patients ask whether they were represented in a study's sample, which uses resemblance to a study population as a stand-in for mechanism. Common diseases will keep splitting into narrower categories until they become a long tail of rare diseases.
ex: Patients often ask: was someone like me in this study's sample?

items.d: A drug or protein just for you

n166|708.c: The path to the clinic is still unclear, but rare-disease communities can move faster.
n166|708.e: She admits clinical research, delivery, and safe deployment all need to change, and Biohub is testing the waters through UCSF's CRISPR Cures program. Single-cell atlases can reveal, before human trials, cells that unexpectedly express a target. For example, a supposedly highly selective target showing up in kidney cells is an early warning of kidney toxicity. Commercial priorities often neglect rare diseases, and neutral shared tools plus patient-organized communities can speed progress dramatically.
ex: Working with Jennifer Doudna on UCSF CRISPR Cures
One patient community advanced a gene therapy in three to five years

n166|709.c: Protein language models learn structure and function implicitly, just by predicting the next token.
n166|709.e: Alex Rives explains that protein language models simply predict the next token along a sequence, yet they form representations of structure and function that were never explicitly labeled. Using interpretability, you can link proteins of unknown function to known ones through an underlying "structural grammar," revealing hidden biological relationships. He doesn't claim the problem is solved.
ex: Structures predicted for more than 1.1 billion proteins

n166|709.c: Protein design emerged on its own: the model designs binders without being trained on antibodies.
n166|709.e: He says this open protein world model predicts structure quickly at atomic accuracy and reaches the best results on nearly every structure prediction benchmark, especially protein-protein and protein-antibody interactions. The model wasn't trained on antibodies or specific targets, yet searching within its world model yields designed proteins and single-chain antibodies. As he sees it, the team simply built a model that understands proteins.
ex: Best results on nearly every structure prediction benchmark

n166|709.c: Screening hundreds of thousands of digital designs down to 96 proteins found nanomolar binders.
n166|709.e: The team filtered hundreds of thousands of digital design trajectories and synthesized just 96 proteins, a single plate. In a very short experimental cycle they found nanomolar binders, meaning very tight binding, which he says is at a level relevant to therapeutic activity. The designs were also tested against therapeutic targets, confirmed in cell experiments, and checked structurally with cryo-electron microscopy. The model and the discovery engine have both been released openly.
ex: Just 96 proteins synthesized to find nanomolar binders

n166|709.c: The next frontier is the virtual cell: linking multi-omics data to phenotype and predicting interventions.
n166|709.e: He thinks a virtual cell must connect the proteome, genome, and transcriptome to phenotype, and predict the effects of new interventions in situations it hasn't seen. That requires generating enormous amounts of data. Good modeling means finding the right representation at each layer and having measurements that span layers. Research is essentially about managing constraints: trading off protein models against cell work, and balancing model size against data.

n166|709.c: Programmable biology could give every patient a drug of their own.
n166|709.e: He thinks the barriers in design, preclinical work, and safety testing are all falling, which could make one drug per patient a reality. Digitally simulating how a drug distributes and binds in the body is a start on the toxicity problem, though he frames this as optimism rather than proven progress. Rare and unusual cases often reveal more biology than repeatedly attacking common diseases. Models are also starting to help build models, but he says it's still very early.
ex: Agents are already hooked up to the open models for automated protein design

n167|714.c: A turnaround starts with crawling: listen to customers, fix the balance sheet, trim products.
n167|714.e: Lip-Bu Tan says he took the job at 66 purely to save Intel, which matters to the semiconductor ecosystem and to the US. He had every engineering group report directly to him so he could hear about failures firsthand and decide faster, and he cut layers of meetings. His sequence is crawl, walk, run, sprint. First, listen humbly to customers, repair a heavy balance sheet, and streamline the product line. Only with that foundation in place does he talk about leadership products and a 5-to-10-year vision.
ex: All engineering groups report directly to him
Trump once demanded he resign over conflicts of interest, then let him stay

items.d: Listen, fix balance sheet, trim products
Leading products and a 5–10 year vision

n167|714.c: Government stakes and long-term shareholders are good, and advanced manufacturing should be treated as infrastructure.
n167|714.e: He welcomes the US government as a major shareholder, arguing that advanced chip manufacturing is infrastructure, as Taiwan, Japan, and Singapore treat it. Jensen Huang's $5 billion investment is now worth roughly $25 billion or more, and SoftBank's Masayoshi Son also helped. He prefers long-term shareholders willing to fund growth over investors focused on buybacks and short-term returns.
ex: He cites about 6x shareholder returns in 14 months
The goal is another 10x over 5 to 10 years

n167|714.c: Inference and agents are pushing the CPU-to-GPU ratio from 1:8 toward 1:4 or even 1:1.
n167|714.e: He says the training era paired roughly one CPU with eight GPUs. Model builders tell him reinforcement learning and agent orchestration run better on CPUs, so the ratio could become 1:4 or even 1:1. Customers have started asking for whole racks, pushing Intel from selling chips toward delivering systems and software. His 10x vision combines XPUs, software, advanced packaging, and foundry into purpose-built systems for PCs, the edge, agents, and physical AI.
ex: CPUs to GPUs were about 1:8 in the training era
Customers now ask for full-rack delivery

n167|714.c: Foundry is a service business and a trust business, and its potential won't show until after 2030.
n167|714.e: He once considered exiting foundry, given the heavy investment and how far behind TSMC Intel was, but chose to double down. Leading companies need resilient supply chains, not one or two geographically concentrated suppliers, and the more advanced the manufacturing, the more the US needs domestic capability. Customers want evidence on IP, yield, defect density, and cycle time before they commit wafers; phone customers, for instance, need low-power IP. 18A is in place, and 14A is entering high-volume production.
ex: Foundry potential expected to show in 2030–2032
Works weekly with Elon Musk's TeraFab team
14A (about 1.4 nanometers) is entering volume production

items: Earn trust with yield and IP

d.verdict: Double down, but win customers with evidence

n167|714.c: Invest in bottlenecks customers urgently need solved, and back teams that can pivot midstream.
n167|714.e: His screen is whether the problem is real and whether customers urgently need it solved. He invests in the most painful bottlenecks first, and he sees AI-assisted chip design software as a gold mine. He wants portfolio companies to land a hyperscaler willing to spend millions over several years from day one, even if it takes warrants. Nine out of ten of his companies change plans along the way, and successful chip companies often nearly die first, so he values adaptable teams and investors who stay in.
ex: Invested in 238 companies; 159 went public or were acquired
Backed Credo (interconnect) and Celestial AI (optical links)

items.d: A gold mine in his view

n168|96.c: Benchmark tables that ignore test-time compute undersell new models; they need a compute axis.
n168|96.e: He says when GPT-5.5 launched, the benchmark table showed it only a few points above 5.4, drawing skepticism, but users found the improvement much bigger. The table didn't control for test-time compute, and 5.5 thinks more efficiently, reaching answers with less compute. He argues for plotting performance against cost, tokens, or time. Best-of-n sampling and using the model as its own judge both inflate scores, so comparisons must be made at equal compute.
ex: GPT-5.5 scored only a few points above 5.4 on the table
Controlling for thinking time, o3 is clearly stronger than o1

items: Plot by cost, tokens, or time

n168|96.c: Capability depends on how much you spend, yet safety frameworks don't say which budget to test at.
n168|96.e: When responsible scaling policies and preparedness frameworks were designed, capability was treated as a fixed property of a model. In the GPT-3 era, spending more didn't make it much stronger. Now $10, $10,000, and $10 million might yield very different capabilities, but current policies don't specify which budget to evaluate at, which matters most for dangerous capabilities like cyber and bio. Models can run for weeks or even months, yet release cycles are only two to three months, and competitive pressure discourages delaying launches.
ex: Cybersecurity evals were still improving past 100 million tokens

items.d: Unclear which budget to test at
A six-month task takes six months to test

n168|96.c: Testing with poker solvers, he finds new models nearly zero-shotting his PhD-level work.
n168|96.e: He uses writing poker bots as a personal test, because there are many papers but little usable open-source code, and the work requires sustained reasoning through lots of small pitfalls. With GPT-5.2, writing a river solver was about 5x faster than doing it himself, but he had to guide it on details like blockers, and it confidently rationalized its mistakes. By 5.5 the task was nearly zero-shot. He expects that within six months to a year, models might zero-shot a full solver, the equivalent of his entire PhD thesis.
ex: GPT-5.2 helped him write a river solver about 5x faster
In testing, a model brushed off an obvious calculation error as roughly right

n168|96.c: Today's models have scientific abilities that remain largely untapped.
n168|96.e: An internal OpenAI model disproved Erdős's unit distance conjecture at very low cost, and mathematicians valued its method even more. Others later reproduced a similar result with GPT-5.5 and a generic scaffold: generate many ideas, pick the promising ones, and push them forward repeatedly. He estimates the cost at between $1,000 and $100,000, which means the capability was already there, just untapped. New models may cut the cost of such discoveries 10 to 100 times, so whether to spend compute now or wait for the next generation becomes a real question.
ex: Reproduction cost estimated at $1,000 to $100,000
New models may cut discovery costs 10–100x

n168|96.c: Recursive self-improvement will be gradual, with research taste and time as bottlenecks.
n168|96.e: He thinks unlimited inference compute won't buy general superintelligence. A fact you don't know won't come back by thinking longer, while search problems like sudoku eventually get solved; research sits in between. Current models lack good research taste: they can optimize his poker algorithm 10 to 100 times but can't invent a better one. Speed up one step a hundredfold and the bottleneck shifts to the parts that didn't speed up. The best results also depend on long runs, so time itself becomes a bottleneck, making a gradual takeoff more likely.
ex: Can optimize his algorithm 10–100x, but can't invent a new one

n169|717.c: Nuclear doesn't need better designs; it needs simple reactors that can be mass-produced.
n169|717.e: He thinks US nuclear stalled because of execution, not ideas. After Three Mile Island the industry froze, its skills drained away, and a stopped industry is hard to restart. America is no longer good at big civil construction, but it is good at advanced manufacturing, so reactors should become factory-built products. Rather than chase high-performance designs that need rare materials and supply chains that don't exist, build a Toyota Camry: simple, safe, made by the tens of thousands, and cheapest overall.
ex: The company's goal: make energy 10 times cheaper
He says no one died at Three Mile Island, yet the industry stalled afterward

d.verdict: Mass manufacturing wins on total cost

n169|717.c: The Energy Department's testing route lets real operating data break the no-data, no-license loop.
n169|717.e: Under the Nuclear Regulatory Commission's commercial licensing process, each hardware iteration costs years and billions of dollars. Regulators want operating data, but companies need approval before they can generate any, so the industry fell back on simulations and paper reactors. He points out that when the Atomic Energy Commission split in 1974, its testing role went to what became the Department of Energy, and that path sat unused for about 40 years. Executive Order 14301 called for three advanced reactors to reach criticality, a self-sustaining chain reaction, by July 4. Valar used it to build W-250 under DOE authorization.
ex: At interview time, W-250 produced 100 kW, splitting about 10^17 atoms per second
In 1974 the AEC split into the NRC and ERDA, later folded into DOE

items.d: Testing goes to ERDA, later DOE
Industry turns to simulations and paper reactors
Three advanced reactors must reach criticality

n169|717.c: Judge safety by consequences: even if everything fails, no one should receive a radiation dose.
n169|717.e: A conventional light-water reactor still produces about 5–6% of its heat after shutdown, from radioactive decay, and needs cooling for about a day. Three Mile Island and Fukushima both involved losing that cooling. He argues advanced reactors should limit the consequences of an accident, not just its probability. Valar plans to run at full power for 72 hours, drop the control rods, then cut all power, the helium circulators and the safety systems, to show the operator is not the last line of defense. In an earlier non-nuclear test, the water jacket boiled, condensed and circulated on its own for two days, purely from its geometry.
ex: TRISO fuel, graphite moderator and helium cooling: an inherently safe combination
He says nuclear is safer than rooftop solar per unit of energy

items.d: Boron carbide control rods go in
Power, fans, pumps and safety systems
Geometry and natural circulation do the work

n169|717.c: He judges the company by how fast milestones arrive, aiming to turn reactors into a speeding production line.
n169|717.e: He measures the company by its cadence: the gap between one fission milestone and the next. It took two years and four months from incorporating in Delaware to first fission, then about seven months to the next. The targets after that are six months, four, one, and eventually minutes. He sees speed as culture that has to be built in when the team is 5 or 20 people. When a project drags, he declares wartime, squeezing a six-month plan into four weeks, even if it ends up taking eight.
ex: The whole plant, control room included, flew to Utah on a C-17
One operator runs W-250 under a senior operator's supervision

n169|717.c: Vertical integration is the secret weapon: build whatever is blocking you, and expose the fake costs.
n169|717.e: He says he'd happily buy a ready-made reactor kit, but none exists, so Valar runs toward the gunfire on fuel, siting, regulation, shielding and controls. After forty years of little building, nuclear suppliers' quotes are full of fake costs, with margins sometimes as high as 100x. Shielding is in-house too: the 78-inch-thick Citadel is stacked from precast concrete blocks whose seams follow a sine-wave path that blocks radiation. It needs no grout and no bolts, and goes up in about 42 hours.
ex: Reactor protection system: a supplier quoted $5 million and 2.5 years
Valar built a similar system in 6 weeks for about $400,000
The Salt Lake City factory can make 3,000 identical shield blocks a year

n169|717.c: Equity should carry the execution risk once the physics is proven; debt comes after about five reactors.
n169|717.e: A decade ago he too believed you could assemble a financeable project from drawings, customer letters of intent and partnerships, and repeated failures changed his mind. US venture capital is best at taking technical risk, and Valar's physics is already proven. What remains is mechanical, thermal and manufacturing work he considers far simpler than a rocket engine. Equity should build the first few reactors and a track record, and only after about five do debt and project finance become workable. He also plans to build gigawatt-scale campuses with fiber on land Valar owns, then wait for customers to come.
ex: He is sure data centers will come; dedicated projects should aim to deliver within a year

result.d: Debt and project finance step in

n169|717.c: Demand for energy is nearly unlimited: the cheaper power gets, the more uses people invent.
n169|717.e: He welcomes AI's appetite for power but doesn't see AI as the whole story. Energy is a commodity: at 1 cent per kilowatt-hour people invent new uses, and at 0.1 cent they invent even more. He says big compute buyers don't expect scalable new power before 2031–2032, so they are bridging with diesel generators and solar plus batteries. Most nuclear companies are tuning simulations instead of iterating on hardware and will struggle to scale even by 2035. Long term, fission could make energy a thousand times cheaper, while AI and robots turn labor into energy use.
ex: Powering Nvidia Blackwell chips directly from W-250
Analogy: cheap electricity turned aluminum from a rarity into a structural material

items.d: From 1 cent to 0.1 cent per kWh

n170|719.c: Scale is an advantage, but not a moat; it has to be won again every day.
n170|719.e: He says there is no such thing as a moat: an advantage can vanish tomorrow, so 25,000 employees have to keep innovating. Scale really pays off in the parts that are hard to copy. Listing properties is easy; the hard part is understanding what hotels and property managers need and fixing their operational headaches. Being the merchant of record, the party that takes the customer's payment, carries heavy regulatory burdens, and scale makes compliance affordable. Anyone hoping to take on the big platforms should understand the business before investing.
ex: Its alternative accommodations bookings are about three-quarters of Airbnb's
Over five years, that category grew faster than Airbnb on a like-for-like basis

items.d: Understanding hotels' and hosts' pain points

n170|719.c: An AI travel agent's biggest value is handling disruptions, not just planning trips.
n170|719.e: He imagines an agent that knows the traveler completely and never forgets, handling complex planning like a wealthy person's concierge, while the user still confirms important choices. He used Penny to plan a family trip. It kept asking for details and came back with a mix of miles and cash plus an overnight connection. The bigger opportunity is disruption management. Travel is like dominoes: one failure knocks over everything else. Ideally, one point of contact fixes the flight, hotel and ground transport at once, or even sees problems coming.
ex: Penny test: seat preferences, a different return city, miles or cash
Penny usage doubled month over month for several months

n170|719.c: Penny's early signals look good, but its unit economics are still unproven.
n170|719.e: Next to $186 billion in annual travel bookings and more than a billion room nights, Penny is still small, and Booking hasn't pushed it hard. The open questions: how much inference cost and how many conversation turns it takes to complete a trip, which model fits each task, and whether gains in conversion, repeat bookings and lifetime value cover those costs. In customer service, cost per contact has fallen and satisfaction has risen, but he stresses that automation isn't the goal. Some customers still want a human.
ex: Last year: $186 billion in bookings and over a billion room nights
He didn't confirm the host's figure of about 10% customer-service savings

d.verdict: Whether gains cover costs is still unproven

n170|719.c: Capital goes in order: internal investment first, then acquisitions, otherwise back to shareholders.
n170|719.e: The host cited about $550 million in reinvestment this year in AI and the platform. He corrected it to about $700 million, spread across many areas, not all of them AI. His order: first check whether internal projects earn a high enough return, then consider acquisitions, and if neither fits, return the money so shareholders can invest it themselves. Over roughly twelve years, Booking has bought back about 40% of its shares outstanding.
ex: Q4: $3.6 billion in buybacks and about $300 million in dividends
About 40% of shares outstanding repurchased over roughly 12 years

items.d: Only if returns clear the bar

n170|719.c: Technology always creates new jobs, but this time old jobs may vanish faster than new ones appear.
n170|719.e: Booking once relied on people to translate hotel content and service into more than 40 languages, and machine translation eliminated those jobs. He accepts that technology has always created new work, but doubts new jobs will appear as fast as old ones disappear. He worries about people like a truck driver in his fifties losing both income and a sense of worth. He is skeptical of government retraining programs over the past fifty years. Booking is paying to train its own staff in AI literacy, and he fears runaway job losses could spark a backlash against technology.
ex: Human translators covered 40-plus languages until machine translation replaced them
He says China hasn't seen this kind of rejection of technology

n171|724.c: Conversational ordering unlocks demand that clunky interfaces were holding back.
n171|724.e: Voice ordering was a bet that didn't pan out, but it left an insight: people can simply say what's on their mind instead of researching restaurants or stringing together keywords. Since Ask DoorDash launched, about half of its restaurant orders go to places the user has never ordered from, and restaurant discovery is one of DoorDash's hardest metrics to move. Grocery baskets are also about 40% bigger. It can cite web and forum discussions newer than the model's knowledge cutoff, which makes recommendations more trustworthy.
ex: About 50% of restaurant orders go to places never ordered from before
Grocery baskets about 40% bigger: snap the fridge to restock, plan around diets

result.d: Half of orders go to new places

n171|724.c: Built from scratch today, DoorDash would be agent-first, but users first need to learn what's possible.
n171|724.e: He won't predict five years out, since AI is too hard to call, but guesses that a student building DoorDash from scratch today would make it agent-first. The new DoorDash CLI, a command-line tool for developers, already has an example: a startup's office manager hooked up a pantry camera that triggers a restock when the shelves run empty. The more practical job right now is showing users what it can do, because a blank chat box leaves people unsure where to start.
ex: Office lunch: gather dietary needs and order before the cutoff
DoorDash CLI plus a pantry camera restocks automatically

items.d: Repeat tasks done automatically in the background

n171|724.c: The network's edge is sending the right kind of courier for each job, while merchants integrate once.
n171|724.e: DoorDash doesn't need one vehicle for everything. DOT suits short suburban trips from strip malls, drones suit light items in rural areas with poor roads, and complex grocery orders that need picking, packing or stair-climbing still go to Dashers. Consumers use one app, and merchants already on the platform get Dashers, drones and autonomous vehicles without integrating again. He thinks this unified interface, spanning 40 to 50 countries, is very hard to copy.
ex: DOT: short suburban trips of 3–5 miles
Dashers: complex grocery orders that need picking or stair-climbing

n171|724.c: Huge volumes of real delivery data are an autonomy asset others can't easily copy.
n171|724.e: DoorDash delivers more than 3 billion orders a year, about 10 billion in total, to over 40 million monthly active consumers. Settings range from San Francisco and Dallas to snowy Helsinki, and items from pizza and groceries to medicine and parcels, so no two deliveries are alike. Map pins often miss the apartment gate or front door, but DoorDash knows where Dashers actually hand things off. Its Tasks product also lets Dashers collect data to train world models, AI that learns how the physical world works.
ex: Over 3 billion deliveries a year, about 10 billion all-time
Over 40 million monthly active consumers

items.d: Trained on data collected via Tasks
3 billion+ a year, about 10 billion total

n171|724.c: Autonomy only improves when it runs 24/7 in the real world.
n171|724.e: When recruiting, he pitches building systems the real world uses rather than prototypes in a PhD lab. DOT has delivered around Phoenix for about two years and reached Level 4 autonomy, fully driverless, last year. Because it switches between roads and sidewalks, it couldn't copy Waymo's approach, so DoorDash built its own autonomy stack. Real deployment surfaced endless surprises: mud covering cameras, regenerative braking jolting the battery during hard stops, and a startup script that crashed about half the time, a big problem across hundreds of robots.
ex: Two wheels on leaves, two on pavement: torque controlled separately
Startup script crashed about half the time, costing 30–45 minutes each

n171|725.c: Since 2018, small autonomy experiments have hedged DoorDash against being disrupted.
n171|725.e: He says DoorDash started on autonomy in 2018, when its importance was still unclear. It began as a small skunkworks project to learn, build partnerships and guard against disruption, not a huge hardware division from day one. That follows the experimental habits the company has had since its Stanford dorm days: test small, scale when demand shows up, and work backward from the customer's problem. The partnership phase convinced them autonomy was a question of when, not if.
ex: Partnering showed they also needed dispatch, merchant integration and operations

items.d: Partners build vehicles, DoorDash supplies the API

n171|725.c: Many autonomy companies build the technology first and look for uses later, which is backwards.
n171|725.e: Borrowing the advice to make something people want, he criticizes autonomy companies that build technology first and then hunt for use cases. For years DoorDash hoped outside robotics companies would supply vehicles while it provided the API and the orders. But hardware built in isolation always fell a bit short of what DoorDash needed. So the company worked backward from one specific problem, dense suburban delivery, and designed its own purpose-built vehicle.

n171|725.c: Sidewalk robots are too slow and robotaxis too heavy; DOT sits in between for suburban delivery.
n171|725.e: Sidewalk robots move at only 2–3 mph, like a water cooler on wheels, and can't cover a typical 3–5 mile delivery in about 15 minutes. Robotaxis weigh around 4,000 pounds and are designed for people. A passenger can get out half a block away and walk, but a package has to reach the door. DOT weighs about 300 pounds, roughly a tenth of a car, tops out at 20 mph, and moves between roads, bike lanes and sidewalks.
ex: Sidewalk robots travel at about 2–3 mph
DOT: about 300 pounds, top speed 20 mph

n171|725.c: Hardware is becoming the bottleneck to scale, which demands reliable components and supply chains.
n171|725.e: Scaling has three parts: getting autonomy working in new cities, operations and fleet management, and hardware. He thinks hardware increasingly looks like the bottleneck. The first 100 robots were built by hand. Reaching 1,000 or 10,000 requires reliable components and a mature supply chain. That's why DoorDash partnered with Also, a micromobility company spun out of Rivian.
ex: The first 100 robots were handbuilt
Partnered with Also, a micromobility company spun out of Rivian

n171|725.c: Automation won't eliminate Dashers; in ten years DoorDash will have more of them.
n171|725.e: DoorDash has more than 9 million Dashers, growing about 25% a year. Growing another 5 to 10 times on human couriers alone is barely realistic, so DOT, drones, robotaxis, sidewalk robots and people all have to work together. Cheaper autonomous delivery will also create new demand, and that demand needs human Dashers too. So his view isn't machines replacing people, but many kinds of couriers growing the pie together.
ex: Over 9 million Dashers, growing about 25% a year

n171|725.c: Internal AI spending rose 20x in six months, so models must be chosen by benchmarked return.
n171|725.e: Acquiring Metis brought AI-native work habits. Coding shows the clearest gains, but seats are growing fastest among analysts, operations staff and account managers, for example auto-generating business reviews for merchants. AI spending in June was about 20 times January's, then leveled off. DashBench, an internal benchmark, compares models and tooling on return on investment and tests whether cheaper open-source models can take over routine work. They also found models are only okay on enterprise data but excellent on lab-cleaned data, and are investigating whether the gap lies in tooling or model capability.

n172|729.c: Scheduling is the hardest part of home services, and AI can take over everything but the physical labor.
n172|729.e: HVAC and plumbing operators are mostly private-equity owned, focused on EBITDA, and grow by hiring nonstop. But call-center staff often quit or miss shifts, and a heat wave sends demand soaring. Services look alike, so an unanswered call sends the customer to a competitor. Netic's agents handle customers by voice, text and web, pull up the household's records, and judge the equipment and urgency. Dispatch isn't just sending the next free technician: it weighs equipment type, today versus tomorrow, customer lifetime value, and whether to use a scarce boiler specialist.
ex: A broken heater at minus 20 degrees, with elderly people or kids at home
Over 70% of customers are now Netic-first, with AI agents handling first contact

items.d: Elderly or kids at home, extreme cold
People still do the physical work

n172|729.c: Build compounding software infrastructure instead of buying service companies and rolling them up.
n172|729.e: Asked why she doesn't just buy HVAC companies and transform them with AI, she gives three reasons. M&A isn't her strength; she's a builder and product engineer. Software built inside a roll-up serves only the companies acquired, so it never becomes infrastructure for the whole market. And she wants a product that compounds. Robots, in her view, are a later chapter: every house is different, cramped spaces demand dexterity, and technicians sometimes have to open a wall to find the problem.

d.verdict: Infrastructure any real-world business can run on

n172|729.c: Counting on AGI to solve industry-specific problems is lazy, both operationally and intellectually.
n172|729.e: She sees OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta not as direct threats but as strong companies and potential partners. Labs launch and kill products quickly, while home-services operators need stable, long-term partners, and researchers naturally chase general solutions. Real deployments face millions of customers with different accents, contexts and requests, so all three layers matter: the model, orchestration and harness, and purpose-built product software. She thinks many founders' real problem is short-termism, chasing a quick exit, when meaningful companies take decades.

n172|729.c: Hire on a full track record of sustained initiative, not one impressive answer.
n172|729.e: She rejects the permanent-underclass anxiety: the fear that if you don't get rich and learn everything within 18 months, you'll be left behind forever. Nor does she think AI will quickly make skills obsolete. Great work takes years, and the deepest lessons come from living through several versions. She uses Martin Luther's story of the cobbler to describe craft: making the best shoe you can is itself a form of reverence. In interviews she looks at what candidates initiated, why it mattered, and whether they saw it through. One weekend project isn't enough.
ex: One new hire has kept an intense daily routine for over fifteen years

n172|729.c: Sell private equity owners on measurable new revenue, not just cost cutting.
n172|729.e: She calls it a misconception that home services is old-fashioned: big operators care intensely about value and can move fast. The old private equity approach of finding an undervalued asset, swapping management and selling is fading, because those hidden gems are gone and value has to be created continuously. She rejects judging an AI product on a one-week trial. Week one is just the start of a relationship, and results should keep improving over a year. PE firms usually lead with cost savings, but she leads with new revenue and better service, with efficiency as a side benefit.
ex: A $500,000 contract signed end to end in 14 days
She estimates over $600 million in revenue created for customers through AI interactions

n173|144.c: Three companies reaching a trillion dollars in five years is an anomaly, not a pattern that will repeat.
n173|144.e: Five years ago Anthropic barely existed, OpenAI was in the GPT-3 era, and SpaceX was valued around $80–100 billion. Now all three are near a trillion, something that historically takes 15–20 years. He describes technology as punctuated equilibrium: a breakthrough sparks a startup boom, then consolidation, then a wait for the next breakthrough. A trillion-dollar company probably needs $50–100 billion in revenue with decent margins. Many companies can reach $100 billion valuations, but he can think of only one that might hit a trillion in three to five years.
ex: A trillion-dollar valuation needs roughly $50–100 billion in revenue
Social, SaaS, cloud, security and crypto all went through these waves

n173|144.c: Fear of the labs is pushing top founders into niches and shrinking their ambitions.
n173|144.e: He sees the best new founders retreating into hardware, American dynamism, narrow applications, or features an inference cloud should provide, to avoid competing head-on with the new labs. Some markets really are on the labs' roadmaps and will be absorbed, but many more can be won on product and distribution. He stresses he means the top founders, not the median. Sarah also finds founders not ambitious enough, but notes her portfolio includes companies challenging the labs' core assumptions.

n173|144.c: A year in AI equals three or four normal years, so boards should discuss exits every six months.
n173|144.e: He thinks Anthropic and OpenAI shouldn't sell anytime soon, but most other companies should at least consider it, since many may have only a 12–18 month window at peak value. An AI year is like three or four normal years, so boards should put exits on a pre-scheduled, unemotional agenda every six months. Founders should ignore the narratives of investors, the press and Twitter and do their own math on dilution, an exit multiple of perhaps 10x, and the years still required. Many 2020–2021 companies are still overcapitalized and struggling.
ex: He expects valuations and fundraising to stay hot for another year or two
He credits Ben Horowitz for the twice-yearly exit discussion

n173|144.c: With compute scarce, budgets should follow return on tokens; the death of SaaS is overstated.
n173|144.e: If compute is split roughly proportionally among the big labs, the result is close to an oligopoly, and no one can accelerate without limit. A few dozen researchers may produce about 80% of a lab's results, and some labs have slowed hiring because every new person consumes scarce compute. Companies will likewise move from everyone using AI to measuring spend, using more open source, and finally deciding explicitly which people and projects get big token budgets, based on return on tokens (ROIT). They'd rather spend tokens on core products or margins than on replacing cheap SaaS.
ex: A few dozen researchers may produce about 80% of results
Minecraft was built by about 5–10 people and sold for billions of dollars

items.d: Big budgets go to high returns

n173|144.c: Heavy regulation in the name of safety can become a moat for incumbents.
n173|144.e: If compliance hurdles keep outsiders out while incumbents keep working internally, one protected year equals a three-to-four-year lead. He relays a drug developer's view that regulators weigh only risks, not benefits equally, and slow progress, though he doesn't say he agrees. Nuclear is his sharpest example: he blames roughly forty years of almost no new US reactors on 1970s safety lobbying. He supports appropriate safeguards but thinks tech overall should be lightly regulated.
ex: Sarah objects that reactors are being built now; he replies that not many are

n173|143.c: Investors size AI markets per head and underestimate how big outcome-based pricing can get.
n173|143.e: She thinks many investors know AI sells the value of a service, yet still size the markets for Harvey or Abridge per seat, per lawyer or per doctor, instead of modeling outcome-based pricing. Coding has already shown that consumption and delivered value could grow another hundredfold from here. Elad agrees the opportunity is huge but cautions that the ultimate size of a market and how fast physical capacity can be built are separate questions.

n173|143.c: Recursive self-improvement is plausible, but the 18-month tipping point has been predicted for five years.
n173|143.e: She relays the fervent expectations inside the labs: coding could be largely solved within six months to year-end, and mild recursive self-improvement (RSI) could arrive by the end of next year, with models doing most of their own training, first in post-training and then pre-training. She sees this as a natural extension of progress in code and math, especially training code and data pipelines. But the 18-month tipping point has been predicted for five years, and data in hard-to-verify domains and physical compute may slow things more than algorithms. Some people now work 16-hour days over it, which she finds a bit tragic.

n173|143.c: Whatever happens to model architectures, all the compute and power will get used.
n173|143.e: She lists possible shocks: investors pulling back on capex because of debt and disappointing returns, restrictions on existing or open-source models, or a new architecture replacing the Transformer, the design behind today's large models. But in every case she expects all existing compute and power to be used up, memory and energy efficiency to become more valuable, and the industry's direction to hold. Elad adds that a new architecture would struggle to match the Transformer's scale and hardware ecosystem, and any breakthrough would likely be copied by compute-rich labs.

n173|143.c: California's billionaire tax would drive away builders, and ecosystems cluster where regulation is lighter.
n173|143.e: She calls California's proposed billionaire tax the fastest way to drive out the people who create value, and says some are already leaving. But neither host expects everyone to move to Miami right away, since ecosystems form around critical mass. She points to Texas, which allows energy experiments and has attracted strong technical talent. Elad adds the hardware corridor SpaceX has spawned, and argues the moves are driven by regulatory differences, not lifestyle preferences.

result.d: Like Texas in energy and hardware

n174|735.c: A business Sand Hill Road called uninvestable grew at the speed of its own cash flow.
n174|735.e: In 2005 he and a friend bought the chess.com domain for about $56,000 at the bankruptcy auction of a failed chess software company, aiming to build the MySpace of chess. His Stanford business school classmates and Sand Hill Road investors called it uninvestable, so he started with money from a previous startup plus a small loan from a friend's mother. The site launched in 2007, began charging for memberships within about 18 months, and turned profitable quickly. They hired only when revenue allowed, growing at the speed of cash.
ex: About 10 million daily users, 40–50 million monthly, 250 million+ registered
Revenue expected just over $200 million this year, with about 650 fully remote staff

items.d: Free, playable right in the browser

n174|735.c: Growth came in waves; each seemed like a fad, but the baseline kept rising.
n174|735.e: Before the pandemic, about 1 million daily users already surprised the team. When the pandemic and The Queen's Gambit set off a surge, they assumed it would fade like the treadmill and sourdough crazes. In 2023, short videos, the Mittens bot, a cheating scandal and scholastic chess drove another wave, and the baseline never dropped back. Only in 2024 were they sure it was a business that would keep compounding. Through the expansion he had sweaty palms; only in the past year has it felt predictable.
ex: He thinks the company made it mainstream to call beginners chess players

items.d: A surge that never fell back

n174|735.c: You don't need the standard funding playbook; software and content businesses can win slowly on product and community.
n174|735.e: Chess can't be patented, so winners are decided by product, community and content. Early rivals FICS, ICC and Yahoo Chess faded because Chess.com focused on the player experience: free, playable in the browser, easy to use. He compares open-source Lichess to Linux; the two can coexist. He rejects the idea that every software company must raise money. Slow bootstrapping suits software and content businesses without big-tech competition, though he grants that hardware, inventory-heavy or speed-driven markets differ. Later deals with GA, Tenzing and CVC mostly bought out existing shareholders.
ex: Early rivals: FICS, ICC and Yahoo Chess
He says private equity owners brought discipline in forecasting and operations

d.verdict: Don't wait for permission; just build it

n174|735.c: Humans want to do human things: however strong engines get, people still want to play people.
n174|735.e: When the host recalls predictions after Deep Blue that chess was dead, he answers that humans fundamentally want to do human things: compete with each other, create and solve problems. Engines have actually pushed humans forward. Grandmasters first used early engines to find ideas, then brought them back to human games. The near-perfect Stockfish made top-level games dull and drawn-out for a while, until the neural-network engine Leela Chess Zero played more aggressive, creative chess and revived the game.

n174|735.c: Expertise comes from repeating small building blocks, and an AI tutor is like a professor in your pocket.
n174|735.e: Chess.com's data shows that improvement comes from repeating small fundamentals. His rule of thumb: multiply any day of your life by a thousand and that's roughly your life, so five puzzles a day adds up to 5,000. AI now powers game reviews, on-demand coaching and personalized puzzles, like carrying a professor around, though he worries about bias, inflated egos and people giving up on thinking. Anti-cheating uses statistics and machine-learning models to compare human and engine move patterns. It can't stop cheating entirely but catches and punishes it well.

n174|735.c: Classic games with no luck and full information endure, and players care about ratings more than money.
n174|735.e: In a world where AI can generate endless new games, chess has no loot boxes, skins, balance patches or luck, and all information is visible, so it endures like classical music. The new product Gambit brings chess ratings to poker: your score depends on opponents' ratings, chips won and hands played, making skill rather than bankroll visible. He says dropping 100 rating points in poker stings more than losing money, and he expects players to care about ratings as much as money.
ex: Small teams plan to launch more classic games next

n175|739.c: Prima shows a moonshot can succeed: patients are reading books and doing sudoku again.
n175|739.e: Prima is a tiny chip implanted under the retina. A laser projector on a pair of glasses beams images onto it, bypassing dead photoreceptors and stimulating the retina directly. In trials, patients with macular degeneration finished sudokus and crosswords and read whole books, which he sees as a crucial existence proof. The team compared targeting the retina, the LGN in the thalamus, and V1, with about 500 million cells, then acquired Pixium, a French company with Stanford roots that he considered far ahead. He rejects the idea that a moonshot is a bet you don't mind losing.
ex: European CE approval in July, with first commercial sales within weeks
Black and white only for now, like looking through a straw
About half of people have early macular degeneration by age 80

items.d: A French company with Stanford roots
Hoping for human trials next year

n175|739.c: The brain literally is a computer, and engineering it is more controllable than drugs.
n175|739.e: To him, any system that arranges matter in some way and runs it to solve a computational problem is a computer. The brain is one, so is the universe, and transistors aren't special. Treating the brain as a computer yields effect sizes that are rare in medicine. By contrast, our grasp of molecular biology isn't good enough to design drugs reliably, and drug development takes a decade and usually fails. Meanwhile a quadriplegic patient with electrodes in the motor cortex can be playing video games within about an hour.
ex: Cochlear implants and deep brain stimulation are examples that work quickly
Pipeline: vision, biohybrid neural interfaces and Vessel perfusion

n175|739.c: A brain-controlled keyboard just replaces your hands, and thoughts can't be read before they take shape.
n175|739.e: He finds silent-speech devices like EEG, MEG and radar useful but beside the point. Hands already work well, and controlling apps requires unambiguous intent, or you might accidentally summon two rideshares during a meeting. He doubts there is decodable pre-linguistic thought; speaking and writing are themselves thinking. Human cognition tops out around 10 bits per second and attention is already maxed out, so brain keyboards may end up like AR glasses. He's more interested in redrawing the brain's boundaries, such as how the two hemispheres are bound into one.
ex: A savant drew Manhattan at about 10 bits per second after a helicopter ride

n175|739.c: Continuity of consciousness matters a lot; even a perfect copy is unlikely to satisfy.
n175|739.e: He imagines scanning himself losslessly, sending the software copy to work while he goes into hospice, and asks: would that make you feel better? People accept a lot of identity drift as long as experience is continuous, but a copy that behaves identically without continuous experience is less satisfying. General anesthesia also interrupts experience, which needs explaining. He thinks a temporary cognitive dip might be acceptable if it recovers within weeks. Once substrate independence is achieved, a mind could go almost anywhere.
ex: A full human connectome is far off; a mouse connectome is closer

cells.d: Maybe acceptable if it recovers in weeks

n175|739.c: AI models and brains are converging on similar representations, so studying AI may beat studying neuroscience.
n175|739.e: He notes that the math inside large models resembles what neuroscience has found: concepts are represented with similar geometry. Science uses this to align animal neural recordings with the internals of AI models. He reads it as an early sign that AI is on the right track and hasn't hit a wall, and cautiously suggests that all learning systems may be converging on the true underlying manifold of the data, which feels like a law of physics. Half-joking, he says models are far easier to study than brains, and his neuroscientist friends at OpenAI and Anthropic have left neuroscience.

result.d: Converging, perhaps like a physical law

n176|741.c: Models and compute cost almost nothing to switch; a company's own data is its most valuable asset.
n176|741.e: He argues models and compute can be swapped at any time, so every company's most valuable asset is its own data. Google paid about $10 million for the data of bankrupt Spirit Airlines; it bought the data, not the airplanes. Real-world training data is scarce, and people still use the public Enron emails to simulate how a real company works. Spirit's data is valuable because it covers a large enterprise's full hierarchy, from frontline staff to executives. Labs are also buying hedge fund data through Wall Street channels.
ex: Google paid about $10 million for Spirit Airlines' data
Enron's emails are still used as a sample of a real company

n176|741.c: Companies sit on data they can't use: it's locked up, hard to reach and expensive to get.
n176|741.e: Eon provides a cloud data foundation that maps and classifies data across the major cloud providers, telling companies what data they have, where it lives and what is sensitive. It ingests both structured and unstructured data for two purposes: low-cost protection and recovery, and making the data queryable by large language models. The core tension is that customers already own this data; it's just locked away, hard to access and expensive to retrieve.

n176|741.c: AI agents with legitimate access are a supercharged insider threat.
n176|741.e: At AWS, a large customer that thought it had disaster recovery covered actually had about 60% of its environment exposed to ransomware, because resources had never been mapped, classified or tagged. That experience shaped why Eon exists. Today agents have legitimate permissions, and a single action can delete an entire table. The old methods of spotting unusual write patterns and entropy changes still work, but the damage happens much faster. Six months ago few people wanted to talk about this; now most executives are either afraid or have already been hit.
ex: One large customer had about 60% of its environment exposed to ransomware
Non-technical staff build apps with tools like Lovable and store company data

items.d: One action deletes a whole table
A chain no one can assess

n176|741.c: Dashboards won't disappear but multiply, and non-human identity security is about to boom.
n176|741.e: When Elad asks whether dashboards vanish in the agent era, he argues the opposite: agents launch other agents, people can barely trace the chain of responsibility, and without dashboards nothing is visible. That explains the wave of startups in non-human identity (NHI) security. It also makes endpoint security important again, because agents run on laptops connected both to outside messaging tools and to the internal network.

n176|741.c: AI adoption pressure dwarfs the cloud era: everyone gets ChatGPT, and boards see opportunity and fear obsolescence.
n176|741.e: The cloud was hard to explain to non-technical people, but after ChatGPT everyone understands what AI is. Boards, shareholders and CEOs see the opportunity and fear being left behind, so the push is far stronger than it was for the cloud. He thinks the era of token maximizing is over: spending more is fine, but you have to squeeze value from every token. The industry is just getting started, and most companies haven't adopted AI yet. Adoption is scary, but it has to happen.

n176|742.c: Misaligned incentives keep data out of reach, scattered across business units and twenty years of legacy systems.
n176|742.e: Data leaders are pushed by CEOs and boards to deliver AI, but business units own the data, and incentives don't line up. Systems span about twenty years, and some legacy servers no one dares to switch off. Moving data can threaten production uptime and compliance, or even leak sensitive information like executive pay into training sets. Eon's approach is to classify first, build a semantic layer, and continuously bring in relevant data without disrupting production or compliance, then protect personal and financial data with audit trails and classification-based access controls.

items.d: With audit trails and access controls

n176|742.c: Legacy data pipelines each handle one piece, and context gets lost along the way.
n176|742.e: He uses buying a coffee as an example: the transaction lands in a database, one process pulls it out, another processes it later somewhere else, and context is lost at every step. Fivetran, dbt and Monte Carlo are good tools, but each was built for a single purpose. Or say one team has data on burger lovers in New York and another has data on pizza lovers; neither knows they could find the people in both. Only clean data with context lets you ask such questions. Data volumes are exploding, much of it agent-generated noise, but there's value in it too.

cells.d: Exists only in the other system

n176|742.c: AI transformation is cloud migration on steroids, and fear of leaks is pausing deployments.
n176|742.e: Drawing on his CloudEndure years helping customers migrate between AWS, Azure and GCP, he calls AI transformation cloud migration on steroids. Customers feel a loss of control and worry about data leaks and intellectual property walking out the door, and many deployments have paused. He argues for assuming breach, whether the cause is malicious or accidental. He also admires how Databricks keeps reinventing itself and building its own agents, a case of if you can't beat them, join them.

items: Fears of lost control and leaks

d.verdict: You must assume breach

n176|742.c: He once thought developer tools couldn't grow through product-led growth; now he believes the opposite.
n176|742.e: He admits he once thought product-led growth (PLG) didn't fit developer tools, and now it works. Cognition started with PLG, then embedded forward-deployed engineers (FDEs) at customers like banks. FDEs have gone from Palantir's niche practice to a common approach that shortens sales cycles, and Eon follows the same path. He believes every company will eventually go through this transformation, and the world will be better for it.

marks.d: FDEs were once a niche model

n177|746.c: Going from IP licensing to selling chips was a gradual step, and Meta's demand was the trigger.
n177|746.e: Arm's core business is licensing CPU designs for phones, data centers and cars, which gives it a view across markets. It first moved from individual IP blocks to pre-assembled compute subsystems, saw strong demand, and naturally moved toward physical products. Product cycles are getting longer, so faster delivery is worth more. Meta wanted a general-purpose CPU for agentic workloads that he says no one else could provide, which led to the Arm AGI CPU. Arm expected customer pushback, but Nvidia, Amazon, Microsoft and Google all backed it, because more Arm software helps the whole ecosystem.
ex: Arm must build a supply chain with TSMC, Samsung and the three memory makers
Hired executives from Broadcom, Qualcomm and Nvidia to fill back-end gaps

n177|746.c: The slowest parts of chip design are verification and debugging, exactly where AI is strongest.
n177|746.e: Designing a chip takes 24–36 months, and the slowest part isn't architecture or RTL generation but verification, validation, debugging and documentation, which happen to be AI's strengths. He estimates 80–90% of Arm engineers use AI daily; taking it away would be like allowing internet access only two hours a day. But AI is still immature at RTL generation and leading-edge physical design, because models train mostly on public material and that know-how is largely proprietary. Arm's IP comes with extensive documentation and test benches, and Arm is working with model makers to make them trainable.
ex: Design cycles run 24–36 months
80–90% of engineers use AI every day
Five-plus years out, simple designs might go straight from idea to GDSII

items.d: Not the slowest; AI still immature

n177|746.c: Export controls are an infinite game with no winners, and there's no downside to being the leader.
n177|746.e: Citing SEMATECH, the US response to cheap Japanese memory in the 1980s, he argues the US needs more fabs for national security and supply-chain diversity, and the UK should build a smaller version. He calls trying to keep chips from China an infinite game with no winners and warns that key technology may end up outside the US. He sees opposition to data centers as mostly about job fears, which he thinks don't hold up: data centers employ few people directly but create many jobs in energy, liquid cooling and more.
ex: He says claims like water contamination are invented to spread fear

d.verdict: There's no downside to leading

n177|746.c: Supply will stay tight for at least three to five years; bubble talk confuses valuations with supply and demand.
n177|746.e: Transformers are hungry for both compute and memory, so demand for wafers, memory and packaging will last; he expects tightness for at least 3 to 5 years. The next bottleneck may be data center construction: few projects finish early or with fewer workers, and some US regions are debating slowdowns or limits, though that beats a wafer or memory crunch. He separates valuation bubbles from oversupply: valuations aside, supply is nowhere near exceeding demand. He advises capital-intensive chip startups to form strategic partnerships early with the supply chain, private equity and banks.

n177|746.c: CPUs matter again in the inference era: something has to deliver the tokens to users.
n177|746.e: After ChatGPT, all the attention went to accelerators and CPUs were overlooked. But as workloads shift toward reinforcement learning and inference, something has to orchestrate and decide where tokens go, and that's the CPU's job. In his analogy: where's the truck that delivers the tokens to the user? From data centers to cars, robots, phones and wearables, systems need CPUs, accelerators and memory working together. Arm has a special edge in small devices that must run AI locally but can't fit a 50-watt GPU.
ex: He says most humanoid robots' brains now run on Arm

n178|750.c: AI agents need their own bank accounts, because most of their payments are under 30 cents.
n178|750.e: His starting point is simple math. A card payment carries a fixed cost of about 30 cents, so a one-cent purchase makes no sense. Yet about 76% of the agent transactions Coinbase sees are under 30 cents. Stablecoins, crypto tokens pegged to the dollar, settle anywhere in the world in about a second for less than a cent. Agents have no government ID, so Coinbase lets an agent get a self-custody wallet with one prompt and no identity check, or a sub-account under a human's identity. The X42 payment protocol, incubated at Coinbase, now lives at the Linux Foundation, with Google, Cloudflare and AWS on board.
ex: Typical small payments: paid research, data scraping, one agent calling another's tool
He expects the agent economy to eventually outgrow the human economy

n178|750.c: Even if AI makes things cheap, land, energy and chips stay scarce, so money won't disappear.
n178|750.e: Elon Musk has suggested money might go away, with value measured in energy and mass instead. Armstrong grants there is something to that, but land, energy and chips will stay scarce for a long time, and even a sci-fi Dyson sphere around the sun would be expensive. His reasoning: AI and robots may push down the price of commodities, food and housing, while governments printing money pushes prices up. Either way, people need a medium of exchange. He thinks crypto suits both humans and AI agents, and for agents it is close to essential, since they cannot walk into a bank.

result.d: Crypto works for people and AI

n178|750.c: Give every team a written "brain," so each human correction stops an agent repeating the mistake.
n178|750.e: His view is that coding tools alone are not enough; the AI has to remember what the company has learned. Coinbase is building a "brain" for every team, service and person: past incidents, financial controls, A/B tests and pull request history, mostly as markdown files today. Before an agent touches code, it reads the relevant brain. When a reviewer corrects the agent, the fix must be written back into the brain, so the same situation never trips it up again, and the share of pull requests approved on the first pass keeps rising. He had a top model split one feature into three phases of ten tasks each, ran ten agents in parallel, and finished phase one before the recording.
ex: He now sends finished pull requests straight to his team for review
He rejects the "ten-person company" idea: AI removes tasks, not people

n178|750.c: 88% of Coinbase revenue now comes from outside Bitcoin, and the next step is an "everything exchange."
n178|750.e: He still calls Bitcoin digital gold, but growth has to come from elsewhere: putting stocks, commodities, derivatives, perpetual futures and prediction markets into one account where margin is shared across them. Clearer regulation makes that possible. Coinbase has already launched tokenized stocks outside the US, and he stresses these are real securities held one-to-one, not synthetic copies; the US path is being worked out with the SEC. About four billion people have no broker or US investment account, much as Tether succeeded abroad by offering a dollar account. Private credit, treasuries and deposits would move on-chain next.
ex: 88% of revenue is non-Bitcoin trading, yet the stock still mostly tracks Bitcoin
Elad backed Harbor, an early real-estate tokenization startup; Armstrong calls it "a bit too early"

n178|750.c: Prediction markets go well beyond sports: they can inform policy and even price opinions.
n178|750.e: Prediction markets inside the Coinbase app reached roughly $100 million in annualized revenue within a few months, more than doubling quarter over quarter. He thinks the value goes far past sports. A market on what unemployment will be if a given policy passes, for example, gives governments real information before they decide. He also floats "opinion markets" with no settlement date at all: does God exist, did life come from evolution or intelligent design. Prices would move as new evidence arrives, a bit like owning a stock.

n178|750.c: Most longevity research is hype; the bet worth making is reprogramming old cells back to a young state.
n178|750.e: After Coinbase went public in 2021, he surveyed the big technology trends and found longevity full of hype and short on strong teams. A few dinners with scientists got him hooked on epigenetic reprogramming, which resets the switches on genes rather than editing the genes, the same way he once got hooked on Bitcoin. New Limit has frontier AI models suggest combinations of transcription factors, the proteins that flip those switches, tests them in large pooled screens, then moves to animals and people. It has reprogrammed at least one human cell type inside humanized mice, is running primate studies now, and plans its first Phase 1 trial next year.
ex: First targets: liver cells, blood vessel cells and T cells of the immune system
He estimates alcoholic liver disease alone is a roughly $20 billion market

n179|751.c: Generative models are the right way to understand data, and diffusion grew out of frustration with older methods.
n179|751.e: When he arrived at Stanford in 2014, producing a blurry handwritten digit counted as progress. Generative modeling papers were hard to publish and often had to be framed as feature learning for supervised tasks. His real goal was world models: systems that imagine the consequences of an action for planning and model predictive control. He expected that to take a career and badly underestimated the pace. He was unhappy with autoregressive image models, VAEs and hard-to-reproduce GANs. In 2019 he and a PhD student proposed score-based generative models, the ancestor of modern diffusion: train a network to remove noise, then refine pure noise step by step into a clean result.

n179|751.c: Word-by-word generation leaves GPUs idle, so diffusion, which refines many words at once, should win.
n179|751.e: Transformers won because training processes every token in parallel. But at inference they still produce one token at a time. Each step moves the full set of weights through memory while doing very little math, so the bottleneck is memory bandwidth, not compute. Diffusion processes many tokens at once, so inference looks like training and matches what GPUs are good at. What matters, he says, is intelligence per watt and intelligence per dollar. Faster inference means more test-time reasoning and more reinforcement learning rollouts. That is why he bets the more parallel approach wins in the end.
ex: A 2024 GPT-2-scale test: same perplexity, generation about 10x faster
Text is discrete, unlike images, so diffusion for text needed new methods

n179|751.c: Speed is the way in: at least 20 to 30 percent of AI workloads are highly latency-sensitive.
n179|751.e: He says Mercury matches speed-tier models like Haiku, Flash, Mini and Nano on benchmarks while running much faster. Because vLLM and SGLang do not support diffusion language models, the company built its own inference engine. The voice-agent company OpenCall shows why speed matters: its pipeline is speech recognition, then an LLM to reason, then speech synthesis, and any delay is obvious to the caller. OpenCall moved from custom Cerebras hardware to Mercury on Nvidia GPUs and got similar speed at lower cost with better quality. Using OpenRouter's task categories, he estimates 20 to 30 percent of workloads depend heavily on latency, and he treats that as a floor.
ex: OpenCall moved from Cerebras hardware to Mercury running on Nvidia GPUs
He thinks users who get used to fast models rarely go back

items.d: Turn the caller's voice into text

n179|751.c: Diffusion may be more controllable and more data-efficient, but so far only speed is proven.
n179|751.e: An autoregressive model can only score an output against constraints after it is finished. Diffusion works coarse to fine, so a half-finished draft can be evaluated and steered mid-generation, for example guiding a molecule toward better solubility. Denoising also shows the model many corrupted versions of each example, which acts like data augmentation, and academic results suggest that helps when data is scarce. To the objection that human-written code is messier than physical data, he answers that both training styles compress data, and which inductive bias works better is an empirical question.

root.d: Ranked by how proven they are

n179|751.c: The real defense is deployment experience: a homegrown inference engine, customer feedback and production evals.
n179|751.e: He admits well-funded incumbents could absorb a better architecture. The first line of defense is research IP and trade secrets; model size and training FLOPs are not disclosed. The deeper one is deployment experience: a proprietary inference engine, customer feedback, evals drawn from production and some of the data. Even a rival that trains a diffusion LLM would lack a serving stack equivalent to vLLM. The company is about 50 people and two years old, and built its own SFT, RLHF and RL infrastructure. Staying closed protects the IP but gives up community contributions, a trade-off he accepts.
ex: He often feels more short of compute than of people
Academia has won contrarian bets before: diffusion over GANs, FlashAttention, DPO

n180|753.c: AI's impact is uneven; in most sectors incumbents have the edge, and frontier engineering lets them lead.
n180|753.e: He started studying AI at Lone Pine in 2017, when CNNs, GANs and LSTMs degraded as soon as you scaled them. ChatGPT showed him an architecture that keeps improving with compute. He splits the economy into three buckets: areas AI barely touches, like restaurants and golf courses; areas startups will win, like coding; and a large set of industries where incumbents hold brand, scale, network effects and regulatory advantages. Most companies, he argues, just bolt AI tools onto human processes. Machines run around the clock and scale with compute, so the right move is to rebuild the company around the machines.

n180|753.c: Incumbents can't transform themselves by any of the usual three routes; only ownership aligns incentives.
n180|753.e: Route one is doing it yourself. Every company has a "key person" role; at Blackstone it is the investor, and in the AI era it should be the engineer, which incumbents struggle to grow internally. That gap is why Palantir exists. Route two is hiring a services firm. Accenture, McKinsey and Palantir make money by expanding their share of a client's wallet, which he calls "the road to incrementalism," and they cannot change the client's organization or incentives. Route three is buying software. Anyone can buy it, so vendors must standardize, and what you get is today's process. Ownership, by contrast, aligns incentives, puts engineers in charge, and buys the years a real transformation takes.

n180|753.c: He runs a permanent holding company instead of a fund, and does only one deal a year.
n180|753.e: His view is that the life of the capital should match a long-term operating commitment. Sequence aims to build market leaders rather than raise fund after fund, and it can reinvest retained earnings. He respects the private equity he saw at Apollo, but a fund's economics force you to deploy on a schedule and exit after about three years. In large, investor-centric buyout funds, young engineers get no say in investment decisions. His screen for a target: a big market, an incumbent with a real advantage, and work that overlaps with what AI does well. He hopes to hold his Sequence equity for life.
ex: One deal a year, and skipping a year is fine

n180|753.c: A bank's heavy regulation is an asset: clear rules and clean data are exactly what AI agents need.
n180|753.e: The cold-start problem was that without capital he could not close a deal, and without a deal he could not hire engineers. He found Jamie Reynolds, co-founder of Avenir, whose family owns a bank in Georgia. The project kicked off on August 4; by late November the family asked Sequence to become a permanent partner, and the investment closed the following March with Federal Reserve and OCC approval. The host worried about regulatory complexity, but Lee sees clear rules and clean data as ideal ground for AI agents. Underwriting is centralized, so tools built at headquarters reach every branch. He credits part of the result to luck.
ex: Consumer loan underwriting workload is down 94% since March
Loan volume doubled from Q1 to Q2 with the same standards

n180|753.c: Insurance brokerage is ripe for rebuilding, and the hardest part is the human engineering, not the code.
n180|753.e: Brokerages handle more than $2 trillion in annual premiums, keep about 90% of clients, and clients do not pay brokers directly, so price competition is limited and startups struggle to break in. Baldwin also has a scalable business, a centralized technology base and an ambitious management team. The Atlas platform, built during the bank project, rests on a judgment that about 80% of a company's basic building blocks are the same across industries, so it can be reused at Baldwin. The harder work, he says, is people: paying attention to employee anxiety, removing repetitive tasks, upgrading the work itself, and making everyone feel the organization is winning.
ex: The Baldwin deal was done with the Dell family office
He says he has never run a bank or brokerage and relies on top management

n181|757.c: AI chips look different on the outside, but underneath they are mostly the same recipe.
n181|757.e: Google's TPU, Meta's MTIA, Microsoft's Maia, OpenAI's in-house chip, and Nvidia and AMD GPUs mostly use HBM memory, tensor cores for matrix multiplication and TSMC's advanced packaging, and they are often implemented by a handful of ASIC partners, Broadcom the largest. He blames the traditional hand-off process: architects define the workload, a front-end team writes the RTL, then partners do physical implementation and the GDSII layout. Each hand-off adds friction and slows iteration. Fractile, about 150 people, keeps workload analysis, front end, physical design, back end and advanced packaging all in house to shorten the feedback loop.
ex: He thinks cloud providers build chips mainly to pressure Nvidia's prices and diversify supply
About 150 people cover the full stack

items.d: Define what the chip must do

n181|757.c: SRAM can't hold big models and long contexts, so Fractile switched to high-bandwidth DRAM.
n181|757.e: For its first two years Fractile built an SRAM architecture like Groq's and Cerebras's: SRAM sits right next to the logic, with enough bandwidth to read weights and the KV cache fast and emit thousands of tokens per second. But from late 2023 into 2024, parameter counts and context lengths kept growing and SRAM capacity became the bottleneck. These fast systems could not handle long contexts and had to fall back to GPUs. So the company moved to DRAM, which is large, cheap and can still deliver very high bandwidth; the platform should be fully running in the second half of next year. At data-center scale, he says, cost per gigabyte of memory largely decides the economics of inference.

items: Long contexts fall back to GPUs

n181|757.c: A faster chatbot is just a faster horse; fast frontier models are what make long-running agents possible.
n181|757.e: He argues that each inference is cheap, but you pay it on every deployment, so at scale it matters structurally. Still, merely speeding up chatbots is like asking for a faster horse. The real shift is running multi-trillion-parameter models at thousands of tokens per second. That is a fundamental step toward long-running AI agents, and the agents themselves would work far faster. When he started the company in summer 2022, he already believed foundation models generalize well enough that spending more compute at inference time could bring AlphaGo-style scaling to language models.
ex: Some chips now entering the inference market were training chips about 18 months ago

items.d: Trillions of parameters, thousands of tokens a second

n181|757.c: AI can speed up chip design but not the physics, so the answer is a portfolio of parallel bets.
n181|757.e: A new model lands roughly every two weeks, and attention and sparsity schemes change every few weeks. But some needs are durable: high bandwidth and fast small-batch autoregressive generation. The physical constraints are harder. Place-and-route is NP-hard and a single run can take days, simulation is just as slow, and as Amdahl's law says the slowest step sets the pace. Final sign-off still runs through Cadence and Synopsys. So faster design does not mean one perfect chip; it means a set of options to bet on, pick the flagship that will last, scale it, and aim to stay three to six months ahead of rivals.
ex: His rule of thumb: question every assumption, then divide the timeline by four

marks.d: A new model about every two weeks

n181|757.c: Bandwidth scales too, and it will shape both model architecture and the chip market.
n181|757.e: Over the past 20 years compute grew about a million-fold while memory bandwidth grew only about 40-fold. Fractile claims per-chip bandwidth 25 times that of an HBM chip and hopes that exerts a pull on future architectures. For example, pushing mixture-of-experts sparsity from 1 in 16 to 1 in 128 or 1 in 256 would deliver the same intelligence with far less compute, but HBM systems struggle to serve such models efficiently. He expects big labs and cloud providers to keep several suppliers for supply resilience and leverage against Nvidia. Betting only on your own proprietary hardware carries asymmetric risk.
ex: A rival five times more efficient on an incompatible architecture could put you about nine months behind

items.d: Playing the hardware lottery on purpose
